records.title: Architecture
records.text: Architecture. How the authorization layer is built — the PDP contract, the PostgresRbacPDP engine, registry-as-code, the open-core seams and enterprise loader, the request lifecycle, and the path to swapping the engine for OpenFGA.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Architecture
records.text: This page is for contributors and operators who want to know *how* authorization is implemented, not just how to use it. It maps the concepts from the rest of this section onto the code.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The PDP contract
records.text:
All authorization goes through one interface — the **Policy Decision Point**:

interface Pdp {
 can(actor, action, resource): Promise ; // boolean + reason
 enforce(actor, action, resource): Promise ; // throws ForbiddenError on deny
 bulkCheck(actor, checks[]): Promise ; // many at once; never loop can()
 listAccessible(actor, action, resourceType): Promise ; // ids you may act on
}

Call sites depend on this interface only — never on a concrete engine. That's what makes the engine swappable.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The community engine: PostgresRbacPDP
records.text:
The default implementation answers a check with a single SQL gather followed by a pure decision:

 
 
**Gather grants.** One query selects the actor's grants that match the org, the principal, and the required permission key (` : `), returning each grant's `resource_id` (where `NULL` = org-wide).
 
 
**Walk the hierarchy.** A recursive CTE computes the target resource's ancestor ids (project → org).
 
 
**Decide (pure).** `coversResource(grantResourceIds, resourceId, ancestorIds)`: a grant with `NULL` resource_id (org-wide) covers everything; otherwise a grant covers the resource if its id is the resource itself or one of its ancestors. No matching grant ⇒ **deny**.
 
 
**Enforce & record.** `enforce` throws `ForbiddenError` (→ 403) on denial and writes the decision to the Activity log; every denial and every successful non-read action is recorded (successful reads are skipped).
 
 

 
The decision logic (`coversResource`, permission-key helpers) is a **pure function** in `evaluate.ts` with no database or IO, so it's exhaustively unit-tested (org-wide grants, exact match, hierarchy inheritance, default-deny, explicit-deny override) without needing a live database. The SQL gathering

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Registry-as-code

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The open-core seams
records.text:
The core exposes extension points and consults them through small accessor functions, each with a community default:

 Seam Accessor Community default Enterprise fills with 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Policy engine `getPdp()` `PostgresRbacPDP` `OpenFgaPdp` (optional) 
 Tenancy scope `getActiveScope(userId)` personal org (`orgId == userId`) the member's active org 
 Auth plugins `getAuthPlugins()` `[]` Better Auth `organization()` + SSO 
 Entitlements `getEntitlements(actor)` all off license-derived flags 

All four read from `lib/enterprise.ts` — if no enterprise module is registered, they return the community default.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The enterprise loader

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Request lifecycle
records.text:
server action sa["authorize(action, resource)"]
 req --> CLI / stream route cli["authorizeCli(req, action, resource)"]
 sa --> scope["getActiveScope(requireOwner) → actor"]
 cli --> vtok[verify token] --> scope
 scope --> enforce["getPdp().enforce(...)"]
 enforce --> deny forbid[403 Forbidden]
 enforce --> allow query["query under withScope() / withOwnerScope()"]
 query --> rls["PostgreSQL RLS restricts rows to the active org"]
`} />

Two independent gates on every path: the **PDP** (permission) and **RLS** (tenancy). On the CLI/stream paths — which use the service connection that bypasses RLS — the route additionally scopes its query explicitly by the active org, so the tenancy guarantee holds there too.

 
There is a deliberate guard against regressions: a lint (`check:authz-scope`) fails the build if any server action, CLI route, or stream route does ad-hoc `user_id` ownership filtering instead of going through `authorize`/`enforce` + org scoping.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Swapping the engine
records.text: Because every call site depends only on the `Pdp` interface and obtains the engine via `getPdp()`, switching from the Postgres engine to **OpenFGA** (for relationship-based authorization at large scale) is a **binding flip plus a tuple backfill** — the enterprise module registers an `OpenFgaPdp`, and not a single call site changes. The community engine remains the default and the fallback.

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.text: Access Control Overview. How Alethia decides who can do what — the Policy Decision Point, roles, permissions, and the tenancy model, with a single mental model that scales from one user to many organizations.

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.heading: Access Control Overview
records.text:
Every action in Alethia — viewing a project, deploying infrastructure, destroying a runner, inviting a teammate — passes through one **authorization layer** before it runs. This page gives you the mental model; the rest of the section is the detail.

 
**One sentence:** an **actor** (you, acting in an **organization**) is granted **roles**, each role carries a set of **permissions**, and a permission is the right to take an **action** on a **resource**. A request is allowed only if the actor holds a matching permission — everything else is denied.

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.heading: The mental model
records.text:
(you + org)"] --> holds grant
 grant --> of a role["role (owner/admin/…)"]
 role --> bundles perms["permissions (project:deploy, …)"]
 perms --> gate act["actions on resources"]
`} />

- **Actor** — a verified user plus their **active organization** (the tenancy scope). In the free Community edition there is exactly one organization per user — your *personal organization* — so "actor" is effectively just "you".
- **Resource** — a thing you act on: an organization, a **project** (an infrastructure application), a **runner**, a **cloud identity** (a connected cloud account), a job, a connector (git / integration provider), a member, alerts, the managed fleet, support cases, Activity logs, or billing.
- **Action** — what you're trying to do: `view`, `create`, `edit`, `plan`, `deploy`, `destroy`, `test`, and the management actions (`manage_identities`, `manage_members`, `manage_connectors`, `view_alerts`, `manage_alerts`, `view_activity`, `export_activity`, `manage_billing`, `manage_support`).
- **Permission** — a single `resource:action` pair, e.g. `project:deploy`. The complete, exhaustive list is fixed in code (see [Roles & Permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.heading: Default-deny
records.text: The system is **default-deny**: if nothing explicitly grants you a permission for what you're attempting, the answer is *no*. There is no implicit "owner of the row can do anything" shortcut scattered through the code — every decision is made in one place (the **Policy Decision Point**, or PDP) and recorded.

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.heading: One decision point
records.text:
A single component answers every authorization question:

- **`enforce(action, resource)`** — the gate at the top of every server action and API route. It allows the request or throws a `403 Forbidden`.
- **`listAccessible(type)`** — the "which ones can I see?" query that powers list views, so a list only ever returns resources you're allowed to see.

Because all decisions flow through this one point, the rules are consistent everywhere, every denial can be audited, and the underlying engine can be swapped without touching a single call site (see [Architecture](/concepts/access-control/architecture)).

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.heading: Two layers of protection
records.text:
Authorization is enforced in **two independent layers**, so a bug in one cannot expose your data:

 
 
 Application-level role + permission checks: *can this actor take this action on this resource?* Rich, hierarchical, role-aware.
 
 
 A coarse PostgreSQL guarantee that a request only ever sees rows belonging to its active organization — enforced by the database itself, beneath the application.
 
 

The PDP decides *what you may do*; Row-Level Security guarantees *whose data you can even touch*. Together they mean a cross-tenant leak would require both layers to fail at once.

records.title: Access Control Overview
records.heading: Community vs Enterprise at a glance
records.text:
The whole model above ships in the **free, open-source (AGPL) Community edition**. Organizations with multiple members are the main thing the commercial **Enterprise edition** adds.

 Community (free) Enterprise 
 --- --- --- 
 Roles & permissions (owner/admin/operator/viewer) ✅ ✅ 
 Per-project grants + inheritance ✅ ✅ 
 Row-Level Security tenant isolation ✅ ✅ 
 Activity log of decisions ✅ ✅ 
 **Organizations, teams, members, invitations** — (single personal org) ✅ 
 **SSO (SAML / OIDC)** — ✅ 
 **Custom roles, the access portal, activity export** — ✅ 
 **OpenFGA fine-grained engine** — ✅ (optional) 

For the authoritative, capability-by-capability breakdown, see the [**Editions** feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix).

In Community, every user is the sole `owner` of their own personal organization — so the org/roles machinery is fully present but you simply never see another member. The same code lights up into real multi-member organizations under an Enterprise license, with **no change to how permissions are decided**. See [Open-Core Model](/concepts/access-control/open-core).

records.title: Open-core model
records.text: Open-core model. The architectural boundary that keeps the AGPL Community build complete and self-contained, and the CI guards that enforce it.

records.title: Open-core model
records.heading: Open-core model
records.text:
Alethia is **open-core**. The entire product — including the authorization engine, roles, grants, hierarchy, and tenant isolation — is free and open source under the **AGPL-3.0**. A separate **Enterprise edition** adds organization-scale features under a commercial license. This page explains the **engineering** that keeps the split honest.

 
 Looking for the *feature* comparison or how licensing works? That's the [**Editions**](/editions) section —
 the [feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix) and [licensing](/editions/licensing). This page is the
 contributor-facing view: the dependency boundary and the CI guards that enforce it.

records.title: Open-core model
records.heading: Where the line is
records.text:
The dividing line is **"single tenant vs many tenants."** Everything needed to run Alethia for yourself is
free; the Enterprise edition is about *organizations with multiple members and identities*. The
capability-by-capability list is the [feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix), and how a license turns
those capabilities on — entitlements, activation, graceful degradation — is [Licensing](/editions/licensing).
This page does not repeat either.

records.title: Open-core model
records.heading: The boundary that makes it work
records.text:
Open-core only stays maintainable if the free edition is genuinely complete on its own. Alethia enforces that with a strict, mechanically-checked rule:

 
**The AGPL core never imports the Enterprise package.** The dependency only goes one way: Enterprise may build on core; core must run without Enterprise even present.
 

How it's enforced:

- **Seams, not branches.** The core has no `if (licensed)` checks scattered through it. It exposes a handful of extension points (the policy engine, the tenancy resolver, the auth plugins, the entitlement gate). In the Community build they return community defaults; the Enterprise package fills them in.
- **One integration file.** Exactly one core file (`lib/enterprise.ts`) is allowed to load the Enterprise package, and it does so *tolerantly* — if the package isn't installed, it quietly falls back to community behavior.
- **CI guards.** Three lint checks run on every build:
 - **boundary guard** — fails if any file outside the allowed integration point imports the Enterprise package;
 - **authz-scope guard** — fails if any code does ad-hoc ownership checks instead of going through the decision point;
 - **no-Supabase guard** — a legacy guard

records.title: Open-core model
records.heading: For self-hosters
records.text: See [Self-Hosting](/guides/self-hosting) for deployment, and [Architecture](/concepts/access-control/architecture) for exactly how the seams and the loader work.

records.title: OpenFGA engine
records.text: OpenFGA engine. The optional relationship-based authorization engine — what it is, how the model is generated, and how to stand it up.

records.title: OpenFGA engine
records.heading: OpenFGA engine
records.text:
Alethia's authorization runs behind one interface (the [Policy Decision Point](/concepts/access-control/architecture)),
so the **engine** underneath can be swapped without touching a single call site. The default engine,
`PostgresRbacPDP`, is open-source and handles everything described in this section. The **OpenFGA engine** is an
optional Enterprise alternative — a dedicated [OpenFGA](https://openfga.dev) relationship-graph server (ReBAC)
for fine-grained authorization at scale.

 
 OpenFGA is **optional even with a license.** Enterprise works perfectly on the Postgres engine; turn OpenFGA
 on when you want a purpose-built relationship engine. Leaving `OPENFGA_*` unset keeps the Postgres engine.

records.title: OpenFGA engine
records.heading: How it stays in sync with everything you've read
records.text:
The key design choice: **Postgres stays the source of truth.** You author roles, grants, and exceptions exactly
as documented elsewhere — they're stored in Postgres — and every change is *also* mirrored into OpenFGA as
relationship **tuples**. The OpenFGA engine reads those tuples to decide.

Two consequences:

- **Custom roles need zero model changes.** A role is a Postgres bundle of permissions that *expands to tuples*
 when granted. Add or edit a role and the tuples update — the OpenFGA model itself never changes.
- **The model is generated from the registry.** The authorization model (types, relations, the deny
 exclusions, the hierarchy inheritance) is produced directly from the same `resource × action` registry that
 drives everything else — so it covers every permission by construction.

The Postgres and OpenFGA engines are kept in **parity**: for any (actor, action, resource), they return the
same decision — including the allow/deny precedence and hierarchy inheritance from
[grants & scopes](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes).

records.title: OpenFGA engine
records.heading: Standing it up
records.text:
The high-level operator steps (the full runbook is in
[Enterprise setup](/guides/self-hosting/enterprise-setup)):

 
 Bring up the `enterprise` compose profile — the OpenFGA server and its own datastore. 
 Create a store and point the app at it (`OPENFGA_API_URL`, `OPENFGA_STORE_ID`). 
 On boot the app writes the generated model and backfills tuples from your existing grants + hierarchy. 
 From then on, every grant/role/team change dual-writes to OpenFGA; the engine answers all checks.

records.title: OpenFGA engine
records.heading: When to use it
records.text:
The Postgres engine is the right default for most deployments. Reach for OpenFGA when you want a dedicated
authorization service — very large tenancies, cross-service authorization, or a relationship graph you'll grow
beyond Alethia. Because the swap is a binding flip, you can start on Postgres and move later with a tuple
backfill, no application changes.

records.title: OpenFGA engine
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- The engine interface and the binding flip: [**architecture**](/concepts/access-control/architecture).
- Turning it on: [**Enterprise setup**](/guides/self-hosting/enterprise-setup).

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.text: Roles & Permissions. The four built-in roles, the complete resource × action permission matrix, how grants assign roles at a scope, and how the Org → Project hierarchy makes a single grant flow downward.

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: Roles & Permissions
records.text: This is the reference for *what each role can do* and *how access is assigned*. The model is **registry-as-code**: the resources, actions, and role templates below are defined in one place in the source and seeded into the database, so the docs, the UI, and the enforcement never drift.

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: Permissions
records.text: A **permission** is a single `resource:action` pair, e.g. `project:deploy`. Permissions are not freeform — only the pairs in the matrix below exist. Anything not listed is not a permission and can never be granted (default-deny by construction).

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: Resources
records.text:
The resource types are the `RESOURCES` union in `apps/console/lib/authz/registry.ts`.

 Resource What it is 
 --- --- 
 `org` An organization (the tenancy boundary). 
 `project` An infrastructure application (owns N [environments](/reference/glossary), each with a cluster + databases + networking + …). 
 `runner` An execution agent that runs provisioning jobs. 
 `cloud_identity` A connected **cloud account** — the keyless-OIDC credential anchor for AWS / GCP / Azure / Hetzner. This is the RBAC resource for a cloud account. 
 `job` A provisioning job (`plan` / `deploy` / `destroy` / …). 
 `connector` A **git / pluggable integration provider** connection (e.g. GitHub, GitLab). The connector catalog names provider *types*; a connected cloud *account* is a `cloud_identity`, not a `connector`. 
 `member` A member of an organization. 
 `activity` The Activity log. 
 `billing` Subscription & billing. 
 `alert` Alert channels, rules, and deliveries. 
 `fleet` Managed warm-pool (in-app scaler) config. Provisions real cloud VMs, so it's an owner/admin-only capability. 
 `support_case` A help-desk support case. Any member may open/track/reply to their own; `manage_support` is the staff-triage

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: The matrix
records.text:
Each resource permits an exact set of actions — the `MATRIX` in `registry.ts`. A `resource:action` pair not listed here is not a permission and can never be granted (default-deny by construction).

 Resource Actions 
 --- --- 
 `org` `view` · `edit` · `manage_billing` 
 `project` `view` · `create` · `edit` · `plan` · `deploy` · `destroy` 
 `runner` `view` · `create` · `edit` · `deploy` · `destroy` 
 `cloud_identity` `view` · `manage_identities` · `test` 
 `job` `view` · `create` · `edit` 
 `connector` `view` · `manage_connectors` 
 `member` `view` · `manage_members` 
 `activity` `view_activity` · `export_activity` 
 `billing` `manage_billing` 
 `alert` `view_alerts` · `manage_alerts` 
 `fleet` `view` · `create` · `edit` · `destroy` 
 `support_case` `view` · `create` · `reply` · `manage_support` 

The `test` action re-runs a cloud identity's server-side connection verify; `plan` / `deploy` / `destroy` map to the corresponding `tofu` provisioning jobs.

 
Adding a capability is a **one-line change** to the `RESOURCES` / `ACTIONS` / `MATRIX` registry in `registry.ts`. Because the resource and action sets are exhaustive string-literal unions, a new action that isn't handled becomes a c

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: The four built-in roles
records.text:
Roles are bundles of permissions. There are four built-in templates:

 
 
 Everything. Full control of the organization including members and billing. The creator of an organization (and every Community user, in their personal org) is an owner.
 
 
 Everything **except billing**. Can manage members, identities, integrations, and all infrastructure — but not the subscription.
 
 
 Operate infrastructure: full control of projects (`view` / `create` / `edit` / `plan` / `deploy` / `destroy`), runners (the same minus `plan`, which runners don't have), and jobs (`view` / `create` / `edit`), plus `view` / `edit` on the org, `view` on connectors, read access to alerts (`view_alerts`), and the Activity log (`view_activity` / `export_activity`; export also needs Enterprise). **Cannot** manage cloud identities, members, billing, or the managed fleet.
 
 
 Read-only. Can `view` everything (including alert config and the Activity log) but change nothing and cannot export the Activity log — plus open/reply to their own support cases.
 
 

 Role Infra (projects/runners/jobs) Cloud identities Connectors Members Alerts Fleet Activity Billing 
 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- 
 **owner** full ma

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: Grants — assigning a role
records.text:
You never attach a permission to a user directly. Instead you create a **grant**:

> *principal* gets *role* at *scope*.

- **principal** — a user (or, in Enterprise, a team).
- **role** — one of the roles above.
- **scope** — what the grant applies to: the whole **organization**, or a single **project**.

A grant scoped to the whole organization is a **wildcard** grant — it applies to every resource in the org. (This is exactly how the single grant each Community user receives works: *owner, org-wide*.)

grant: alice → operator → project "production" # operator on that project
grant: bob → viewer → org # read-only across the whole org
grant: you → owner → org # the Community default — full control of your personal org

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: Inheritance: the Org → Project hierarchy
records.text:
Resources form a tree — the parent chain in `apps/console/lib/authz/fga-hierarchy.ts`. `project`, `runner`, `cloud_identity`, and `connector` all hang directly off the `org`:

 project
 org --> runner
 org --> cloud_identity
 org --> connector
`} />

A grant **flows downward**. If you grant someone `operator` on the **organization**, they automatically have those permissions on **every project inside it** — you don't grant each project separately. A project-scoped grant covers just that project.

grant: dana → operator → project "staging-api"
 ⇒ dana can plan/deploy/destroy project "staging-api"
 ⇒ dana CANNOT touch project "production-api" (no grant)

This is why a handful of grants covers an entire estate: assign at the highest scope that makes sense and let inheritance do the rest. The decision engine resolves this by walking up from the target resource to see whether any of your grants cover it or an ancestor — see [Architecture](/concepts/access-control/architecture).

records.title: Roles & Permissions
records.heading: How this shows up
records.text:
- **List views** only show resources you can `view` — the list itself is filtered by your grants, not just hidden in the UI.
- **Actions** (deploy, destroy, invite, …) are checked the instant you trigger them; if you lack the permission you get a clear *Forbidden*, and the attempt is recorded in the Activity log.
- **Community**: with a single org-wide `owner` grant, you can do everything in your own personal organization — the role machinery is invisible until you add teammates under [Enterprise organizations](/guides/access/organizations).

records.title: Authentication flows
records.text: Authentication flows. Why the console, the CLI and the runner each authenticate differently — OAuth and email OTP sessions for the web, a device grant and service tokens for the CLI, and hashed tokens for runners.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Authentication flows
records.text: The platform has three distinct authentication mechanisms — one for each component.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Web Authentication (Console)
records.text:
Console uses **Better Auth** (in-process, with the Drizzle adapter) for web sessions. Two sign-in paths are supported — social OAuth and email OTP:

 Provider Method 
 ---------- -------- 
 GitHub OAuth 2.0 (native) 
 Google OAuth 2.0 (native) 
 GitLab OAuth 2.0 (genericOAuth) 
 Bitbucket OAuth 2.0 (genericOAuth) 
 Email 6-digit OTP (email OTP plugin)

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: User clicks provider button
records.text: The sign-in page shows buttons for each OAuth provider.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Redirect to provider
records.text: Better Auth redirects to the provider's authorization endpoint (e.g., `github.com/login/oauth/authorize`).

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: User authorizes
records.text: The user grants the application access to their account.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Callback with code
records.text: The provider redirects back to `/api/auth/[...all]` with an authorization code. Better Auth exchanges it for access and refresh tokens.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Session created
records.text:
Better Auth creates a **server-side session** (a row in the `session` table) and sets a signed,
HTTP-only session cookie. The web session is a cookie-backed Better Auth session — **not** a JWT (the
`jwt()` plugin is not enabled); JWTs are used only for the CLI and workload identity (see
[**Standards → JOSE**](/reference/standards/jose)).

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Email OTP Flow
records.text: For password-less email sign-in, the user enters their email, receives a **6-digit one-time code**, and submits it back. Better Auth verifies the code and issues the same cookie-backed session as the OAuth path.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Session Management
records.text:
- Sessions are managed by Better Auth (creation, refresh, revocation)
- The session lives in a signed HTTP-only cookie backed by the `session` table; the Next.js middleware validates it on every request
- Data access runs through the app's Policy Decision Point (PDP), which sets the active org via `set_config('app.current_org', …)` before queries
- Coarse Postgres RLS keyed on `org_id` enforces per-organization data isolation (not `auth.uid()`)

Authentication is *who you are*; **authorization** is *what you can do*. Once you're signed in, the PDP decides
every action — see [**Access Control**](/concepts/access-control) for roles, permissions, grants (allow/deny), and the
org/team model.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: CLI authentication (alethia)
records.text:
A terminal cannot host an OAuth redirect, and a person should never type a password into one. So
`alethia login` uses a flow modeled on the OAuth 2.0 **Device Authorization Grant**
([RFC 8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628)) — the same browser-hands-off-to-terminal pattern
as GitHub CLI, Azure CLI and AWS SSO. The browser does the real sign-in, with any provider the console
supports; the terminal waits, then receives a token pair.

- It works with every web sign-in method, because the browser handles the login.
- The access token is short-lived (1 hour); the refresh token lasts 90 days, so people rarely sign in
 again.
- The CLI tokens are their own HS256 JWTs, separate from the cookie-backed web session.

A pipeline has no browser and no person, so it uses a **service-account token** instead: minted once,
passed in `$ALETHIA_TOKEN`, acting as its creator inside one organization.

Where to read more:

- The protocol, its endpoints and its deviations from RFC 8628:
 [Standards → Device Authorization Grant](/reference/standards/device-code).
- Signing in, refusing a login you did not start, token storage and service tokens:
 [CLI → Authentication](/reference/cli/authenticati

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Runner Authentication
records.text: Runners authenticate with Console using **token-based auth** via HTTP headers.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Registration
records.text:
When a Runner is registered (via UI or CLI), the server:

1. Generates a random token
2. Hashes it with SHA-256
3. Stores the **hash** in `runners.token_hash`
4. Returns the **plaintext** token to the user (shown once, never stored)

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Request Authentication
records.text:
Every Runner API call includes two headers:

X-Runner-ID: {runner-uuid}
X-Runner-Token: {plaintext-token}

The server:
1. Looks up the runner by `X-Runner-ID`
2. Hashes the provided `X-Runner-Token` with SHA-256
3. Compares against `runners.token_hash` in constant time
4. Rejects if mismatch (401)

 
The plaintext token is shown only once at registration. If lost, the Runner must be re-registered. This is intentional — it prevents token reuse and ensures tokens are not stored in a recoverable location.

records.title: Authentication flows
records.heading: Authentication Summary
records.text:
Component Method Token Lifetime Storage 
 ----------- -------- --------------- --------- 
 **Console** (web) Better Auth (OAuth + email OTP) Session-based (auto-refresh) Signed HTTP-only cookie (session table) 
 **alethia** (CLI) Device grant (RFC 8628 variant), or a service-account token Access: 1h, Refresh: 90d; service token: until revoked or expired `~/.config/alethia/credentials.json`, or `$ALETHIA_TOKEN` 
 **Runner** (agent) SHA-256 token hash Permanent (until re-registration) Environment variable

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.text: Bring-your-own charts. Point an add-on at a Helm chart in your own git repository — Alethia deploys it through ArgoCD under a hardened project that confines it to its own namespace, auto-syncs it, and never prunes or reverts what you change.

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: Bring-your-own charts
records.text:
Alethia's add-on marketplace installs charts from public Helm registries. **Bring-your-own charts**
let you install a Helm chart from **your own git repository** instead, alongside marketplace add-ons
in the same cluster.

Your chart is not Alethia's code, so it runs under a deliberately narrower contract than a
marketplace add-on. This page is that contract: what gets deployed, what your chart is allowed to
create, what Alethia will and will not do to it afterwards, and how to remove it. To attach a chart,
scan it, and bind its workloads, follow [Bring your own Helm charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts).

 
 **A BYO chart is a Helm chart in git.** It is a different thing from
 [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac), which points an environment at your own
 **OpenTofu root module** and provisions the infrastructure itself. They can be used together;
 neither requires the other.

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: What happens when you enable one
records.text:
Each deploy, Alethia:

1. creates the destination **namespace**, because your chart is not permitted to create one itself
 (see [What your chart may create](#what-your-chart-may-create));
2. registers a **repository credential** for your chart's repo, in a Secret scoped to that repo
 alone — no BYO chart can read another's token, or the apps repo's;
3. applies a hardened **ArgoCD AppProject** that confines the chart; and
4. applies the **Application**, which then syncs on its own.

Nothing about this is a one-time setup. The Application is re-applied on every deploy, so a change
to any of the above takes effect on your next deploy rather than needing the add-on removed and
re-added.

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: A push to the tracked ref deploys
records.text:
Your chart is attached at a git **ref**, and a ref is usually a branch — the default is `HEAD`.
ArgoCD watches that ref, so **a commit to it deploys, on its own, without an Alethia deploy and
without an approval step.** That is ordinary GitOps, and for most people it is the point: your
chart repo is the source of truth and the cluster follows it.

It is worth being deliberate about, though, because it means write access to that branch is
effectively deploy access to that namespace.

 
 **Attach a tag or a commit SHA if you want deploys to be explicit.** The `ref` accepts any git
 revision, so pinning it to `v1.4.2` or a full SHA means the cluster changes only when you change
 the ref — pushing to your branch then does nothing until you do. Use a branch when you want
 continuous delivery; use a tag or SHA when you want a release step.
 

What a push **cannot** do is escape the chart's confinement — every sync is validated against the
same hardened project, so a new commit is held to exactly the rules in
[What your chart may create](#what-your-chart-may-create).

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: Sync behaviour
records.text:
Your chart is deployed automatically. Two things Alethia deliberately does **not** do:

 Marketplace add-on Your chart 
 --- :---: :---: 
 Deployed automatically yes **yes** 
 Prune — delete resources no longer declared yes **no** 
 Self-heal — revert changes made in the cluster yes **no** 

**Prune is off, so a resource you delete from your chart keeps running.** If you remove a Deployment
from the chart and deploy, the old Deployment is still there. This is deliberate: Alethia will not
delete a workload of yours because your chart stopped mentioning it. To remove it, either delete it
yourself with `kubectl`, or [disable the add-on](#removing-a-chart), which removes everything.

**Self-heal is off, so changes you make in the cluster stick.** If you `kubectl edit` a resource
your chart owns, ArgoCD reports the Application `OutOfSync` and leaves your change alone. That is
what you want while debugging; it also means an `OutOfSync` BYO chart is informational, not an
error.

To put it back, you have to give ArgoCD something to do — **a deploy on its own will not revert it**,
because the chart is already at the revision it is meant to be at and there is nothing to sync. Any
of these wo

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: What your chart may create
records.text:
The AppProject Alethia applies is default-deny. Your chart may create **namespaced** resources in
its **own destination namespace** and nothing else:

- **No cluster-scoped resources.** No `Namespace`, `ClusterRole`, `ClusterRoleBinding`,
 `CustomResourceDefinition`, `StorageClass`, or any other cluster-scoped kind. A chart that
 declares one fails its sync with a message naming the resource.
- **No `Role`, `RoleBinding` or `ServiceAccount`,** even namespaced ones — a chart that could mint
 its own identity could grant itself more than this project allows.
- **Only the repositories you declared.** The project is locked to your chart's repo, so an
 Application cannot be re-pointed at a source you did not configure.
- **Only its own namespace.** The project's destinations list that namespace and no other.

 
 **If your chart needs a cluster-scoped resource, it cannot be a BYO chart as-is.** The usual
 answers are to split the cluster-scoped part out and have an operator apply it once, or to request
 the capability as a marketplace add-on. Relaxing the project for one chart would relax it for
 every chart in the environment.

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: Removing a chart
records.text:
Disabling the add-on deletes its Application, and the Application carries ArgoCD's
`resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io` finalizer — so deletion **cascades to everything the chart
created**, including resources that prune would have left behind. The namespace Alethia created for
it remains.

So the two removal paths differ, and the difference is worth remembering:

- **Remove a resource from the chart** → it keeps running (prune is off).
- **Disable the add-on** → everything the chart created is deleted.

records.title: Bring-your-own charts
records.heading: Troubleshooting
records.text:
**The Application is `OutOfSync` and I did not change anything.** Some charts render a value that
differs on every render — a generated password, a timestamp, a self-signed certificate. ArgoCD
compares each render against the cluster, so such a chart is permanently `OutOfSync`. Pin the value
in your chart, usually through an `existingSecret`-style option, and it settles.

**The Application is `Missing`.** Its resources do not exist. Check the sync result in ArgoCD: the
most common causes are a resource the project forbids (see
[What your chart may create](#what-your-chart-may-create)) and a chart path that does not exist at
the configured revision.

**The Application is `Progressing` and stays there.** ArgoCD is waiting for a workload to become
ready. Check the pods: a pod stuck `Pending` with `Insufficient memory` or `Insufficient cpu` is
asking for more than any node in your cluster can give it, which no amount of waiting fixes — lower
the request or provision a larger node type.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.text: Bring-your-own IaC. Attach a git repo holding your own OpenTofu root module to a project environment — Alethia provisions from your module instead of its built-in template, behind a fail-closed static safety gate, a frozen variable contract, and the same verify gate as template provisioning.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Bring-your-own IaC
records.text:
Alethia normally provisions from its own per-cloud project templates (EKS / GKE / AKS / ACK / Talos +
supporting services). **Bring-your-own IaC (BYO IaC, "E3")** lets you point a project **environment** at
a git repository holding your **own OpenTofu root module** — Alethia then provisions that environment
from *your* module instead of the built-in template.

Because a customer's OpenTofu is arbitrary code, running it is a trust decision. This page describes the
contract Alethia gives your module, the static safety gate that vets it, who is allowed to run it, and
the lifecycle that keeps the whole thing TOCTOU-safe. To attach a module, write a minimal one, or
detach it, follow the how-to guide [Bring your own IaC](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-iac).

 
 **v1 is REPLACE mode.** A BYO source attached to an environment provisions *instead of* the built-in
 template — not alongside it. There is at most **one** source per environment. Attaching is rejected if
 the environment already has deployed (or in-flight) template state; destroy it first. Composing your
 module *with* an Alethia template is not a v1 capability.
 

 
 **Flagged off by default.** BYO IaC is gated by `ALETHI

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Why a gate at all
records.text:
Running `tofu plan` on arbitrary HCL is **remote code execution**. Providers are arbitrary binaries
fetched at `init` time; an `external` data source executes a program during `plan`; `local-exec` /
`remote-exec` provisioners run commands at `apply`. So BYO IaC is protected by two independent controls:

1. A **fail-closed static safety gate** (`iacsafety`) that *parses* the module — never evaluates
 expressions, never runs `tofu`, never fetches remote modules — and blocks anything dangerous before a
 single `tofu` command runs.
2. The **execution sandbox** (on the managed fleet) that contains a hostile provider even if it slips the
 gate. See [Isolated Execution](/concepts/isolated-execution).

The gate is the first line; the sandbox is the backstop. Neither is trusted alone.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: The Alethia variable contract
records.text:
When Alethia runs your module it injects **platform context** as OpenTofu variables via `TF_VAR_*`
environment variables. This set is a **frozen public contract** — author your module's `variable` blocks
against these exact names:

 Variable Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `alethia_project` The project name 
 `alethia_environment` The environment stage (e.g. `production`, `staging`) 
 `alethia_region` The primary region 
 `alethia_project_id` The Alethia project/config id 
 `alethia_environment_id` The Alethia environment id 

Declare the ones you want in your root module:

variable "alethia_project" { type = string }
variable "alethia_environment" { type = string }
variable "alethia_region" { type = string }

 
 **Frozen means additive-only.** These names never rename or disappear — new keys may only be *added*.
 A module that declares **none** of them is unaffected (OpenTofu silently ignores undeclared
 `TF_VAR_*`); a module that declares one receives its value.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: The alethia_ namespace is reserved
records.text:
Your own variable values (`var_values`) are passed to `tofu` as a var-file, which is **higher precedence**
than `TF_VAR_*` env vars. To stop a customer value from *shadowing* the platform context (e.g. spoofing
`alethia_project_id`), any `var_values` key starting with **`alethia_`** is **dropped** with a warning.
Name your own variables anything outside that prefix.

Customer variable values are also **coerced to scalars** at the write step: only `string` / number /
`bool` pass through. Nested objects, arrays, and other shapes are rejected (skipped with a warning) so
nothing structured or injectable reaches the tfvars file; a `null` is skipped so your module's own default
applies.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: The static safety gate
records.text:
Before any `tofu` runs, `iacsafety.Scan` walks the root module and every **local** child module it
references (staying inside the clone), parsing configuration only. It produces `error`- and
`warning`-severity findings; **any error-severity finding fails the deploy closed** — the provisioner
never reaches `tofu`. The gate runs at **attach/scan time** *and* is **re-run inline on every
plan/deploy/destroy** (defense in depth — the recorded scan result is never trusted on its own).

What the gate enforces:

 Rule Severity Why 
 --- --- --- 
 **Provider not on the allowlist** error `tofu init` downloads and executes provider binaries; only vetted providers are allowed. Covers both explicit `required_providers` sources and providers *implied* by a resource/data type. 
 **`provisioner` blocks** error `local-exec` / `remote-exec` run arbitrary commands at apply. 
 **`data "external"`** error Executes a program during `plan`. 
 **Remote / absolute module sources** error A non-local (`./` or `../`) module source — registry, git, http, s3/gcs, absolute or `~` path — cannot be statically vetted (`tofu init` would fetch and run code the gate never saw, including provider binaries the unfetched

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Provider allowlist
records.text:
The default allowed provider set:

hashicorp/aws hashicorp/google hashicorp/google-beta
hashicorp/azurerm hashicorp/azuread hashicorp/alicloud
hashicorp/kubernetes hashicorp/helm hashicorp/tls
hashicorp/random hashicorp/time hashicorp/cloudinit
hashicorp/dns hashicorp/local hashicorp/null
hashicorp/template aliyun/alicloud hetznercloud/hcloud

Registry-host prefixes are normalized away, so `registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/aws` and
`registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws` both match `hashicorp/aws`; a provider on **any other** registry
host keeps its host and therefore never matches — **unknown registries fail closed**. An operator can
override the set with `ALETHIA_BYO_IAC_PROVIDER_ALLOWLIST` (comma-separated provider source addresses);
an unset or empty value falls back to the default.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: State is Alethia's, not yours
records.text:
Your module may declare a `backend` / `cloud` block, but Alethia **overrides it**: an empty `http`
backend override is written into the cloned module (under both `.tf` and `.tofu` extensions, to close the
OpenTofu 1.8+ precedence gap), and its `-backend-config` binds to Alethia's per-job **console HTTP state
proxy**. So:

- Your backend block is **ignored** (and flagged as a warning; a customer-committed *override file* is
 rejected outright as a footgun).
- State lives behind Alethia's **per-job state proxy**, keyed per environment. The runner holds no
 authoritative state and no object-storage credential — one job's token can only touch its own state.

See [OpenTofu State Management](/concepts/terraform-state) for the state model, and
[Isolated Execution](/concepts/isolated-execution) for how the state-proxy source-drop is part of the sandbox.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Cluster wiring is opportunistic
records.text:
Alethia's post-apply steps — the reachability gate, kubeconfig capture, ArgoCD install, infra-services —
key off the module's OpenTofu **outputs**:

- A module that outputs **`cluster_name`** (and the kubeconfig inputs below) opportunistically gets the
 reachability gate and ArgoCD/GitOps wiring, exactly like a template-provisioned cluster.
- A module that outputs **neither degrades gracefully**: Alethia provisions it, captures its outputs, and
 stops there — no kubeconfig probe, no ArgoCD. Perfectly valid for a module that provisions something
 other than a cluster.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: The cluster-output contract
records.text:
The runner reads the cluster wiring from your outputs. For each field it checks the **provider-prefixed**
key the built-in templates emit first, then falls back to the **generic** key — so a BYO module only needs
to emit the generic names:

 Field Generic key (BYO) Provider-prefixed keys (templates) Purpose 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Cluster name `cluster_name` `eks_cluster_name` · `gke_cluster_name` · `aks_cluster_name` · `talos_cluster_name` · `ack_cluster_name` **Gates all post-apply wiring.** Empty ⇒ Alethia treats the deploy as cluster-less and skips kubeconfig/reachability/ArgoCD/add-ons. 
 API endpoint `cluster_endpoint` `eks_cluster_endpoint` · `gke_cluster_endpoint` · `aks_cluster_endpoint` · … The API server URL the kubeconfig points at. 
 Cluster CA `cluster_ca_certificate` `gke_cluster_ca_certificate` · `aks_cluster_ca_certificate` Base64 CA the kubeconfig trusts (GKE/AKS-style clouds). 
 Ready kubeconfig `kubeconfig` (Talos/ACK emit `kubeconfig` directly) A complete kubeconfig. If present it is used **verbatim** — for a self-managed / non-cloud-managed cluster (incl. a non-EKS cluster on AWS, where it short-circuits the EKS `DescribeCluster` path). 

How the two kubeconfig sh

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Required: your module must self-admin the cluster
records.text:
Alethia installs ArgoCD (and every add-on) over the kubeconfig from your outputs. That kubeconfig
authenticates as **the identity your provisioning runner runs as** — so **your module MUST grant that
identity `cluster-admin` on the cluster it creates.** Alethia cannot inject this for you (it never holds a
static admin credential for a BYO cluster); if you skip it, the cluster comes up reachable but the ArgoCD
install **401s** and the deploy fails at the GitOps step. Grant it in-module, at create time:

 Cloud Grant the apply/runner identity cluster-admin via 
 --- --- 
 **AWS (EKS)** An `aws_eks_access_entry` + `aws_eks_access_policy_association` (`AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy`) for the runner's IAM role — or add it to `access_entries` / the aws-auth mapping — so the role that ran `apply` is a cluster admin. 
 **GCP (GKE)** Bind the runner's service account `roles/container.admin` (or `roles/container.clusterAdmin`) on the project/cluster. 
 **Azure (AKS)** An `azurerm_role_assignment` of **Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin** to the runner principal (Azure-RBAC clusters), or include its Entra group in the cluster's `admin_group_object_ids`. 
 **Talos / self-managed** Emit

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Verification: the same gate as templates
records.text:
A BYO plan flows through the **same fail-closed [Elench](/concepts/elench) verify gate** as template
provisioning — the deterministic controls (keyless / least-privilege / OIDC-sub, with honest
`not_evaluable` for what the plan can't show) run between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`, and a hard
control failure blocks the apply unless an authorized override waives it. Every plan/apply also produces
an **ed25519-signed evidence receipt** sealing the report to the exact plan (`plan_sha256`).

 
 The receipt seals the *plan* (`plan_sha256`) + control catalog + verdict. The **git provenance** of a
 BYO deploy — which commit actually ran — is pinned separately on the environment's source record
 (the scanned `commit_sha`, and the `deployed_commit_sha` of the last successful deploy), not embedded
 in the receipt itself.

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Lifecycle
records.text:
1. **Attach** (console, per environment) — you attach a repo + ref + module path (+ optional variable
 values and a git credential). Rejected if the environment already has a source, or has deployed /
 in-flight **template** state (replace mode would orphan it — destroy first).
2. **`IAC_SCAN`** — a scan job clones the repo, **pins the exact commit SHA it checked out**, inventories
 the module (providers + module sources), runs the static safety gate + `tofu validate`, and writes the
 report back. Provisioning stays **locked** until a clean scan pins a `commit_sha`; a failed / not-ok
 scan clears the pin.
3. **Plan / Deploy** — run the **pinned commit** (never the moving ref). The gate is re-run inline
 (fail-closed), the backend is overridden to the state proxy, the frozen `TF_VAR_alethia_*` context is
 published, and the plan flows through the verify gate. A successful deploy records its
 `deployed_commit_sha`.
4. **Detect drift** — the pinned commit is refreshed against real state, producing a drift posture like
 any environment.
5. **Destroy** — runs the **last-deployed** commit (`deployed_commit_sha`), then purges the state. A
 source that never deployed is freely detachable;

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Operator model — who can run BYO IaC
records.text:
This is the honest availability boundary. BYO IaC runs **untrusted customer code**, so *where* it runs
determines whether it is available:

- **Self-hosted runners (`operator=self`)** run BYO IaC at the **customer's own risk boundary** — the
 runner is in the customer's own cloud with native permissions. This is the **generally-available** path
 under the `ALETHIA_BYO_IAC_ENABLED` flag.
- **Managed runners** are **fail-closed blocked** from executing untrusted BYO IaC **unless** the
 per-job container sandbox with egress enforcement is active — i.e. `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container`
 **and** `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` **and** `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_ENFORCE_MANAGED`. That sandbox
 itself stays disabled until the **real-VM isolation canary** is proven on the fleet (nested podman,
 `/proc` isolation, IMDS unreachable, domain-allowlist egress).

 
 **Managed BYO IaC is trusted-only / gated until the isolation canary passes.** Do not assume managed
 availability. The container sandbox and its turn-on sequence are documented in
 [Isolated Execution → Architecture](/concepts/isolated-execution/architecture) and the
 [Managed provisioning runbook](/guides/self-hosting/managed-provisioni

records.title: Bring-your-own IaC
records.heading: Where to go next
records.text:
Attach a module to an environment, read its safety scan, and detach it — with a minimal module
 that exercises the whole path at zero spend.
 
 
 The per-job container sandbox that contains untrusted BYO code on the managed fleet — the runtime
 backstop behind the static gate.
 
 
 The fail-closed verify gate and signed evidence receipt every plan/apply flows through.
 
 
 How state is stored — and why Alethia overrides your backend with its per-job state proxy.
 
 
 Config snapshot → ProjectConfig → tfvars → infrastructure, shared by template and BYO paths.

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.text: Cloud Provider Abstraction. What Alethia can provision, and how it abstracts AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud, and Hetzner behind one interface.

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.text: Alethia provisions across **five providers** — AWS, GCP, Azure, and Alibaba Cloud (full managed clouds) plus Hetzner (a lean, self-managed Talos Kubernetes cluster on cheap VMs). A single form, a single CLI, and a single Runner agent work across all of them, through a multi-layered abstraction.

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: What Alethia can provision
records.text:
Alethia models a cloud-indifferent set of **capability categories** (the `ProjectConfig` service model in `packages/core/types/project_config.go`). Each maps to a concrete resource per provider and is gated by a `create_*`/`provision_*` toggle the Runner emits from your Project config:

Kubernetes cluster · VPC/network · managed SQL database · managed Redis/cache · message queue · pub/sub topic · object storage · NoSQL table · container registry · DNS zone · secrets manager · WAF · CDN / managed TLS certificate — plus the cluster autoscaler and the [pluggable-connector seam](/concepts/connectors) (swap the cloud-native DNS/secrets/registry for a tool you already run).

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Provider capability matrix
records.text:
The registry (`lib/cloud-providers/registry.ts`) maps each capability to the provider's cloud-native service. The **four managed clouds are at feature parity** across every category.

**Hetzner is different in kind, not merely leaner.** Hetzner sells compute, private networking and object storage; it sells no database, cache, queue, registry or secret store. So Alethia provisions the cluster and the network with OpenTofu and delivers the rest as components **it installs and operates in the cluster** — CloudNativePG, Valkey, RabbitMQ, Harbor and HashiCorp Vault, one release per component, each converging as its own ArgoCD Application. You design the same canvas; what lands differs.

Two consequences worth knowing before you pick Hetzner:

- **You own the data plane.** A managed database is backed up, patched and failed over by the cloud. An in-cluster one is backed up, patched and failed over by you (and by the add-ons you choose for it). The canvas will not pretend otherwise.
- **The secret store's seal is only as strong as the cluster.** Hetzner sells no KMS, so the platform Vault is Shamir-sealed and its unseal key lives in a Kubernetes Secret in the same cluster. Against a clust

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Infra services (post-apply)
records.text:
After `tofu apply`, the Runner wires a set of **in-cluster infra services** over ArgoCD (external-dns, the external-secrets store, ingress, the default storage class, the ArgoCD URL). Not every service maps cleanly to every cloud — some are cloud-inherent gaps, not bugs. Rather than silently omit a service (or ship it broken), the pipeline records a **machine-readable per-service decision** with an honest reason — the same `not_evaluable`/"honest N/A" discipline the [verify gate](/concepts/security) applies to the plan.

The decisions come from `argocd.InfraServiceDecisions` (`packages/core/argocd/decisions.go`), computed from the **same gates** the templates render against (`InfraFacts.DNSProvider()`, the per-cloud ClusterSecretStore conditions), so a recorded decision can never drift from what actually shipped. The Runner forwards them on `execution_metadata["infra_services"]` (status + reason only — non-sensitive), and the console renders them alongside the add-on status.

 Infra service AWS GCP Azure Alibaba Hetzner 
 --------------- ----- ----- ------- --------- --------- 
 external-dns installed (Route 53, IRSA) installed when Workload Identity SA present installed when manag

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Region Mapping
records.text:
Regions are mapped across providers for cross-cloud Project duplication:

AWS us-east-1 ←→ GCP us-east4 ←→ Azure eastus
AWS eu-west-1 ←→ GCP europe-west1 ←→ Azure westeurope
AWS ap-south-1 ←→ GCP asia-south1 ←→ Azure centralindia

Each provider has a default region: `us-east-1` (AWS), `us-east4` (GCP), `eastus` (Azure).

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Instance Type Mapping
records.text:
Compute instance types are mapped for Project conversion:

 AWS GCP Azure Profile 
 ----- ----- ------- --------- 
 t3.medium e2-standard-2 Standard_B2s General (2 vCPU, 4 GiB) 
 t3.large e2-standard-2 Standard_D2s_v5 General (2 vCPU, 8 GiB) 
 m5a.large n2-standard-2 Standard_D2as_v5 Compute (2 vCPU, 8 GiB) 
 c5.large c2-standard-4 Standard_F2s_v2 Compute-optimized 
 r5.large n2-highmem-2 Standard_E2s_v5 Memory-optimized

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Database Engine Mapping
records.text:
AWS GCP Azure 
 ----- ----- ------- 
 aurora-postgresql cloudsql-postgresql azure-postgresql 
 aurora-mysql cloudsql-mysql azure-mysql 

Capacity units differ: AWS uses **ACUs** (Aurora Capacity Units, 0.5–128), GCP uses **vCPUs** (1–96), Azure uses **vCores** (1–64). When converting across providers, the platform maps equivalent capacity ranges and warns when units change.

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Cache Engine Availability
records.text:
The abstraction has a limit, and the cache engine is where you meet it. Not every cloud sells every
engine, so this axis is **narrowed per cloud** rather than mapped across them.

 Cloud Redis Valkey Service 
 ------- :-----: :------: --------- 
 AWS yes yes ElastiCache — replication group for Redis, Serverless for Valkey 
 GCP yes yes Memorystore — separate products, sized differently 
 Azure yes — Azure Managed Redis 
 Alibaba yes — ApsaraDB for Redis (KVStore) 
 Hetzner — yes in-cluster Valkey chart 

Azure and Alibaba have no Valkey product, so the canvas does not offer it there. Hetzner is the
mirror image: its data services run as in-cluster charts, and the cache chart is Valkey.

Two consequences follow, and both are visible in the product rather than left implicit:

- The engine picker shows only what the selected cloud can build. You cannot choose an engine that
 would provision nothing.
- Converting a project to a cloud that lacks its engine **switches the engine and tells you**. A
 Valkey cache moving to Azure becomes Redis, with a warning naming the change.

The same rule governs databases. Hetzner runs PostgreSQL in-cluster through CloudNativePG and offers
no MySQL, so

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: The provider_config JSONB Column
records.text:
Provider-specific configuration that doesn't fit the shared schema is stored in a `provider_config` JSONB column on component tables. For example:

- **Cluster**: `{ "enable_karpenter": true }` (AWS) vs `{ "enable_autopilot": true }` (GCP) vs `{ "enable_cluster_autoscaler": true }` (Azure)
- **DNS**: `{ "waf_cloudfront": true, "waf_alb": false }` (AWS) vs `{ "cloud_armor": true }` (GCP) vs `{ "azure_waf": true }` (Azure)
- **NoSQL**: `{ "global_table": true }` (AWS DynamoDB) vs `{ "multi_region": true }` (Azure Cosmos DB)

This keeps the shared schema clean while allowing provider-specific features.

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: How the Form Adapts
records.text:
When the user switches providers via the Provider Ribbon in the Design a Project form:

1. **Instance types** update to the target provider's catalog
2. **Kubernetes versions** update (e.g., 1.32 for AWS EKS, 1.31 for GCP GKE)
3. **Database engines** switch (Aurora → Cloud SQL → Azure Database)
4. **Cache node types** switch (cache.r6g.large → M2 → C2)
5. **Network options** adapt (VPC → VPC Network → VNet)
6. **DNS/WAF options** change (CloudFront WAF → Cloud Armor → Azure WAF)
7. **Autoscaler** toggles change (Karpenter → GKE Autopilot → Cluster Autoscaler)
8. **Region dropdown** repopulates with the provider's regions

All form fields reset to provider-appropriate defaults. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion) for how existing Projects are converted across providers.

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: OpenTofu Templates
records.text:
Each provider has its own set of OpenTofu templates:

- `infra/templates/project/aws/` — EKS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, S3, ECR, etc.
- `infra/templates/project/gcp/` — GKE, Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Firestore, GCS, Artifact Registry, etc.
- `infra/templates/project/azure/` — AKS, Azure Database, Azure Cache, Cosmos DB, Blob Storage, ACR, etc.
- `infra/templates/project/alibaba/` — ACK, ApsaraDB RDS, KVStore, Tablestore, OSS, CR, etc.
- `infra/templates/project/hetzner/` — Talos Kubernetes + private network (Cilium CNI, hcloud CCM/CSI).

The runner selects the correct template directory based on the project's cloud provider and generates `terraform.tfvars.json` (the tfvars file `tofu` reads) from the project configuration (`packages/core/cloud/ _provider.go` `ProviderTfvars`).

records.title: Cloud Provider Abstraction
records.heading: Pluggable connectors
records.text: The same registry pattern extends one level down to **per-category connectors** — letting a Project swap the cloud-native default for a tool you already run (Cloudflare DNS, Vault secrets, Docker Hub registry, Datadog/Grafana Cloud observability). See [Connectors Architecture](/concepts/connectors).

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.text: Connectors architecture. How pluggable per-category connectors are declared, stored, and composed into a provision.

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: Connectors architecture
records.text:
Connectors decouple **what** a Project needs (a DNS zone, secrets, a registry, observability) from **who** provides it. A **connector** is a provider *type* in the catalog; an account you actually connect to a cloud is a **cloud identity** (see the [glossary](/reference/glossary#connectivity)). Cloud and Git connectors are first-class; the **pluggable per-category** connectors are added by registration, not by editing call sites.

This page explains how the catalog is built and how credentials flow. To connect an account, read its status, or disconnect it, see [Connectors](/guides/connectors).

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: Single source of truth
records.text:
Every pluggable provider is declared once in a manifest, `packages/core/categories/catalog.json` (slug, category, `auth_method`, icon, credential fields, provider-config fields, module path). That manifest is consumed three ways so the provider set never drifts:

- **Go** loads it with `go:embed` (`packages/core/categories`) to resolve which module to compose and what credential a provider needs.
- **Codegen** (`pnpm -F console gen:connectors`) emits the typed TS registry (`lib/connectors/registry.generated.ts`) that drives the credential form and the Project provider selectors, plus the SQL seed of `connectors` catalog rows.
- **Behavior** that can't be data — `Tfvars()` and `Validate()` — lives in small per-slug Go impls.

This mirrors the [cloud-provider registry](/concepts/cloud-abstraction) one level down, per category.

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: The CategoryProvider contract
records.text: Each provider impl exposes a small interface: `Category()`, `Slug()`, `ModulePath()`, `Tfvars(ctx)` (maps the component's config + decrypted credential into module variables), and `Validate(ctx)` (rejects nonsensical combinations before a plan is produced). A registry resolves a provider by `(category, slug)`.

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: Credential storage
records.text: API-key credentials live in the `connector_credentials` table, owner/org-scoped under the same RLS as everything else. Secret fields are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM (`ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`); non-secret fields (a Vault address, a Docker Hub username) are stored in clear.

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: Runtime credential flow
records.text:
The zero-credential model is preserved end to end:

1. A Project's `config_snapshot` carries only **identifiers** — including each component's chosen provider slug — never secrets.
2. When a runner **claims** a job, the claim endpoint (`app/api/jobs/claim/route.ts`) resolves the connectors the Project references, decrypts their credentials **in the console**, and attaches the plaintext to the claim response (alongside the cloud identity). The runner never holds the encryption key.
3. The runner injects them into OpenTofu variables **in memory** at provision time.

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: Module composition
records.text: For each component with a pluggable provider, the runner copies the provider's module from `infra/templates/categories/ / /` into the working directory, writes a generated `_categories.tf.json` wiring the module with its variables, and sets a ` _provider` guard variable. The cluster-cloud templates gate their native resources on that variable (`count = var.dns_provider == "native" ? 1 : 0`), so the native resource is **skipped** when a pluggable provider is chosen. Observability is purely additive (no native default).

records.title: Connectors architecture
records.heading: Open-core
records.text: Connectors are core value and stay AGPL/community — the registry-of-record (`connectors` table) and the category contract are community. Only premium connectors or org-scoped connector governance would live in `ee/` (see [Open Core](/concepts/access-control/open-core)).

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.text: Cost Estimation. How the platform estimates infrastructure costs in real-time and via Infracost analysis.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Cost Estimation
records.text: The platform provides two layers of cost estimation: a **real-time cost sidebar** during Project configuration, and a **post-plan Infracost analysis** for precise per-resource costs.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Cost Sidebar (Real-Time)
records.text: The cost sidebar appears on the right side of the Design a Project form. As the user configures infrastructure, the estimated monthly cost updates immediately.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: How Pricing Works
records.text:
1. When a region is selected, the `fetchPrices(region)` action fetches pricing from the AWS Pricing API
2. Prices are cached in the Zustand store with a 24-hour TTL
3. Each component contributes a cost line item

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Pricing Sources
records.text:
The `getRegionPrices(region)` server action fetches:

 Resource Pricing Key Source 
 ---------- ------------ -------- 
 EKS control plane Fixed $0.10/hour Hardcoded 
 EC2 instances Per instance type AWS Pricing API (on-demand, Linux, shared tenancy) 
 NAT Gateway $0.048/hour AWS Pricing API 
 Aurora ACU $0.14/ACU-hour AWS Pricing API 
 ElastiCache nodes Per node type AWS Pricing API 
 WAF web ACL ~$5/month Hardcoded 
 Secrets $0.40/secret/month Hardcoded

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Cost Calculation
records.text:
Monthly cost = Σ (hourly_rate × 730 hours/month)

Per component:
- **Cluster**: EKS control plane ($73/mo) + node_desired_size × average_instance_rate × 730
- **NAT Gateway**: $0.048 × count × 730 (single = 1, HA = AZ count)
- **Database**: min_capacity × ACU_rate × 730 per instance
- **Cache**: node_rate × num_cache_nodes × 730 per cache
- **WAF**: $5 per enabled WAF option
- **Secrets**: $0.40 per secret
- **NoSQL/Queues/Topics**: $0 (usage-based, not estimable from config)

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Fallback Pricing

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Infracost Analysis (Post-Plan)
records.text: After a runner runs `tofu plan`, it optionally runs [Infracost](https://www.infracost.io/) for a precise cost breakdown based on the actual planned resources.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: tofu plan completes
records.text: The runner generates a plan JSON via `tofu show -json plan.tfplan`.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Infracost analyzes the plan
records.text:
If an `INFRACOST_API_KEY` is configured, the runner runs:
infracost breakdown --path plan.json --format json

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Cost data stored
records.text: The Infracost output is parsed and stored in the job's `execution_metadata.cost_breakdown` field.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: UI displays breakdown
records.text: The Plan tab in the Project detail page shows per-resource costs and a total monthly estimate.

records.title: Cost Estimation
records.heading: Why Both?
records.text:
Cost Sidebar Infracost 
 --- --- --- 
 **When** During form editing After plan generation 
 **Speed** Instant Requires plan job 
 **Accuracy** Approximate (simple formulas) Precise (analyzes actual planned resources) 
 **Scope** Major cost drivers only Every resource in the plan 
 **Use case** Quick feedback while configuring Final review before apply 

The sidebar gives instant feedback to guide decisions. Infracost gives the precise number for sign-off before deploying.

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.text: Domain Model & Terminology. The entity graph — organization, project, environment, component — and the lifecycle states each moves through.

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Domain Model & Terminology
records.text:
Every object in Alethia maps to one row in one Postgres table under `apps/console/lib/db/schema/`.
This page describes that graph and the state machines its rows move through. For the canonical name
of each concept — and the words the product deliberately avoids — start with the
[Glossary](/reference/glossary); this page assumes those terms.

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: The core shape
records.text:
The tenancy and configuration graph is four levels deep:

 (RLS boundary, org_id)"] --> 1:N Proj["project (projects)"]
 Proj --> N:1 CI["cloud identity (cloud_identities)"]
 Proj --> 1:N Env["environment (project_environments)"]
 Env --> Comp["components (project_* tables)"]
 Env --> Jobs["jobs (provisioning work)"]
 Jobs --> Logs["job_logs"]
`} />

- An **organization** (`org_id`) is the tenancy boundary. Coarse Postgres RLS keyed on `org_id`
 filters every org-scoped table (see [Security](/concepts/security#row-level-security-rls)).
- A **project** (`projects`) is a declarative infrastructure *app*. It links to **exactly one**
 [cloud identity](/reference/glossary#connectivity) (`projects.cloud_identity_id`) and carries the
 `region` and `iac_version`. It owns **N** environments.
- An **environment** (`project_environments`) is an independently-provisionable deployment target.
 This is the level most other tools collapse to 1:1 — here it is **1:N**: `staging` and `production`
 are two rows of the same project, each with its own state file, its own components, and its own
 provisioning `status`.
- **Components** are the cloud resources an environment declares (`project_cluster`,

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Environments
records.text:
`project_environments` is the pivot of the whole model. Each row has:

 Column Type Meaning 
 --- --- --- 
 `name` `text` Slug feeding the OpenTofu state key (`{project}-{name}-{region}/tofu.tfstate`) and the URL. Unique per project. 
 `stage` `environment_stage` `development` \ `staging` \ `production`. Drives provider template defaults (instance sizing, HA knobs). Distinct from `name`. 
 `status` `project_status` The per-environment provisioning lifecycle (see below). 
 `is_default` `boolean` Exactly one row per project is the representative for single-value surfaces — the CLI wire, the project list's "Env"/status column, the project-detail header. Enforced by a partial unique index. 
 `lifecycle` `environment_lifecycle` `persistent` (long-lived dev/staging/prod) or `ephemeral` (disposable, TTL'd). 
 `region` `text` `NULL` inherits `projects.region`.

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: The ephemeral seam (inert today)
records.text:
`lifecycle`, `expires_at`, `cost_cap`, and the reaper bookkeeping columns (`reap_attempts`,
`last_reap_at`, `reap_gave_up_at`) exist so a future reaper — a `drift`-style reconciler — and the UI
can build disposable "sandbox" environments on top. **Nothing reads them yet**: every environment is
effectively `persistent`. The column is a forward seam, not a live feature.

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Components attach to (project, environment)
records.text:
Two shapes, distinguished only by their unique constraint (`apps/console/lib/db/schema/project-components.ts`):

**Singletons** — `UNIQUE (project_id, environment_id)`, so zero-or-one per environment:

 
 VPC / VNet / VPC Network 
 EKS / GKE / AKS / ACK / Talos 
 Route 53 / Cloud DNS / Azure DNS 
 Log/metric delivery config 
 GitOps repo references 
 Bring-your-own IaC module (E3) 
 

**Multi-instance** — `UNIQUE (project_id, environment_id, name)`, so zero-or-many per environment,
each addressed by `name`:

 
 Aurora / Cloud SQL / Azure DB / RDS 
 ElastiCache / Memorystore / Azure Cache (redis \ valkey) 
 SQS / Pub/Sub / Service Bus 
 SNS / Pub/Sub / Service Bus Topics 
 DynamoDB / Firestore / Cosmos DB 
 ECR / Artifact Registry / ACR 
 Secrets Manager / Secret Manager / Key Vault 
 S3 / Cloud Storage / Storage Account 
 Marketplace add-ons via ArgoCD (keyed by `addon_id`)

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Environment lifecycle
records.text:
The per-environment `status` (`project_status` enum) is the state machine a provision walks. It is a
property of the **environment**, not the project — provisioning `production` never moves `staging`.

 DRAFT
 DRAFT --> QUEUED: submit plan/deploy
 QUEUED --> PROVISIONING: runner claims the job
 PROVISIONING --> ACTIVE: tofu apply succeeds
 PROVISIONING --> FAILED: apply fails
 FAILED --> QUEUED: retry
 ACTIVE --> QUEUED: re-deploy a change
 ACTIVE --> DESTROYING: destroy
 DESTROYING --> DESTROYED
 DESTROYING --> FAILED
 DESTROYED --> [*]
`} />

 Status Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `DRAFT` Configuration written but never submitted for provisioning 
 `QUEUED` A provisioning job is waiting for a runner to claim it 
 `PROVISIONING` A runner is actively executing `tofu` for this environment 
 `ACTIVE` Infrastructure is provisioned and live 
 `FAILED` A plan/apply/destroy failed (retryable — re-enters `QUEUED`) 
 `DESTROYING` A `DESTROY` job is tearing the environment down 
 `DESTROYED` Infrastructure has been torn down

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Component status
records.text:
Each component carries its own `component_status`, independent of its environment's status — a
cluster can be `ACTIVE` while a newly-added database is still `CREATING`.

 Status Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `PENDING` Declared, awaiting first provisioning 
 `CREATING` Being created by `tofu apply` 
 `ACTIVE` Successfully provisioned 
 `UPDATING` A configuration change is being applied 
 `FAILED` Creation or update failed 
 `DESTROYING` Being torn down 
 `DESTROYED` Successfully removed

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Jobs
records.text:
A **job** (`jobs`) is one unit of runner work. It references a `(project_id, environment_id,
cloud_identity_id)` and, once claimed, a `runner_id`. Its `provision_job_status` walks:

 QUEUED
 QUEUED --> CLAIMED: claim_next_job / SKIP LOCKED
 CLAIMED --> PROCESSING: runner starts execution
 PROCESSING --> SUCCESS: reported ok
 PROCESSING --> FAILED: error / stale-job sweep
 QUEUED --> CANCELLED: user cancels
 CLAIMED --> CANCELLED
 SUCCESS --> [*]
 FAILED --> [*]
 CANCELLED --> [*]
`} />

See [Job queue](/concepts/job-queue) for the atomic-claim mechanics and
[Warm-pool scaling](/concepts/runner/scaling) for how capacity appears.

records.title: Domain Model & Terminology
records.heading: Job types
records.text:
The `provision_job_type` enum (`apps/console/lib/db/schema/enums.ts`) is the full catalog of work a
runner can claim — not just plan/apply/destroy. Each type is described once, in
[Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types).

Promotions (`staging → production`) do **not** add a job type — a promotion reuses `PLAN` then
`DEPLOY` under a `promotions` row.

records.title: Drift detection
records.text: Drift detection. How Alethia runs scheduled refresh-only OpenTofu plans to detect when live cloud infrastructure diverges from its provisioned state, records a per-environment drift posture, and what that posture means on the Evidence page.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Drift detection
records.text:
Provisioning proves an environment matches its configuration at one moment — the moment of apply. Drift
detection is the other half: it **keeps proving it**. On a recurring schedule, Alethia reconciles each
environment's recorded OpenTofu state against the live cloud and records whether anything has diverged.

The unit of this feature is a dedicated job type, `DETECT_DRIFT`, whose result is a compact
per-environment **drift posture** — in-sync or not, how many managed resources drifted, and which ones.

 
 Drift detection is a **read-only** operation. It runs `tofu plan -refresh-only` and never applies —
 it mutates nothing in the cloud (`RunDriftDetection` in `packages/core/provisioner/drift.go`).

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: What "drift" means here
records.text:
Drift is the difference between the resources OpenTofu recorded in state and how those resources actually
look in the cloud now. A refresh-only plan asks each provider what the live resource looks like and
compares it to state. The `drift` package (`packages/core/drift`) classifies each diverged managed
resource into one of three kinds:

 Kind Meaning 
 ------ --------- 
 `modified` The resource still exists, but its live configuration diverged from state (an out-of-band update). 
 `deleted` The resource was deleted out-of-band — it is gone from the cloud but still in state. 
 `other` Any other drift action shape.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Honest coverage
records.text:
A refresh-only plan only sees resources that are **in state** — the ones OpenTofu manages. It **cannot**
see *unmanaged* resources that exist in the cloud but were never recorded in state. Detecting those needs
a separate cloud inventory source (for example AWS Config or Cloud Asset Inventory).

The posture is honest about this gap. Its `unmanaged` count stays at `0` and its `unmanaged_known` flag
stays `false`, so a consumer never mistakes "we did not check for unmanaged resources" for "there are
none" (`Posture` in `packages/core/drift/drift.go`).

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: The drift posture
records.text:
`drift.Analyze` turns the `resource_drift` section of a refresh-only plan JSON into a `Posture`. It is
pure and deterministic — a nil plan, or a plan with no drift section, yields an in-sync posture. Data
sources and no-op changes are ignored, because they do not represent managed-infrastructure drift.

The posture the runner produces carries:

- `in_sync` — `true` when no managed resource has drifted.
- `drifted` — the count of diverged managed resources.
- `details` — one entry per drifted resource: its OpenTofu `address`, its `type`, and its `kind`.
- `unmanaged` / `unmanaged_known` — the honest-coverage fields described above.
- `scanned_at` — an RFC3339 timestamp for when the refresh-only plan was taken.
