records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: The lifecycle of a drift check
records.text:
Drift detection runs end to end without a user in the loop. The stages below trace one `DETECT_DRIFT`
job from schedule to stored posture.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: 1. Scheduling — which environments are due
records.text:
A reconcile loop tick calls the drift scheduler (`sweepDriftSchedule` in `apps/console/lib/drift/dispatch.ts`).
It selects environments whose last drift check is older than their tier's cadence. The cadence is tiered
by environment criticality so provider-API cost stays bounded, with production rechecked most often
(`DRIFT_CADENCE_MS` in `apps/console/lib/drift/schedule.ts`):

 Tier Cadence 
 ------ --------- 
 `prod` 6 hours 
 `staging` 1 day 
 `dev` 7 days 

An environment's stage maps onto a tier via `tierForStage`, and an environment that has never been
checked is always due. The selection itself is the unit-tested, deterministic `selectDueForDrift`.

The sweep runs **in-process**, driven by the reconcile loop (`lib/reconcile/loop.ts`).
`/api/internal/drift/sweep` exposes the same sweep to an external scheduler; nothing calls it today.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: 2. Enqueue — one job per due environment
records.text:
For each due environment, the scheduler enqueues a `DETECT_DRIFT` job. The job's config snapshot is
**copied from the environment's latest successful `DEPLOY` job**, so the refresh-only plan reads the exact
provisioned configuration and state.

Two guards keep duplicates from piling up:

- **Anti-stampede.** An environment that already has a `DETECT_DRIFT` job in flight
 (`QUEUED`, `CLAIMED`, or `PROCESSING`) is excluded from the candidate set.
- **Cross-replica dedup.** The insert is guarded by a partial unique index that permits at most one
 in-flight `DETECT_DRIFT` per environment, so a racing replica's concurrent insert is dropped rather
 than duplicated.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: 3. Execution — the runner's refresh-only plan
records.text:
A runner claims the job and executes it (`executeDriftDetection` in `apps/runner/internal/agent/drift.go`).
It reconstructs the project config from the snapshot, then runs `RunDriftDetection`, which:

1. Prepares the workspace — copies the provider template (or, for bring-your-own IaC, clones the
 customer's module at its pinned commit).
2. Reads the environment's state through the Console's per-job state proxy — the same backend the deploy
 writes, so drift reads exactly the state the deploy produced. See
 [OpenTofu State Management](/concepts/terraform-state).
3. Runs `tofu plan -refresh-only`, renders the plan to JSON, and calls `drift.Analyze` to build the
 posture.

The runner posts the posture back on the job's `execution_metadata.drift_posture`.

 
 A bring-your-own IaC drift run executes **untrusted customer OpenTofu** — a refresh-only plan still
 runs provider plugins. On a managed runner this is fail-closed: `byoManagedGate` refuses the job unless
 the egress-enforced container sandbox is active, and the customer module runs inside that sandbox. See
 [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac) and
 [Security → Execution isolation](/concepts/security#execution-isola

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: 4. Recording — the per-environment posture
records.text:
When the job reaches `SUCCESS`, the Console's job-status route reads `drift_posture` from the job metadata
and upserts it into the `environment_drift` table (`recordDriftPosture` in
`apps/console/app/server/actions/drift.ts`). There is one row per `(project, environment)`, upserted each
run — latest wins.

The `environment_drift` schema (`apps/console/lib/db/schema/drift.ts`) stores:

 Column Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 `in_sync` `true` when no managed resource has drifted. 
 `drifted` Count of diverged resources. 
 `details` Per-resource drift list (OpenTofu address, type, kind). 
 `scanned_at` When the refresh-only plan was taken (runner-supplied). 

If the environment drifted, the status route may also consider auto-healing it. Auto-heal is opt-in, and
production stays approval-gated.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Running a check on demand
records.text:
Besides the schedule, you can queue a `DETECT_DRIFT` job for one environment from the canvas **Run**
menu with **Detect drift**. It runs the same refresh-only plan and records the posture the same way.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: What the Evidence page shows
records.text:
The Evidence page and the drawer's **Drift** tab render the stored posture as one mark per environment:

 Mark Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **In sync** The last refresh-only plan found no managed resource had drifted. 
 **N drifted** That many managed resources diverged from the provisioned state. 
 **Not scanned** No drift check has run for this environment yet — an honest unknown, never a green pass.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Reading the posture
records.text:
The stored posture is the single source consumers read. The latest posture for a project (optionally
scoped to one environment) is available through `getLatestDriftPosture`, which is authorization-gated and
returns `null` when no `DETECT_DRIFT` job has run yet. This is the read behind the assistant's
[`get_drift_posture`](/concepts/elench/agent-runtime) tool, which external agents can also call over
MCP; the CLI's drift endpoint and other server-side reads query the same
`environment_drift` table directly through their own authorization-scoped queries rather than calling
that function.

 
 `environment_drift` is a project-child table without its own row-level security policy, so the org
 boundary is enforced in the query: it joins to the parent project and filters on the caller's org. A
 foreign project UUID returns no row.

records.title: Drift detection
records.heading: Where it fits
records.text:
Drift detection is the continuous companion to the apply-time [Elench](/concepts/elench) verification
gate: verification checks the **plan** before apply; drift checks the **live cloud** after. Both feed the same evidence
timeline. Together they back the claim that Alethia does not just stand
infrastructure up — it keeps proving the infrastructure still matches what was declared.

- The plan itself: [Provisioning Pipeline](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline).
- Where state comes from: [OpenTofu State Management](/concepts/terraform-state).
- How untrusted modules are isolated during a drift run: [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

records.title: Agent harness
records.text: Agent harness. One tool registry exposed read-only to external agents, per-agent identities with isolated memory, a stateless executor, and a supervisor that delegates to a colony.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Agent harness
records.text:
The harness exposes the platform's tools **once** and reuses them everywhere — the in-app agent, and the
customer's own agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) — without ever forking the tool definitions. It then
layers scoped agent identities, isolated memory, and a supervisor on top.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Tool registry — the single source of truth
records.text:
Every agent tool is an AI-SDK `tool()` definition in `apps/console/lib/ai/tools/`, classified by
**audience** in `registry.ts`:

 Audience Who sees it 
 --- --- 
 `in-app` Dashboard agent only — HITL proposals, canvas-context tools, and job-queuing writes. 
 `external` / `both` Read-only, PDP-gated, stateless — safe to expose to a customer's agent. 

`buildExternalAgentTools()` is the **read-only projection** (`externalToolsOnly`, audience
`external both`). An anti-drift test (`assertAudienceCoverage`) fails CI if a new tool ships without an
explicit audience, so the external surface can never silently widen.

 
 Authorization is **not** re-implemented in the registry. Each tool's `execute` still resolves the
 actor and enforces its PDP verb at call time; the audience map only decides *visibility*.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The MCP surface — read-only at launch
records.text:
The remote MCP server (`app/api/mcp/route.ts`, OAuth 2.1 via Better Auth + actor binding) consumes
`buildExternalAgentTools()` — so HITL proposals, canvas tools, and job-queuing writes (`scan_repo`) never
reach an external agent. A single endpoint serves Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex, and Gemini/Zed-via-ACP.

 
 Writes stay **out** of the external surface until an approval-over-MCP design exists: a multi-turn
 HITL approval (propose → human click → resume) does not project onto a single stateless MCP
 `tools/call`. The endpoint is a connector, not the moat — the moat is the governed, provable execution
 behind it.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The proof surface over MCP
records.text:
The evidence half of Elench is readable by an external agent, not just the dashboard:

 Tool Audience Returns 
 --- --- --- 
 `get_plan_result` `both` A job's status + the Elench `verify_verdict` / `verify_result` (the signed gate report). 
 `get_drift_posture` `both` The latest day-2 [drift `Posture`](/concepts/elench/engine-internals) for a project environment. 
 `audit_infrastructure` `in-app` Queues an `AUDIT` job over a bring-your-own plan / manifests (a job-queuing write → stays in-app). 

So a customer's own agent can ask "is this cluster still in sync, and did the last deploy pass the gate?"
over the read-only MCP surface — the "keep proving it" evidence, not just the build.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Agents are DATA, not processes
records.text:
A "colony of per-project agents" is realized as **durable per-tenant data on stateless compute**, not
standing daemons (a long-lived in-context process accrues context rot). An agent is a row
(`agent_identities`, migration `0045`): persona, mission, tool-scope, and a memory namespace. A stateless
executor reconstructs context per turn.

Memory lives in `agent_memory`, keyed by `(namespace, path)`. The namespace is the per-tenant prefix
(`org/{orgId}` for the organization, `org/{orgId}/project/{projectId}` for a project); the path is
validated by the tenant-isolation guard `lib/agent/memory-path.ts`, which **rejects every traversal
escape** (`..`, absolute paths outside the `/memories` mount, backslashes, null bytes) so one tenant can
never read another's memory.

Alongside memory, a scope carries **pinned context** — custom instructions and named knowledge documents
— in `agent_context`, one row per `(org_id, project_id)` (the org row keyed with a null project). Its
`(organization, project)` shape mirrors the memory namespace 1:1. On each turn the executor layers the
org context under the project's and appends live, auto-derived project facts, all into the cached system
prompt — so

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The stateless executor
records.text:
`lib/agent/executor.ts` is the deterministic core of running a turn *as* an agent:

- `buildAgentSystemPrompt(identity, memorySummary?)` composes the persona + mission (+ just-in-time
 memory) into a system prompt.
- `scopeToolsToAgent(tools, tool_scope)` narrows the tool set to the agent's allowlist (least privilege
 per agent — deployer / auditor / cost-optimizer roles).

The agent-scoped chat route (`/api/agent/[agentId]`) loads the identity, applies these, and runs the turn
via the AI SDK — mirroring the main agent route, tools still PDP-gated at execute time.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The supervisor / colony
records.text:
`lib/agent/supervisor.ts` is a deterministic, replayable orchestrator. It delegates tasks to sub-agents
and drives them via a **Magentic-style Task / Progress ledger** (facts + plan + per-task status) with a
**stall counter that triggers a bounded re-plan** (`stall > 2 → re-plan`). The actual sub-agent execution
is **injected** (`SubAgentRunner`) — exactly the "AI executes, deterministic code decides" pattern, so the
control flow is testable without a model and always terminates.

 
 **Use it where it pays.** A standing colony costs roughly 15× the tokens of a single agent and loses on
 work over one convergent state (e.g. IaC plan/apply). The supervisor is for breadth-first **read**
 fan-out (drift / cost / security surveys across accounts) and tenant-isolated tasks; write/converge
 work stays on a single-threaded path.

records.title: Architecture
records.text: Architecture. The full system — repos to a verified GitOps Kubernetes cluster on your cloud. The "A" (infer-and-generate) and "B" (bring-your-own + audit) flows, stage by stage, and where the Elench proof layer sits.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Architecture
records.text:
Alethia is **one product**: connect your repos and get a **verified GitOps Kubernetes cluster on your own
cloud**. Two operators — **managed** (Alethia's runner fleet assumes a role into your account) and
**self** (a runner you run) — and two entry flows that share the same design surface, provisioner, and
proof layer:

- **"A" — infer & generate.** Scan repos → infer the stack → propose a project → provision the cluster +
 backing services + ArgoCD → generate app manifests → GitOps deploy → **verify**.
- **"B" — bring your own + audit.** Point at existing OpenTofu/Terraform or Kubernetes manifests →
 **audit** them with the same engine → get a signed report.

 
 **Core vs Enterprise.** The generate/provision **"A" flow is core** (open-source, self-hostable). The
 **Elench proof layer — verify · audit · drift · agent · MCP — is Enterprise.** This page is the map;
 the proof-layer pages carry the badge.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The "A" pipeline
records.text:
Each stage names its source-of-truth code so the docs stay honest to the implementation.

 connect 1:N] --> scan[scan Go scanner · per-svc]
 scan --> infer[infer + merge lib/scanner → to-project]
 infer --> propose[propose canvas design]
 propose --> provision[provision RunDeployV2 · tofu]
 provision --> generate[generate manifests .FromServices]
 generate --> gitops[GitOps ArgoCD apps · path .]
 gitops --> verify[VERIFY elench gate + receipt]
 verify --> drift[day-2 drift DETECT_DRIFT → Posture loop]
`} />

1. **Connect repos (1:N, monorepo-aware).** `project_source_repos` (migration `0050`) holds every scanned
 repo + its detected services.
2. **Scan.** `packages/core/scanner` clones + statically reads a repo (never executes it) into a
 `RepoDigest`, and detects per-directory **services** (Dockerfile / workspace manifests) — so a monorepo
 yields several deployable services, not one blob.
3. **Infer + merge.** `apps/console/lib/scanner/infer.ts` turns the digest into an `InferredStack` (LLM,
 structured output); `to-project.ts` `mergeScansToFormData` folds **N repos / services** into one
 guaranteed-valid `ProjectFormData` (union backing needs, de-duped names, one `source_repos`

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The "B" pipeline — bring your own + audit
records.text:
The verification engine is **plan-agnostic**, so auditing infrastructure Alethia *didn't* generate needs
no new controls:

 B[AUDIT job]
 B --> C[verify same controls]
 C --> D[signed report]
 D --> E[VerifyBlock]
`} />

- **OpenTofu / Terraform plan:** `verify.ParseCustomerPlan(planJSON)` → `Evaluate` — the same AWS/GCP/Azure controls.
- **Kubernetes:** `verify.EvaluateManifests(yaml)` → the Kubernetes [control set](/reference/control-catalog).
- The `AUDIT` job (migration `0052`) runs on the runner (`executeAudit`) and posts the report to
 `jobs.execution_metadata.verify_result`, surfaced by the existing `get_plan_result` tool + the
 `VerifyBlock`. Queue it from the assistant (`audit_infrastructure` tool) or `queueAudit`.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The data model
records.text:
Table / field What it holds 
 --- --- 
 `project_source_repos` (0050) Scanned source repos (1:N) + detected services (JSONB). 
 `environment_drift` (0051) Latest day-2 `Posture` per environment. 
 `jobs.job_type` `ANALYZE_REPO` · `PLAN` · `DEPLOY` · `DESTROY` · `DETECT_DRIFT` · `AUDIT` · `*_RUNNER`. 
 `jobs.execution_metadata` `repo_digest` · `verify_result` (the signed report) · `drift_posture`.

records.title: Verification engine
records.text: Verification engine. How the deterministic policy gate works — the Evaluate seam, statuses, fail-closed gating, overrides, Access Analyzer corroboration, signed receipts, and drift.

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: Verification engine
records.text:
The engine (`packages/core/verify`) is a deterministic policy gate over the OpenTofu **plan JSON**. It
runs **between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`** inside `provisioner.RunDeployV2`, and it is **fail-closed**:
a hard control failure blocks the apply before any infrastructure changes.

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: The Evaluate seam
records.text:
The whole engine sits behind one entrypoint:

func Evaluate(ctx context.Context, plan *tfjson.Plan) (*Report, error)

It is deterministic and side-effect free — the same plan always yields the same verdict, which is what
the evidence receipt relies on. The seam is **engine-agnostic**: Phase 0 ships a pure-Go evaluator
(builds and tests offline, no external policy runtime); an OPA/Rego backend for customer-authorable
control bundles can be swapped in behind the identical `Report` contract without touching any caller.

`EvaluateWithOptions(ctx, plan, opts)` is the same path with optional AWS Access Analyzer corroboration
(below).

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: Three ways in — same Report
records.text:
The engine is plan-agnostic, so the same `Report` (and receipt) shape serves three inputs:

 Entrypoint Input Use 
 --- --- --- 
 `Evaluate(plan)` An Alethia-generated OpenTofu plan The apply-time gate. 
 `ParseCustomerPlan(json)` → `Evaluate` A **bring-your-own** `tofu show -json` plan Audit infrastructure Alethia didn't generate — **zero control changes**. 
 `EvaluateManifests(yaml)` Kubernetes manifests (multi-doc) The Kubernetes [control set](/reference/control-catalog); `Provider` = `k8s`. 

The **"B" flow** (bring-your-own + audit) rides the latter two: an `AUDIT` job (migration `0052`) runs on
the runner (`executeAudit`) — parsing the customer's plan or manifests, evaluating them, and posting the
report to `jobs.execution_metadata.verify_result`. It provisions nothing; the console surfaces it through
the same `get_plan_result` tool + `VerifyBlock` a PLAN job's gate uses. Queue it with the
`audit_infrastructure` agent tool or the `queueAudit` action, or run it locally with
[`elench-verify -manifests`](/concepts/elench/extending).

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: Statuses and the verdict
records.text:
Every control reports one of four statuses, and the report's overall verdict follows a strict
precedence:

 Status Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `pass` The control was evaluated and the plan satisfies it. 
 `fail` Evaluated and violated. On a real apply this **blocks** (unless overridden). 
 `warn` A recorded concern that does not block. 
 `not_evaluable` The plan JSON lacked the information to judge it. **Never** treated as a pass. 

> **Verdict precedence:** `fail` › `warn` › `not_evaluable` › `pass`.

The `not_evaluable` rung is the heart of the engine's honesty.

 
 **Never a silent pass.** A policy body that is computed until apply (`after_unknown`), or an
 AWS-managed policy referenced only by ARN (whose body is not in the plan), is reported `not_evaluable`
 with a plain-language coverage note — never a quiet `pass`. A silent pass on an un-inspectable
 resource is exactly the false result the verification claim must never make.

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: Fail-closed, with a real exception path
records.text:
A fail-closed gate with no escape hatch gets disabled within a week. Elench ships the exception path
**with** the gate:

- A `verify.Override` is an **authorized, time-boxed** waiver of *specific* control ids — never a way to
 disable the gate wholesale.
- It is persisted on the deploy job (`jobs.verify_override`, migration `0043`), stamped server-side with
 the authorizing actor and an expiry by the `recordVerifyOverride` action.
- The runner reconstructs it (`buildVerifyOverride`) and passes it to the gate; `Report.Unwaived(ov)`
 returns any failing control the override does **not** cover. A non-empty result keeps the apply blocked.
- The waiver is recorded in the evidence receipt as an exception (who, why, expiry) — the verdict itself
 is **not** rewritten to pass.

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: AWS IAM Access Analyzer corroboration
records.text:
Beyond the pattern checks, the gate can corroborate IAM policies with **AWS IAM Access Analyzer's
automated reasoning** — a *provable* statement about what a policy could grant, run pre-apply without
deploying anything.

- `verify.PolicyChecker` is the seam (the pure `verify` package carries no cloud SDK); the AWS-backed
 implementation lives in `packages/core/accessanalyzer` and calls `CheckAccessNotGranted` per action.
- Control `ACCESS-ANALYZER-001` fails when a planned policy could grant any action in a sensitive-action
 denylist; a checker error is `not_evaluable`, never a pass.
- It is **off by default** (no AWS calls). The runner enables it for AWS jobs when
 `ALETHIA_VERIFY_ACCESS_ANALYZER=1`, building the checker from the assumed-role config.

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: Signed evidence receipt
records.text:
After the gate decides (and any override is applied), the runner seals a **`Receipt`** for the apply and
signs it (ed25519 detached signature → tamper-evident; offline `Verify`).

 
 

 Field Why 
 --- --- 
 `plan_sha256` Binds the receipt to the exact plan evaluated. 
 `tofu_version`, `catalog_version` A verdict is only meaningful against the schema + controls that produced it. 
 `report` The full per-control result, including `not_evaluable` and coverage. 
 `exception` Any recorded override (controls, reason, by, expiry). 
 `runner`, `evaluated_at` Provenance. 

 
 

A receipt signed by Alethia's own runner is **tamper-evidence on self-attestation** — it proves "Alethia's
runner asserted these controls passed on plan `sha256` and the file wasn't edited since", not independent
compliance proof. To make it meaningful to a customer's auditor, anchor the root of trust outside Alethia:
sign with a **customer-controlled key** and/or log the signature to a **transparency log (Rekor)**. The
key is loaded from `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY`; with none configured the receipt is attached
**unsigned** rather than blocking the apply — signing is additive evidence, not a precondition.

records.title: Verification engine
records.heading: Continuous drift — "keep proving it"
records.text:
`packages/core/drift` turns a refresh-only plan into a per-environment **`Posture`** via
`Analyze(plan)` — the after-apply half of the same evidence. The scheduler, the `DETECT_DRIFT` job,
the stored posture and its honest-coverage fields are described once, in
[Drift detection](/concepts/drift).

records.title: Extending & running
records.text: Extending & running. Adding a control, the injection seams that keep AI advisory, the elench-verify CLI for CI, and the gated live exercises.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: Write the control
records.text:
Add a `control…` function in `packages/core/verify` returning a `ControlResult`. Use `resolveStatus` so
the pass / fail / warn / not_evaluable / vacuous-pass precedence stays consistent, and reuse the policy
helpers (`parseIAMPolicy`, `attrUnknown`, `toStringSlice`) — they already handle string-vs-array IAM
fields and unknown values.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: Add a fixture and a test
records.text:
Drop a plan-JSON fixture under `testdata/` and a case in the test suite. **Always include a
`not_evaluable` case** for any control that reads a body that can be computed — that path is the
engine's honesty guarantee.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: Bump the catalog version
records.text:
Change `CatalogVersion` whenever the new (or changed) control could alter a verdict. Old receipts are
only meaningful against the catalog that produced them.
 

 

A **Kubernetes** control is the same shape in `packages/core/verify/k8s.go`: add a `control…` function over
the decoded `k8sResource` list, wire it into `EvaluateManifests`, and add a fixture (an insecure manifest
→ fail, a clean one → pass). Reuse the `podSpec` / `containers` helpers.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: Adding a cloud
records.text:
Extending the provisioner + GitOps seam to a new cloud is a separate, documented checklist — the
`CloudProvider` impl, the OpenTofu template + keyless workload-identity outputs, runner credential
activation, and the per-cloud ArgoCD facts. See **[Multi-cloud](/concepts/elench/multi-cloud)** and
`packages/core/cloud/README.md`.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: The injection seams — "AI proposes, the gate disposes"
records.text:
Elench keeps AI strictly advisory through a set of injected interfaces, so the deterministic engine
always has the final say:

 Seam Role 
 --- --- 
 `PolicyChecker` AWS Access Analyzer corroboration (real implementation in `packages/core/accessanalyzer`). 
 `Remediator` Proposes a fix + re-plans; the loop only accepts a gate-confirmed result. 
 `SubAgentRunner` Runs one delegated colony task; the supervisor decides what to do with the outcome. 
 injected model call The LLM in `explainFindings` / the agent runner — swappable, so logic is tested with a fake. 

The safety spine is `ReVerify(original, candidatePlan)`: it re-runs the gate on a proposed fix and reports
which original failures it **resolved**, which **still fail**, and which it made **newly fail**. A fix is
`Accepted` only when every original failure is resolved with no regression. `RunRemediationLoop` wraps it
in a bounded harness so "AI proposes, the gate disposes" can never loop forever or apply an unverified fix.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: The elench-verify CLI
records.text:
`cmd/elench-verify` runs the gate over any plan JSON outside the runner — for local checks, CI gating, or
producing the go/no-go corpus measurement:

go build -o elench-verify ./packages/core/verify/cmd/elench-verify
tofu show -json tfplan elench-verify # human report; exit 2 if the verdict blocks
elench-verify -json plan.json # machine-readable report on stdout
elench-verify -manifests deploy.yaml # audit Kubernetes manifests instead of a plan

The default mode accepts a **bring-your-own** plan (via `ParseCustomerPlan`), not just an Alethia-generated
one — the same controls run either way. `-manifests` runs the Kubernetes control set. Exit codes: `0`
pass/warn/not_evaluable · `2` blocking (fail) · `1` usage/parse error — so it drops straight into a CI step.

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: Gated live exercises
records.text:
The deterministic logic is unit-tested with injected fakes; the live integrations are proven by **gated**
tests (skipped in normal CI, run explicitly) that exercise the real services end-to-end:

 
 

ELENCH_LIVE=1 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-… \
 pnpm -F console exec vitest run tests/lib/agent/llm-live.test.ts

Drives the supervisor → LLM sub-agent runner → **real Claude model** → parse → completion.

 
 

ELENCH_LIVE_AWS=1 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 \
 go test ./packages/core/accessanalyzer -run TestLive -v

Calls the **real `CheckAccessNotGranted` API**: an admin policy is reported as granting the denied
actions; a scoped policy grants none.

 
 

bash

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: verify a real OpenTofu plan
records.text: tofu show -json plan.out elench-verify # blocks an admin policy (exit 2)

records.title: Extending & running
records.heading: remediation re-verify across two real plans
records.text:
ELENCH_PLAN_BAD=bad.json ELENCH_PLAN_FIXED=fixed.json \
 go test ./packages/core/verify -run TestLiveReVerifyRealPlans -v

`ReVerify(bad, fixed)` over genuine `tofu show -json` output resolves the failing control with no
regression (`accepted=true`).

 
 

 
 These tests stay **gated** so CI remains deterministic and never spends credits or hits a cloud; the
 env flags above run them on demand against real services.

records.title: Elench
records.text: Elench. The verification layer and agent harness — Alethia generates infrastructure and proves it, then keeps proving it.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Elench
records.text:
**Elench** (Greek _elenchus_ — proof by cross-examination) is Alethia's verification layer and agent
harness. The thesis is simple: don't just generate infrastructure — **scrutinise it and produce
evidence**. Every change, human- or agent-initiated, runs through a deterministic gate between
`tofu plan` and `tofu apply`, and leaves a signed evidence receipt; drift re-checks keep proving it
after apply.

 
 **Honest framing.** Elench produces *evidence that named, versioned controls passed on a specific
 plan* — not a claim of "provably compliant" or "guaranteed least-privilege". A verdict is
 reproducible **given the same plan**; compliance is an auditor's judgment, not a property of one
 apply. The docs here are deliberately precise about what the engine can and cannot see.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: The load-bearing principle
records.text:
> The **deterministic engine is the trusted verdict. The LLM only proposes** — and every proposal is
> re-validated by that engine before it is trusted.

This division of labor runs through the whole system. The policy gate over the OpenTofu plan JSON is
pure, reproducible code. An LLM may explain a failing control or suggest a fix, but a suggested fix is
offered only if re-running the gate confirms it resolves the failure with no regression. The model is
never the gate and has no write path.

records.title: Elench
records.heading: Layered architecture
records.text:
native AI SDK MCP
 EXT --> remote MCP MCP
 MCP[Exposure — one adapter: remote MCP server read-only at launch]
 MCP --> CORE
 CORE[Elench core Tool Registry SSOT · agent-as-data runtime · supervisor]
 CORE --> calls ACT[Platform actions PDP-gated]
 CORE --> calls VER[Verification engine plan-JSON gate · override · signed receipt · drift]
 VER --> new verify stage RUN[Go runner · OpenTofu]
`} />

Two halves, joined at the runner:

- **The verification engine** (`packages/core/verify`, `packages/core/drift`,
 `packages/core/accessanalyzer`) — the deterministic gate, the signed receipt, and continuous drift.
 This is the headline.
- **The agent harness** (`apps/console/lib/ai/tools`, `lib/agent/*`, `app/api/mcp`) — one tool registry
 exposed read-only to external agents, scoped per-agent identities with isolated memory, and a
 supervisor that delegates to a colony of sub-agents.

system (the "A" infer-and-generate flow and the "B" bring-your-own + audit flow); the pages below go deep
on each layer.

 in-console **assistant** — its workspaces, knowledge base, dashboards, and artifacts, written for

records.title: Multi-cloud
records.text: Multi-cloud. How AWS, GCP and Azure all deploy apps — the cloud-agnostic GitOps seam, per-cloud workload identity, manifest generation, and the checklist for adding a cloud.

records.title: Multi-cloud
records.heading: Multi-cloud GitOps seam
records.text:
The provisioner was already ~95% cloud-agnostic — the `CloudProvider` interface, `ProviderTfvars`, and
`ConfigureKubeconfig` all work for AWS, GCP and Azure. The **one** thing keeping GCP/Azure from actually
*deploying apps* was the GitOps seam: `argocd.BuildFromOutputs` + the ArgoCD templates were
AWS/IRSA/EKS-hardcoded. That seam is now `Provider`-discriminated, so all three clouds render a working
ArgoCD layer.

records.title: Multi-cloud
records.heading: Cloud-agnostic InfraFacts
records.text:
`packages/core/argocd/infra_facts.go` carries **common facts** (cluster name/endpoint, region, DNS) plus a
**per-cloud workload-identity block**, and `BuildFromOutputs` extracts the right outputs per provider:

 Provider Cluster output Workload identity external-dns SA annotation 
 --- --- --- --- 
 AWS `eks_cluster_name` IRSA role ARN `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn` 
 GCP `gke_cluster_name` Workload Identity SA email (`external_dns_service_account`) `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` 
 Azure `aks_cluster_name` Federated Identity client id (`external_dns_client_id`) `azure.workload.identity/client-id` 

`InfraFacts.DNSProvider()` maps the cloud to the external-dns `provider` value (`aws` / `google` /
`azure`). The ArgoCD templates (`infra/templates/argocd/*.yaml`) switch on `.Provider`; AWS-only apps
(`aws-load-balancer-controller`, `karpenter`, `storage-class-gp3`) are guarded so they **render empty →
are skipped** on other clouds. `render_test.go` pins AWS-unchanged and asserts the GCP/Azure output.

records.title: Multi-cloud
records.heading: Per-cloud workload identity, keyless
records.text:
Each cloud binds the in-cluster `external-dns` service account to a cloud identity with **no static key**:

- **GCP** — `infra/templates/project/gcp/workload-identity.tf`: a Google service account with `roles/dns.admin`,
 bound to `external-dns/external-dns-sa` via GKE Workload Identity; exported as `external_dns_service_account`.
- **Azure** — `azure/workload-identity.tf`: a user-assigned managed identity + a **federated credential** on
 the AKS OIDC issuer (`oidc_issuer_url` output added to the AKS module), `DNS Zone Contributor`; exported as
 `external_dns_client_id`.

Both templates are `tofu validate`-clean.

records.title: Multi-cloud
records.heading: Manifest generation (the "generate" apps path)
records.text:
`packages/core/manifests` renders a hardened Deployment/Service/Ingress per detected service
(`FromServices` → `WriteManifests`): non-root, `drop: [ALL]`, read-only rootfs, resource limits, no
privilege escalation — so the generated manifests **pass the Kubernetes [audit](/reference/control-catalog) by
construction**. At deploy, `RunDeployV2` commits them to the GitOps repo **only when the repo has no
manifests yet** (`hasManifests` guard):

 
 **Never clobbers bring-your-own.** Generation is safe-by-construction: it writes to an *empty* apps repo
 or does nothing, and is **non-fatal** — a git edge case warns, it never fails an otherwise-healthy
 cluster. "Bring your own manifests" simply means ArgoCD points at a repo that already has them.

records.title: Multi-cloud
records.heading: Adding a cloud
records.text:
The deploy flow itself never changes — a new cloud is five edits (mirrors
`packages/core/cloud/README.md`):

records.title: Multi-cloud

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.text: Receipts & signing. What an evidence receipt is, how ed25519 signing makes it tamper-evident and offline-verifiable, waivers, and the root-of-trust model.

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: Receipts & signing
records.text:
An **evidence receipt** is the record Alethia seals on every apply. It is the artifact that turns "the
console says it passed" into something you can verify independently, later, without trusting the console.

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: What a receipt binds
records.text:
Each receipt is bound to the exact change it describes:

- **`plan_sha256`** — the hash of the exact OpenTofu plan that was applied.
- **verdict** — the Elench gate's decision (`pass` / `warn` / `fail` / `not_evaluable`).
- **catalog version** — which control catalog produced the verdict (an old receipt is only meaningful
 against the catalog that generated it).
- the full per-control report, the provider, OpenTofu version, the runner, and the evaluation time.
- any **sealed exception** (see waivers below).

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: Signing — what it buys you
records.text:
When a signing key is configured, the receipt is signed with **ed25519**. A signed receipt is
**tamper-evident** and **verifiable offline**: anyone with the public key can confirm the receipt wasn't
altered after the fact — the signature is over the receipt's canonical JSON, so any change breaks it. Even
with the platform-held key, this upgrades "trust the database row" to "cryptographically bound to this
plan and verdict."

 State Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Signed** An ed25519 signature seals the receipt; it's tamper-evident and offline-verifiable. 
 **Unsigned** A receipt was sealed, but no signing key is configured — still a faithful record, not signed. 
 **—** No apply has sealed a receipt for this environment yet.

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: Enabling signing
records.text:
Signing is off until a key is set. Provide an ed25519 key to the runner (via
`ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY`) and every subsequent receipt is signed. Absent a key, receipts are still
attached — just unsigned — so an apply is never blocked on signing.

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: Checking one yourself
records.text:
alethia verify receipt --job 

Pulls the receipt, checks its signature, and **exits non-zero when it cannot** — so a deployment
pipeline can gate on it. `alethia verify show --job ` prints the per-control report behind
the verdict. See [Verify Commands](/reference/cli/verify).

The signature is checked against a key the control plane **vouches for**, not against the public key
the receipt carries about itself. That distinction is the whole point: a receipt always verifies
under its own embedded key, whoever produced it, so checking only that would prove the document was
not altered — never who signed it. To verify against a key you hold out of band, pass
`--key-file `.

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: Root of trust
records.text:
A receipt signed by Alethia's own runner attests "Alethia asserted this" — `alethia verify receipt`
reports that honestly as trust `platform`, and reports `org` when your own registered key signed it.
For auditor-grade non-repudiation, sign with a **customer-controlled key** and/or anchor the receipt
in a **transparency log** (Rekor) so its existence and integrity are provable by any third party
offline. Both are on the roadmap; the signing seam is already in place.

records.title: Receipts & signing
records.heading: Waivers
records.text:
A fail-closed gate blocks an apply on a hard failure. A **waiver** (override) is the authorized, escape
hatch: a time-boxed pass of **specific** failing control IDs, recorded with who granted it, why, and when
it expires. The waiver is sealed into the receipt as an **exception**, so the record shows the gate was
passed deliberately — not disabled. Active waivers are listed on the Evidence page.

records.title: Security scanning
records.text: Security scanning. How Alethia rolls up in-cluster vulnerability findings from Trivy-Operator, and what "Not scanned" means on the Evidence page.

records.title: Security scanning
records.heading: Security scanning
records.text:
The Evidence page's **Security** column reports the vulnerability posture of the workloads running in an
environment's cluster. The data is real — it comes from [Trivy-Operator](https://aquasecurity.github.io/trivy-operator/),
read live from the cluster — never a synthetic all-clear.

records.title: Security scanning
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
When Alethia inspects a cluster (on the deploy finalizer and on the day-2 drift refresh), it reads the
Trivy-Operator `VulnerabilityReport` custom resources across all namespaces and sums the findings by
severity — **critical / high / medium / low** — along with the number of reports that fed the aggregate.
That rollup is stored per environment and surfaced as the Security posture.

records.title: Security scanning
records.heading: What the Evidence page shows
records.text:
Mark Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **N critical** / **N high** The highest-severity findings across the cluster's Trivy reports. 
 **N low** Only medium/low findings remain. 
 **Clean** Trivy scanned and found no critical/high/medium/low vulnerabilities. 
 **Not scanned** Trivy-Operator isn't installed (or has produced no reports yet) — an honest unknown.

records.title: Security scanning
records.heading: Enabling scans
records.text:
"Not scanned" means the **Trivy-Operator add-on** isn't running in the cluster. Install it from the add-on
marketplace; once it produces `VulnerabilityReport`s, the next cluster inspection picks them up and the
Security posture fills in automatically. Nothing to wire on the Alethia side — if the reports exist,
Alethia reads them.

records.title: Fabrics & Placement
records.text: Fabrics & Placement. How an environment is decoupled from its cluster — placed onto a Fabric as a namespace, a virtual cluster, or a dedicated cluster.

records.title: Fabrics & Placement
records.heading: Fabrics & Placement
records.text:
Most tools tie an environment to a cluster one-to-one: one `staging`, one cluster. Alethia
decouples the two. An **environment** is *where you deliver* (a target for your apps). A **Fabric**
is *the infrastructure that hosts it* (a control plane, a network, shared add-ons, its own OpenTofu
state). A **Placement** connects them — it says *how* an environment sits on a Fabric.

This decoupling lets several environments share one Fabric, so a preview or a `dev` target costs a
namespace instead of a whole cluster. This page explains the model. For the wider entity graph, start
with the [Domain Model](/concepts/domain-model).

records.title: Fabrics & Placement
records.heading: The three parts
records.text:
(project_environments)"] --> placement_mode Place{"Placement"}
 Place --> dedicated FabA["Fabric A (project_fabrics)"]
 Place --> namespace / vcluster FabB["Fabric B (shared)"]
 FabA --> ClusterA["cluster (1:1)"]
 FabB --> ClusterB["cluster (shared)"]
`} />

- An **environment** (`project_environments`) is a delivery target — `production`, `staging`, a
 preview. It owns its delivered apps and its managed data.
- A **Fabric** (`project_fabrics`) is the infrastructure unit: a control plane plus its network,
 cluster-scoped shared add-ons (ingress, `cert-manager`, ArgoCD), and **its own OpenTofu state**. A
 project owns one or more Fabrics. A Fabric can be Alethia-templated or
 [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).
- A **Placement** is how an environment sits on a Fabric. It is the `placement_mode` column on
 `project_environments`, plus the `fabric_id` that names the host Fabric.

records.title: Fabrics & Placement
records.heading: Placement modes
records.text:
An environment is placed in one of three modes. They form an isolation ladder — each tier isolates
more, and costs more.

 Mode What the environment gets Isolation Cost 
 --- --- --- --- 
 `namespace` A Kubernetes namespace on a **shared** Fabric cluster Soft — same nodes and API server as its neighbors, bounded by `ResourceQuota`, `LimitRange`, `NetworkPolicy`, and Pod Security Admission Lowest 
 `vcluster` A **virtual cluster** on a shared Fabric cluster — its own API server, custom resources, and Kubernetes version Medium — an isolated control plane, but workloads still run on shared nodes Medium 
 `dedicated` The environment **owns its Fabric** one-to-one — a whole cluster Hard — a separate cluster Highest 

 
 **Tell the truth about the tier.** A `vcluster` isolates the control plane, not the nodes — its
 pods share the host's nodes, so it is not a hard boundary for untrusted node-level workloads. Use
 `dedicated` when you need a hard boundary. `namespace` is for same-trust targets like `dev` and
 previews.
 

 
 **Maturity.** `dedicated` is generally available — it is the classic environment-owns-a-cluster
 shape and the default for a new project's first environment. `namespa

records.title: Fabrics & Placement
records.heading: Infrastructure and delivery split apart
records.text:
Because a Fabric owns the infrastructure and an environment owns the delivery, the two halves track
separately:

- **Infrastructure is per-Fabric.** Each Fabric has its own OpenTofu state (see
 [OpenTofu State](/concepts/terraform-state)), and infrastructure [drift](/concepts/drift) is
 detected per Fabric with `tofu plan -refresh-only`.
- **Delivery is per-environment.** Each environment's apps sync through
 [ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd) into its own destination — the namespace for a `namespace` or
 `vcluster` placement, the whole cluster for a `dedicated` one. Delivery drift is an ArgoCD concern,
 not an OpenTofu one.
- **Managed data is per-environment.** A database or cache belongs to the environment that declares
 it, even when several environments share a Fabric.

A `dedicated` environment is the simple case of this model: it owns its Fabric, so its infrastructure
and delivery collapse back to one cluster — the same behavior as before Fabrics existed.

The split also decides who can get a kubeconfig. A `dedicated` environment's cluster is its own, so
`alethia cluster kubeconfig` can mint a short-lived kubeconfig for it. A `namespace` or `vcluster`
environment sits on a sh

records.title: Fabrics & Placement
records.heading: How it maps to the schema
records.text:
Key columns on `project_environments`:

 Column Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `fabric_id` The Fabric this environment is placed onto. 
 `placement_mode` `namespace` \ `vcluster` \ `dedicated`. Empty is treated as `dedicated`. 
 `namespace` The Kubernetes namespace for a `namespace` or `vcluster` placement. Ignored for `dedicated`. 

A cluster belongs to its **Fabric**, not to a single environment — a partial unique index
(`project_cluster_fabric_id_key`) keeps at most one cluster per Fabric, shared by every environment
placed on it.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.text: GitOps & ArgoCD. How ArgoCD is installed automatically and configured with the App of Apps pattern.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.text: After a successful `tofu apply`, the runner automatically installs **ArgoCD** on the provisioned Kubernetes cluster. ArgoCD manages all subsequent application deployments via GitOps — Git is the source of truth.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: What Gets Installed
records.text:
Every provisioned cluster comes with ArgoCD and a set of supporting components:

 Component Purpose 
 ----------- --------- 
 **ArgoCD** GitOps continuous delivery engine 
 **AWS Load Balancer Controller** Kubernetes ingress via ALB/NLB (AWS) 
 **External DNS** Automatic DNS record management from Kubernetes resources 
 **External Secrets Operator** Sync secrets from cloud stores to Kubernetes Secrets 
 **Karpenter** Just-in-time node provisioning (AWS) 
 **Metrics Server** Resource metrics for Horizontal Pod Autoscaler 
 **Storage Class** EBS / Persistent Disk / Managed Disk provisioner

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: tofu apply completes
records.text: The runner provisions all infrastructure (VPC, cluster, databases, etc.) via `tofu`. Outputs include cluster name, endpoint, and ARN.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: Exec-plugin kubeconfig (CLI-free)
records.text:
The runner is **CLI-free** — it does not shell out to `aws eks update-kubeconfig`, `gcloud`, or `az`.
It writes an **exec-credential** kubeconfig (`packages/core/cloud.writeExecKubeconfig`) built from the
`tofu` cluster outputs (endpoint + CA), whose exec block invokes the runner itself as the credential
plugin: `runner kube-token --provider ` (`apps/runner/internal/agent/kube_token.go`).
So kubectl/helm mint a fresh short-lived token in-process on demand, exchanging the keyless cloud
credential for cluster access — no cluster CLIs, no long-lived kubeconfig secret.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: ArgoCD installed via Helm
records.text: The Runner runs `helm upgrade --install argocd` with the ArgoCD Helm chart. It waits for all ArgoCD pods to become Ready.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: Admin password stays in the cluster
records.text:
The ArgoCD admin password lives in the `argocd-initial-admin-secret` Kubernetes Secret and is **never extracted or stored by Alethia** — retrieve it on demand:

kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
 -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' base64 -d

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: Infrastructure facts rendered
records.text: `tofu` outputs (cluster name, VPC ID, RDS endpoints, ElastiCache endpoints, etc.) are rendered into a **Helm values file** called "infra facts." This file provides concrete resource identifiers to ArgoCD applications.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: App of Apps configured
records.text: ArgoCD Application manifests are rendered from templates and applied to the cluster.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: Metadata reported
records.text: The ArgoCD URL and cluster metadata are stored in the job's execution metadata and written to the Project's component tables. Credentials (the admin password, kubeconfigs, generated secret values) are scrubbed and never persisted.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: App of Apps Pattern
records.text:
ArgoCD uses the **App of Apps** pattern: a single "parent" Application watches a directory of YAML files, each defining a child Application.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

The parent Application points to this directory. When a new YAML file is added (via Git push), ArgoCD automatically deploys the new application.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: Infrastructure Facts
records.text:
`tofu` outputs are injected into ArgoCD applications as Helm values. This bridges the gap between infrastructure provisioning (OpenTofu) and application deployment (ArgoCD).

Example infra facts:

cluster:
 name: api-backend-production
 endpoint: https://ABC123.gr7.eu-west-1.eks.amazonaws.com
 oidcProviderArn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/...

database:
 endpoint: api-backend-production.cluster-abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com
 port: 5432

cache:
 endpoint: api-backend-production.abc123.euw1.cache.amazonaws.com
 port: 6379

dns:
 domain: api.example.com
 zoneId: Z1234567890

ArgoCD applications reference these values in their Helm charts. For example, an application's database connection string uses `{{ .Values.database.endpoint }}`.

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: ArgoCD Templates
records.text:
Templates are stored in `infra/templates/argocd/` and staged into the Runner Docker image during the release build. Each template is a Kubernetes manifest with Helm-style placeholders:

 Template What It Deploys 
 ---------- ---------------- 
 `aws-load-balancer-controller.yaml` ALB/NLB ingress controller 
 `external-dns.yaml` Route53/Cloud DNS/Azure DNS sync (renders only when DNS is enabled with a domain and the cloud has a supported backend + workload identity) 
 `external-secrets-operator.yaml` Secrets Manager → Kubernetes Secrets 
 `karpenter.yaml` Node auto-provisioning 
 `metrics-server.yaml` CPU/memory metrics for HPA (renders on AWS and Hetzner only — GKE, AKS and ACK ship their own) 
 `storage-class-gp3.yaml` GP3 EBS storage class 
 `project-infra.yaml` ArgoCD AppProject boundary

records.title: GitOps & ArgoCD
records.heading: Post-Installation
records.text:
After ArgoCD is installed:

1. **All infrastructure components are managed by ArgoCD** — changes to Git repos are automatically synced
2. **The ArgoCD URL is displayed** in the Console Clusters page with a clickable link
3. **Applications can be added** by pushing new YAML files to the `manifests/applications/` directory
4. **Drift detection** — ArgoCD continuously compares the live cluster state against Git and alerts on drift

records.title: Platform Overview
records.text: Platform Overview. High-level architecture of the multi-cloud infrastructure orchestration platform.

records.title: Platform Overview
records.heading: Platform Overview
records.text: This platform is a hybrid multi-cloud infrastructure orchestration system. It combines a visual web interface, a command-line tool, and autonomous execution agents to provision production-grade Kubernetes clusters with databases, caches, networking, DNS, secrets, and GitOps — across AWS, GCP, and Azure.

records.title: Platform Overview
records.heading: Three-Component Model
records.text:
Component Type Language Role 
 ----------- ------ ---------- ------ 
 **Console** Web application TypeScript (Next.js) Visual configuration, job management, real-time monitoring 
 **alethia** CLI tool Go Terminal-based operations, scripting, CI/CD integration 
 **Runner** Execution agent Go Runs OpenTofu (`tofu`), installs ArgoCD, streams logs back to Console

records.title: Platform Overview
records.heading: Data Flow
records.text:
Q["Job Queue (Postgres)"]
 CLI["alethia CLI"] --> Q
 Q --> claim Runner["Runner (agent)"]
 Runner --> keyless assume Cloud["Cloud Provider"]
 Runner --> logs Notify["LISTEN/NOTIFY"]
 Notify --> SSE Web
`} />

1. The user configures infrastructure through Console (web form) or the `alethia` CLI
2. Actions are queued as jobs in Postgres
3. A runner claims the job atomically and assumes temporary, keyless cloud credentials
4. The runner executes `tofu` and streams logs back in real time over LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE
5. On completion, ArgoCD is installed for GitOps-managed deployments

records.title: Platform Overview
records.heading: Multi-Cloud Support
records.text:
Every infrastructure component has provider-specific implementations across three clouds:

 Capability AWS GCP Azure 
 ----------- ----- ----- ------- 
 Kubernetes EKS GKE AKS 
 Relational DB Aurora PostgreSQL/MySQL Cloud SQL Azure Database 
 Cache ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey) Memorystore Azure Cache for Redis 
 NoSQL DynamoDB Firestore Cosmos DB 
 Messaging SQS + SNS Pub/Sub Service Bus 
 DNS Route 53 Cloud DNS Azure DNS 
 Secrets Secrets Manager Secret Manager Key Vault 
 Container Registry ECR Artifact Registry ACR 
 Object Storage S3 Cloud Storage Storage Account 
 WAF AWS WAFv2 Cloud Armor Azure WAF
