records.title: Architecture
records.text: Architecture. How isolated execution works — the per-job container, the environment allowlist, PID and network isolation, the state-proxy source-drop, per-job and per-VM tokens, and default-deny domain-allowlist egress.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Architecture
records.text:
Isolated execution is a **seam** in the runner (`packages/core/sandbox`): the runner calls `Sandbox.Run`
instead of invoking the provisioner directly, and a backend decides how much isolation the work gets. Trusted
templates use the in-process `Passthrough` backend; untrusted bring-your-own on the managed fleet uses the
`Container` backend described here.

 
 This page is the customer/operator view. The full engineering reference — types, the re-exec contract, the
 allowlist tables, and the shipped dependency chain — lives in the
 [`packages/core/sandbox` README](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/main/packages/core/sandbox/README.md).

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The per-job container
records.text:
A container can't run a Go closure, so the runner **serializes** the work and **re-execs itself** inside a
fresh per-job container. The child reconstructs the exact work from a serialized stage
(`deploy` / `plan` / `destroy` / `drift` / `chart_scan` / `iac_scan`), runs it, and writes its result back into the per-job working
directory for the parent to read. One job, one container, torn down after — the fleet VM itself is disposable
(one job per VM).

Hardening on the container: dropped Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, its own PID namespace (so it
cannot read the parent runner's `/proc`), only the per-job workdir mounted writable, and pid/memory
limits.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The environment allowlist (and a fail-closed guard)
records.text:
The child gets **only** an allowlisted set of environment variables:

- the cloud-auth vars the credential activators set — file paths and non-secret ids (`AWS_CONFIG_FILE` /
 `AWS_PROFILE`, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `ARM_*` / `AZURE_*`, `ALIBABA_CLOUD_*`),
- the token-cloud tokens the provider needs (e.g. `HCLOUD_TOKEN`),
- the state-proxy auth and the egress-proxy vars,
- a minimal toolchain (`PATH`, locale).

Everything else — the runner token, the storage master key, the receipt-signing key, static cloud keys — is
**dropped**. A **fail-closed guard** runs on the final child environment and refuses to start the container
if any denylisted secret survived, so a mistake that widens the allowlist is caught *before* untrusted code
runs. Credentials that are files are mounted **read-only** at their original paths (as directories, so the
runner's ~5-minute token refresh stays visible to a long `apply`).

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Removing secrets at the source
records.text:
The container can only contain what it isn't handed. Three source-drops keep the allowlist short and the
fleet's boot configuration secret-free:

- **OpenTofu state via a console proxy, not storage keys.** Project templates use an `http` backend pointed
 at the console; auth is a **per-job, key-scoped** token, and the state object key is derived server-side
 from the job. The runner never holds an object-storage credential, and one job's token can only reach its
 own state.
- **Per-job cloud tokens.** Cloud credentials are minted per job and bound to it — a stolen runner token
 can't mint another cloud's credentials.
- **Per-VM bootstrap tokens.** Each fleet VM self-registers with its own short-TTL, instance-bound token
 rather than a shared fleet secret.

Together these mean a managed VM's boot configuration carries no long-lived secret — so the network control
below closes the *last* read rather than being the only line of defense.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Network: default-deny + domain allowlist
records.text:
The untrusted child has **no network route of its own**. On the managed fleet:

- the VM runs an internal-only network (no gateway → no route off the box) plus a **forward proxy** that
 allowlists egress **by domain** (registries, Git hosts, the target cloud's API);
- the runner — and the child, which inherits the runner's network namespace — reach the internet *only*
 through that proxy;
- so the cloud metadata service (`169.254.169.254`) and arbitrary exfiltration endpoints are **unreachable by
 construction**, not merely blocked by a rule.

A `chart_scan` stage needs no network at all and runs fully **deny-all** (`--network none`) with zero secrets.

The backend is **fail-closed on managed**: it refuses to run untrusted work unless egress enforcement is
confirmed on the fleet — it never silently falls back to running unsandboxed.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Where to go next
records.text:
The trust model, the guarantees, and availability.
 
 
 Where the sandbox seam sits in the runner's poll loop and job dispatch.
 
 
 Enabling the container sandbox on the fleet (the 3b turn-on sequence + the real-VM canary).

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.text: Isolated Execution. When Alethia runs your bring-your-own OpenTofu/Terraform or Helm on the managed fleet, each job runs in a per-job sealed sandbox — no shared secrets, no cloud metadata, default-deny domain-allowlisted egress.

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.heading: Isolated Execution
records.text:
Zero-credential connections control **who** can touch a cloud. Isolated execution controls what the
**provisioning code itself** can do once it runs. When Alethia runs *your* code — bring-your-own OpenTofu/Terraform
providers, `external` data sources, Helm charts and their hooks — on the **managed fleet**, that code is
arbitrary. Isolated execution is the boundary that runs it **sealed off** from the platform.

 
 **What this is — and isn't.** This is the isolation boundary that makes *managed bring-your-own execution*
 safe: a per-job sandbox with an allowlisted environment and a locked-down network. It is **not** a
 general-purpose "spin up a sandbox and run anything" service, and there is no customer-invokable sandbox API
 today — a customer-facing sandbox/preview surface is on the roadmap. What ships now is the **guarantee**
 underneath managed BYO: your code can't reach the platform's secrets, the cloud metadata service, or the
 open internet.

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.heading: The trust model
records.text:
Alethia runs two kinds of code, and treats them differently:

- **Trusted templates** — Alethia's own project templates (EKS / GKE / AKS / ACK / Talos + supporting
 services). Reviewed platform code, so it runs in-process on the runner. This is every managed provision
 today.
- **Untrusted bring-your-own** — your OpenTofu/Terraform or Helm. Arbitrary code, so on the managed fleet it runs in a
 **per-job container sandbox**: a fresh container per job, its own PID namespace, an allowlisted environment
 (no runner token, no storage key, no signing key — only the short-lived, job-scoped cloud credentials the
 job actually needs), read-only credential mounts, and a **default-deny, domain-allowlisted** network.

The container is what actually contains a hostile provider. Scrubbing environment variables at the last
moment does **not** — a child process sharing the worker's PID namespace can just read the parent's
`/proc/1/environ`. Only a real uid / pid / net namespace boundary contains it.

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.heading: The guarantees
records.text:
For an untrusted job on the managed fleet:

 Guarantee How 
 --- --- 
 **No platform secrets** The child gets an allowlist-only environment; a fail-closed guard refuses to start the container if any platform secret (runner token, storage key, signing key) would leak in. 
 **No cross-job state** OpenTofu state goes through a console **state proxy** with a per-job, key-scoped token — one job's token can only touch its own state. The runner holds no object-storage credential. 
 **No cloud metadata** The child has no network route of its own; it reaches only a domain-allowlist forward proxy, so `169.254.169.254` (which serves the VM's boot config) is unreachable by construction. 
 **No open egress** Only the registries, Git hosts, and the target cloud's API are reachable — everything else is default-denied. 
 **No host reach** Its own PID namespace, dropped capabilities, no-new-privileges, resource limits.

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.heading: Why it matters
records.text:
Alethia sits in the gap between IaC orchestrators (which run *your IaC* on shared workers) and BYOC PaaSes
(which run *your apps*). Running **bring-your-own infrastructure code in a per-job sealed sandbox** is the
execution-trust complement to the [zero-credential](/concepts/security) connection model — and the safety
floor under the "proof, not just generation" story ([Elench](/concepts/elench) verifies *what* the change does; this
contains *how* it runs).

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.heading: Availability
records.text:
Isolated execution applies to the **managed fleet**. Bring-your-own Helm/IaC is gated by
`ALETHIA_BYO_HELM_ENABLED` and, until the container backend is enabled and verified on the fleet, stays
trusted-templates-only. Operators turn it on per the
[managed provisioning runbook](/guides/self-hosting/managed-provisioning#untrusted-byo-container-sandbox-3b).

records.title: Isolated Execution
records.heading: Where to go next
records.text:
The mechanism: the per-job container, the environment allowlist + fail-closed guard, PID/network
 isolation, read-only credential mounts, the state-proxy source-drop, per-job / per-VM tokens, and the
 default-deny domain-allowlist egress.
 
 
 Where isolated execution sits in the overall zero-credential / OIDC security model.
 
 
 The operator guide to the managed fleet + the 3b turn-on sequence for the container sandbox.

records.title: Job queue
records.text: Job queue. How infrastructure operations are queued, claimed atomically, and executed by Runners.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Job queue
records.text:
Every provisioning operation in the platform — planning, deploying, destroying, drift detection,
bring-your-own scans — is modeled as a **job** in a PostgreSQL queue. Runners poll for jobs, claim
them atomically, execute them, and report results. (Cloud-account connection is *not* a job; it runs
server-side in the Console — see [Connectors](/concepts/connectors).)

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Why a Job Queue?
records.text:
Infrastructure provisioning is slow (minutes to hours) and must be reliable. A job queue provides:

- **Decoupling** — the web UI and CLI queue work without waiting for completion
- **Exactly-once execution** — atomic claiming prevents two Runners from running the same job
- **Resumability** — if a runner dies, the job can be retried from persisted OpenTofu state
- **Auditability** — every operation is logged with timestamps, status, and metadata

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Job types
records.text:
Plan, deploy and destroy are the common jobs, but the `provision_job_type` enum also covers runner
lifecycle, scans, drift, probes, builds and break-glass state repair. The full catalog is
[Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types).

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Job Lifecycle
records.text:
QUEUED
 QUEUED --> CLAIMED: claim_next_job()
 CLAIMED --> PROCESSING: execution starts
 PROCESSING --> SUCCESS
 PROCESSING --> FAILED
 QUEUED --> CANCELLED: user cancels
 CLAIMED --> CANCELLED
 SUCCESS --> [*]
 FAILED --> [*]
 CANCELLED --> [*]
`} />

 Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 `QUEUED` Waiting for a Runner to pick it up 
 `CLAIMED` A Runner has locked it (prevents double-execution) 
 `PROCESSING` Runner is actively running `tofu` 
 `SUCCESS` Completed successfully 
 `FAILED` Failed with error message 
 `CANCELLED` User cancelled before completion

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Atomic Job Claiming

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Config Snapshot
records.text:
When a job is created, the current Project configuration is serialized as a **config_snapshot** in the job record. This ensures the Runner executes exactly the configuration that was planned, even if the user modifies the Project after queuing.

When a signing key is configured, the config_snapshot is also signed (HMAC-SHA256, stored as `config_snapshot_sig`) and the signature is re-verified when a Runner claims the job — if the snapshot was altered after it was enqueued, the job is failed as tampered rather than executed. A DEPLOY reuses its `PLAN` job's saved plan by reference via `plan_job_id`.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Job Created
records.text:
User plans / applies / destroys an environment in the Console (or runs `alethia project plan` /
`alethia project apply` / `alethia project destroy` in the CLI). A `jobs` row is inserted with status `QUEUED`.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Runner Claims Job
records.text: The runner's wake stream (SSE) signals that a job is claimable — or, while that stream is down, a 30-second fallback poll fires — and the runner calls `POST /api/jobs/claim`. The server executes `claim_next_job()`. If a job is returned, the runner proceeds.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Credential Assumption
records.text: The runner reads the `cloud_identity` from the job and assumes temporary, **keyless** credentials — `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` (AWS), Workload Identity Federation token exchange (GCP), or federated identity (Azure) — using a minted OIDC assertion, no static key. See [Security](/concepts/security).

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Execution
records.text: The runner runs the job-type-specific logic (`tofu` plan/apply/destroy, ArgoCD install, etc.) while streaming logs.

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Result Reporting
records.text: On completion, the runner calls `PUT /api/jobs/{id}/status` with SUCCESS or FAILED, plus execution metadata (`tofu` outputs, cost data, cluster info, and the verify report).

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Finalization
records.text: For DEPLOY jobs, the Console calls `finalizeDeployment()` to extract cluster metadata from `tofu` outputs and update the environment's component tables (cluster endpoint, ArgoCD URL, database endpoints, etc.).

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Failure Recovery
records.text:
When a Runner dies mid-job:

1. Heartbeat stops → Console marks the Runner OFFLINE once its last heartbeat is older than 45 seconds (the SSE wake connection refreshes it every ~10 seconds, so a 45-second gap means the runner is genuinely gone)
2. Job stays in `CLAIMED`/`PROCESSING` with no new log updates
3. A background sweep (`recover_stale_jobs`) **requeues** the job automatically once it is stale — a dead runner (claimed over 15 minutes ago with no heartbeat in the last 5 minutes) or a live-but-stalled runner (no forward progress for 30 minutes)
4. Each recovery increments `attempts`; below `max_attempts` (5) the job is requeued (back to `QUEUED`, runner cleared) so another Runner picks it up — at the cap it is failed **terminally** to protect the queue
5. OpenTofu state is preserved in S3-compatible storage, so the requeued run continues from the last successful state

records.title: Job queue
records.heading: Status in the UI
records.text: The job detail page streams a job's **logs** live over [Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE](/concepts/realtime). Job **status** is not pushed: the jobs list and the job detail page poll, fast while a job is in flight — see [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime#poll-everything-else).

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.text: Multi-Cloud Conversion. How Project configurations are converted across AWS, GCP, and Azure when duplicating.

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.text:
Users can duplicate an existing Project and target a different cloud provider. The platform converts the configuration automatically, mapping resources, instance types, and capacity units across providers.

 

 
 A converted project doesn't just *provision* on the new cloud — it **deploys apps** there too. The
 ArgoCD/GitOps layer is cloud-agnostic (per-cloud workload identity), so GCP and Azure get a working
 external-dns + app-sync just like AWS. See [Multi-cloud GitOps seam](/concepts/elench/multi-cloud).

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: When Conversion Happens
records.text:
1. User clicks **"Duplicate & Edit"** on an existing Project
2. Selects a different cloud identity (e.g., switching from AWS to GCP)
3. The `convertProjectConfig()` function transforms the configuration
4. Conversion **warnings** are displayed for items that need manual review
5. User adjusts the converted config and submits

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Region
records.text:
Regions are mapped via a cross-provider table:

AWS us-east-1 → GCP us-east4 → Azure eastus

If no mapping exists, the target provider's default region is used, and a warning is shown.

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Cluster
records.text:
- **Instance types**: Mapped via `INSTANCE_TYPE_MAP` (e.g., `t3.medium` → `e2-standard-2` → `Standard_B2s`). Unmapped types generate a warning. A mapping never targets a machine type too small to run the cluster add-ons, so a conversion to GCP can land on a larger node than the capability match alone would pick.
- **Kubernetes version**: Reset to the target provider's default (versions differ across providers)
- **Autoscaler**: Key name converted in `provider_config` (`enable_karpenter` → `enable_autopilot` → `enable_cluster_autoscaler`)

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Databases
records.text:
- **Engine**: Mapped (e.g., `aurora-postgresql` → `cloudsql-postgresql` → `azure-postgresql`)
- **Capacity**: Clamped to target provider's min/max range. Units change (ACU → vCPU → vCores), and a warning explains the difference.

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Caches
records.text: - **Node type**: Mapped (e.g., `cache.t3.medium` → `M2` → `C2`). Unmapped types fall back to the target provider's default.

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Network
records.text:
- If the source Project uses an **existing network** (`provision_network = false`), the conversion switches to **create new** (`provision_network = true`) with a warning: "Existing network cannot be reused across providers."
- CIDR blocks are preserved (they're provider-agnostic).

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: DNS & WAF
records.text:
- **Zone ID and domain**: Cleared (DNS zones are provider-specific)
- **WAF config**: Cleared with a warning (WAF rules differ significantly across providers)
- User must re-select a DNS zone and re-configure WAF in the target provider.

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: NoSQL
records.text:
- **DynamoDB → Firestore**: Warning about data model differences ("Firestore is document-based, not key-value")
- **Range key support**: Checked per provider. If the target doesn't support range keys natively, a warning is shown.

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Messaging
records.text: - **FIFO queues**: Warning when targeting GCP Pub/Sub ("No direct FIFO support; consider ordering keys")

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: Conversion Warnings

records.title: Multi-Cloud Conversion
records.heading: What Cannot Be Converted
records.text:
Some configurations are fundamentally provider-specific:

- **IAM roles / service accounts** — identity models differ
- **Cluster admin ARNs** — IAM identifiers are provider-specific
- **Existing network references** — VPC IDs don't translate across providers
- **DNS hosted zones** — zone IDs are provider-specific
- **WAF rules** — rule schemas differ significantly

These are cleared during conversion and must be re-configured manually.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.text: Environment Promotion. How Alethia carries a source environment's structural design onto a higher-stage environment through a gated, two-phase plan-then-deploy state machine.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Environment Promotion
records.text:
Each environment in a project owns a full design — the same shape the canvas reads and writes. **Promotion** is how a change proven in one environment moves up to another: it carries the *source* environment's structural design onto a *target* environment, runs a plan, evaluates the target's protection gates, and then deploys (or waits for a human).

Promotion is a first-class subsystem with its own table, status enum, gate engine, and approval flow. It does not add a new job type — it reuses the existing `PLAN` then `DEPLOY` jobs.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Structural vs. environment-tunable
records.text:
A promotion changes *what a resource is*, not *how much of it there is* or *where it lives*.

- **Structural** — engine, version, topology, presence, and similar identity fields. These are what promotion carries. The exact structural field set per component lives in `lib/promotions/diff.ts` (for example a database promotes `engine`, `engine_version`, `port`, and `iam_auth`).
- **Environment-tunable** — sizing, capacity, node counts, retention, and env-specific domains or repos. A field that is not in a component's structural list is never overwritten by a promotion.

This is why promoting an "add redis" change from development up to production keeps production's own cluster size and retention: the merge (`mergeChangeset`) applies only structural fields onto the target and preserves everything else.

 
 The **diff** and **merge** engines are pure and deterministic — no database, no I/O. The diff produces a machine-readable `changes` list plus a human `summary`, and is also available as a side-effect-free `previewPromotion` for the promote dialog.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Stage order
records.text:
A promotion may only move to an **equal or higher** stage. The stage rank is:

 Stage Rank 
 ------- ------ 
 `development` 0 
 `staging` 1 
 `production` 2 

Promoting a target whose stage rank is lower than the source's is rejected before any work is done.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: The two phases
records.text: Promotion is a two-phase flow: **write the candidate and plan it**, then **evaluate gates and deploy**.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Compute the diff and candidate
records.text: `promoteEnvironment` authorizes the caller for `deploy` on the project, confirms both environments belong to it, checks the stage order, and confirms the target is not currently `QUEUED`, `PROVISIONING`, `DESTROYING`, or `DESTROYED`. It then diffs the two designs. An empty diff (nothing structural to carry) is rejected.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Record the promotion
records.text: A row is inserted with status `PENDING_PLAN`, the computed `diff_summary`, and a `candidate_hash` — a structural fingerprint of the source design. A partial unique index rejects a second in-flight promotion into the same target here, before the target design is touched.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Write the candidate and queue the plan
records.text: The merged candidate design is written into the target environment, and a `PLAN` job is queued for it. The `plan_job_id` is recorded on the promotion. `promoteEnvironment` returns the promotion id and the plan job id.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Evaluate gates on plan success
records.text: When the `PLAN` job succeeds, `advancePromotionOnPlan` assembles the gate context (predecessor state, verify outcome, cost delta, approvals) and evaluates every gate. The result decides what happens next — deploy, wait for approval, or block.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
If every gate passes, the target environment is moved to a deployable state and a `DEPLOY` job is enqueued, reusing the plan job's frozen config snapshot so the deploy is idempotent. The promotion moves to `DEPLOYING`. When that deploy job succeeds, `finalizePromotionOnDeploy` marks the promotion `SUCCEEDED`.

 

If the `PLAN` or `DEPLOY` job fails, the promotion is marked `FAILED`.

See [Provisioning Pipeline](/concepts/provisioning-pipeline) for how `PLAN` and `DEPLOY` jobs run, and [Cost Estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation) for how the plan's cost is produced.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Status state machine
records.text:
The `promotion_status` enum drives the lifecycle:

 Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 `PENDING_PLAN` Candidate written; the `PLAN` job is queued to produce verify + cost. 
 `PENDING_APPROVAL` Gates need a human — manual approval, or cost over the threshold. 
 `APPROVED` Approvals satisfied; the deploy is about to enqueue. 
 `DEPLOYING` The `DEPLOY` job is queued or running. 
 `SUCCEEDED` The deploy job succeeded. 
 `FAILED` The plan or deploy job failed. 
 `BLOCKED` A hard gate failed (for example the predecessor is unhealthy or verify hard-failed). 
 `CANCELLED` The promotion was rejected or cancelled. 

 PENDING_PLAN
 PENDING_PLAN --> DEPLOYING: all gates pass
 PENDING_PLAN --> PENDING_APPROVAL: a gate needs a human
 PENDING_PLAN --> BLOCKED: a hard gate failed
 PENDING_APPROVAL --> DEPLOYING: approvals satisfied
 PENDING_APPROVAL --> CANCELLED: rejected
 DEPLOYING --> SUCCEEDED: deploy job succeeds
 PENDING_PLAN --> FAILED: plan job fails
 DEPLOYING --> FAILED: deploy job fails
`} />

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Protection gates
records.text:
After the candidate plan completes, the pure gate engine (`lib/promotions/gates.ts`) evaluates five gates against the target environment's protection rules. Each rule is individually toggleable; a rule that is off (or whose threshold is `NULL`) is **skipped**.

 Gate Turned on by Passes when 
 ------ ------------- ------------- 
 **Predecessor healthy** `require_predecessor` The predecessor environment exists, is in sync (no drift), and has already deployed *this* design (its deployed hash matches the candidate hash). 
 **Verify** `require_verify_pass` The plan's Elench verify report has no unwaived hard control failures. A missing report leaves the gate **pending**. 
 **Soak timer** `soak_minutes` At least that many minutes have elapsed since the predecessor's last deploy. Before then the gate is **pending**; if there is no predecessor deploy to soak from, it **fails** (blocks). 
 **Cost delta** `cost_delta_threshold` The candidate plan's monthly cost minus the target's prior cost does not exceed the threshold. If there is no prior cost to compare, the gate is **skipped**. 
 **Manual approval** `require_approval` The recorded approvals reach the required count. Otherwise the gate

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Protection rules
records.text:
Protection rules live one-per-environment in `environment_protection_rules`. Defaults are fully permissive: an environment with no rule row (or with every toggle off) promotes freely. The columns map directly to the gates:

 Column Effect 
 -------- -------- 
 `require_predecessor` Enables the predecessor-healthy gate. 
 `require_verify_pass` Enables the verify gate. 
 `require_approval` Requires manual approval before deploy. 
 `approvers` Who may approve, and how many are required (`user_ids`, `role`, `min_count`). 
 `soak_minutes` Minutes to soak since the predecessor deploy. `NULL` = off. 
 `cost_delta_threshold` Cost delta (USD/mo) above which approval is required. `NULL` = off.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Classification can force gates on
records.text: A classification value assigned to the target environment can force gates on top of the environment's own rules — the label is the policy. An enforcing value can OR the approval or verify gate on, and can raise the required approval count. The effective required approvals is the strictest of the environment's own `min_count` and every enforcing value's minimum, with a floor of 1 when approval is required at all. The gate detail records which value labels drove the requirement.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Approvals
records.text:
When a promotion enters `PENDING_APPROVAL` because of the manual-approval gate, Alethia materializes one approval slot per required decision. The slot count is the effective minimum described above.

- **Approve** — `approvePromotion` claims one slot through a race-safe per-slot check, then re-runs the exact same gate evaluation the plan step runs. Once every gate clears, the deploy is enqueued; if approvals still remain, the promotion re-parks.
- **Reject** — `rejectPromotion` records the decision and moves the promotion to `CANCELLED`.
- **Cancel** — `cancelPromotion` cancels an in-flight promotion. The candidate design already written into the target is left in place.

An approver is eligible when the environment's `approvers` spec lists their user id, or names a role they hold. Organization `owner` and `admin` roles always satisfy a role requirement. When no spec is set, any user authorized to `deploy` may approve.

records.title: Environment Promotion
records.heading: Concurrency
records.text: A partial unique index (`env_promotions_one_active_per_target`) permits **at most one in-flight promotion per target environment** — one whose status is `PENDING_PLAN`, `PENDING_APPROVAL`, `APPROVED`, or `DEPLOYING`. A second `promoteEnvironment` into the same target is rejected at insert time, before the target's design is modified.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.text: Provisioning Pipeline. How project form values flow through config snapshots and provider-specific mappings into OpenTofu variables.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Provisioning Pipeline
records.text:
When a user plans or applies an environment, the platform transforms the project's form configuration into OpenTofu variables through a five-stage pipeline. Each stage has a single responsibility: serialize, freeze, deserialize, map, execute.

 

 
 The Project config can be authored by hand **or inferred from repos** — the "A" flow scans one or more
 repos (monorepo-aware), infers the stack, and produces the same `ProjectFormData` this pipeline
 consumes. See the [Elench Architecture](/concepts/elench/architecture) page for the full repos → verified cluster
 loop.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Stage 1: Form → Database
records.text:
The project form in Console (or `alethia project plan` in the CLI) calls `createProject()`, which inserts the configuration into normalized component tables:

 Table Data 
 ------- ------ 
 `projects` Project name, region, environment, cloud_identity_id, iac_version 
 `project_network` CIDR block, provision_network flag, existing network_id 
 `project_cluster` Kubernetes version, instance types, node min/max/desired, cluster_admins, provider_config 
 `project_dns` Enabled flag, zone_id, domain_name, WAF settings (in provider_config) 
 `project_repositories` Apps destination (GitOps) repo URL 
 `project_source_repos` Scanned source repos (1:N) + detected services — used to generate app manifests 
 `project_databases` Engine, instance class, scaling config (per database) 
 `project_caches` Node type, cluster size (per cache) 
 `project_queues` Queue name, config (per queue) 
 `project_topics` Topic name, subscriptions (per topic) 
 `project_nosql_tables` Table/collection config with provider_config 
 `project_secrets` Secret name and metadata 

Each table stores the shared schema. Provider-specific options live in `provider_config` JSONB columns — see [Cloud Provider Abstraction](/co

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Stage 2: Database → Config Snapshot
records.text:
When a job is queued, `buildConfigSnapshot()` in `app/server/actions/projects.ts` queries all component tables in parallel and assembles a single JSON object. This object is stored in `jobs.config_snapshot`.

The snapshot is a **point-in-time freeze**. Even if the user edits the Project after queuing, the job executes the exact configuration that was planned.

config_snapshot = {
 ...project fields,
 provider: "aws" "gcp" "azure",
 network: { provision_network, cidr_block, network_id, ... },
 cluster: { cluster_version, instance_types, node_min_size, ... },
 dns: { enabled, zone_id, domain_name, provider_config, ... },
 databases: [...],
 caches: [...],
 queues: [...],
 topics: [...],
 nosql_tables: [...],
 secrets: [...],
 git_access_token: "" // fetched at runtime, not stored
}

 
The git access token is intentionally left empty in the snapshot. The Runner fetches it at runtime via `POST /api/jobs/{id}/git-token` to avoid storing secrets in the job record.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Stage 3: Config Snapshot → ProjectConfig
records.text:
The Runner claims the job and deserializes the JSON snapshot into a strongly-typed Go struct:

func snapshotToProjectConfig(snapshot map[string]any) (*types.ProjectConfig, error) {
 data, _ := json.Marshal(snapshot)
 var sc types.ProjectConfig
 json.Unmarshal(data, &sc)
 return &sc, nil
}

The `ProjectConfig` struct in `packages/core/types/project_config.go` mirrors the snapshot shape with typed fields: `Network`, `Cluster`, `DNS`, `Databases[]`, `Caches[]`, and so on.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Stage 4: ProjectConfig → terraform.tfvars.json
records.text:
Each cloud provider implements a `ProviderTfvars()` method that maps `ProjectConfig` fields to provider-specific OpenTofu variable names:

 ProjectConfig Field AWS GCP Azure 
 ----------------- ----- ----- ------- 
 `ProjectName` `project_name` `project_name` `project_name` 
 `Region` `region` `region` `location` 
 `CloudAccountID` `aws_account_id` `project_id` `subscription_id` 
 `Network.ProvisionNetwork` `provision_vpc` `provision_network` `provision_vnet` 
 `Network.CIDRBlock` `vpc_cidr` `network_cidr` `vnet_cidr` 
 `Cluster.ClusterVersion` `eks_cluster_version` `gke_cluster_version` `aks_cluster_version` 
 `Cluster.InstanceTypes` `eks_instance_types` `gke_instance_types` `aks_instance_types` 
 `Databases[]` `rds_config` `cloud_sql_engine`, ... `azure_db_engine`, ... 
 `Caches[]` `redis_instance_type` `memorystore_instance_type` `azure_cache_sku` 
 `Queues[]` + `Topics[]` `sqs_queues`, `sns_topics` `pubsub_topics` `service_bus_queues`, `service_bus_topics` 
 `NosqlTables[]` `ddb_table_configuration` `firestore_databases` `cosmos_db_collections` 
 `StorageBuckets[]` `bucket_configuration` `cloud_storage_buckets` `storage_containers` 

The result is a `map[string]interface{}` wri

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Template Selection
records.text: The Runner resolves the template directory based on `ProjectConfig.Provider` — one of `aws/`, `gcp/`, or `azure/` under the templates path.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Backend Configuration
records.text: OpenTofu state is stored in S3-compatible storage. The backend key follows the pattern `{project}-{env}-{region}/tofu.tfstate`. See [OpenTofu State](/concepts/terraform-state).

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Plan
records.text: `tofu plan` runs with the generated tfvars. For PLAN jobs, an Infracost analysis is also generated. The plan artifact is uploaded to S3-compatible storage.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Apply
records.text: For DEPLOY jobs, `tofu apply` runs the plan. If a `plan_job_id` is linked, the cached plan artifact is downloaded and applied directly.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Post-Apply
records.text:
After apply, the runner extracts `tofu` outputs (cluster endpoint, database endpoints, ARNs), writes an exec-plugin kubeconfig in-process (CLI-free — see [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)), installs ArgoCD, and renders application templates (per cloud — see [Multi-cloud](/concepts/elench/multi-cloud)). It then **generates app manifests** for the detected services and scaffolds them into the GitOps repo — only when that repo has no manifests yet, so a bring-your-own repo is never overwritten. See [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).

Between `plan` and `apply` the [Elench verification gate](/concepts/elench/engine-internals) runs (fail-closed) and seals a signed receipt.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Plan Hash Validation
records.text: When a DEPLOY job references a prior PLAN job, the platform validates that the configuration hasn't changed between plan and apply. If the `config_snapshot` hash differs, the deploy fails with a hash mismatch error and the user must re-plan. This prevents applying a stale plan against a modified Project.

records.title: Provisioning Pipeline
records.heading: Key Implementation Files
records.text:
Component Location 
 ----------- ---------- 
 Config snapshot builder `apps/console/app/server/actions/projects.ts` — `buildConfigSnapshot()`

records.title: Real-time updates
records.text: Real-time updates. How the console pushes live job logs and support messages over Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY and SSE, and why everything else refreshes by polling.

records.title: Real-time updates
records.heading: Real-time updates
records.text:
The console has two ways to keep a page current. A stream that must feel instant — a job's log, a
support thread — is **pushed**: Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` fanned out to the browser over SSE
(Server-Sent Events). Everything else — job status, the runner list, an environment's status — is
**polled**, and polls fast only while something is in flight.

records.title: Real-time updates
records.heading: Push: LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE
records.text:
When a row is inserted, the database emits `pg_notify` on a named channel with a small JSON payload
that names the row, not its contents. Each console instance holds **one** dedicated `LISTEN`
connection per channel and dispatches each notification to the SSE subscribers for that key. Because
every instance listens for itself, this scales to several console instances without a message
broker. The implementation lives in `apps/console/lib/realtime/index.ts`.

 N["pg_notify(channel, {key, id})"]
 N --> L["Console LISTEN (1 per channel per instance)"]
 L --> S["SSE stream for that key"]
 S --> B["Browser EventSource"]
`} />

Two channels are wired:

 Channel Emitted by Payload SSE route 
 --- --- --- --- 
 `job_logs` the `insert_job_log` RPC `{jobId, logId}` `/api/stream/jobs/{id}` 
 `support_messages` `notify_support_message()` `{caseId, messageId}` `/api/stream/support/cases/{id}` 

The payload carries only ids because `NOTIFY` caps a payload at 8 KB. On each notification the SSE
route reads the rows newer than the last one it sent and writes them to the stream. Each route
checks that the caller may see the job or case before it opens the stream.

For the log path end to end — the r

records.title: Real-time updates
records.heading: Poll: everything else
records.text:
Lists and statuses refresh through TanStack Query, which dedupes every component that asks for the
same data into one request:

 Data Refresh 
 --- --- 
 Jobs page (`useJobsPageQuery`) every 5 seconds while a listed job is in flight; every 30 seconds otherwise 
 Shared jobs cache (`useJobsQuery`) — palette, overview, notifications every 5 seconds while any job is in flight; idle otherwise 
 One job (`useJobQuery`) every 3 seconds while it is `QUEUED`, `CLAIMED` or `PROCESSING`; idle once terminal 
 Runners (`useRunnersQuery`) every 10 seconds while the tab is focused 
 Environment status (canvas) every 4 seconds while a job is active on the environment; every 30 seconds once settled 

There is no SSE stream for job status, runners, or environments. A status change shows up on the
next poll, not instantly.

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.text: Internal Architecture. Main loop, heartbeat mechanism, graceful shutdown, and the core shared package.

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Internal Architecture
records.text: Runner is a single Go binary with a straightforward architecture: a main poll loop, a heartbeat goroutine, and shared libraries from the `core` package.

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Main Loop
records.text:
Reg[Register with Alethia API]
 Reg --> HB[Start heartbeat goroutine · every 30s]
 Reg --> Wake[Start wake-stream goroutine · SSE /api/runners/wake]
 Reg --> Poll{Claim loop · on wake or 30s safety poll POST /api/jobs/claim}
 Wake --> wake Poll
 Poll --> no job Wait[await next wake / safety tick]
 Wait --> Poll
 Poll --> job claimed Mint[Mint per-job cloud creds · keyless OIDC]
 Mint --> Exec[Execute via sandbox seam · tofu, ArgoCD]
 Exec --> Logs[Stream logs]
 Logs --> Report[Report result]
 Report --> Poll
`} />

The claim loop runs on the main goroutine; the wake-stream listener and the heartbeat each run as a
background goroutine. All share the runner configuration.

Provisioning work runs through the **sandbox seam** (`packages/core/sandbox`), not by invoking the provisioner
directly. For trusted Alethia templates the default `Passthrough` backend runs it in-process; on the managed
fleet, untrusted bring-your-own IaC/Helm runs in a per-job **container** with an allowlisted environment and a
locked-down network. See the [`sandbox` package README](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/main/packages/core/sandbox/README.md)
and [Security Architecture → Execution isola

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Job types
records.text:
The dispatch switch (`internal/agent/runner.go`) routes each claimed job to its handler. The handler
for each type, and how it runs, is in [Job execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution#dispatch); what
each type does is in [Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types).

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Configuration
records.text:
Runner receives its configuration via environment variables:

 Variable Description 
 ---------- ------------- 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` Base URL of the Alethia instance 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_ID` Unique Runner identifier (assigned at registration) 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_TOKEN` Authentication token for API calls 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_OPERATOR` `managed` or `self` (the legacy `ALETHIA_RUNNER_MODE` with `cloud-hosted`/`self-hosted` still works as a back-compat fallback) 
 `INFRACOST_API_KEY` Optional, for cost estimation 

The runner holds **no object-storage credentials**. tofu state goes through the console **state proxy**
(`backend "http"` → `/api/jobs/{id}/state`) authenticated by a per-job token in `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`, and cloud
auth is minted per job via keyless OIDC — so a managed fleet VM's cloud-init carries no long-lived secret.
Managed fleet VMs additionally self-register with a per-VM, short-TTL bootstrap token rather than any static
credential.

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Heartbeat Mechanism
records.text:
The heartbeat goroutine sends `POST /api/runners/heartbeat` every 30 seconds. The payload carries:

- The runner version
- The cloud providers this runner can claim (per-cloud routing)

The runner's identity travels in the `X-Runner-ID` / `X-Runner-Token` headers, not the body. The
response returns any server-side-cancelled job IDs (`cancelled_job_ids`) — the fallback cancel path
when a wake-stream cancel was missed.

Alethia uses the heartbeat to:
- Mark Runners as ONLINE (heartbeat within 60s) or OFFLINE (heartbeat missed)
- Detect dead Runners and requeue their jobs
- Track which Runner is running which job

If a Runner crashes mid-job:
1. Heartbeat stops arriving
2. After 60 seconds, Alethia marks the Runner OFFLINE
3. If no log updates for 5+ minutes, the job is marked FAILED
4. User can retry the job — tofu state is preserved in the console state proxy (`project-tofu-state`, with fenced locks so a reclaimed lock can't clobber a slow writer)

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Graceful Shutdown
records.text:
When Runner receives SIGINT or SIGTERM:

1. Enters a local **draining** state — stops claiming new jobs
2. Lets the in-flight job (if any) run to completion, up to a 10-minute grace period, after which the
 context is cancelled to force shutdown
3. Exits

In the managed fleet, a warm-pool VM claims jobs until the scaler decides it is surplus. Scale-down
is a two-step **drain then destroy**: the controller marks the runner `DRAINING` (it stops claiming
but finishes its in-flight job), and the next tick destroys it once idle — so the SIGTERM the VM
sends always lands on a runner that already drained gracefully. See
[Warm-pool scaling](/concepts/runner/scaling). (Self-operated runners get the same on any orchestrator's
stop signal.)

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: API Client
records.text:
The `RunnerAPIClient` handles all communication with Alethia:

 Method Endpoint Purpose 
 -------- ---------- --------- 
 `ClaimJob()` `POST /api/jobs/claim` Atomic job claiming 
 `Heartbeat()` `POST /api/runners/heartbeat` Keepalive 
 `UpdateJobStatus()` `PUT /api/jobs/{id}/status` Status transitions 
 `SendLog()` `POST /api/jobs/{id}/logs` Log batch delivery 
 `UploadPlanArtifact()` `POST /api/jobs/{id}/plan-artifact` Plan JSON upload 
 `DownloadPlanArtifact()` `GET /api/jobs/{id}/plan-artifact` Plan JSON download 

All requests include `X-Runner-ID` and `X-Runner-Token` headers for authentication.

records.title: Internal Architecture
records.heading: Shared core Package
records.text:
Runner and Alethia CLI both import from `packages/core/`:

 Package Purpose 
 --------- --------- 
 `provisioner/` Bootstrap, deploy, destroy orchestration 
 `tofu/` OpenTofu CLI wrapper (init, plan, apply, destroy) — drives the `tofu` binary via `terraform-exec` 
 `cloud/aws/` AWS SDK for provisioning (keyless `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, EKS kubeconfig) 
 `cloud/` (`http_backend.go`) The console HTTP state backend (per-job token via `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`) — no storage credential on the runner 
 `sandbox/` The per-job isolation seam (Passthrough / Container backends) 
 `cloud/gcp_provider.go` GCP Workload Identity Federation provider tfvars + kubeconfig 
 `cloud/azure_provider.go` Azure federated-auth provider tfvars + kubeconfig 
 `argocd/` ArgoCD installation and configuration (App-of-Apps rendering) 
 `git/` Git clone, branch, commit, push 
 `k8s/` kubectl operations 
 `infracost/` Infracost CLI wrapper and output parsing 

This shared package ensures both the CLI and Runner use the same provisioning logic.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.text: Cloud credentials. How Runner assumes temporary credentials per job — AWS, Alibaba, GCP, and Azure, plus token clouds (DigitalOcean / Hetzner / Civo) with an optional self-managed path where the token never leaves your infrastructure.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Cloud credentials
records.text: Runner assumes temporary cloud credentials at the start of every job and clears them when the job completes. No credentials persist between jobs.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Per-job credential lifecycle
records.text:
B[Read cloud_identity from the claim]
 B --> C[Provider-specific keyless minting]
 C --> D[Set env vars · OIDC token file]
 D --> E[Execute tofu · reads env vars]
 E --> F[defer: clear credentials + remove token file]
`} />

The `defer` ensures credentials and any on-disk assertion are always cleared, even if the job fails
or panics.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: AWS: keyless AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
records.text:
**Input from cloud_identity:**
- `role_arn` — ARN of the IAM role in the user's AWS account (its trust policy trusts the Alethia issuer)

**Execution (managed runner — keyless, no ambient AWS identity):** the runner mints a web-identity assertion
(audience `sts.amazonaws.com`) from the console and writes a single AWS profile that federates **straight into
the customer role** — no platform account, no ExternalId:

[profile alethia-customer]
web_identity_token_file = /tmp/alethia-aws-XXXX/web-identity-token
role_arn = arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AlethiaProvisionerRole
role_session_name = alethia-runner

It points OpenTofu's aws provider at that profile (`AWS_CONFIG_FILE` + `AWS_PROFILE=alethia-customer`). A
background refresher re-mints the assertion into the token **file** every few minutes; the SDK re-reads it
and re-assumes on session expiry, so a `tofu apply` longer than the ~1 hour session keeps a live assertion
(parity with GCP/Azure/Alibaba). No access key ever reaches the runner (see
[Security architecture → AWS](/concepts/security#aws-keyless-issuer-direct-iam-role)).

**Self-operated runners** (`operator=self`) run in the customer's own cloud with their own ambient
crede

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Alibaba Cloud: RAM Role via OIDC (keyless, account-free)
records.text:
Alibaba is **keyless** — there is no platform AccessKey (the old `ALETHIA_ALIBABA_ACCESS_KEY_*` was
retired). The runner authenticates the same way the console does: an anonymous **`AssumeRoleWithOIDC`**
using a short-lived assertion minted by the Alethia issuer. Alethia holds no Alibaba account.

**Input from cloud_identity:**
- `role_arn` — ARN of the RAM role in the user's account (`acs:ram:: :role/ `)
- `oidc_provider_arn` — ARN of the customer's RAM OIDC provider (fixed name `alethia`)

**Execution:**

func ActivateAlibabaOIDC(ctx, fetcher, roleArn, oidcProviderArn string) (cleanup func(), err error) {
 token, err := fetcher.FetchAlibabaToken() // mint an assertion from the console (/api/runners/alibaba-token)
 tokenFile := writeToTempFile(token)

 // The alicloud provider runs AssumeRoleWithOIDC itself from these — no AccessKey on the runner.
 os.Setenv("ALIBABA_CLOUD_ROLE_ARN", roleArn)
 os.Setenv("ALIBABA_CLOUD_OIDC_PROVIDER_ARN", oidcProviderArn)
 os.Setenv("ALIBABA_CLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE", tokenFile)
 // …a background refresher re-mints into tokenFile every ~5 min; cleanup stops it + removes the file
 return cleanup, nil
}

The `alicloud` provider reads `ALIBABA_CLOUD_OIDC

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: GCP: Workload Identity Federation
records.text:
**Input from cloud_identity:**
- `project_id` — GCP project ID
- `wif_config` — the Workload Identity Federation credential configuration (pool, provider, and the
 service account to impersonate)

**Execution** (`ActivateGcpOIDC` in `internal/agent/gcp_credentials.go`): the runner fetches a
short-lived assertion from the console (`POST /api/runners/gcp-token`, runner-authed; audience
`alethia-gcp-wif`), writes it to a token file, points the WIF configuration's `credential_source` at that
file, and hands the configuration to OpenTofu's google provider. google-auth exchanges the assertion at
GCP STS for a temporary access token and re-reads the file to exchange again. A background refresher
re-mints into the file every 5 minutes, so a long apply keeps a live assertion (parity with
AWS/Azure/Alibaba). Cleanup stops the refresher and removes both files. No service account key file is
involved.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Azure: Federated Identity
records.text:
Azure is **keyless** — no client secret reaches the runner. The runner authenticates **as the customer's
user-assigned managed identity** (there is no platform Entra app) by fetching a short-lived OIDC assertion
from the console (the console holds the issuer signing key) and handing it to OpenTofu as the client
assertion for that identity's federated credential.

**Input from cloud_identity:**
- `tenant_id` — the customer's Azure Entra tenant
- `client_id` — the customer's managed-identity application id (per-connection)
- `subscription_id` — Target Azure subscription

**Execution:**

func ActivateAzureFederated(fetcher azureTokenFetcher, tenantId, clientId, subscriptionId string) (cleanup func(), err error) {
 // Mint an assertion from the console (POST /api/runners/azure-token, runner-authed).
 token, err := fetcher.FetchAzureToken()
 if err != nil {
 return nil, err
 }
 tokenFile := writeToTempFile(token)

 os.Setenv("ARM_CLIENT_ID", clientId)
 os.Setenv("ARM_TENANT_ID", tenantId)

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Token Clouds: DigitalOcean / Hetzner / Civo
records.text:
These providers have no cross-account role federation — they authenticate with a single API token.
Alethia supports two models.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Stored scoped token (encrypted)
records.text:
The customer pastes a scoped API token; Alethia stores it **encrypted at rest** and decrypts it only at
claim time, passing it to the runner. The runner exports the provider's env var
(`DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN` / `HCLOUD_TOKEN` / `CIVO_TOKEN`) for the job and clears it after.

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Self-managed — token stays in your infrastructure (true zero-trust)
records.text:
For clouds without federation, the honest zero-trust path: the token lives **only** in your self-hosted
runner's environment, never in Alethia's database.

- The connection is recorded with `self_managed: true` and **no token**.
- Its jobs are flagged `requires_self_runner`, and `claim_next_job` **excludes managed runners** from
 them — so only *your* runner, which holds `HCLOUD_TOKEN` / `CIVO_TOKEN` / `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN`
 in its own env, can claim and run them.
- The runner reads the token from its environment (the `selfManaged` path) and never receives it from
 Alethia.

Pick the model in the connect sheet: **"Store a scoped token"** (encrypted at rest) vs **"Self-hosted
runner — token stays in your infra."** See [Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated).

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: Security Properties
records.text:
Property Guarantee 
 ---------- ----------- 
 No persistent credentials Env vars are cleared after every job via `defer` 
 No credential sharing Each job gets its own assumed session 
 Time-bounded Each minted assertion lives ≤10 minutes; the cloud session it buys lasts about an hour 
 Scoped Credentials only have the permissions of the customer's IAM role / service account / managed identity / RAM role 
 Revocable The customer deletes the IAM role / WIF provider / managed identity / RAM role → instant revocation 
 No file leaks Temporary credential and token files are deleted in `defer` cleanup 
 Optional zero-storage Self-managed token clouds keep the secret in your runner's env — it never enters Alethia's database

records.title: Cloud credentials
records.heading: CloudIdentity Structure

records.title: Runner Agent
records.text: Runner Agent. Autonomous execution agent that runs OpenTofu, installs ArgoCD, and streams logs.

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Runner Agent
records.text:
Runner is the execution engine — a single Go binary shipped as a container image. Runners claim
provisioning jobs from the queue, mint per-job cloud credentials keylessly, execute the `tofu`
binary (OpenTofu), install ArgoCD, and stream logs back in real time. The binary is **CLI-free**:
it bundles no `aws`/`gcloud`/`az`, and mints cluster tokens in-process via `runner kube-token` (see
[Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials)).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Key facts
records.text:
Property Value 
 ---------- ------- 
 Language Go (single binary) 
 IaC engine OpenTofu (`tofu`) `v1.9.0`, baked into the image 
 Base image Alpine 3.21, non-root `runner` user 
 Registries GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner*`) 
 Versioning release-please (`runner-v*` tags). See [Release System](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/release-system.md). 
 Job dispatch Push wake stream (SSE `GET /api/runners/wake`) + 30-second safety poll (`POST /api/jobs/claim`) 
 Heartbeat interval 30 seconds (`POST /api/runners/heartbeat`) 
 tofu state Console HTTP state proxy — no object-storage credential on the runner 
 Cloud auth Keyless OIDC per job (no static keys)

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Where a runner runs — the managed fleet vs. self-deployed
records.text:
The word "runtime" splits cleanly into two paths. Do not conflate them.

 Managed fleet Self-deployed (AWS) 
 --- --- --- 
 Operator `managed` `self` / `deployed` 
 Substrate **Hetzner VM warm pool** AWS ECS Fargate (ARM64) 
 Provisioned by the in-app scaler (`apps/console/lib/fleet/`) a `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job running `infra/templates/runner/aws/` 
 Image source GHCR per-cloud image, self-registers via `ALETHIA_RUNNER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` GHCR image, registration token injected as an ECS env var 
 Scaling 60s warm-pool loop, sized by queue depth ([Warm-pool scaling](/concepts/runner/scaling)) ECS service `desired_count`, managed by the customer 
 Billing provisioned hours via `runner_usage_sessions` the customer's own AWS bill 

The **managed fleet** is Alethia running runners in the platform account and assuming into the
customer cloud — cheap Hetzner VMs from a GHCR image, sized by an in-app scaler. **ECS Fargate is
not the managed substrate anymore** (the retired AWS ECS + Lambda fleet lived under `infra/fleet-aws`
and is gone). ECS Fargate is real only for a **self-deployed** runner, which a `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job
provisions into the customer's own AWS account from `infra/templates/runne

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Operator & provisioning
records.text:
A runner is described by two orthogonal axes: **operator** (`managed` `self`) and, for self
runners, **provisioning** (`deployed` `registered`). This yields three effective categories:

 Category Operator Provisioning Description 
 ---------- ---------- -------------- ------------- 
 **Managed** `managed` — Alethia runs the runner in the platform account (Hetzner VM warm pool) and bills it by provisioned hours. Automatic scaling, no user setup. 
 **Self · Deployed** `self` `deployed` Provisioned into the customer's cloud by an existing runner running `tofu` (Console "Deploy" tab / `alethia runner deploy`). AWS lands on ECS Fargate. 
 **Self · Registered** `self` `registered` Customer brings their own runner — their own IaC or just `alethia runner start` — and registers it for a token. For on-prem or air-gapped environments. 

The legacy `ALETHIA_RUNNER_MODE` (`cloud-hosted`/`self-hosted`) still works as a back-compat
fallback (`cloud-hosted` → `managed`, `self-hosted` → `self`), but `ALETHIA_RUNNER_OPERATOR` is
canonical.

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Picks up jobs
records.text:
A push wake stream (SSE) signals when a job is claimable; the runner calls `POST /api/jobs/claim` on
each wake, with a 30-second safety poll as the fallback if the stream drops. See
[Job queue](/concepts/job-queue).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Claims atomically
records.text: PostgreSQL `claim_next_job()` with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` prevents double-execution.

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Mints credentials
records.text:
Keyless OIDC per job — AWS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, GCP Workload Identity Federation, Azure
federated identity, Alibaba `AssumeRoleWithOIDC` — no stored cloud keys. Token clouds
(DigitalOcean / Hetzner / Civo) use an API token, either stored encrypted or kept entirely in a
self-operated runner. See [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Executes OpenTofu
records.text:
`tofu init` → `tofu plan` → the [verify gate](/concepts/runner/job-execution/plan-jobs) → `tofu apply` or
`tofu destroy`. Provisions **greenfield** infrastructure, or **attaches to existing** resources when
the config marks a component "existing" (brownfield — e.g. an existing VPC/VNet). See
[Job Execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Installs ArgoCD
records.text: Helm chart deployment with the App-of-Apps pattern. See [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Streams logs
records.text:
Batched POST (notify-driven, flushed on write with a ~1-second backstop) → Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`
→ SSE → browser. See
[Log Streaming](/concepts/runner/log-streaming).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Reports results
records.text:
Updates job status with execution metadata (timing, tofu outputs, and the verify report on
`execution_metadata["verify_result"]`).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Sends heartbeat
records.text: Every 30 seconds to confirm it is alive.

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Container contents
records.text:
The image builds `FROM` a shared `runner-base` (Alpine 3.21, non-root `runner` user). The base
carries everything cloud-agnostic; each per-cloud image adds only that cloud's project template.

 Tool Purpose 
 ------ --------- 
 Go binary (`runner`) The runner executable — also the `kube-token` exec-credential plugin 
 OpenTofu (`tofu`) `v1.9.0` Infrastructure provisioning (SHA256-verified download, baked in) 
 kubectl Kubernetes cluster access 
 Helm ArgoCD and component installation 
 Infracost `v0.10.39` Cost estimation 
 Infrastructure templates Per-cloud project templates + runner + ArgoCD manifests 
 podman / crun / fuse-overlayfs Nested rootless sandbox runtime — **inert** until `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container` 

 
 **No cloud CLIs.** The image bundles **no** `aws-cli`, `gcloud`, or `azure-cli` — the
 `Dockerfile`s say so explicitly. EKS/GKE/AKS cluster tokens are minted **in-process** by
 `runner kube-token --provider `, invoked by the exec-credential kubeconfig the runner
 writes. See [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Runner Agent
records.heading: Documentation
records.text:
Main loop, heartbeat, sandbox seam, graceful shutdown 
 Per-job-type execution details 
 Keyless, per-job credential minting 
 Real-time log delivery 
 In-app scaler + Hetzner VM fleet 
 Running a runner you operate yourself 
 OpenTofu modules for all providers 
 Shared Go packages

records.title: ArgoCD Components
records.text: ArgoCD Components. Pre-installed Kubernetes components managed by ArgoCD after cluster provisioning.

records.title: ArgoCD Components
records.heading: ArgoCD Components
records.text: After cluster provisioning, Runner installs ArgoCD and deploys a set of supporting components via the [App of Apps pattern](/concepts/gitops-argocd). These templates live in `infra/templates/argocd/`.

records.title: ArgoCD Components
records.heading: Component Manifests
records.text:
Template Component Purpose 
 ---------- ----------- --------- 
 `aws-load-balancer-controller.yaml` AWS Load Balancer Controller Provisions ALB/NLB for Kubernetes Ingress and Service resources 
 `external-dns.yaml` External DNS Syncs DNS records from Kubernetes Ingress annotations. Backends: Route53/Cloud DNS/Azure DNS via workload identity, **Hetzner Cloud DNS** via the official webhook sidecar (the connector's Cloud API token; the domain's zone must already exist in Hetzner Cloud DNS), and **Cloudflare** whenever the Cloudflare DNS connector is attached (any cloud). Renders only when DNS is enabled with a domain and the selected backend's identity/token is actually present — otherwise it is skipped rather than deployed broken 
 `external-secrets-operator.yaml` External Secrets Operator Pulls secrets from Secrets Manager/Secret Manager/Key Vault into Kubernetes Secrets. The AWS SecretsManager `ClusterSecretStore` renders on AWS only; the operator itself ships on every cloud 
 `karpenter.yaml` Karpenter Just-in-time node provisioning based on pod resource requests (AWS) 
 `metrics-server.yaml` Metrics Server Provides CPU/memory metrics for the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and `kubectl

records.title: ArgoCD Components
records.heading: How Templates Are Rendered
records.text:
Each template is a Kubernetes manifest with Helm-style placeholders. During deployment, the Runner:

1. Extracts **infrastructure facts** from tofu outputs (cluster name, VPC ID, database endpoints, etc.)
2. Renders the facts into a Helm values file
3. Applies each component manifest as an ArgoCD Application

The ArgoCD Application resources reference Helm charts from public repositories with the infrastructure facts injected as values.

records.title: ArgoCD Components
records.heading: Infrastructure Facts
records.text:
Example facts passed to component Helm charts:

cluster:
 name: api-backend-production

records.title: AWS Resources
records.heading: Key Features
records.text:
**IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts)** — Kubernetes pods can assume IAM roles via their service account, eliminating the need for static credentials in containers. The EKS module creates an OIDC provider and the IRSA module creates per-service-account IAM roles.

**Karpenter** — Just-in-time node provisioning. Instead of pre-scaling node groups, Karpenter watches for pending pods and launches appropriately-sized EC2 instances within seconds. Supports spot instances and multiple instance families.

**Aurora Serverless v2** — Auto-scaling database with ACU-based capacity (0.5–128 ACUs). Scales to zero-ish (0.5 ACU minimum) during idle periods.

records.title: Azure Resources
records.heading: Key Features
records.text:
**Azure AD Integration** — AKS integrates with Azure AD for RBAC. Cluster admins are Azure AD users or groups, not separate IAM identities.

**Flexible Server** — Azure's latest managed database tier with zone-redundant HA, automatic backups, and vCore-based scaling (1–64 vCores).

**Cosmos DB** — Globally distributed multi-model database supporting SQL (document), Table (key-value), MongoDB, Cassandra, and Gremlin APIs. Multi-region writes for global distribution.

**Ingress through an Application Gateway** — Azure has no per-Ingress load balancer. Instead, the template provisions one Application Gateway v2, and the Application Gateway Ingress Controller (AGIC) turns every `Ingress` object in the cluster into listeners and routing rules on that gateway. Set `ingressClassName: azure-application-gateway` on your `Ingress` to publish through it. AGIC authenticates with a workload identity, so it holds no static credential.

records.title: Infrastructure Templates Overview
records.text: Infrastructure Templates Overview. OpenTofu modules the runner uses to provision infrastructure across AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, and Hetzner.

records.title: Infrastructure Templates Overview
records.heading: Infrastructure Templates
records.text:
The runner provisions infrastructure using pre-built OpenTofu modules (HCL). These templates are
baked into the runner image at build time — each per-cloud image pre-runs `tofu init` on its
template so no provider/module download happens at job time.

records.title: Infrastructure Templates Overview
records.heading: Template Categories
records.text:
Category Path Purpose 
 ---------- ------ --------- 
 AWS project `infra/templates/project/aws/` User infrastructure on AWS 
 GCP project `infra/templates/project/gcp/` User infrastructure on GCP 
 Azure project `infra/templates/project/azure/` User infrastructure on Azure 
 Alibaba project `infra/templates/project/alibaba/` User infrastructure on Alibaba Cloud 
 Hetzner project `infra/templates/project/hetzner/` Self-managed Talos Kubernetes on Hetzner VMs 
 Runner `infra/templates/runner/aws/` Self-deployed runner infrastructure (ECS Fargate)
