 EKS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, and more 
 GKE, Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Firestore, and more 
 AKS, Azure Database, Azure Cache, Cosmos DB, and more 
 Pre-installed cluster components

records.title: Infrastructure Templates Overview
records.heading: Template staging (image build)
records.text:
During the [runner release pipeline](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/release-system.md), templates are `COPY`d into the image
and pre-initialized. The full `runner` image carries all five project templates; each per-cloud image
(`runner-aws`, `runner-hetzner`, …) carries only its own:

infra/templates/project/ → /home/runner/project-templates/ (+ tofu init)
infra/templates/runner/ → /home/runner/runner-templates/
infra/templates/argocd/ → /home/runner/argocd-templates/

records.title: Infrastructure Templates Overview
records.heading: Variable generation
records.text:
When executing a job, the runner materializes a tfvars file from the environment's config snapshot
(`tofu.OverrideTfvarsFromMap`). The provisioner in `packages/core/provisioner/` maps each component
to specific tofu variables (`ProviderTfvars`). See
[Cloud Provider Abstraction](/concepts/cloud-abstraction) for the mapping layer.

records.title: Infrastructure Templates Overview
records.heading: tofu state
records.text:
The runner holds **no object-storage credentials**. State for every template is written through the
**Console HTTP state proxy** — the templates declare `backend "http" {}`, and the runner fetches a
per-job token it exposes as `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`, so state I/O flows through
`/api/jobs/{id}/state`. See [tofu state](/concepts/terraform-state).

records.title: Build Jobs
records.text: Build Jobs. How the runner executes BUILD jobs — kaniko image builds scheduled in the customer's own cluster, pushed to ECR, reported as a per-service digest map.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Build Jobs
records.text:
`BUILD` jobs turn a project's repo-sourced services into real, pushed container images. For each
service whose source is a repository, the runner schedules a [kaniko](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/kaniko)
build **inside the customer's own provisioned cluster**, waits for it to finish, captures the pushed
image digest, and reports a per-service digest map. `BUILD` is a first-class job type (`JobType =
"BUILD"`), dispatched to `executeBuild` alongside `PLAN`, `DEPLOY`, and the others.

 
 **Where the build runs.** The customer's Dockerfile executes in **their own cluster**, never on the
 runner. Runner-side work is limited to rendering the Job manifest, running `kubectl` against the
 cluster's API server, and a commit-pinning clone that only fetches data. Because nothing from the
 repository executes on the runner, no BYO sandbox is required for a `BUILD`.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: What gets built
records.text:
The runner builds every service whose `source.kind == "repo"`. Prebuilt-image services
(`source.kind == "image"`) are not buildable and are skipped. If the environment has no repo-sourced
services, the job posts an empty result map and finishes with nothing to do.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Read environment outputs
records.text:
The runner reads the environment's OpenTofu outputs through the per-job
[state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state). Two outputs drive the build:

- `ecr_repository_urls_map` — the per-service registry destination map (service name → repository URL).
- `ecr_build_service_account` — the build identity as `namespace:serviceaccount`.

If `ecr_repository_urls_map` is missing, the job fails: the ECR wiring has not been provisioned, so
there is nowhere to push. Provision the infrastructure before running a `BUILD`. When the
service-account output is absent, the runner falls back to the fixed defaults `alethia-build` /
`kaniko-builder`.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Configure cluster access (keyless)
records.text:
The runner builds an exec-plugin kubeconfig from the already-active federated cloud credentials — the
same CLI-free `runner kube-token` mechanism used by [Deploy Jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs).
A `BUILD` needs the cluster, so a kubeconfig failure fails the job.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Ensure the build namespace
records.text:
The runner applies the build namespace (idempotently) so the kaniko Jobs have somewhere to land. The
namespace is labelled `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: alethia`.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Pin the commit
records.text:
For each service, the runner shallow-clones the repository runner-side and resolves `HEAD`, pinning
the exact commit the image is built from. When the repository is private, the job's git token is used
for this clone only — it never reaches the in-cluster Job spec or `execution_metadata`.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Render and apply the kaniko Job
records.text:
The runner renders a kaniko build Job (`imagebuild.RenderBuildJob`) named `build- ` and applies
it. The image is tagged with the resolved commit SHA (immutable and reproducible). Any prior build Job
for the same service is deleted first, so a re-run is idempotent.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Watch to completion
records.text:
The runner polls the Job's conditions until it reports `Complete`, `Failed`, or the per-build deadline
passes. A build has a 30-minute ceiling and is polled every 10 seconds. If the Job fails, the runner
surfaces the last 50 lines of the kaniko log so the Console shows why the Dockerfile build failed.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Capture the digest
records.text:
On success the runner captures the pushed image's digest, in priority order:

1. The build pod's **termination message** — kaniko writes ` @sha256:…` to
 `/dev/termination-log`, so the digest is readable after completion without depending on log retention.
2. The digest line from the kaniko **log** (`sha256:` followed by 64 hex characters).
3. As a loud fallback, the **immutable git-SHA tag** (` : `) — still a pinned reference.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Report results
records.text:
Job status → `PROCESSING`/final with `execution_metadata.build_result`: a map of
`service_name → image_digest_uri`. The Console persists each entry into
`project_services.resolved_image`, so the workload no longer runs a placeholder image.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Fail-closed behavior
records.text:
A `BUILD` never lets the Console treat an unbuilt service as built. The whole job fails when:

- a service has no provisioned ECR destination (infra not provisioned),
- a service's build Job fails, or
- a digest cannot be captured.

Digests captured **before** the failure are still posted — a completed, pushed image is real and
persisting it is idempotent.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: The kaniko build Job
records.text:
The build uses kaniko because it runs rootless, needs no Docker daemon, and pushes to the registry via
the pod ServiceAccount's IRSA. The renderer is pure and deterministic (a fixed service + options
produces the same YAML). Key facts of the rendered Job:

 Field Value 
 --- --- 
 Executor image `gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor:v1.23.2` (pinned; overridable) 
 Namespace `alethia-build` (default) 
 Dockerfile the service's `build.dockerfile`, else `Dockerfile` 
 Build context sub-path the service's `build.context`, else its `source.path` 
 Destination tag the resolved commit SHA 
 `backoffLimit` `1` (default) 
 `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` `3600` 
 Resource requests `cpu: 500m`, `memory: 1Gi` 

The kaniko executor image bundles the Amazon ECR credential helper and auto-detects
`*.dkr.ecr.*.amazonaws.com` destinations; IRSA is picked up through the default AWS credential chain
because the container sets `AWS_SDK_LOAD_CONFIG=true`.

When the repository is private, its git token never enters the rendered manifest: it is used only for
the runner-side commit-pinning clone (`resolveHeadSHA`) and is not passed to the in-cluster kaniko
build. No secret material is ever inlined into the rendered

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: Secret boundary
records.text:
Registry credentials never enter `execution_metadata`: the build authenticates in-cluster via IRSA,
the runner holds no registry credential at all, and the digest URI is non-secret. The git token used
for commit pinning stays runner-side and is never written into the Job spec or job metadata.

records.title: Build Jobs
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Deploy Jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs) — provisions the cluster and the ECR wiring a
 `BUILD` depends on.
- [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials) — the keyless per-job credential minting.
- [OpenTofu state](/concepts/terraform-state) — the per-job state proxy the runner reads outputs from.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.text: Deploy Jobs. How the runner executes DEPLOY jobs — the verify gate, tofu apply, keyless kubeconfig, and ArgoCD.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Deploy Jobs
records.text:
`DEPLOY` jobs apply the OpenTofu plan and install ArgoCD on the provisioned cluster. Between the
plan and the apply sits the **fail-closed verify gate** — a real apply will not run while a hard
control is failing.

 
 **Brownfield attach.** A DEPLOY doesn't only create new infrastructure — it can attach to what you
 **already have**. When the environment config marks a component "existing" (e.g. an existing
 VPC/VNet — see [Reuse existing resources](/guides/design-project/network#reuse-existing-resources)),
 the runner passes the resource's id into the tofu template instead of creating it, and the template
 `data`-sources the existing resource (and, for networks, resolves its subnets) so the rest of the
 graph wires into it. The provision-vs-existing seam is a `count = var.provision_X ? 1 : 0` guard on
 the create path plus a data source on the existing path. Today this covers networks on AWS/GCP/Azure.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Mint cloud credentials
records.text: Same keyless per-job minting as PLAN jobs. See [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Validate against the plan job
records.text:
Fetches the bound PLAN job and fails unless it finished `SUCCESS`. When both jobs carry a
`configuration_hash` and the two differ (the project was edited after planning), the job fails:

> "configuration changed since plan was generated"

Only jobs queued through the jobs API (`POST /api/jobs`, which the CLI uses) carry the hash; a
console-queued job relies on the saved artifact below. See
[Config hash validation](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#config-hash-validation).

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Download plan artifact
records.text:
Fetches the binary plan from the PLAN job (`GET /api/jobs/{planJobId}/plan-artifact`) into the job
workdir and applies it. If it can't be fetched, the runner re-plans.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: tofu init
records.text:
Initializes against the Console HTTP state proxy (`backend "http"`, per-job `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`) —
same as PLAN. No cloud storage credential is involved.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Verify gate (fail-closed)
records.text:
`provisioner.RunDeployV2` re-derives the plan JSON and runs `verify.Evaluate`
(`packages/core/verify`). It attaches a `verify.Report` and, on this **non-dry-run** apply, calls
`gateRequiresReport` + `Report.Unwaived(override)` **before `tofu apply`**:

- A hard control failure with no waiver → the job **fails here**, before any resource is touched.
- An authorized `verify.Override` (time-boxed, carrying `Reason`/`By`) waives specific control IDs
 so the apply can proceed deliberately.
- An ed25519 evidence **receipt** is sealed for the apply (unsigned `algorithm: "none"` when no
 `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` is set).

The report and receipt ride back on `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` /
`["verify_receipt"]` and render in the Console **Plan tab**
(`components/agent/artifact-panel.tsx`). See [Engine internals](/concepts/elench/engine-internals).

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: tofu apply
records.text:
tofu apply plan.tfplan
State is written back through the state proxy as each resource settles. (`RunDeployV2` writes
`apply` to a phase file just before this, so an interrupted apply can be flagged orphan-risk.)

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Extract tofu outputs
records.text: Reads cluster name / endpoint / ARN, database endpoints, cache endpoints, VPC id, etc.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Generate kubeconfig (CLI-free)
records.text:
No cloud CLI is invoked. The runner writes an **exec-credential kubeconfig** whose `user` runs the
runner itself as the credential plugin:

users:
 - name: alethia
 user:
 exec:
 apiVersion: client.authentication.k8s.io/v1beta1
 command: runner
 args: ["kube-token", "--provider", "aws", "--cluster", " ", "--region", " "]

`runner kube-token` mints a short-lived cluster token in-process from the already-active keyless
cloud credentials — a presigned STS `GetCallerIdentity` for EKS, a cloud-platform OAuth token for
GKE, an AAD workload-identity token for AKS. kubectl/Helm re-invoke it on expiry, so tokens
auto-refresh with no `aws`/`gcloud`/`az` present.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Install ArgoCD
records.text:
Deploys ArgoCD via Helm and waits for pods Ready. The admin password stays in the cluster's
`argocd-initial-admin-secret` (never extracted, never persisted to `execution_metadata`). See
[GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Configure App of Apps
records.text:
Renders ArgoCD Application manifests with infrastructure facts (cluster name, DB endpoints, …) as
Helm values and applies them.

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Report results
records.text:
Job status → SUCCESS with `execution_metadata`:
- Cluster name, endpoint, `cluster_ready` (a real reachability gate — not just "tofu apply exited 0")
- ArgoCD URL
- tofu outputs, credential-bearing keys scrubbed (kubeconfigs, passwords, tokens, generated secrets
 never leave the runner — `scrubSensitiveOutputs` + a whole-blob `scrubMetadataTree` backstop)
- `verify_result` / `verify_receipt`
- Per-phase execution timing

records.title: Deploy Jobs
records.heading: Finalization
records.text:
On the Alethia side, when the job reaches SUCCESS the `finalizeDeployment()` server action:
- Updates `project_cluster` with cluster metadata and ArgoCD credentials
- Updates `project_databases` with writer/reader endpoints and credential ARNs
- Updates `project_caches` with primary/reader endpoints
- Sets the environment's `status` to `ACTIVE`

This data appears in the [Clusters page](/guides/clusters) and the environment detail.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.text: Destroy Jobs. How the runner executes DESTROY jobs — tofu destroy with state cleanup.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: Destroy Jobs
records.text: `DESTROY` jobs tear down all infrastructure provisioned for an environment.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: Mint cloud credentials
records.text: Same keyless per-job minting as other job types. See [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: tofu init
records.text:
Initializes against the Console HTTP state proxy (`backend "http"`, per-job `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`) to
read the existing state — no cloud storage credential on the runner.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: tofu destroy
records.text:
tofu destroy -auto-approve
Removes all resources tracked in the tofu state. No confirmation prompt — the user already confirmed
via the Console or CLI.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: State cleanup
records.text: The state managed by the proxy is left in place (empty or minimal) for audit purposes.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: Report results
records.text: Job status → SUCCESS. The environment's `status` is set to `DESTROYED`.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: Partial destroy recovery
records.text:
If the destroy fails mid-way (resource dependency, timeout):

1. tofu state reflects which resources were already destroyed.
2. The job is marked FAILED with the error message.
3. The user retries — the next destroy only attempts the remaining resources.
4. This continues until all resources are removed.

records.title: Destroy Jobs
records.heading: What gets destroyed
records.text:
Everything provisioned for the environment:
- VPC/VNet and all networking resources (subnets, NAT gateways, security groups)
- Kubernetes cluster (EKS/GKE/AKS) and node groups
- Databases (Aurora/Cloud SQL/Azure Database instances)
- Caches (ElastiCache/Memorystore/Azure Cache)
- NoSQL tables, queues, topics
- Container registries
- Secrets
- DNS records and certificates
- WAF rules
- IAM roles (IRSA)

 
Destroy is permanent for stateful resources. Database data, cache contents, and secret values are **lost**. tofu state is preserved so re-apply is possible, but the data is gone.

records.title: Job execution
records.text: Job execution. How the runner claims and executes each job type.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Job Execution
records.text:
All jobs share the same claiming mechanism and keyless credential handling, but differ in what they
execute. For the queue mechanics, see [Job queue](/concepts/job-queue); for what each job type does, see
[Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types).

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Claiming
records.text:
A push wake stream (SSE) signals when a job is claimable; the runner then calls
`POST /api/jobs/claim` (a 30-second safety poll is the fallback if the stream drops). The server
runs `claim_next_job()` — a PostgreSQL function using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` for atomic,
exactly-once claiming. Job status walks `QUEUED → CLAIMED → PROCESSING → SUCCESS FAILED CANCELLED`.

When a job is returned, the runner:
1. Sets status to `PROCESSING`.
2. Reads the environment config snapshot and cloud identity from the claim.
3. Mints cloud credentials keylessly ([details](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials)).
4. Dispatches on `types.JobType` (the switch in `internal/agent/runner.go`) to the handler.
5. Sets status to `SUCCESS` or `FAILED`.

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Dispatch
records.text:
The switch in `internal/agent/runner.go` routes each `provisionJobType` to its handler. What each type
does is in the [Job types](/guides/jobs/job-types) catalog; this table adds only how the runner
executes it.

 Job type Handler Execution 
 ---------- --------- ----------- 
 `PLAN` / `DEPLOY` / `DESTROY` `executePlan` / `executeDeploy` / `executeDestroy` Through the **sandbox seam**. [Plan](/concepts/runner/job-execution/plan-jobs) · [Deploy](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs) · [Destroy](/concepts/runner/job-execution/destroy-jobs) 
 `DEPLOY_RUNNER` / `UPDATE_RUNNER` / `DESTROY_RUNNER` `executeDeployRunner` / … [Runner lifecycle jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/runner-jobs) 
 `ANALYZE_REPO` `executeAnalyzeRepo` Posts the `RepoDigest`. 
 `DETECT_DRIFT` `executeDriftDetection` Posts the posture on `execution_metadata.drift_posture`. Bring-your-own modules need the container sandbox on a managed runner. 
 `AUDIT` `executeAudit` Posts `execution_metadata.verify_result`; a verdict that cannot be persisted fails the job. 
 `CHART_SCAN` `executeChartScan` Always runs inside the sandbox. 
 `IAC_SCAN` `executeIacScan` On a managed runner, refuses unless the container sandbox

records.title: Job execution
records.heading: Error handling
records.text:
When any step fails:
1. The error is logged to the STDERR stream.
2. Job status is set to `FAILED` with the error message.
3. tofu state is preserved through the [Console state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state) (partial
 apply state, with fenced locks so a reclaimed lock can't clobber a slow writer).
4. Cloud credentials are cleared (the deferred cleanup always runs).
5. The runner returns to the poll loop for the next job.

Users can retry failed jobs — since state is preserved, retries continue from the last successful
resource rather than starting over.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.text: Plan Jobs. How the runner executes PLAN jobs — tofu plan, the verify gate, structured output, and Infracost.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Plan Jobs
records.text:
`PLAN` jobs run `tofu plan` to preview infrastructure changes without applying them, and run the
plan JSON through the [Elench verify gate](/concepts/elench/engine-internals) so the Plan tab shows both the
diff and the policy verdict.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Mint cloud credentials
records.text:
Keyless per job — AWS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, GCP WIF, Azure federated identity, Alibaba
`AssumeRoleWithOIDC`. No stored keys. See [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Generate tofu variables
records.text:
The project's config snapshot is transformed into a tfvars map by the provisioner
(`tofu.OverrideTfvarsFromMap`). Each environment component maps to specific tofu variables.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: tofu init
records.text:
Initializes against the **Console HTTP state proxy**, not a cloud bucket the runner can reach:
backend "http" {} # /api/jobs/{id}/state, auth via TF_HTTP_PASSWORD (per-job token)
The runner holds no object-storage credentials. See [tofu state](/concepts/terraform-state).

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: tofu plan
records.text:
tofu plan -out=plan.tfplan
Generates a binary plan file describing what will change.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: tofu show (plan JSON)
records.text:
tofu show -json plan.tfplan
Converts the binary plan to structured JSON — the input both to the UI diff and to the verify gate.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Verify gate (fail-closed)
records.text:
`provisioner.RunDeployV2` calls `verify.Evaluate` on the plan JSON right after it is produced. The
gate runs the deterministic Elench control set (keyless / least-privilege / OIDC-subject, with
honest `not_evaluable` for what the plan can't show) and attaches a `verify.Report` to the result.
On a PLAN this is **advisory** — the report is surfaced but nothing is applied — but the same code
path is **fail-closed on apply**: a `DEPLOY` will refuse before `tofu apply` if a hard control is
failing and unwaived. See [Deploy Jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs) and
[Engine internals](/concepts/elench/engine-internals).

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Infracost analysis (optional)
records.text:
If `INFRACOST_API_KEY` is configured:
infracost breakdown --path plan.json --format json
Parses per-resource cost estimates. See [Cost Estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation).

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Upload plan artifact
records.text:
The binary `plan.tfplan` is uploaded to the Console (`POST /api/jobs/{id}/plan-artifact`) for a
later `DEPLOY` job to apply verbatim.

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: Report results
records.text:
Job status → SUCCESS with `execution_metadata`:
- Resource change counts (add / change / destroy)
- `verify_result` — the `verify.Report` (rendered in the Plan tab)
- Cost breakdown (if Infracost ran)
- Plan artifact reference

records.title: Plan Jobs
records.heading: What the user sees
records.text:
After the plan completes, the [Plan tab](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply) in the environment detail
shows:
- Resource groups with create / update / delete actions
- The verify report — per-control `pass` / `fail` / `warn` / `not_evaluable`
- Per-resource costs and total estimated monthly cost
- An "Apply" button (blocked, or requiring an override, if a hard control failed)

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.text: Probe Jobs. How the runner executes PROBE_CLUSTER jobs — a bounded, read-only liveness dial of the cluster API server that mutates nothing.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Probe Jobs
records.text:
`PROBE_CLUSTER` jobs answer one question: **is the environment's cluster reachable right now?**
This is the live half of day-2 monitoring, alongside `DETECT_DRIFT`. A probe reads the
environment's OpenTofu outputs in-process, acquires the cluster kubeconfig, and dials the
Kubernetes API server's `/readyz` endpoint. It provisions nothing and mutates nothing.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Mint cloud credentials
records.text:
Keyless per job, the same as other job types. Credentials are activated by the runner before the
handler runs. See [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Read environment outputs from the state proxy
records.text:
The runner runs `tofu output -json` against a throwaway workspace whose config is **only** a
`backend "http" {}` block, initialized against the [Console state proxy](/concepts/terraform-state)
(per-job `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`). No module is cloned and no template is copied — outputs live in state,
so no providers or resources are needed.

Output values stay **in-process only**. The sensitive `kubeconfig` output (used by Hetzner and
Alibaba) is never written to the workdir, logged, or persisted.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Acquire the cluster kubeconfig
records.text:
The provider configures a private kubeconfig from the outputs:

- **Hetzner / Alibaba** read the sensitive `kubeconfig` output from state.
- **AWS / GCP / Azure** synthesize an exec-plugin kubeconfig from the cluster name.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Dial the API server
records.text:
kubectl get --raw=/readyz
The dial is bounded by both a `kubectl --request-timeout` and a context deadline (default 30s), so a
dead endpoint fails fast instead of hanging the job. The cluster is **reachable** only when
`/readyz` returns exactly `ok`.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Enrich a reachable result (best-effort)
records.text:
When the API server answers, the probe additionally reads the Kubernetes server version and node
readiness (`total` / `ready`). A failure here does **not** flip the result to unreachable — the API
server already answered.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Report the result
records.text: The runner posts the result on `execution_metadata.probe_result` and the job ends `SUCCESS`.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Reachable is a fact, not a job outcome
records.text:
An unreachable cluster is a **successful** probe carrying `reachable: false`. That is the whole
point of the job — the honest "it's down" signal, not a job failure.
 

The handler returns an error only when the probe cannot **run** — an unreadable state proxy or an
unknown provider. That is an operational failure, distinct from an honest "the cluster is down".

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: What the probe reports
records.text:
The result carries a non-secret `ProbeResult` — no kubeconfig, token, or certificate:

 Field Meaning 
 ------- --------- 
 `reachable` `true` when the API server answered `/readyz` with `ok`. 
 `message` Short human-readable summary (especially why a cluster is unreachable). 
 `detail.endpoint` The API-server endpoint that was dialed (a public control-plane address). 
 `detail.method` The liveness mechanism — `apiserver-readyz`. 
 `detail.statusCode` The HTTP status the health endpoint returned (`200` on `ok`). 
 `detail.serverVersion` The Kubernetes server version (reachable clusters only). 
 `detail.nodeCount` / `detail.readyNodeCount` Nodes seen and Ready (best-effort). 
 `detail.latencyMs` Round-trip latency of the liveness check, in milliseconds. 
 `detail.error` The failure reason when unreachable (dial / TLS / timeout) — a message, never a secret.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: No sandbox gate
records.text:
Unlike `DETECT_DRIFT`, a probe carries **no** BYO-managed sandbox gate. It never executes the
customer's module: reading state outputs runs OpenTofu against a backend-only workspace, and the
reachability dial is Alethia's own code. There is no untrusted plugin execution to contain, so a
safe, read-only probe runs on a managed runner without the gate.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: How probes are dispatched
records.text:
The Console enqueues `PROBE_CLUSTER` jobs two ways:

- **On a schedule.** A sweeper on the reconcile loop enqueues a probe for every `ACTIVE`
 environment whose last probe is older than its tier cadence: production every 10 minutes, staging
 every hour, development every 6 hours. An environment with a probe already in flight
 (`QUEUED` / `CLAIMED` / `PROCESSING`) is skipped, so a slow runner cannot pile up duplicates.
- **On demand.** The canvas **Run** menu queues a single probe for one environment. Only one probe
 runs per environment at a time.

Both paths reuse the config snapshot from the environment's latest successful `DEPLOY`, so the
runner reads the exact provisioned state.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: What the Console does with the result
records.text:
On a `SUCCESS`, the Console appends the result as an `environment_probes` history row. When a probe
records a **true → false** transition — a cluster that was reachable and now is not — it raises a
`system.project.cluster_unreachable` alert once. A first-ever probe that is already unreachable does
not alert, and a cluster that is still down does not re-alert.

records.title: Probe Jobs
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Job Execution Overview](/concepts/runner/job-execution) — every job type and the dispatch switch.
- [tofu state](/concepts/terraform-state) — the Console HTTP state proxy the probe reads.
- [Cloud Credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials) — keyless per-job minting.

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.text: Runner Lifecycle Jobs. DEPLOY_RUNNER, UPDATE_RUNNER, and DESTROY_RUNNER jobs.

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.text:
These job types manage Runner infrastructure.

 
 Connection verification and resource discovery are **not** runner jobs. Cloud connections are
 verified server-side by the console the moment you connect (an instant auth + provisioning-permission
 probe), and the asset inventory is maintained server-side + event-driven — see
 [Connection health & inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory). The runner is
 provisioning-only.
 

These are the **self-deployed** runner path — `operator=self`, `provisioning=deployed`. They are
distinct from the [managed fleet](/concepts/runner/scaling), which the in-app scaler sizes over Hetzner
VMs (no job runs to create a managed runner — it self-registers with a bootstrap token).

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: DEPLOY_RUNNER
records.text:
Provisions a new self-deployed runner into the customer's cloud account. On AWS this is ECS Fargate,
from [`infra/templates/runner/aws/`](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates/aws).

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: Use platform credentials
records.text: Runner lifecycle jobs use the platform's own cloud credentials (not a customer cloud identity).

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: Generate tofu config
records.text:
Writes the tfvars for the AWS runner template — an ECS cluster + Fargate service (ARM64), execution
+ task IAM roles, a CloudWatch log group, and security groups. State goes through the Console proxy
(`backend "http"`).

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: tofu apply
records.text: Provisions the infrastructure in the specified region.

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: Register with Alethia
records.text:
Calls `POST /api/runners/register` to create a runner record. The runner ID and token are injected
as environment variables into the ECS task.

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: Report results
records.text:
Job status → SUCCESS. The new runner boots, sends its first heartbeat, and appears as ONLINE on the
[Runners page](/guides/runners).

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: UPDATE_RUNNER
records.text:
Updates an existing self-deployed runner to the latest release.

1. Updates the ECS task definition with the latest image tag.
2. Forces a new ECS Fargate deployment (`--force-new-deployment`).
3. The old task drains gracefully; the new task starts on the updated image.

records.title: Runner Lifecycle Jobs
records.heading: DESTROY_RUNNER
records.text:
Tears down a self-deployed runner's infrastructure.

1. Runs `tofu destroy` on the runner's ECS resources.
2. Removes the runner registration from Alethia.
3. Any jobs assigned to that runner are requeued to other available runners.

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.text: Real-time log streaming. How the runner streams OpenTofu output to the browser in real-time.

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: Real-time log streaming
records.text:
The runner streams all `tofu` output back to Alethia in real time. Users see `tofu plan` and
`tofu apply` output in the browser as it happens.

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: Architecture
records.text:
Out[JobLogger STDOUT]
 Tofu --> Err[JobLogger STDERR]
 Out --> Buf[Buffer]
 Err --> Buf
 Buf --> POST /api/jobs/id/logs Tbl[(job_logs)]
 Tbl --> NOTIFY on INSERT Listen[Console LISTEN]
 Listen --> SSE stream Browser[Browser EventSource]
`} />

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: JobLogger
records.text:
The `JobLogger` is a Go struct that wraps an `io.Writer`. It buffers output and flushes to the
Alethia API periodically.

**Two loggers per job:**
- **STDOUT logger** — captures normal `tofu` output (plan details, resource progress)
- **STDERR logger** — captures errors and warnings

**Buffer flush triggers:**
- Within ~100ms of a write (a coalescing wake), backed by a **1-second** ticker as a backstop
- When the buffer exceeds **10 KB** (size-based flush)
- On job completion (final flush)

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: API Delivery

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: Log display
records.text:
The job detail page renders logs in a terminal-like viewer, one row per chunk with a line number and
a timestamp. **STDERR** chunks render in the destructive (error) color; STDOUT and SYSTEM chunks
render in the muted text color. The viewer scrolls to the bottom as new chunks arrive.

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: Local Echo
records.text:
All log output is also written to the container's stdout — journald/`docker logs` on a managed
Hetzner fleet VM, CloudWatch Logs for a self-deployed runner on ECS Fargate, or the local terminal
for a registered runner. This provides a secondary log source for debugging.

records.title: Real-time log streaming
records.heading: Timing
records.text:
Event Latency 
 ------- --------- 
 tofu writes to stdout 0ms (piped to JobLogger) 
 JobLogger buffer flush ~100ms (coalescing wake; 1s backstop ticker) 
 API POST to Alethia ~50ms (network) 
 Database INSERT ~5ms 
 NOTIFY → SSE delivery ~50ms (server-sent event) 
 **Total: tofu output → browser** **~200ms**

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.text: Warm-pool scaling. How the managed fleet sizes itself — the in-app scaler's 60-second loop that keeps a warm pool of runners per provider, lifts it with queue depth, and destroys the idle surplus.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Warm-pool scaling
records.text:
The managed fleet runs as a **warm pool** per provider. A pool keeps a small floor of runners ready
even when the queue is empty — one by default — so the common job starts without a VM boot. When
jobs back up, an **in-app scaler** creates more VMs; when the backlog clears, it destroys the idle
surplus down to the floor again. There is no separate scaling service: the loop runs inside the
Console process (`apps/console/lib/fleet/`).

 
 **The old mechanism is retired.** The managed fleet used to be AWS ECS Fargate services scaled by
 a Python Lambda on an EventBridge schedule (`infra/fleet-aws`). That is gone. There is no Lambda,
 no EventBridge rule, and no `ecs:UpdateService` desired-count toggle in the managed path. ECS
 Fargate survives only in the **self-deployed** runner template (`infra/templates/runner/aws/`) —
 see [Self-operated runners](/guides/runners/self-operated). For the managed-fleet operator's guide
 see [Managed provisioning](/guides/self-hosting/managed-provisioning).

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: The control loop
records.text:
`apps/console/lib/fleet/` splits into a pure planner and an impure driver:

 File Role 
 --- --- 
 `scaler.ts` Hosts the 60-second tick and the fire-on-enqueue `wakeFleetScaler`. Serializes passes within a process, and lets only the fleet leader reconcile. 
 `plan.ts` **Pure** `plan(project, observed)` — diffs a pool target against observed reality and returns the minimal, safe create/drain/destroy actions. Reconciles four axes in priority order: **health → count → placement → version**. 
 `controller.ts` Applies the planned actions idempotently through the provider and records each to the `fleet_actions` ledger. 
 `provider.ts` Selects the `FleetProvider`. 
 `hcloud.ts` The Hetzner `FleetProvider` — `list`/`create`/`destroy` over the Hetzner REST API (`fetch`, no SDK). 
 `pools-db.ts` Loads the enabled `fleet_pools` rows each tick. 

`startFleetScaler()` arms a `setInterval` on a **60-second** tick (`TICK_INTERVAL_MS = 60_000`)
whenever `ALETHIA_DATABASE_URL` is set. On top of the interval, every job enqueue calls
`wakeFleetScaler()`, so a fresh `QUEUED` job does not wait up to a minute for the next tick.

 wakeFleetScaler Tick
 Timer["60s tick"] --> Tick["scaler.ts (serialized pa

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Concurrency
records.text:
Two layers keep overlapping passes from over-provisioning:

- **Within a process**, `scheduleTick()` allows at most one pass in flight. A wake that arrives
 mid-pass coalesces into a single follow-up, so a burst of enqueues cannot fan out into parallel
 read → plan → act passes that each read the same stale VM list.
- **Across replicas**, every replica runs the interval, but a tick first tries to hold the
 fleet-controller **leader lease** (`tryBecomeFleetLeader`). Only the holder reconciles. The lease
 is time-bounded, so a crashed leader is replaced once its lease expires. A per-provider apply lock
 (`tryFleetScaleLock`) stays in the controller as an inner defence.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Pools
records.text:
A pool is a row in the `fleet_pools` table, one per provider. The scaler reads the enabled rows
fresh each tick, so a pool edited in the console goes live without a redeploy, and a tick with no
enabled pools is a cheap no-op. The `FLEET_POOLS` environment variable is deprecated: it only seeds
an empty table on an existing deployment.

 Knob Default Meaning 
 --- --- --- 
 `warm_min` `1` The warm floor — healthy runners kept ready even at zero backlog. 
 `max` `10` Hard ceiling on healthy instances. 
 `buffer` `1` N+1 headroom added on top of demand, so an idle spare always exists. 
 `slots_per_runner` `1` Concurrent jobs one runner claims. 
 `surge` `1` Extra instances allowed above the target during a version rollout (`maxSurge`). 
 `scale_down_grace_ticks` `5` Consecutive over-target ticks before idle surplus is destroyed. 
 `locations` `["fsn1"]` Locations to spread across. 
 `min_per_location` `0` Minimum healthy instances to keep in each listed location.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Sizing: targetCount
records.text:
The desired healthy-instance count is a pure function (`plan.ts`, `targetCount`):

demand = max(recentPeak, ceil(backlog / slotsPerRunner))
target = clamp(max(warmMin, demand + buffer), 0, max)

 Input Source Meaning 
 ------- -------- --------- 
 `backlog` `deps.backlog(provider)` `QUEUED` jobs targeting this provider 
 `recentPeak` `deps.recentPeak(provider)` in-flight (`CLAIMED`/`PROCESSING`) jobs — auto-grows the floor 

So a pool holds `warm_min` runners warm, lifts toward `demand + buffer` as the queue grows, and never
plans the claimable (online) count below the warm floor. The default floor of one trades a little idle
cost for **no cold start** on the common case. Set `warm_min` to `0` to let a pool that tolerates boot
latency scale to zero.

Scale-down is not a desired-count decrement. Once the pool has been over target for
`scale_down_grace_ticks` consecutive ticks, the planner **destroys** idle online runners down to the
target — never a busy one, and never below a location's `min_per_location` (`scale-down-idle`).
`deps.retire()` closes each destroyed runner's `runner_usage_sessions` billing row. **Draining** is for
runners that may still hold a job: during a version ro

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Provider seam
records.text:
`getFleetProvider()` (`provider.ts`) selects the `FleetProvider` implementation. The default is
`manual`, a no-op that only logs what it would create or destroy. **`FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud`** selects
the Hetzner provider (`hcloud.ts`), a thin `list` / `create` / `destroy` over the Hetzner REST API
(`https://api.hetzner.cloud/v1`). All diff logic lives in the pure planner, so the whole reconcile is
unit-testable against a fake world (`fake-provider.ts`).

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: VM shape and self-registration
records.text:
`create` boots a Hetzner VM whose **cloud-init** does a single `docker run` of the per-cloud runner
image from GHCR:

ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner-${provider}:${tag}

The server type is a preference list: cheap ARM `cax21` first, x86 `cpx31` as the fallback
(`HCLOUD_SERVER_TYPES` overrides it). The image is `ubuntu-24.04` unless `HCLOUD_IMAGE` says
otherwise.

The VM carries **no long-lived credential**:

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Create
records.text:
`controller.ts` calls `hcloud.create()`; the VM boots with cloud-init carrying an
`ALETHIA_RUNNER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` — a **short-TTL, instance-bound** token minted for that one VM and
swept by `sweepBootstrapTokens`, not a shared fleet secret.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Self-register
records.text:
The runner exchanges the bootstrap token for its identity via `POST /api/runners/bootstrap`,
receiving its own runner id and token.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Claim and work
records.text:
The runner enters its claim loop (`POST /api/jobs/claim`) and starts claiming jobs for the clouds it
serves. Cloud auth is minted per job via keyless OIDC, and state goes through the Console state proxy.
See [Job queue](/concepts/job-queue).

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Destroy
records.text:
When backlog falls and the grace window passes, the planner destroys the idle surplus (a runner
being rolled out or torn down is drained first). The VM is deleted; billing stops.

 

 
 The container-sandbox knobs on the cloud-init (`ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container`,
 egress-enforced proxy) are **inert** until enabled — trusted provisioning boots a byte-identical
 cloud-init. See [Architecture → sandbox seam](/concepts/runner/architecture).

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: The fleet_actions ledger
records.text:
Every applied action appends a durable row via `deps.recordAction()` — the audit trail behind each
VM lifecycle event. Each `FleetActionRecord` (`controller.ts`) carries:

 Field Meaning 
 ------- --------- 
 `action` `create` \ `drain` \ `destroy` 
 `reason` `scale-up-demand`, `min-per-location`, `rollout-surge`, `rollout-drain`, `scale-down-idle`, `reap-dead`, `reap-drained`, `teardown` 
 `runnerId` correlated runner (drain/destroy); `null` for a create (the runner self-registers later) 
 `queueDepth` `QUEUED` backlog for the provider at decision time 
 `poolSize` observed online (claimable) pool size at decision time 

A ledger write is best-effort and never breaks a reconcile.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Cold start
records.text:
A cold start happens only when demand outgrows the warm floor, or for a pool set to `warm_min: 0`.
While the new VM comes up:

1. **Hetzner VM boot + image pull** — cloud-init pulls `runner- ` from GHCR.
2. **Runner boot + self-register** — `POST /api/runners/bootstrap` with the bootstrap token.
3. **First heartbeat** — `POST /api/runners/heartbeat` (30-second cadence).
4. **First job claim** — the runner drains the backlog on startup, then reacts to push wakes.

During this window the job stays `QUEUED`. The `wakeFleetScaler()` call on enqueue is what starts the
VM immediately rather than at the next 60-second tick.

records.title: Warm-pool scaling
records.heading: Cost model
records.text:
You pay for Hetzner VM-hours for the warm floor you keep (`warm_min` runners per pool, one by
default), plus the VMs above it while a backlog lasts. Managed runner cost is billed by provisioned
hours through the `runner_usage_sessions` ledger — a session opens when a managed runner comes online
and closes when `retire()` reaps it. There is no Lambda invocation cost and no idle Fargate task.

records.title: Security architecture
records.text: Security architecture. The zero-credential model — Alethia's own OIDC issuer, how each cloud federates against it and what it may do there, execution isolation, and data isolation.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Security architecture
records.text: The platform's security model is built on one principle: **never store static cloud credentials**. Every cloud access is temporary, scoped, and revocable.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Zero-Credential Model
records.text:
Traditional infrastructure tools require users to provide long-lived access keys (AWS Access Key ID, GCP service account JSON, Azure client secret). These keys are stored in configuration files, environment variables, or vault systems — creating a persistent attack surface.

Console takes a different approach. The platform never stores cloud credentials. Instead, the control plane is **its own OIDC identity provider** (see [the Alethia OIDC issuer](#the-alethia-oidc-issuer-workload-identity) below): it mints short-lived, audience-scoped assertions that each cloud federates against. **All four managed clouds are keyless** — no access key, service-account JSON, or client secret anywhere:

 Provider Mechanism Session 
 ---------- ----------- ---------
