 GCP Workload Identity Federation (OIDC token exchange) ~1 hour, auto-refreshed 
 Azure Client assertion into the customer's user-assigned managed identity (federated credential — no platform Entra app) ~1 hour, auto-refreshed 
 Alibaba `AssumeRoleWithOIDC` (anonymous — no AccessKey, no Aleth

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: The Alethia OIDC issuer (workload identity)
records.text:
Rather than assume into each cloud with a static platform key, the control plane runs a minimal,
single-purpose **workload-identity OIDC issuer** at `${APP_URL}/api/oidc` (`lib/oidc/issuer.ts`). It is
the trust root every managed cloud federates against:

- **Mint.** `mintWorkloadToken({ audience })` signs a short-lived (≤10 min) RS256 assertion with a fixed
 subject (`alethia-connector`) and the cloud's expected **audience** (`sts.amazonaws.com`,
 `alethia-gcp-wif`, `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, `sts.aliyuncs.com` — one per cloud, from
 `packages/workload-identity`). The audience scopes the token so it can't be replayed at a
 different cloud.
- **Publish.** The public half is served as a JWKS at `${APP_URL}/api/oidc/jwks` (plus an OIDC discovery
 document). The customer's cloud fetches it to verify signatures — the private key never leaves the vault.
- **Verify.** Each cloud validates the assertion (issuer + subject + audience + signature) and exchanges it
 for its own ~1 hour credential. A successful exchange **is** the proof of access.

Because the exchanged credential is short-lived, the runner re-mints the assertion into a token **file**
that the provider re-reads, so a `tofu

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The user deploys a CloudFormation template (or OpenTofu module) in their AWS account. This creates:

1. **An IAM OIDC provider** for the Alethia issuer (`${APP_URL}/api/oidc`) — the account's trust root for Alethia
2. **`AlethiaProvisionerRole`** — an IAM role whose trust policy allows **only** `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` from that provider, pinned to the fixed audience (`sts.amazonaws.com`) and subject (`alethia-connector`)

There is **no ExternalId and no trust in an Alethia AWS account** — the cryptographic sub/aud pin replaces the
confused-deputy shared secret entirely, and no other identity (not even a different Alethia token) can assume
the role.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Runtime Flow
records.text:
The control plane (for server-side connection health / inventory) and managed runners (for provisioning)
federate **directly** into the customer role with a minted assertion — a single hop, no platform account:

 >STS: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity(customer RoleArn, OIDC assertion) — no access key
 STS-->>R: Temporary customer credentials (~1h)
 Note over R: tofu runs; the assertion auto-refreshes from the re-read token file
`} />

How a managed runner hands the assertion to OpenTofu, and how a self-operated runner differs, is in
[Cloud credentials → AWS](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials#aws-keyless-assumerolewithwebidentity).

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Permissions scope
records.text:
The OIDC trust above controls *who* may assume the role. This section is *what* the role is allowed to do —
a separate, independent axis.

**Exactly what Alethia provisions in AWS** (every service the project templates can touch — feature-gated,
so a given Project uses a subset): EC2/VPC (subnets, NAT, route tables, security groups, VPC endpoints),
EKS (cluster, managed node groups, add-ons, IRSA OIDC provider + roles), RDS (Aurora), ElastiCache
(Redis/Valkey), Route 53, ACM, Secrets Manager, DynamoDB, SQS/SNS, ECR, S3, KMS (envelope keys), CloudWatch
Logs + Kinesis Firehose (log delivery), EventBridge (Karpenter interruption), Application Auto Scaling, and
the IAM roles for the in-cluster controllers (external-dns, the AWS Load Balancer Controller, EBS CSI,
Karpenter, …).

 
**Least-privilege by default — no account admin, fully action-enumerated.** The setup attaches **five
scoped policies** instead of `AdministratorAccess`: `ComputeNet`, `ComputeScale`, `Data`, `Edge` (the
data-plane, split into net/scale to stay under AWS's 6144-char managed-policy limit — each lists the
**specific `ec2:`/`eks:`/`rds:`/… actions** the templates issue, not `service:*`), and an action-enumerated

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The user configures a Workload Identity Pool and Provider in their GCP project:

1. Creates a Workload Identity Pool
2. Adds an OIDC Provider with the Console issuer URL and audience
3. Binds a GCP service account to the pool with `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser`

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Runtime Flow
records.text:
>STS: Present minted OIDC token (Console issuer)
 STS-->>R: Short-lived GCP access token (~1h)
 Note over R: tofu runs with the exchanged credentials
`} />

No service account JSON key files are created or stored. The OIDC token exchange happens at runtime for each job.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Permissions scope
records.text:
**Exactly what Alethia provisions in GCP:** Compute/VPC (networks, subnets, Cloud Router + NAT, firewall
rules, Cloud Armor), GKE (cluster + node pools), Cloud SQL, Memorystore (Redis), Cloud DNS, Artifact
Registry, Secret Manager, Cloud Storage, Firestore, Pub/Sub, and the workload-identity service accounts +
bindings for in-cluster controllers.

 
**Least-privilege by default — no `roles/editor`.** The service account gets **11 predefined roles + 5
custom roles**. The predefined roles are kept for services whose Google-maintained admin set is already
tightly scoped and churns with new features (container / compute.network / compute.security /
servicenetworking / cloudsql / redis / dns / artifactregistry / secretmanager / cloudkms, plus
`iam.serviceAccountUser`) — hand-enumerating those buys nothing. `cloudkms.admin` lets the provisioner
create the customer-managed key that encrypts Kubernetes Secrets; it carries no permission to *use* that
key, so the provisioner writes the key's encrypt/decrypt binding for the cluster and can never read a
Secret with it. The **5 custom roles replace the predefined admin roles that bundled
data-plane access a provisioner must never hold**, granti

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Azure: Federated Identity
records.text:
Azure is keyless and **customer-side** — there is **no platform Entra app** and no `ALETHIA_AZURE_CLIENT_ID`.
The customer creates a **user-assigned managed identity** in their own subscription (a plain ARM resource —
no App Registration, no directory-admin rights) with a **federated-identity credential** trusting the
Alethia OIDC issuer (subject `alethia-connector`, audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`). The console and the
runner authenticate **as that customer identity** (its `client_id` is stored per-connection) via a client
assertion — **no client secret**. This is parity with the GCP Workload Identity Federation model.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The customer runs the connect script (Azure Cloud Shell or OpenTofu), which creates everything in **their**
subscription and stores nothing but three public identifiers:

1. `az identity create` — a user-assigned managed identity in the customer's subscription
2. `az identity federated-credential create` — a credential trusting the Alethia issuer (subject
 `alethia-connector`, audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`)
3. `az role definition/assignment create` — the least-privilege **Alethia Provisioner** custom role (below)

The customer pastes back their **tenant id**, **subscription id**, and the **managed identity's client id**.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Runtime Flow
records.text:
>AZ: Present minted OIDC assertion as a client assertion
 AZ-->>R: Access token for Azure Resource Manager (~1h)
 Note over R: tofu runs; the runner re-mints into the token file so long applies refresh
`} />

No client secret is ever generated or stored. Access revocation is instant by deleting the managed
identity (or its role assignment) in the customer's subscription.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Permissions scope
records.text:
**Exactly what Alethia provisions in Azure:** Resource Group, AKS (+ node pools), VNet (subnets, NSGs, NAT
gateway, public IPs), PostgreSQL Flexible Server (+ private DNS zone), Redis Cache, DNS zones, Container
Registry, Key Vault (+ secrets), Storage, Service Bus, Cosmos DB, WAF policy, and the managed identities +
role assignments for in-cluster workload identity.

 
**Least-privilege by default — a custom role, not `Contributor`.** The customer's managed identity is granted a
**custom role definition** ("Alethia Provisioner") enumerating only the actions the services above need —
including the AKS credential-list and per-resource-provider registration that `Contributor` omits (so this
also *fixes* a gap: pure `Contributor` cannot create the external-dns role assignment the templates require).
The one escalation-grade permission it needs — `roleAssignments/write` — is **constrained by an ABAC
condition** to a single built-in role (*DNS Zone Contributor*), so the connector can grant that to the
external-dns identity and **nothing else** (no path to Owner). See the
[Azure connector guide](/guides/connectors/azure).

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Alibaba: RAM Role via OIDC (account-free)
records.text:
Alibaba is keyless **and account-free** — Alethia holds no Alibaba account and no AccessKey. The customer
applies an OpenTofu module that creates a **RAM OIDC provider** (fixed name `alethia`) trusting the Alethia
issuer plus a **RAM role**, then pastes the role ARN (Alethia derives the provider ARN from it).

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Runtime Flow
records.text:
>STS: AssumeRoleWithOIDC(RoleArn, OIDCProviderArn, minted token) — anonymous, no AccessKey
 STS-->>R: Temporary STS credentials (~1h)
 Note over R: tofu runs; the runner re-mints into the token file so long applies refresh
`} />

`AssumeRoleWithOIDC` is an anonymous STS action — the OIDC token itself authenticates the call, so there is
no AccessKey and no request signature. On the runner, the `alicloud` provider performs the exchange itself
from `ALIBABA_CLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE` (re-read on refresh). Revocation is instant by deleting the RAM role.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Permissions scope
records.text:
**Exactly what Alethia provisions in Alibaba Cloud:** ACK (managed cluster + node pool), VPC (vSwitches, NAT,
SNAT), EIP, RDS, Container Registry EE, KVStore (Redis), AliDNS, KMS, Message Service (MNS), OSS, and
Tablestore (OTS). Not a WAF: Alibaba's WAF 3.0 instance is an account-level purchase, so Alethia does not
buy one on your behalf and the role is granted no `yundun-waf` actions.

 
**Least-privilege by enumerated custom policy — never account admin.** The Alibaba RAM role attaches **4
enumerated custom policies** (replacing the per-service `*FullAccess` System policies): `ComputeCluster`
(ACK + its transitive node-pool ECS + API-server/Service SLB), `Network` (VPC/vSwitch/NAT/SNAT + EIP),
`Data` (RDS/KVStore/OSS/Tablestore/KMS), and `EdgeReg` (Container Registry/AliDNS/MNS). Each lists the
**specific create/read/modify/delete/tag actions** the templates issue (reads stay `Describe*`/`Get*`/`List*`
so a provider bump doesn't break a real apply) — never `service:*`, `AliyunRAMFullAccess`, or an admin
policy. The service-linked roles ACK/NAT need are covered by a **narrow custom policy granting only
`ram:CreateServiceLinkedRole`** (service-linked roles are cloud-managed with f

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Key rotation
records.text:
The issuer's signing key is the trust root for all four clouds, so it rotates with **zero downtime** via an
overlap: the JWKS publishes the outgoing and the new key at once, and each assertion's `kid` header selects
the right one. New assertions are signed by the new key while in-flight ones still verify; the old key is
retired once every cloud's cached JWKS has refreshed. The operator steps are in the
[rotation runbook](/guides/self-hosting/managed-cloud-connectors#rotating-the-issuer-signing-key).

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Execution isolation (managed untrusted BYO)
records.text:
Keyless auth controls *who* can touch a cloud; **execution isolation** controls what the *provisioning code
itself* can do. In **managed** mode Alethia runs the provisioning fleet, so the trust question is: whose code
runs on it?

- **Trusted templates** — Alethia's own project templates (EKS/GKE/AKS/ACK/Talos + supporting services) run
 in-process on the runner. They are reviewed platform code, so this is safe.
- **Untrusted bring-your-own** — customer OpenTofu / Helm (a provider, an `external` data source, a chart
 hook) is arbitrary code. It runs inside a **per-job container sandbox**: a fresh container per job with its
 own PID namespace, an **allowlisted environment** (no runner token, no storage key, no signing key — only
 the short-lived, job-scoped cloud credentials it needs), read-only credential mounts, and a **default-deny,
 domain-allowlisted network**. A fail-closed guard refuses to start the container if any platform secret
 would leak into it.

Three properties keep the blast radius of a single job to that one job:

- **No storage master key on the runner.** OpenTofu state goes through a Console **state proxy**
 (`backend "http"` → `/api/jobs/[id]/state`) authenticat

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Signing in
records.text:
People sign in to the console with Better Auth (OAuth or email OTP, a cookie-backed session) and to the
CLI with a device grant or a service-account token. Runners authenticate with a per-runner token stored
only as a hash. Each is explained in [Authentication flows](/concepts/authentication).

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Row Level Security (RLS)
records.text:
Every org-scoped table in the database has a coarse Row Level Security policy keyed on `org_id`. The current org is set per request via `set_config('app.current_org', …)`, driven by a Policy Decision Point (PDP) in the app:

CREATE POLICY "Org members can only access own org data"
 ON projects FOR ALL
 USING (org_id = current_setting('app.current_org')::uuid);

This means even if there is a bug in application code that constructs a query without a `WHERE org_id = ?` clause, PostgreSQL will filter the results to only the current org's data. A raw `SELECT * FROM projects` returns only the current org's Projects.

RLS is the coarse, unbypassable backstop; fine-grained role/permission decisions are made by the PDP. See [Access Control](/concepts/access-control) for the full authorization model (roles, permissions, grants, and the org/tenancy model).

Cloud identities are additionally filtered by provider — an AWS identity will not appear in a GCP context.

records.title: Security architecture
records.heading: Git Token Management
records.text:
OAuth tokens for Git providers (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) are stored on the Better Auth `account` table:

- Better Auth persists each linked provider's `accessToken` / `refreshToken` / expiry on `account` at login
- The `getValidProviderToken()` server action checks token expiry before use
- Expired tokens are automatically refreshed via the provider's refresh flow
- Access is scoped to the owning user (the `org_id` RLS backstop + the PDP)

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.text: OpenTofu State Management. How OpenTofu state is stored in S3-compatible object storage, organized by environment, and shared across runner executions.

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: OpenTofu State Management
records.text:
OpenTofu tracks the real-world resources it manages in a **state file**. Alethia never hands a runner an
object-storage key. Instead, **every** provisioning job reaches state through the Console **state proxy**
using OpenTofu's built-in `http` backend, and the Console persists the bytes to S3-compatible object
storage (SeaweedFS by default, swappable for Garage, MinIO, AWS S3, or R2). This lets runners share state
across executions and resume from failures while holding zero storage credentials.

 

 
 The state proxy is the **universal** path — trusted Alethia templates and managed **untrusted**
 bring-your-own code alike. The runner authenticates to `/api/jobs/{id}/state` with a per-job,
 key-scoped token minted at claim time (`stateBackend()` in `apps/runner/internal/agent/runner.go`),
 passed to `tofu` only via `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD` — never written to the workdir. See
 [Security → Execution isolation](/concepts/security#execution-isolation-managed-untrusted-byo).

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: State Backend
records.text:
The runner writes a `backend "http"` config (`WriteBackendHCL` in `packages/core/cloud/http_backend.go`)
and runs `tofu init -backend-config= `. The state, lock, and unlock endpoints all point at the
Console proxy for that job; the per-job token travels out-of-band in `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD` (App Router can't

hcl

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: backend.hcl — generated per job, consumed by tofu init -backend-config=backend.hcl
records.text:
address = "{console_url}/api/jobs/{job_id}/state"
lock_address = "{console_url}/api/jobs/{job_id}/state/lock"
unlock_address = "{console_url}/api/jobs/{job_id}/state/lock"

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: TF_HTTP_USERNAME=alethia, TF_HTTP_PASSWORD=<per-job state token>  (from the process env, not this file)
records.text:
Behind the proxy, the Console reads and writes each environment's state object in S3-compatible storage,
keyed as `{project}-{environment}-{region}/tofu.tfstate`. The S3 endpoint/bucket/credentials live
**server-side on the Console**, never on the runner.

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: Path Structure
records.text:
The state key is `{project}-{environment}-{region}/tofu.tfstate`, so **every environment** — not
just every project — gets its own state file:

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

This is why a project's `staging` and `production` are fully isolated: they are separate state files.
The key is derived from the environment's `name` (see [Domain Model](/concepts/domain-model#environments)).

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: During tofu plan
records.text:
1. The runner mints a per-job state token and writes `backend.hcl` pointing at the Console proxy
2. `tofu init` pulls the existing state (if any) from the proxy via the `http` backend
3. `tofu plan` compares the desired configuration against the current state
4. The plan output describes what will change

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: During tofu apply
records.text:
1. `tofu apply` executes the plan, taking a state lock via `POST` to the lock address
2. After each resource is created/updated/destroyed, OpenTofu writes the updated state back through the proxy
3. If the apply fails mid-way, the state reflects the partial progress

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: During tofu destroy
records.text:
1. `tofu destroy` removes all resources tracked in the state
2. The state file is left empty (or removed)

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: Why proxy the state?
records.text:
- **Zero storage credentials on the runner** — the runner never sees an S3 key; it holds only a per-job,
 key-scoped state token in `TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`. This is what lets managed untrusted BYO code run safely.
- **Locked coordination** — the `http` backend takes a lock via the proxy's lock address (`POST`/`DELETE`),
 keeping concurrent runs on the same environment safe.
- **Consistent across runners** — every runner reads and writes the same state through the proxy, so
 executions share a single source of truth.
- **Portable storage** — behind the proxy, any S3-compatible backend works (SeaweedFS, Garage, MinIO, AWS
 S3, R2); the Console's endpoint is swappable, so you are never locked to one provider.
- **Cross-provider** — works regardless of whether the environment targets AWS, GCP, Azure, or Hetzner.

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: State and Failure Recovery
records.text:
Because state is persisted after every resource operation:

- If a runner dies mid-apply, the state reflects all resources created so far
- A retry (new job) runs `tofu init` → downloads the existing state → `tofu plan` only shows remaining resources
- No resources are double-created

This is why OpenTofu state is the foundation of the platform's reliability model.

records.title: OpenTofu State Management
records.heading: Plan Artifacts
records.text:
In addition to state, **plan artifacts** are stored in a separate S3-compatible bucket (`plan-artifacts`). These are the binary `plan.tfplan` files that capture exactly what OpenTofu will do.

When a user applies after reviewing a plan, the runner downloads the plan artifact and passes it to `tofu apply plan.tfplan`. This ensures the apply executes exactly what was planned, even if the configuration has changed since the plan was generated.

 
Plan artifacts are validated with a **config hash**. If the environment's configuration was modified after the plan was generated, the hash won't match and the apply will fail, forcing the user to re-plan. This prevents stale plans from being applied.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.text: How Alethia compares. Where Alethia sits between IaC orchestrators and BYOC app-PaaSes — and the honest tradeoffs versus Porter, Qovery, and Spacelift.

records.title: How Alethia compares
records.heading: How Alethia compares
records.text:
Most infrastructure tools fall into two camps, and Alethia deliberately sits in the gap
between them:

- **IaC orchestrators** (Terraform Cloud, Spacelift) run the IaC *you* write. Powerful, but
 they hand you plumbing — you still author and operate everything.
- **BYOC app-PaaSes** (Porter, Qovery, Northflank) give you a product, but the control plane
 is *their* hosted SaaS, the deploy pipeline is proprietary, and pricing meters your compute.

**Alethia is a self-hostable control plane that designs and provisions real infrastructure
with zero stored credentials, and hands you standard EKS + ArgoCD + OpenTofu you own.**

 Alethia IaC orchestrators BYOC app-PaaS 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Self-host the control plane **Yes** (~4 containers, AGPL) Top tier only No 
 Stores your cloud credentials **No** (role assumed at run time) N/A (you run IaC) Usually yes / privileged 
 Runs your bring-your-own code **Per-job [sealed sandbox](/concepts/isolated-execution)** (no shared secrets, no cloud metadata, allowlisted egress) Shared workers / your own runners Their hosted pipeline 
 App delivery **Real ArgoCD, GitOps, portable** CI apply on push Proprietary pipeline 
 What you own when you leave Cl

records.title: Alethia vs Porter
records.text: Alethia vs Porter. Porter is a BYOC app-PaaS with a hosted control plane and a proprietary deploy pipeline. Alethia is self-hostable, GitOps-native, and open source — same ownership of your cloud, opposite ownership of the platform.

records.title: Alethia vs Porter
records.heading: Alethia vs Porter
records.text:
**Porter** ("Heroku in your own cloud") points at a GitHub repo and builds, deploys, and
autoscales your app on a managed cluster in your cloud account. It's a mature, YC-backed
BYOC PaaS. The key difference is **who owns the platform layer**.

 Dimension Alethia Porter 
 --- --- --- 
 Own / self-host the **control plane** **Yes** — ~4 containers (Postgres + S3 + app + runner) No — control plane is Porter's hosted SaaS 
 Zero stored cloud credentials **Yes** — runner assumes roles at run time Yes for AWS/GCP (AssumeRole / WIF); Azure SP is the exception 
 App delivery **Real ArgoCD wired to your repo** (GitOps, portable) Proprietary build+deploy pipeline (`porter.yaml`) 
 Lock-in if you leave Cluster + OpenTofu + ArgoCD keep working Cluster keeps working; the deploy pipeline + console don't 
 Open source **AGPL core** + small commercial `ee/` Closed product (launched MIT, monorepo since pulled) 
 Pricing Free self-host; commercial for orgs/SSO Usage-based per vCPU/GB-RAM on top of your cloud bill; no free tier 
 Multi-cloud EKS today; GKE/AKS in progress AWS/GCP/Azure all GA 
 Day-2 ops (logs/metrics/rollbacks) Thinner today Mature, SRE-monitored

records.title: Alethia vs Porter
records.heading: Where Alethia wins
records.text:
- **You can own the entire control plane** — self-host with no SaaS dependency. Porter's
 control plane is irreducibly their hosted service (self-host was promised in 2021, never shipped).
- **Standard, portable GitOps** — real ArgoCD wired to your Git; if Alethia disappears, apps
 still deploy from a `git push`. Porter's pipeline is proprietary.
- **Open source + no compute meter** — no per-vCPU/GB markup on top of your cloud bill.

records.title: Alethia vs Porter
records.heading: Where Porter wins (honest)
records.text:
- **Maturity of day-2 ops** — logs, metrics, autoscaling, preview environments, rollbacks,
 alerting, all SRE-monitored.
- **Multi-cloud is GA today** across AWS/GCP/Azure; Alethia leads with AWS.
- **Polished app-deploy UX** for the "push a repo, get a running app" path.

 
Bottom line: pick Porter if you want a managed, batteries-included app-deploy experience and
don't mind a hosted control plane + usage pricing. Pick Alethia if you must **own the control
plane**, keep **standard portable GitOps**, and avoid a compute meter.

records.title: Alethia vs Qovery
records.text: Alethia vs Qovery. Qovery is the closest structural analog — a BYOC Kubernetes control plane. The difference is a hosted, privileged orchestrator vs a self-hostable, credential-free one.

records.title: Alethia vs Qovery
records.heading: Alethia vs Qovery
records.text:
**Qovery** is a BYOC Kubernetes control plane / app-PaaS — connect a repo + your cloud, and it
provisions managed Kubernetes in your account and deploys into it (recently repositioned around
"Kubernetes for humans **and AI agents**"). It's the closest structural analog to Alethia; the
divergence is **ownership and the credential model**.

 Dimension Alethia Qovery 
 --- --- --- 
 Control plane **Self-hostable** (~4 containers, AGPL) Qovery-hosted SaaS by default; self-host only on Enterprise 
 Credential model **Runner assumes roles at run time; control plane holds nothing** Hosted control plane is a privileged orchestrator into your account (even with STS) 
 App delivery **Real ArgoCD wired to your repo** (portable) Qovery's engine *is* the delivery layer (remove it → rebuild your pipeline) 
 Provisioned stack Cluster **+ Aurora/ElastiCache/DynamoDB/SQS-SNS/ECR/S3/Secrets/Route53/WAF** in one Project App-platform-centric; most managed data services left to you 
 Pricing Free self-host; commercial for orgs/SSO Per-org + seats + deploy-minutes; self-host gated to Enterprise 
 Open source **AGPL core** Proprietary

records.title: Alethia vs Qovery
records.heading: Where Alethia wins
records.text:
- **Truly credential-free** — the control plane never holds privileged access; Qovery's hosted
 brain is always a privileged orchestrator into your account.
- **Self-host on day one, for free** — AGPL, ~4 containers. Qovery gates self-host behind Enterprise.
- **Portable app-delivery** — real ArgoCD; delete Alethia and your cluster + GitOps keep running.
- **Broader stack in one Project** + no per-seat / per-deploy-minute meter.

records.title: Alethia vs Qovery
records.heading: Where Qovery wins (honest)
records.text:
- **Multi-cloud breadth GA** (EKS/GKE/AKS/Scaleway + bring-your-own clusters) today.
- **Mature platform** — well-funded, established, with a polished console and the new
 AI-agent guardrails/policy story.
- **Managed app-platform UX** is further along than Alethia's V1 dashboard.

 
Bottom line: Qovery is the more mature managed control plane. Choose Alethia when "the control
plane must be ours and hold no credentials" is a hard requirement.

records.title: Alethia vs Spacelift
records.text: Alethia vs Spacelift. Spacelift orchestrates the IaC you write. Alethia delivers the outcome — a complete cluster + ArgoCD + data services — and still hands you OpenTofu you own.

records.title: Alethia vs Spacelift
records.heading: Alethia vs Spacelift
records.text:
**Spacelift** is an IaC orchestration platform (a "TACOS" — Terraform Automation and
Collaboration Software): point it at a repo of Terraform / OpenTofu / Pulumi / etc. and it runs
plan/apply pipelines with policy-as-code, drift detection, and state management. It does **not**
ship you a cluster — it orchestrates whatever IaC *you* author.

 Dimension Alethia Spacelift 
 --- --- --- 
 What you get **A complete production cluster** (EKS + Aurora/ElastiCache/DynamoDB/SQS-SNS/ECR/S3/Secrets/Route53/WAF) + ArgoCD + operators A runner for **IaC you write & maintain** 
 App delivery **Real ArgoCD/GitOps wired to your repo** CI apply-on-push; not a live GitOps loop, not an app platform 
 Effort to first cluster Design a Project → provision Author all the IaC yourself first 
 Self-host the control plane **Yes — AGPL, a handful of containers** Self-hosted edition only on the top Enterprise+ tier 
 Open source **AGPL core** Proprietary SaaS (only the worker is OSS) 
 Credentials Runner assumes roles at run time You wire cloud creds into the runner

records.title: Alethia vs Spacelift
records.heading: Where Alethia wins
records.text:
- **Delivers an outcome, not plumbing** — one Project → a batteries-included cluster, handed to you.
 Spacelift only runs IaC you must author and maintain.
- **Real GitOps app-delivery** wired to your repo — Spacelift is a CI runner, not ArgoCD.
- **Self-hostable for everyone** (AGPL), and you still **own the OpenTofu** it generates.

records.title: Alethia vs Spacelift
records.heading: Where Spacelift wins (honest)
records.text:
- **Best-in-class for orchestrating existing, complex IaC** at scale — multi-tool (Terraform,
 Pulumi, CloudFormation, Ansible), policy-as-code (OPA/Rego), drift detection, mature collaboration.
- **Established, well-funded**, OpenTofu founding member; deep governance for large IaC estates.
- If you already have a big hand-written IaC codebase, Spacelift manages it; Alethia generates a new one.

 
Bottom line: Spacelift orchestrates IaC you own and operate. Alethia gives you the cluster +
GitOps as a product *and* hands you portable OpenTofu — choose it when you want the outcome,
not just the pipeline.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.text: Feature matrix. The authoritative, capability-by-capability comparison of the open-source Community edition and the licensed Enterprise edition.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Feature matrix
records.text:
The single source of truth for what each edition includes. Community is free and
open-source (AGPL-3.0); Enterprise is licensed.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Authorization core
records.text:
Everything here is **open-source** — the authorization model is the same in both editions.

 Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Policy Decision Point (`can` / `enforce` / `bulkCheck` / `listAccessible`) ✅ ✅ 
 Built-in roles — owner · admin · operator · viewer ✅ ✅ 
 Per-resource grants + Org → Project inheritance ✅ ✅ 
 Explicit **deny** with hierarchy + exceptions ✅ ✅ 
 Single-permission grants (not just roles) ✅ ✅ 
 Row-Level Security tenant isolation (the blast wall) ✅ ✅ 
 Full **Activity log** (every action + denials) ✅ ✅ 
 Registry-as-code (resources × actions, exhaustively typed) ✅ ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Organizations & teams
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Personal organization (single owner — you) ✅ ✅ 
 **Multi-member organizations** — ✅ 
 **Member invitations** (email → accept → join) — ✅ 
 **Active-organization switcher** — ✅ 
 **Teams** (group-based grants) — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Roles & access
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Built-in role catalog (read-only) ✅ ✅ 
 **Custom roles** — the permission-matrix editor — ✅ 
 **Access portal** — AWS-IAM-style grant assignment — ✅ 
 Grant to a **user or a team**, allow/deny, any scope — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Authentication
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Email OTP + social sign-in (GitHub · Google · GitLab · Bitbucket) ✅ ✅ 
 **SSO — OIDC** (Okta · Entra ID · Google · AWS IAM Identity Center · …) — ✅ 
 **SSO — SAML** — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Activity
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Browse the Activity log in the console ✅ ✅ 
 **Export** the Activity log (CSV) — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Engine
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 `PostgresRbacPDP` — the Postgres-backed engine ✅ ✅ 
 **OpenFGA fine-grained engine** (ReBAC at scale) — ✅ (optional) 
 Dual-write tuple sync (Postgres → OpenFGA) — ✅ 

 
 The OpenFGA engine is **optional even with a license** — Enterprise runs perfectly on `PostgresRbacPDP`.
 Turn OpenFGA on when you want a dedicated relationship-graph engine. See the
 [OpenFGA operator guide](/concepts/access-control/openfga).

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Operations
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 **Alerting** — alert policies, channels, delivery log — ✅ 
 **Advanced alerting** — security/governance rules from Activity events — ✅ 
 **Bring-your-own runners** — deploy into your cloud or register your own — ✅ 
 **Managed warm-pool fleet** operations — ✅ 

 
 On the hosted service, entitlements follow each organization's billing plan
 (`apps/console/lib/billing/plan.ts`). The **Team** plan sits between the two columns: it unlocks
 multi-member organizations, alerting and bring-your-own runners, but not teams, custom roles,
 Activity export, advanced alerting, SSO or managed pools.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: How the line is drawn
records.text:
Community is a **complete single-tenant product**: roles, grants, hierarchy, deny, the PDP, RLS, and the Activity
log all ship open-source. Enterprise is about **organizations of people** — inviting and grouping members,
authenticating them with SSO, authoring fine-grained custom roles, assigning access through the portal, and
(optionally) deciding it with OpenFGA.

Next: [how licensing works](/editions/licensing).

records.title: Editions
records.text: Editions. Alethia is open-core — a free, open-source Community edition and a licensed Enterprise edition. What each includes, and why the split is where it is.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Editions
records.text:
Alethia is **open-core**. There are two editions, built from the *same codebase*:

- Community — the free, **open-source** edition, licensed **AGPL-3.0**. The complete
 single-tenant product. You can run it for yourself or your team forever, at no cost, with no license key.
- Enterprise — the **licensed** edition (commercial). Everything in Community **plus**
 multi-member organizations, teams, SSO, custom roles, the fine-grained access portal, the OpenFGA policy
 engine, and activity export.

 
 You can **self-host either edition.** "Self-hosting" is about *where Alethia runs* (your own
 infrastructure); "edition" is about *which features are licensed*. Community needs nothing extra; Enterprise
 needs a license key and a couple of extra services (see [Licensing](/editions/licensing)).

records.title: Editions
records.heading: The dividing line
records.text:
The simplest way to think about it:

> **Everything you need to run Alethia for yourself, or for a team that shares one account, is free and
> open-source. The Enterprise edition is about *many people, many identities* — organizations with multiple
> members, the teams and roles to organize them, the SSO to let them in, and the engine to authorize them at
> scale.**

Concretely:

 
 
 The Policy Decision Point, built-in roles, per-resource grants with Org → Project inheritance,
 Row-Level Security tenant isolation, and the authorization Activity log — all open-source. Your account is a
 single-owner "personal organization".
 
 
 Multi-member organizations, teams, member invitations, SSO (OIDC + SAML), configurable custom roles, the
 AWS-IAM-style access portal (allow/deny, per-resource), the OpenFGA fine-grained engine, and activity export.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Why open-core?
records.text:
The authorization *model* — how a decision is made — is the same in both editions, and it's open. What
Enterprise adds is the machinery for **organizations of people**: ways to invite and group them (members,
teams, invitations), authenticate them (SSO), describe what they can do (custom roles, allow/deny), and decide
it quickly at scale (OpenFGA). None of that is needed to run Alethia for a single tenant — so it isn't in the
free core.

The boundary is enforced in code: **the open-source core never depends on the Enterprise package, and runs
completely without it present.** See the [open-core architecture](/concepts/access-control/open-core) for how that's
guaranteed (a one-way dependency + CI guards), and [Licensing](/editions/licensing) for how a license turns
the Enterprise features on.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- The complete [**feature matrix**](/editions/feature-matrix) — every capability, Community vs Enterprise.
- How [**licensing**](/editions/licensing) works (entitlements, activation, graceful degradation).
- The [**Enterprise setup runbook**](/guides/self-hosting/enterprise-setup) — turning Enterprise on, end to end.
- The [**Access Control**](/concepts/access-control) section — the full authorization reference.

records.title: Licensing
records.text: Licensing. How the Enterprise license works — entitlements, activation, and graceful degradation back to the open-source defaults.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Licensing
records.text:
The Enterprise features are gated by a license. This page explains the mechanism;
the [Enterprise setup runbook](/guides/self-hosting/enterprise-setup) walks through turning it all on.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Entitlements, not scattered checks
records.text:
Alethia never sprinkles `if (licensed)` through the code. Instead, the licensed layer answers a small set of
**entitlements**, and the product reads those:

 Entitlement Unlocks 
 --- --- 
 `organizations` Multi-member orgs, members, invitations, the active-org switcher 
 `teams` Team (access-group) management — create teams and scope grants to them 
 `sso` SSO sign-in (OIDC + SAML) 
 `customRoles` The custom-role editor + the access portal 
 `activityExport` CSV export of the Activity log (viewing is free) 
 `alerting` The alerting surface — policies, channels, and the delivery activity log 
 `advancedAlerting` Security/governance alert rules sourced from PDP Activity events 
 `byoRunners` Bring-your-own runners — deploy into your cloud or register your own 
 `managedPools` Managed warm-pool fleet operations (pools, versions, economics) 

A license also carries runner-scheduling `quotas` (max concurrent jobs, priority band, included
runner-minutes, activity retention).

Without a license, **every entitlement is `false`** and the console shows the open-source experience: a single
personal organization, the four built-in roles (read-only), and a browsable (non-exportable) Activity l

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Where entitlements come from
records.text:
Entitlements are produced by the Enterprise package (`@alethia/ee`), which the core loads through **one
tolerant seam** (`lib/enterprise.ts`). The rule that makes this open-core:

> **The open-source core never imports the Enterprise package, and runs completely if it's absent.** The seam
> tries to load `@alethia/ee`; if it isn't installed, the core falls back to the Community defaults — nothing
> breaks.

So there are really two ways a deployment is "Community":

1. **The open-source build** — `@alethia/ee` isn't installed at all.
2. **An Enterprise build without an active license** — `@alethia/ee` is present, and each organization's
 entitlements fall back to its billing record (`resolveOrgEntitlements` in
 `apps/console/lib/billing/queries.ts`). An organization with no live paid plan resolves to all-`false`.

For an organization without a paid plan, both behave identically: the Community product. See the
[open-core architecture](/concepts/access-control/open-core) for the boundary guarantees and CI guards.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Graceful degradation
records.text:
Because the seam is tolerant, an Enterprise deployment **never hard-fails** if the license is missing or
expires — it degrades to Community behavior. Members already in an organization keep their data; the org
simply stops accepting new enterprise-only operations until the license is restored.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Activating Enterprise
records.text:
At a high level, enabling Enterprise is: install `@alethia/ee`, provide a license, run the extra migrations,
and (optionally) bring up OpenFGA. The full, ordered checklist is in the
[**Enterprise setup runbook**](/guides/self-hosting/enterprise-setup).

 
 Self-hosting an Enterprise deployment requires a commercial license. Running the **open-source Community
 edition** never does. If you only need a single-tenant Alethia, you never touch any of this.

records.text: Quickstart. Sign up, connect a cloud and a Git provider, create a project, deploy it, and open the cluster it provisions.

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Quickstart
records.text:
This page takes you from a new account to a running Kubernetes cluster in the Alethia console.
To do the same from a terminal, see [The CLI](/get-started/the-cli).

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- An account on one of the supported clouds: AWS, GCP, Azure, Hetzner, or Alibaba Cloud.
 You need permission to create roles or API tokens in that account.
- A GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket account.

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Sign up
records.text:
1. Open the console.
2. Select **Continue with email**, or sign in with GitHub, Google, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
 The email path sends a 6-digit code. A self-hosted console shows only the sign-in providers it configures.
3. On first sign-in, choose a plan and name your organization.

The console then opens your organization's **Overview**.

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Connect a cloud
records.text:
1. Select **Connectors** in the sidebar.
2. On your cloud's card, select **Connect**. A setup sheet opens.
3. Follow the steps for your cloud:

 
 
 1. Select **Open CloudShell**. AWS CloudShell opens in your browser.
 2. Copy the setup command from the sheet and run it in CloudShell. The command creates an IAM role that trusts Alethia. No access keys are created.
 3. Paste the `role_arn` that the command prints into **IAM Role ARN**.
 4. Select **Connect**. Alethia verifies that it can assume the role.
 
 
 1. Select **Open Cloud Shell**.
 2. Copy the setup command, replace `YOUR_PROJECT_ID`, and run it. The command creates a Workload Identity Pool that trusts Alethia. No service account keys are created.
 3. Enter the **Project ID** and **Project Number** that the command prints.
 4. Select **Connect**.
 
 
 1. Select **Open Cloud Shell**. Azure Cloud Shell opens in your browser.
 2. Copy the setup command, replace `YOUR_SUBSCRIPTION_ID`, and run it. The command creates a managed identity with a federated credential. No client secret is created.
 3. Enter the **Tenant ID**, **Client ID**, and **Subscription ID** that the command prints.
 4. Select **Connect**.
 
 
 1. Select **Op

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Connect a Git provider
records.text:
1. On the **Connectors** page, find the GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket card.
2. Select **Connect**.
3. Authorize Alethia in the provider's OAuth screen. The provider returns you to **Connectors**.

See [Git providers](/guides/connectors/git-providers) for the scopes Alethia requests.

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Create a project
records.text:
1. On the **Overview** page, select **Create**, then **Project**.
 With no projects yet, you can select **Create a Project** instead.
2. Under **Start from scratch**, select **Start from a template**.
 The **Configure your project** screen opens.
3. Enter a name under **Project**.
4. Under **Template**, select **Standard**, **AI Workloads**, or **Custom**.
 Standard and AI Workloads each name a starter repository to copy. Custom names none.
5. Under **Cloud & region**, select the cloud account you connected and a region.
6. Under **Environments**, keep or change the environments.
7. Select **Create project**.

Alethia creates the project as a draft and opens its **Architecture** canvas.
Nothing is provisioned yet. For what each template contains, see
[Starter templates](/guides/design-project/starter-templates).

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: Deploy
records.text:
1. On the canvas, select **Run**, then **Plan**. Alethia queues a plan job.
2. Select **Jobs** in the project sidebar, then open the plan job.
3. Read the plan output in the job log.
4. When the plan succeeds, select **Apply**.
5. Select **Any available**, or a specific runner, then select **Confirm**.

Alethia queues a deploy job and opens it. Before the runner applies the plan, it runs the
[verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate). A failed gate stops the deploy before
any change is applied. When the apply succeeds, the runner installs ArgoCD on the cluster.

When you edit the design on the canvas later, a **Pending changes** bar appears.
Select **Deploy** on that bar to deploy your changes.

records.title: Quickstart
records.heading: See the cluster
records.text:
1. Select **Clusters** in the sidebar.
2. Find the card for your project.

The card shows the cluster endpoint, the ArgoCD URL, and a command that gets the ArgoCD
admin password. For AWS clusters, the card also shows the `aws eks update-kubeconfig` command.
For GCP and Azure, use the command in [Clusters](/guides/clusters#kubeconfig-commands).
To get a short-lived kubeconfig without a cloud login of your own, on any of the five clouds, see
[Get a kubeconfig for your cluster](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).

records.title: Installation
records.text: Installation. Install the Alethia CLI via Homebrew, Scoop, an install script, a Linux package, Docker, a binary download, or from source.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Installation
records.text:
The `alethia` CLI ships for **macOS, Linux, and Windows** (amd64 + arm64). Pick whichever
method fits your platform. Every method installs the same released binary.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: alethia update
records.text:
Update the CLI. One command regardless of how you installed it:

alethia update

Alethia checks the release published by your control plane. It delegates Homebrew and Scoop
installs to those package managers. It downloads and checksum-verifies a writable standalone
installation before replacing it. For Linux packages and Docker images, it prints the exact native
update command instead of changing the package database or host from inside a container.

Alethia never invokes `sudo` or opens a User Account Control prompt. If the binary is not writable,
the command stops and tells you how to rerun the installer with administrator privileges.

Interactive commands check for a new release at most once per day. Set
`ALETHIA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to disable these automatic notices. Explicit `alethia version` and
`alethia update` checks still contact the control plane.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Homebrew (recommended)
records.text:
One line, no prior setup:

brew install alethialabs-io/tap/alethia

Or tap once, then install (and reinstall) by the short name:

brew tap alethialabs-io/tap
brew install alethia

`alethia update` runs `brew update` and upgrades this formula. You can also run
`brew upgrade alethialabs-io/tap/alethia` directly. (The literal tap-free `brew install alethia` requires
[Homebrew core](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/homebrew-core.md) — a future adoption milestone.)

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Install script
records.text:
No Homebrew? Pipe the installer — it detects your OS/arch, verifies the SHA-256 checksum, and
drops the binary in `~/.local/bin`:

curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io sh

Pin a version or change the install dir with env vars:

curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io ALETHIA_VERSION=0.3.0 sh
curl -fsSL https://get.alethialabs.io ALETHIA_INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin sh

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Linux packages (.deb / .rpm / .apk)
records.text:
Every release attaches Debian, RPM, and Alpine packages. Download the one for your arch from the
[latest release](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-cli/releases) and install it:

bash

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Debian / Ubuntu
records.text: sudo dpkg -i alethia_*_linux_amd64.deb

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Fedora / RHEL
records.text: sudo rpm -i alethia_*_linux_amd64.rpm

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Alpine
records.text: sudo apk add --allow-untrusted alethia_*_linux_amd64.apk

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Scoop (recommended)
records.text:
scoop bucket add alethia https://github.com/alethialabs-io/scoop-bucket
scoop install alethia

`alethia update` delegates to `scoop update alethia`.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Install script
records.text:
irm https://get.alethialabs.io/install.ps1 iex

Honors `$env:ALETHIA_VERSION` and `$env:ALETHIA_INSTALL_DIR`; installs to
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Alethia\bin` and adds it to your user `PATH`.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Docker
records.text:
docker run --rm ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/alethia --version

Images are published to GHCR for every release (`:latest` and `:X.Y.Z`, amd64 + arm64).

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Binary download
records.text:
Pre-built archives are on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-cli/releases)
for every tagged version:

 Platform Architecture Archive 
 ---------- ------------- --------- 
 macOS Intel (amd64) `alethia_Darwin_x86_64.tar.gz` 
 macOS Apple Silicon (arm64) `alethia_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz` 
 Linux amd64 `alethia_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz` 
 Linux arm64 `alethia_Linux_arm64.tar.gz` 
 Windows amd64 `alethia_Windows_x86_64.zip` 
 Windows arm64 `alethia_Windows_arm64.zip` 

tar xzf alethia_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz
mv alethia /usr/local/bin/
alethia --version

Each release also ships `checksums.txt` — verify with `sha256sum -c` (Linux) or
`shasum -a 256 -c` (macOS) before installing.

records.title: Installation
records.heading: From source
records.text:
Requires Go 1.27+:

cd apps/cli
go build -o alethia .
./alethia --version

records.title: Installation
records.heading: Build system
records.text:
Alethia releases are built by [GoReleaser](https://goreleaser.com/) via GitHub Actions on each
`cli-v*` tag. See [Release System](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/release-system.md) for the full pipeline.

The GoReleaser config (`apps/cli/.goreleaser.yml`) produces:
- binaries for macOS / Linux / Windows × amd64 / arm64 (CGO disabled), archived with checksums
- Linux packages (`.deb` / `.rpm` / `.apk`) and Docker images (GHCR)
- the Homebrew formula (`alethialabs-io/tap`) and Scoop manifest (`alethialabs-io/scoop-bucket`), updated automatically

The binary's default control plane is `https://alethialabs.io`. It is a constant in the source, not a
build variable. To use another control plane, run `alethia init` or set the `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN`
environment variable.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.text: alethia CLI. Go command-line tool for managing multi-cloud infrastructure via the Alethia platform.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: alethia CLI
records.text: alethia is the command-line interface for the platform. It provides terminal-based access to all infrastructure operations — planning and deploying Projects, monitoring jobs, and managing Runners.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Overview
records.text:
Property Value 
 ---------- ------- 
 Language Go 
 Framework [Cobra](https://github.com/spf13/cobra) (commands) + [Charmbracelet](https://charm.sh/) (TUI) 
 Version Managed by release-please (`cli-v*` tags) 
 Distribution Homebrew · Scoop · install script (get.alethialabs.io) · .deb/.rpm/.apk · Docker · GitHub Releases (macOS/Linux/Windows, amd64/arm64)

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: How It Works
records.text:
alethia is a **thin client** that communicates with the Alethia API over HTTPS. It does not run OpenTofu directly — instead, it queues jobs that [Runners](/concepts/runner) execute. The CLI handles:

1. **Authentication** — [Device code flow](/concepts/authentication) with tokens stored locally
2. **Configuration** — Creating and inspecting Projects
3. **Job submission** — Queuing Plan / Deploy / Destroy jobs
4. **Monitoring** — Streaming logs, checking job status, waiting for completion
5. **Management** — Listing clusters, managing Runners

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Command Groups
records.text:
Connect AWS, GCP, Azure, Hetzner, and Alibaba Cloud accounts.
 
 
 List and inspect infrastructure configurations.
 
 
 Queue plan, deploy, and destroy jobs.
 
 
 List, stream logs, and cancel jobs.
 
 
 Register, list, and remove Runners.
 
 
 List provisioned Kubernetes clusters.
 
 
 Switch the active org and manage members and teams.
 
 
 Alerts and channels (console-managed today).
 
 
 `whoami`, `config`, output formats, and utility commands.

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Global Flags
records.text:
Every command accepts four persistent flags:

 Flag Default Description 
 ------ --------- ------------- 
 `-o, --output ` `table` Output format. `json`/`csv` print static, machine-readable output, and never open an interactive table. 
 `--no-input` off Disable interactive prompts; fail instead of prompting. Auto-enabled when stdin is not a terminal. A form is refused separately when the stream it would draw on is redirected, so `alethia … 2> log` still renders the rich table. 
 `--token ` unset Service-account token for non-interactive use. Prefer the `ALETHIA_TOKEN` environment variable in CI: a flag value lands in the process table and in shell history. 
 `--org ` the active org Organization to act in for this invocation, instead of the active one. Sent as the `X-Alethia-Org` header on every request, and used as the org in the request path of `members` and `teams`. It selects a scope rather than granting one: the control plane refuses it with `403` when you are not a member of that organization. Under a service token it must name the token's OWN organization — a different one is refused with `403`, never quietly ignored, so a pipeline cannot believe it is acting on one org while

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Quick Start
records.text:
The recommended path declares the project in an `alethia.yaml` file and applies it.

bash

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Install
records.text: brew install alethialabs-io/tap/alethia

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Sign in. The default control plane is https://alethialabs.io
records.text: alethia login

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Connect a cloud account: aws, gcp, azure, hetzner, or alibaba
records.text: alethia connector gcp --project my-gcp-project

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Write ./alethia.yaml for a project named boutique
records.text: alethia init --project boutique

records.title: alethia CLI
records.heading: Create what the file declares, show the plan, and deploy every environment
records.text:
alethia apply

On a terminal, `alethia init` shows a form for the values you do not pass as flags. It skips
the sign-in when this machine is already signed in. `alethia apply` shows the plan and asks
before it deploys. Pass `--yes` to skip the question.

`alethia up` runs the same first run in one command. It skips each step that is already done.
It cannot connect a cloud account for you, so it stops and names the `alethia connector`
command when none is connected.

See [`alethia init`](/reference/cli/init) and [Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply) for every flag.

records.title: Console
records.text: Console. Alethia's web control plane for multi-cloud infrastructure orchestration.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Console
records.text: The Console (`apps/console`) is Alethia's web control plane. It provides a visual interface for configuring infrastructure, managing [cloud identities](/guides/connectors), monitoring [jobs](/guides/jobs), and viewing provisioned clusters — all from the browser. Alethia is the platform; the Console is the web app you drive it from.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Key Pages
records.text:
Project overview grid, plus project detail with services and infrastructure.
 
 
 The in-console AI — grounded in your real infrastructure, with per-project workspaces, a knowledge base, dashboards, and artifacts.
 
 
 Visual canvas for designing a project's infrastructure, with the cost from its last plan.
 
 
 Connect AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, and Hetzner cloud accounts (each a cloud identity) plus GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket Git providers.
 
 
 Monitor infrastructure operations with real-time log streaming.
 
 
 Register, monitor, and manage your own Runners. The sidebar shows Runners only when your organization runs its own.
 
 
 View provisioned Kubernetes clusters with ArgoCD access.
 
 
 Runner, CLI, and Auth API endpoints.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Architecture
records.text:
A[Next.js App Router]
 A --> SA[Server Actions Drizzle · org-scoped RLS]
 A --> API[API Routes Runner + CLI token auth]
 A --> SSE[LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE]
 SSE --> ST[Live job-log & message streams]
`} />

All database access goes through Drizzle with org-scoped RLS policies enforcing per-org data isolation through a Policy Decision Point (PDP). Server Actions set the current org context (`app.current_org` via `set_config`) automatically.

records.title: The Access portal
records.text: The Access portal. The AWS-IAM-style UI for assigning access — pick a principal, a role or permission, a scope, and allow or deny.

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: The Access portal
records.text:
**Settings → Access** is where you assign access, the way you'd attach policies in the AWS IAM portal. It shows
every grant in the organization and lets you create new ones.

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: Granting access
records.text: Click **Grant access** and fill in the four parts of a [grant](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes):

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: Who
records.text: Pick a **member** or a **team** . A team grant reaches everyone on the team.

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: Allow or Deny
records.text: **Allow** confers access; **Deny** is an explicit exception that overrides any inherited allow.

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: What
records.text:
Choose a **Role** (built-in or [custom](/guides/access/custom-roles)) **or** a **single permission**
(e.g. `project:deploy`).

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: Scope
records.text:
**Entire organization**, or a specific **project / runner / cloud identity**. A grant on a container flows
down to its children.
 
 

The grants table lists each entry with its **principal**, **effect** (Allow/Deny), **role or permission**, and
**scope**, and a button to revoke it.

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: The deny-exception workflow
records.text:
The portal is where you build the canonical exception — broad access with a precise carve-out:

 
 Grant **Allow · viewer · organization** to Dana. 
 Grant **Deny · `project:view` · project `S`** to Dana. 
 Dana sees the other projects, but not `S`. 
 

See [grants & scopes](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes) for the precedence rules behind this.

records.title: The Access portal
records.heading: What you can pick from
records.text:
- **Principals** — the org's members and teams.
- **Roles** — the four built-ins plus your [custom roles](/guides/access/custom-roles).
- **Permissions** — the full `resource:action` catalog for single-permission grants.
- **Resources** — your projects, runners, and cloud identities, for scoped grants.

 
 In the open-source Community edition there's a single owner who already holds every
 permission, so there's nothing to assign — the Access portal is an Enterprise surface.

records.title: Activity
records.text: Activity. A record of everything that happens in your organization — every action and every denied attempt — browsable in Community, exportable in Enterprise.

records.title: Activity
records.heading: Activity
records.text:
Every Alethia deployment keeps a full **Activity log**, browsable in **Settings → Activity**. This is
 open-source — it works in the free edition.

records.title: Activity
records.heading: What it records
records.text:
The Activity log is a **complete record of what happens in the org**. The Policy Decision Point writes a row for:

- **Every action** — create, edit, deploy, destroy, the `manage_*` operations (identities, members, integrations,
 billing), exports, and more.
- **Every denied authorization** — someone tried something they weren't allowed to do.
- **Governance changes** — custom roles created/edited/deleted, access grants assigned/revoked, and member
 lifecycle (joins, removals, role changes).

Successful **reads** (viewing a page or listing resources) are not recorded — they fire constantly and would
drown out the signal; their *denials* still are.

Each entry reads as a natural-language line: the **actor**, what they did, the **resource**, and **when**. Denied
attempts are flagged. Filter by time range, user, project, and event type.

 
 The log is engine-agnostic: whether the deployment uses the Postgres engine or the
 [OpenFGA engine](/concepts/access-control/openfga), decisions are recorded the same way, so Activity looks
 identical.

records.title: Activity
records.heading: Export
records.text:
Exporting the log to **CSV** (for a SIEM, a spreadsheet, or a compliance archive) is an Enterprise feature,
gated by the `activityExport` entitlement. The **Export CSV** button appears in the header when the entitlement is
held; the export is also enforced server-side.

records.title: Activity
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- How decisions are made (and recorded): [**architecture**](/concepts/access-control/architecture).
- The edition split: [**feature matrix**](/editions/feature-matrix).

records.title: Custom roles
records.text: Custom roles. Author your own roles with a tailored permission set — the permission-matrix editor, grouped per resource, like an AWS IAM policy.

records.title: Custom roles
records.heading: Custom roles
records.text:
The four [built-in roles](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions) cover the common cases. When you need
something exact — "can plan and deploy projects, but never destroy, and nothing else" — author a **custom role**.

Custom roles are **organization-scoped**: they live in your org, alongside the built-ins, and can be granted
just like them through the [Access portal](/guides/access/access-portal).

records.title: Custom roles
records.heading: The permission matrix
records.text:
Open **Settings → Roles → New role**. The editor groups every permission **per resource** ("per service",
like AWS IAM), so you toggle exactly what the role can do:

 Group Example permissions 
 --- --- 
 Projects `project:view` · `project:create` · `project:edit` · `project:plan` · `project:deploy` · `project:destroy` 
 Runners `runner:view` · `runner:create` · `runner:edit` · `runner:deploy` · `runner:destroy` 
 Cloud identities `cloud_identity:view` · `cloud_identity:manage_identities` · `cloud_identity:test` 
 Jobs · Connectors · Org · Members · Alerts · Fleet · Support · Activity · Billing … 

Because the provisioning operations are themselves distinct permissions, you get **job-type granularity**: a
role can grant `project:plan` without `project:deploy`, or `runner:deploy` without `runner:destroy`. Every job type a
member can trigger is independently grantable.

 
 The permission catalog is **registry-as-code** — one typed list of resources × actions. New capabilities
 appear in the editor automatically when the registry grows; see
 [architecture](/concepts/access-control/architecture).

records.title: Custom roles
records.heading: Editing re-derives access instantly
records.text:
Change a role's permissions and **every grant that uses it updates immediately** — no re-assigning. Under the
hood the change re-expands the role into the underlying permission set (and, when OpenFGA is enabled,
re-syncs the relationship tuples).

records.title: Custom roles
records.heading: Roles vs single permissions
records.text:
A custom role is a reusable *bundle*. For a one-off — grant or deny a single `resource:action` to one person —
you don't need a role at all; grant the [single permission](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes) directly in the
Access portal.

records.title: Custom roles
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- Assign roles in the [**Access portal**](/guides/access/access-portal).
- The full permission catalog: [**roles & permissions**](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions).

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.text: Grants & scopes. How access is actually assigned — grants of a role or a single permission to a user or team, scoped to the org or a resource, as an allow or an explicit deny.

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.heading: Grants & scopes
records.text:
A **grant** is the unit of access. Every grant answers four questions:

 
 --- --- 
 **Who** a principal — a **user**, or a **team** (everyone on the team) 
 **What** a **role** (a bundle of permissions) **or** a **single permission** (e.g. `project:deploy`) 
 **Where** a **scope** — the whole organization, or one specific resource (a project, runner, …) 
 **Effect** **allow** (the default) or an explicit **deny** 

This is the same shape as an AWS IAM statement, and you create them through the
[Access portal](/guides/access/access-portal) (or, in Community, the single owner already holds everything).

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.heading: Scope and inheritance
records.text:
Resources form a hierarchy: **Org → Project** (runners, cloud identities, and connectors hang directly off
the org). A grant flows *down* that hierarchy:

- A grant on the **organization** applies to every resource in it.
- A grant on a single **project** applies to just that project.

So "let Dana view this one project" grants exactly that — you grant once, at the right
level, instead of enumerating children.

 
 This inheritance is the same in both editions and in both engines. Community resolves it by walking the
 `resource_hierarchy` table; the OpenFGA engine resolves it through relationship tuples. The decision is
 identical.

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.heading: Explicit deny — the exception you actually need
records.text:
Inheritance is convenient until you need an *exception*: "Dana can view the org's projects — **except this one
project**." That's an **explicit deny**.

Deny has AWS-IAM semantics:

- A **deny always wins** over an allow, no matter how the allow was granted (directly or inherited). There's no
 "most specific wins" tie-breaking — if any deny covers the resource, access is refused.
- A deny **inherits down** the hierarchy just like an allow. A deny on the *organization* excludes all of its
 projects; a deny on a single *project* excludes just that one.

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.heading: Worked example
records.text:
Give Dana org-wide read access, then carve out one project:

 
 **Allow** the `viewer` role on **the organization**. Dana can now view every project. 
 **Deny** the `project:view` permission on **project `S`** (one of the org's projects). 
 Result: Dana sees the *other* projects, but **not `S`**. The deny on `S` overrides the inherited allow. 
 

The decision rule, in one line:

> **allowed ⟺ an allow covers the resource (directly or via an ancestor) AND no deny covers it.**

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.heading: Role grants vs single-permission grants
records.text:
Two ways to say "what":

- **Grant a role** — the managed-policy model. Roles bundle permissions; assign the whole bundle. Use built-in
 roles, or author a [custom role](/guides/access/custom-roles) for an exact set.
- **Grant a single permission** — the inline model. Attach one `resource:action` (e.g. `project:deploy`) without a
 role. Handy for one-off exceptions, and for denies (deny exactly `project:view` on `S`, nothing more).

Editing a role's permissions instantly re-derives every grant that uses it — there's no need to re-assign.

records.title: Grants & scopes
records.heading: Where this lives
records.text:
- Create and revoke grants in the [**Access portal**](/guides/access/access-portal). 
- The permissions you can pick come from the [**roles & permissions**](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions)
 registry.
- How the two engines evaluate all of the above: [**architecture**](/concepts/access-control/architecture).

records.title: Members & invitations
records.text: Members & invitations. How people join an organization — the invitation lifecycle from email to membership, and how membership becomes authorization.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Members & invitations
records.text:
In the open-source Community edition your organization has exactly one member: you, the
owner. The Enterprise edition adds **multiple members** and the flow to bring them in.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Invite
records.text:
In **Settings → Members → Invite member**, enter an email and pick a role. An invitation is created and an
email is sent with an accept link.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Accept
records.text:
The invitee clicks the link and lands on the accept page. If they're not signed in, they're sent to sign-in
first and returned afterward — and because email sign-in doubles as sign-up, this works even if they don't have
an account yet.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Join
records.text: Accepting creates their **membership** in the organization with the chosen role.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Authorize
records.text:
Membership is turned into real authorization: the member's role is synced into a **grant**, so the
[Policy Decision Point](/concepts/access-control/architecture) starts authorizing them immediately.
 
 

 
 The last step matters. An organization's membership role and the authorization **grant** are kept in step
 automatically — adding a member, changing their role, or removing them updates their access without any
 manual grant management.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Roles for members
records.text:
When you invite or edit a member you pick one of the [roles](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions) — the four
built-ins or a [custom role](/guides/access/custom-roles). For finer control (scoped or deny grants), use the
[Access portal](/guides/access/access-portal) after they've joined.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Switching organizations
records.text:
A member can belong to more than one organization and switch between them with the **organization switcher** in
the dashboard header. The active organization scopes everything — what you see, and what the PDP and Row-Level
Security enforce.

records.title: Members & invitations
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- Group members for bulk grants with [**teams**](/guides/access/teams).
- Manage the org itself in [**organizations**](/guides/access/organizations).

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.text: Organizations & Teams. How tenancy works — the personal organization in Community, and multi-member organizations with invitations and per-member roles in Enterprise.

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: Organizations & Teams
records.text: An **organization** is the tenancy boundary: every project, runner, cloud identity, and job belongs to exactly one organization, and members of that organization see only its resources. Your **active organization** is half of your [actor](/concepts/access-control) identity — it's the scope every permission check runs against.

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: Community: your personal organization
records.text:
In the free Community edition there is **one organization per user** — your *personal organization* — and you are its sole `owner`. You never see another member. Everything you create is scoped to it automatically.
 

Under the hood, your personal organization's id is simply your user id, and you're given a single org-wide `owner` grant when your account is created. That's the entire setup — no organization to create, no members to manage. The full roles-and-grants engine is present and enforcing; it just has one member: you.

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: Enterprise: multi-member organizations
records.text:
The commercial Enterprise edition turns the organization into a real, shared, multi-member tenancy boundary:

 
 
 Named, shared tenancy boundaries. The creator becomes the owner . All existing resources stay scoped to their organization.
 
 
 Users who belong to an organization, each holding a role ( owner / admin / operator / viewer ) that determines what they can do.
 
 
 Invite a teammate by email; they accept and join with the role you choose.
 
 
 Group members so grants can target a whole team at once (rather than each user).

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: Lifecycle
records.text:
**Create an organization.** The creator is automatically its `owner` — they get an org-wide owner grant, so the authorization engine recognizes them as fully privileged within the new org immediately.
 
 
**Invite members by email.** Each invitation carries the role the new member will hold. The invitee accepts and becomes a member.
 
 
**Members act within the org.** Every request a member makes is checked against *their* role in *that* organization — an `operator` can deploy infrastructure but not manage billing; a `viewer` can only look.
 
 
**Scope flows everywhere.** Because the member's organization is their active scope, list views, actions, and the database isolation layer all key off it — a member of org A can never see org B's resources.

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: How a member's role becomes access
records.text:
When a member makes a request, the system resolves their **active organization** and checks their grant in it:

member: carol, role = operator, in org "Acme"
 request: deploy project "Acme/payments"
 ⇒ operator includes project:deploy → ALLOWED (and scoped to Acme only)

 request: invite a new member
 ⇒ operator does NOT include member:manage_members → FORBIDDEN

Roles compose with the [Org → Project hierarchy](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions#inheritance-the-org--project-hierarchy): you can give someone `operator` org-wide, or narrow them to just one project.

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: Tenancy isolation
records.text:
Organization isolation isn't only an application-level check. The database enforces it too: every query runs with the active organization in scope, and PostgreSQL Row-Level Security only returns rows for that organization. So even a flaw in the application layer cannot surface another organization's data. See [Security → Row-Level Security](/concepts/security).

 
A member can belong to **several organizations** and switch between them with the **organization switcher** in
the dashboard header; the active organization scopes everything the PDP and Row-Level Security enforce.
[**SSO**](/guides/access/sso) sign-in, [**teams**](/guides/access/teams), the
[**invitation flow**](/guides/access/members-and-invitations), and the [**access portal**](/guides/access/access-portal)
are all part of the Enterprise edition.

records.title: Organizations & Teams
records.heading: Relationship to roles
records.text: Organizations are *where* you have access; [roles](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions) are *what* that access is. A member always has both: an organization (the scope) and a role within it (the capability). Changing someone from `viewer` to `operator` changes what they can do; moving them between organizations changes what they can see.

records.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
records.text: Single Sign-On (SSO). Let your team sign in through your own identity provider over OIDC or SAML — Alethia as the service provider.

records.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
records.heading: Single Sign-On
records.text:
SSO lets members sign in through **your** identity provider (IdP) instead of (or alongside) email and social
login. Alethia is the **Service Provider** that *consumes* your IdP — it never runs an identity provider of its
own.

You bring the IdP. Supported via standard protocols (see [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) and [SAML & SCIM](/reference/standards/scim-saml) for the protocol details):

- **[OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc)** — Okta · Microsoft Entra ID · Google Workspace · **AWS IAM Identity Center** · OneLogin · Ping · …
- **[SAML 2.0](/reference/standards/scim-saml)** — the same IdPs over SAML.

Under the hood SSO is the Better Auth `@better-auth/sso` plugin (shipped in the enterprise package); a provider stores either an `oidcConfig` or a `samlConfig` and can be scoped per organization (`sso_provider.organizationId`) or left instance-wide.

 
 There's nothing to run on Alethia's side — no Hydra, no Alethia-as-IdP. Each organization registers its own
 provider, so different orgs can use different IdPs.

records.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
records.heading: Registering a provider
records.text:
In **Settings → Single Sign-On → Register provider**, choose the protocol and fill in the IdP's details:

 
 

 Field What it is 
 --- --- 
 Provider ID A short slug for the provider (e.g. `okta`) 
 Email domain The domain whose users route to this provider (e.g. `company.com`) 
 Issuer URL Your IdP's issuer / discovery URL 
 Client ID / Client secret The OIDC application credentials from your IdP 

 
 

 Field What it is 
 --- --- 
 Provider ID A short slug (e.g. `entra`) 
 Email domain The domain whose users route to this provider 
 IdP Entity ID Your IdP's SAML entity / issuer ID 
 SSO URL (entry point) The IdP's SAML sign-in endpoint 
 X.509 certificate The IdP's signing certificate

records.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
records.heading: Provisioning into the organization
records.text:
When a member signs in through SSO for the first time, Alethia **provisions** them into the organization with the
least-privileged role. From that point they're a
