normal [member](/guides/access/members-and-invitations) — the [PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) authorizes
them exactly as it would anyone else.

records.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- How members are authorized once they're in: [**grants & scopes**](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes).
- Turning SSO on for a deployment: the [**Enterprise setup runbook**](/guides/self-hosting/enterprise-setup).

records.title: Teams
records.text: Teams. Group members so you can grant access to a whole team at once — group-based grants.

records.title: Teams
records.heading: Teams
records.text:
A **team** is a named group of organization members. Grant access to a team, and **everyone on it inherits the
grant** — add or remove people from the team and their access follows automatically.

records.title: Teams
records.heading: Why teams
records.text:
Without teams, sharing a project with five engineers means five grants — and five revokes when the work ends.
With a team, it's **one grant to the team**, and membership is the only thing you manage afterward.

Teams are the natural principal for durable, role-based access: "the platform team can deploy the
production projects" is one grant on one team.

records.title: Teams
records.heading: Managing teams
records.text:
In **Settings → Teams**:

 
 **New team** — give it a name (e.g. `platform`). 
 **Manage** — add or remove organization members. 
 Grant access to the team in the [Access portal](/guides/access/access-portal) — pick the team as the principal.

records.title: Teams
records.heading: How team grants resolve
records.text:
A grant whose principal is a team applies to a user whenever they're a member of that team. This is resolved in
**both** authorization engines:

- The Postgres engine matches team grants by joining your team memberships at decision time.
- The OpenFGA engine models a team as a group (`team:… # member`), so a team grant reaches members through the
 relationship graph.

Either way, removing someone from a team **immediately** removes the access that came from it.

 
 Teams compose with everything else: grant a [custom role](/guides/access/custom-roles) to a team, scope it
 to a [project](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes), and add per-member [deny](/guides/access/access-portal)
 exceptions on top.

records.title: Teams
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- Assign team grants in the [**Access portal**](/guides/access/access-portal).
- Bring people into the org first via [**members & invitations**](/guides/access/members-and-invitations).

records.title: Alerts
records.text: Alerts. Route platform events to Slack, Teams, Discord, PagerDuty, webhook, and email channels. Chat channels authenticate with a pasted incoming-webhook URL (PagerDuty with a routing key) — no OAuth.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Alerts
records.text:
Alerting turns platform activity into notifications. A **policy** decides *what* fires, a **channel**
decides *where it goes*, and every routed event is recorded as a **delivery**. Find it under
**Dashboard → Alerts**, organised into **Policies · Channels · Activity**.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: How alerting works
records.text:
deploy fails · action denied · cloud-identity token breaks"] --> P["policies match event + conditions"]
 P --> C["route to channels"]
 C --> D["delivery attempted now, retried on failure, logged in Activity"]
`} />

- **Events** are emitted by the platform as things happen — you don't wire anything up.
- **Policies** watch a chosen set of events and route matches to channels.
- **Channels** are destinations — Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Google Chat, Mattermost, Rocket.Chat, a generic webhook, PagerDuty, or email.
- **Deliveries** are the audit trail: what fired, where it went, and whether it succeeded.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Policies
records.text:
A policy is a set of events plus the channels they route to. Under **Alerts → Policies**:

1. **Create a policy** — click **New policy** to open the guided form. It starts blank; give it a
 name and description.
2. **Pick events** from the catalog, grouped by category (see below). A policy can watch one event or many.
3. **Set conditions** — an optional **scope** filter, a **minimum severity**, and a **dedup/throttle
 window** (collapse repeats of the same event into one notification for N seconds).
4. **Route to channels** — toggle which channels this policy notifies; one policy can fan out to several,
 and one channel can serve many policies.
5. **Enable** it. Disabled policies keep their config but fire nothing.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: What you can alert on
records.text:
Events are grouped into categories. Most (~35) are **live** today; the rest are configurable now but inert
until their emitter ships (the UI tags these "soon").

 Category Example events Status 
 --- --- --- 
 **Deploy & drift** deploy started / succeeded / failed, destroy requested / completed Live · drift *soon* 
 **Policy (PDP)** action denied, sensitive action allowed, role permissions changed Live · policy-override *soon* 
 **Access & roles (RBAC)** grant added / revoked, role created / changed / deleted Live 
 **Members** member invited / joined / removed Live · suspended *soon* 
 **Cloud identities** identity connected / revoked, credential failed Live · rotation *soon* 
 **Cost** budget threshold, spend spike, overage started Live · spike / overage *soon* 
 **Workers & runners** worker unhealthy (runner offline) Live · stalled / exhausted *soon* 
 **Authentication** SSO sign-in failed, new-device sign-in, sign-in blocked *Soon* 
 **Platform health** background loop degraded / recovered Live 
 **Support** case opened / replied / resolved / reopened / closed Live · assignment *soon*

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Free vs Business+
records.text:
Alerting itself is in the open-source core. The split is by **event kind**:

- **Operational events are free** — deploys, destroys, members, cloud-identity connect/revoke, connector
 health, and runner health. These work in the community build with no license.
- **Security & governance events require Business+** (the `advancedAlerting` entitlement) — PDP **policy
 denials / sensitive actions**, and **access-control changes** (grant added/revoked, role
 created/changed/deleted). Without the entitlement these patterns are visible but won't deliver.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Severity
records.text:
Every event carries a severity — **info**, **warning**, or **critical** — surfaced in the channel payload
(e.g. a Slack colour/emoji, or a field your webhook consumer can route on). A policy's **minimum severity**
condition drops anything below the chosen level.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Channels
records.text:
There is no Alethia-hosted Slack/Teams app and no OAuth. A chat channel is just an **incoming-webhook
 URL** you create in your own Slack or RocketChat workspace and paste in. Alethia signs (where applicable) and POSTs to that
 URL — nothing more.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Prerequisite: the encryption key
records.text:
Every channel except email stores a **secret** — a webhook URL for the chat and generic-webhook transports,
or a routing key for PagerDuty. That secret *is* the credential (anyone holding it can post to your
destination), so Alethia encrypts it at rest. That requires an encryption key:

bash

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: 32-byte base64 key — set once, keep it stable across restarts
records.text:
openssl rand -base64 32

Set it in your environment and restart:

ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY= 

Until it's set, secret-bearing channels are **disabled in the UI** (the channel dialog tells you so). The
same key protects `api_key` connector credentials, so a configured deployment already has it. **Email
channels need no key** — recipients aren't secret.

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Add a channel
records.text:
In the console, open **Alerts → Channels → New channel**, pick a type, and follow the matching steps. Use
**Test** afterwards to send a synthetic event before any policy routes real alerts to it.

 
 
 The generic escape hatch — delivers to any HTTPS endpoint you control. No third-party account, so it's
 also the easiest way to test alerting end to end (point it at your own service, or a throwaway
 request-bin / `ngrok` URL).

 

 ### Endpoint URL
 Paste the HTTPS URL that should receive the POST. The body is JSON: `{ channel, event, sent_at }`.

 ### Signing secret (optional)
 If you set one, Alethia signs each request:

 X-Alethia-Signature: sha256=HMAC-SHA256(secret, body)
 
 Recompute the HMAC over the raw body on your side and compare — the outbound mirror of how Alethia
 verifies inbound Stripe webhooks.

 ### Test
 Click **Test**. Your endpoint should receive one POST with a `Test alert from Alethia` payload.

 
 

 
 Slack delivery uses an **Incoming Webhook** — a per-channel URL Slack issues. No bot token, no OAuth,
 no Alethia Slack app to install.

 

 ### Create the incoming webhook
 In Slack, add the **Incoming Webhooks** app (or create a Slack app and enable the *Inco

records.title: Alerts
records.heading: Activity
records.text:
Every routed event becomes a row under **Alerts → Activity**: the event, the channel, status, attempts, and
any error. Status moves **pending → sent**, or **failed → dead** once it exhausts its retries. A background
sweeper retries failed deliveries with backoff, so a briefly-unreachable endpoint recovers on its own — no
cron to configure. (A channel's **Test** button writes no Activity row; it just probes the destination.)

records.title: Artifacts
records.text: Artifacts. Save a dashboard as a named, reusable artifact — private to you by default, and shareable with your organization, a team, or a role.

records.title: Artifacts
records.heading: Artifacts
records.text:
A [dashboard](/guides/assistant/dashboards) lives inside one conversation. An **artifact** is a
dashboard you've saved by name so it outlives that chat — a reusable, org-shared board you can open from
anywhere.

records.title: Artifacts
records.heading: Saving one
records.text:
From the grid, use **Save as artifact** (on the whole grid, or a single widget) and give it a name. A
saved artifact is **private to you** and unique by name in your library; you can then share it with your
whole org, a team, or a role from the viewer's **Share** control.

records.title: Artifacts
records.heading: The library
records.text:
The rail's **Artifacts** item opens the library, split into **Yours** (artifacts you saved) and **Shared
with you** (ones a teammate shared into your org, a team you're on, or a role you hold). Each card shows
its kind and widget count. **New artifact** starts a fresh chat with a few starter prompts to build one
from scratch.

records.title: Artifacts
records.heading: Opening one
records.text:
Clicking an artifact opens a **read-only viewer** — its widgets rendered exactly as saved. Looking at an
artifact never touches a conversation; every action is explicit (and available only on an artifact you
own — one shared to you is view-only):

- **Add to this chat** — drop its widgets onto the open conversation's grid (available when a chat is
 open).
- **Open in new chat** — start a fresh conversation with the artifact materialized on its grid.
- **Share** — grant it to your whole org, a team, or a role (paid orgs with more than one member).
- **Delete** — remove it from the library.

 
 Because a saved dashboard keeps each widget tied to its source tool, opening it onto a chat's grid can
 refresh those widgets against live data — so an artifact is a living board, not a stale screenshot.

records.title: Artifacts
records.heading: Referencing an artifact in chat
records.text:
Tag a saved artifact with `@` (see [tagging resources](/guides/assistant)) to have Elench act on it —
for example, ask it to explain or extend the artifact, and it resolves the `@name` to the right saved
board.

records.title: Dashboards
records.text: Dashboards. Elench's answers land as widgets on a per-chat grid — ask for a full dashboard and it composes stat cards and charts from your live infrastructure.

records.title: Dashboards
records.heading: Dashboards
records.text:
Elench doesn't just reply in text. When it reads your infrastructure, structured results **pin as
widgets** onto a grid beside the chat — a live, per-conversation dashboard you can arrange and keep.

records.title: Dashboards
records.heading: The grid
records.text:
Open the grid from the conversation's top bar (or it opens on its own when Elench builds something). It's
a five-column bento canvas that grows downward, shown in a **resizable split pane** next to the
transcript. Drag the divider to resize; drag it past a quarter of the width and the pane **snaps
closed** — a chevron at the edge brings it back.

records.title: Dashboards
records.heading: Widgets
records.text:
Each answer that returns structured data becomes a **widget** — a stat card, a table, a chart. Every
widget has a lean header:

- **Live / Frozen** — a live widget refreshes on its own cadence; freeze it to keep a fixed snapshot.
 Toggle either way.
- **Refresh** — pull the latest now.
- **Save** — promote the widget (or the whole grid) to an [artifact](/guides/assistant/artifacts).
- **Move / resize** — drag the grip to move (or press Enter on it for keyboard mode); drag the corner
 to resize.

records.title: Dashboards
records.heading: Ask for a whole dashboard
records.text:
Ask for something like *"Build a dashboard of my infrastructure — clusters, jobs, cost, and drift"* and
Elench gathers the data and composes it into stat cards and charts, laid out on the grid. The empty grid
shows the same invitation.

records.title: Dashboards
records.heading: Fill a specific cell
records.text:
Click any empty cell and a small **"describe what goes here…"** composer opens right there. Type what you
want and Elench answers with a single read and pins the result into exactly that cell — a fast way to
build a dashboard one tile at a time.

 
 The grid is per-conversation. To keep a dashboard around — or share it — save it as an
 [artifact](/guides/assistant/artifacts); the widgets stay tied to their source tools, so a saved
 dashboard can refresh against live data when you reopen it.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.text: Assistant (Elench). Elench is the in-console AI — it reads your real infrastructure, answers in grounded dashboards, and proposes changes that the deterministic engine still has to approve.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: Assistant
records.text:
**Elench** is the AI built into the Console. Ask it about your infrastructure and it answers from your
*real* state — clusters, jobs, cost, drift — not a generic guess. Ask it to change something and it
proposes a plan; it never applies on its own.

 
 Elench needs an AI provider configured (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). It's on by default on hosted Alethia;
 self-hosters opt in by setting the key. Without it, the **Ask AI** button is inert and the routes
 return a "not configured" state.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: The one rule
records.text:
> The **deterministic engine is the verdict. The model only proposes.**

Every change Elench suggests is re-run through the [verification engine](/concepts/elench) between `tofu plan`
and `tofu apply`, and a real apply is human-gated. The model has no write path of its own — it drafts,
you and the gate decide. Everything below is built on that line.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: Opening it
records.text:
Click **Ask AI** (top-right of any Console page). Elench opens as a **docked panel** beside your work;
the **expand** control turns it into a full-screen **modal** with a thread rail, a knowledge panel, and
a side-by-side dashboard grid. **Minimize** docks it back to a panel — the conversation is preserved
across both.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: How you talk to it
records.text:
An **Organization** chat for the whole account, or a **Project** workspace scoped to one
 infrastructure project — its own chats, knowledge, and memory.
 
 
 Pin custom instructions and named knowledge documents so every chat in a scope inherits them —
 plus the live facts Elench already derives on its own.
 
 
 Answers land as widgets on a per-chat grid. Ask for a full dashboard and it composes stat cards
 and charts from your live data.
 
 
 Save a dashboard as a named, reusable artifact your whole org can open, view, and drop into any
 chat.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: Ask vs Auto
records.text:
A pill on the composer sets what Elench may do with a proposed change:

- **Ask** (default) — it drafts changes and waits; you review and approve each one.
- **Auto** — it may apply edits for that conversation without stopping to ask each time.

Auto still can't bypass the apply gate — it only removes the per-change confirmation click inside the
chat.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: Model: Fast vs Thinking
records.text:
The composer's settings control picks the response style:

- **Fast** — quick answers for everyday questions.
- **Thinking** — deeper reasoning for complex work.

On the **Max** tier a per-message **Deep reasoning** toggle spends more on a single hard question. The
underlying model names are an internal detail — the transcript only ever shows *Elench*.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: Tagging resources with @
records.text:
Type `@` to tag a specific resource — a **project**, **cluster**, **job**, **connector**, **runner**,
**cloud identity**, or **artifact**. A scrollable menu opens above the composer; pick one and it drops
in as a pill. Tagging tells Elench exactly what you mean, so `@my-cluster` resolves to that cluster's id
and Elench reaches for the right read tool without guessing.

records.title: Assistant (Elench)
records.heading: What it can see, and can't do
records.text:
Elench reads through the same **PDP-gated, org-scoped** actions the rest of the Console uses, so it can
never read across tenants. Its write-capable tools queue **proposals** (plan / deploy) that a human
accepts; the actual apply runs on a runner behind the [verification gate](/concepts/elench/engine-internals).
Usage is metered against your organization's AI plan, which sets the included monthly allowance.

 
 Elench is grounded, not omniscient. It answers from what your account exposes and from what you pin in
 its [knowledge base](/guides/assistant/knowledge); it does not invent state it can't read, and a
 wrong suggestion is caught by the gate, not by the model second-guessing itself.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.text: Knowledge base. Pin custom instructions and named knowledge documents so every chat in a workspace inherits them — alongside the live facts Elench derives on its own.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Knowledge base
records.text:
The **Knowledge** panel (in the rail) is where you tell Elench how to behave and what it should always
know for the current [workspace](/guides/assistant/workspaces). Everything here rides the system prompt
of **every chat in that scope**, so the first answer is already grounded — you don't repeat yourself
each conversation.

It has three parts.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Custom instructions
records.text:
A free-text field for *how* Elench should act here. Examples:

> This is production — always require approval before an apply, and never propose destroy.

> Prefer Hetzner for non-prod. Our region is `eu-central-1` unless a project says otherwise.

Instructions save on blur and apply to every chat in the workspace.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Knowledge documents
records.text:
The knowledge itself is a **list of named documents**, not one blob — so each is titled, sized, and
removable on its own, and Elench can tell you *which* document it drew on.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Add a document
records.text: Click **Add knowledge**, give it a title (e.g. *Runbook: production deploys*), and write the body.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Save it
records.text:
**Save document** persists it to the workspace. It appears in the list with its size and when it was
last edited.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Edit or remove
records.text:
Hover a document for **edit** and **delete**. Deleting it drops it from every future chat immediately.

 

Because knowledge rides **every** turn's prompt, its size is a real cost — a **capacity meter** shows
how much of the budget (50,000 characters) you've used. Keep documents tight and factual: conventions,
owners, on-call, runbooks, gotchas — the things Elench can't work out on its own.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: Already known (auto-derived)
records.text:
Inside a **project** workspace, the panel also shows an **Already known** section: the live facts Elench
derives from your account on every turn — the project's identity and region, its environments and their
status, and its recent jobs and outcomes. You don't need to write any of this down; it's read fresh each
time. The section makes it obvious what's *already* grounded versus what's worth pinning by hand.

 
 The organization workspace has no auto-derived section — it's the general assistant, grounded by the
 org-wide instructions and documents you pin, plus the tools it can call on demand.

records.title: Knowledge base
records.heading: How it reaches the model
records.text:
Under the hood, a scope's instructions and documents are the `agent_context` row for that
`(organization, project)` pair; they're assembled — org first, project second, then the derived facts —
into the cached system prompt for each turn. The [agent runtime](/concepts/elench/agent-runtime) covers the
prompt assembly and the tenant-isolation guards.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.text: MCP server (external agents). Connect an external agent — Claude or a claude.ai connector — to Alethia over MCP so it can read your infrastructure with the same tools Elench uses, read-only.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: MCP server
records.text:
Elench's read tools are re-exposed as an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server so an agent
*outside* the Console — Claude, or a claude.ai connector — can read your real infrastructure without
you copying anything in by hand. It calls the **same PDP-gated, org-scoped tools** the in-console
assistant uses, so it can only see what you can see.

The external surface is **read-only by design**. It exposes just the read tools; the assistant's
proposal, canvas, and job-queuing tools (including repo scans) are excluded. An external agent can
read your projects, clusters, jobs, and drift — it can never queue an apply.

 
 The connector requires AI to be enabled for your organization. On self-host it is always enabled
 (no hosted billing). On hosted Alethia every org has at least the free AI tier, which is enabled,
 so the endpoint is available by default — it returns a `403` only if AI is explicitly disabled for
 the org. See [Assistant](/guides/assistant).

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- Your Alethia Console origin, e.g. `https://app.alethialabs.io`. The MCP endpoint is that origin
 plus `/api/mcp`.
- An MCP client that speaks remote MCP over Streamable HTTP with OAuth — for example Claude or a
 claude.ai connector.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: Connect a client
records.text:
The endpoint authenticates with OAuth 2.1. Clients register themselves (dynamic client
registration), so there is no key to paste — you sign in to Alethia and approve access.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: Add the connector
records.text:
In your MCP client, add a custom / remote MCP server pointing at your endpoint:

https:// /api/mcp

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: Sign in to Alethia
records.text:
The client discovers Alethia's authorization server and sends you to the Console sign-in page. Sign
in as you normally would.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: Approve access
records.text:
If the client requests consent, approve it. The token issued is bound to **your** user — the tools
run as you, under your organization's grants, with no new authority.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: Use the tools
records.text:
The connector now lists Alethia's read tools. Ask the external agent about your infrastructure and
it calls them on your behalf.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: What the agent can read
records.text:
The external projection is the read-only subset of Elench's tools:

 Area What the agent can do 
 --- --- 
 Projects List projects and read one project's full configuration (components + sizes). 
 Jobs List recent provisioning jobs; read a job's status and error; read a plan/deploy result, including the Elench verification verdict. 
 Runtime List clusters (endpoints, databases, caches — no secrets), runners, connectors, and verified cloud accounts; read a cloud account's live inventory. 
 Drift Read a project's latest day-2 drift posture. 
 Catalog Browse the provider-neutral service catalog and its options; compute a CIDR for a host count. 
 Docs Search the Alethia documentation. 
 Scans Read a completed repo-scan result and compare its estimated cost across providers. 
 Usage Read the org's managed-runner usage, standalone AI standing, and billing summary. 

Returns are trimmed and secret-free — never ArgoCD passwords, tokens, or credentials.

records.title: MCP server (external agents)
records.heading: What it can't do
records.text:
The connector deliberately excludes every write and every stateful, UI-bound tool:

- It cannot **queue a repo scan or an audit** — those start a runner job. Start them from the
 [assistant](/guides/assistant) instead.
- It cannot **propose a plan or deploy**. A real apply stays human-gated behind the
 [verification engine](/concepts/elench).
- It cannot open Console UI, build dashboards, pin widgets, or read and write
 [artifacts](/guides/assistant/artifacts).

 
 The read-only boundary is enforced at the source: only tools classified as externally safe are
 ever projected onto the MCP endpoint, and a tool with no explicit classification is excluded. The
 same server actions still re-check their own permission on every call, so the agent can never read
 across tenants.

records.title: Workspaces
records.text: Workspaces. An Organization chat for the whole account, or a Project workspace scoped to one infrastructure project — each with its own chats, knowledge, and memory.

records.title: Workspaces
records.heading: Workspaces
records.text:
Elench borrows its shape from the idea of a project workspace: a self-contained place with its own
chats, its own pinned knowledge, and its own memory — and nothing leaks between them.

There are two kinds of workspace:

- **Organization** — the general assistant for your whole account. It has the org-wide tools and reads
 across all your projects.
- **Project** — a workspace scoped to a single [infrastructure project](/guides/design-project). It
 inherits the org's settings *and* adds that project's own instructions, knowledge, and live-state
 grounding.

records.title: Workspaces
records.heading: Switching workspace
records.text:
Your workspace follows **where you open the assistant**. Click **Ask AI** on an org-level page and you
land in the `Organization` workspace; open it from inside a [project](/guides/design-project) — its
pages or its canvas — and Elench scopes itself to that project. (The panel header's switcher steps
between the *conversations* in your current scope, not between workspaces.)

Each scope keeps three things apart:

- **The chat list** — you see only that scope's conversations (org chats are unscoped; a project's chats
 are keyed to its id).
- **The knowledge panel** — you edit *that* scope's [instructions and
 knowledge](/guides/assistant/knowledge).
- **The conversation** — an organization chat's transcript never follows you into a project, and a
 project's tools never bleed into an org chat.

 general assistant · org knowledge · org memory"]
 P1["Project: checkout + project knowledge · project memory"]
 P2["Project: analytics + project knowledge · project memory"]
 ORG --> P1
 ORG --> P2
`} />

records.title: Workspaces
records.heading: What a project workspace inherits
records.text:
Inside a project chat, Elench is grounded three ways, layered in order:

1. **Organization instructions and knowledge** — your account-wide policy applies everywhere.
2. **This project's instructions and knowledge** — the project's specifics sit on top of the org's.
3. **Live, auto-derived facts** about the project — its identity, environments, and recent jobs — so
 the very first answer is grounded without a tool round-trip.

A project's pinned context is **inherited by every chat inside it** and **never leaks out** to
organization chats or to other projects. See [Knowledge base](/guides/assistant/knowledge) for what you
can pin and how it's used.

records.title: Workspaces
records.heading: Memory
records.text:
Elench keeps a separate memory per workspace: one for the organization and one for each project. A
project's memory is addressed under the organization's, never mixed with it, and never shared with
another project — the same isolation the rest of the platform enforces. The
[agent runtime](/concepts/elench/agent-runtime) covers how that namespacing works underneath.

 
 **Your workspace is yours.** The chats, pinned knowledge, and instructions in a workspace are
 owner-scoped — Elench reads and writes only what you own, so a teammate can't see your pinned grounding
 or your conversations.

records.title: Classification
records.text: Classification. Organize every resource with a governed taxonomy — named dimensions and their allowed values, assigned across projects, clusters, cloud identities, runners, members and more.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: Classification
records.text:
Classification is **governed, structured labeling** for everything in your organization — the
opposite of free-form tags. Instead of anyone typing `env=prod`, `Environment=Production`, or
`PROD` and drifting, an admin defines a fixed set of **axes** and their **allowed values** once, and
every resource is labeled from that closed vocabulary. Find it under **Settings → Classification**.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: The model
records.text:
Three concepts, in a strict hierarchy:

 an axis — 'Environment'"] --> V["Value an allowed answer — dev · staging · prod"] --> A["Assignment pinned to a resource — this project's Environment = prod"]
`} />

- **Dimension** — a named axis: one question you can ask about every resource (*Environment*,
 *Team*, *Data classification*, *Cost center*). It has a label, an immutable `key` slug, an
 optional description, and a **single/multi** mode.
- **Value** — an allowed answer on that axis (`dev` / `staging` / `prod`). A closed set the admin
 curates; each value has a label, a slug, and an optional color accent.
- **Assignment** — a value pinned to one concrete resource. This is what you set on a project, a
 cluster, a cloud identity, and so on.

Two mental models that make it click:

- **Spreadsheet** — dimensions are the **columns**, values are a column's allowed **dropdown
 entries**, and assignments are the **filled-in cells**.
- **Governed cloud tags** — like AWS/GCP resource tags, except the keys *and* the permitted values
 are curated, so there's no typo or casing drift and every resource speaks the same vocabulary.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: Single vs multi
records.text:
Every dimension is either **single-valued** or **multi-valued**, and it's the most important choice
you make when creating one:

 Mode Meaning Example 
 --- --- --- 
 **Single** A resource holds **at most one** value on this axis. Assigning a new value **replaces** the current one. *Environment* — a thing is exactly one of dev / staging / prod. 
 **Multi** A resource may hold **several** values on this axis. *Team* — a service can belong to platform *and* payments.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: Where you can apply it
records.text:
Classification is assignable across the main resource types. On each, you'll see the value **chips**
and — if you can edit — a **picker** to change them:

 Resource Where in the console 
 --- --- 
 Projects Project → **Settings → General** 
 Environments A project's **Environments** 
 Clusters **Clusters** 
 Cloud identities (& pluggable connector credentials) **Connectors** → a cloud identity's detail 
 Runners **Runners** 
 Members **Settings → Members** 
 Roles **Settings → Roles** 
 Alert policies **Alerts → Policies** 
 Alert channels **Alerts → Channels** 
 Support cases A support case's detail 

 
 A few internal record types (alert *deliveries* and runner *usage sessions*) aren't
 classifiable — classification applies to the things you manage, not to the audit trail they
 generate.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: What it's for today
records.text:
Once resources carry consistent labels, classification gives you:

- **Organization** — a single, drift-free vocabulary across every resource type.
- **Filter & group** — read the chips to slice your fleet ("show the `prod` resources", "everything
 owned by the `payments` team").
- **Usage insight** — the **Settings → Classification** page surfaces how the taxonomy is actually
 used: an assignment count per value, a coverage figure per dimension, a per-resource-kind
 breakdown, and which values are **unused** (safe to delete or repurpose).

records.title: Classification
records.heading: What it is *not* — yet
records.text:
**Classification does not enforce anything.** No policy, permission check, provisioning step, or
 the verification gate reads these labels to allow, deny, route, or require. Today classification is
 **organizational metadata and a governance foundation** — it describes your resources, it does not
 govern them. Rules built *on top of* classification (for example, "a `prod` resource must carry a
 data-classification", or a policy scoped to a dimension) are a future step, not current behavior.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: Authoring the taxonomy
records.text:
Under **Settings → Classification** (requires the **Editor** role — `org:edit`; everyone else sees a
read-only view):

1. **Create a dimension.** Give it a label; the `key` slug auto-fills from it. Add a description and
 choose **single** or **multi**. The `key` is **immutable** after creation (it's wire-stable), so
 pick it deliberately — the label and everything else stay editable. Starting fresh? The empty
 state offers **templates** (Environment, Data classification, Team, Cost center) you can drop in
 and then adjust.
2. **Add values.** Type a label and press Enter for a quick add, or open the editor to set the slug
 and a **color accent** (a swatch, a custom color, or none).
3. **Reorder** dimensions and values by dragging — the order is what the pickers show everywhere.
4. **Drill into usage** — click a value's count to see which resource kinds carry it.

 
 Deleting a **dimension** removes its values *and every assignment of those values across all
 resources*; deleting a **value** clears it from every resource it was on. Both are irreversible.

records.title: Classification
records.heading: Assigning values to resources
records.text:
On a supported resource, the classification control shows the current values as chips. The **picker**
to change them appears only when you can edit **that** resource *and* you hold `org:edit` — so you'll
never see a control you'd be denied on. For a single-valued dimension, picking a new value swaps out
the old one; for a multi-valued dimension, you add and remove values freely.

records.title: Clusters
records.text: Clusters. Viewing provisioned Kubernetes clusters with ArgoCD access and kubeconfig.

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Clusters
records.text: The **Clusters** page (`/{org}/~/clusters`) shows all provisioned Kubernetes clusters from active projects.

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Cluster Cards
records.text:
Each cluster displays:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Project Name** The project's name + a **derived** status badge (Active / Reconciling / Degraded / Provisioning) — rolled up from the cluster and every data service, never hardcoded to "Active" 
 **Provider** Provider icon with region, environment, and Kubernetes version (e.g., `K8s 1.32`) 
 **Cluster Endpoint** API server URL (copy button) 
 **kubeconfig Command** The command that writes a kubeconfig with your own cloud CLI (copy button), or a note saying why a cloud has none — the same answer `alethia cluster get` prints (see below). To get one through Alethia instead, see [Get a kubeconfig](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig). Under it, people with read-only cluster access see **Download kubeconfig (1h, read-only)**: see [From the console](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig#from-the-console). 
 **ArgoCD URL** External link to the ArgoCD dashboard, plus a command to retrieve the admin password 
 **Components** Control plane, databases, caches, and DNS — each with its endpoint (copy buttons) and its own derived status

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: kubeconfig Commands
records.text:
There are two ways to get a kubeconfig:

- **Through Alethia**, with no cloud login of your own: `alethia cluster kubeconfig` gets a
 short-lived, read-only or admin kubeconfig that a runner mints for you. It works on all five
 clouds, including Hetzner and Alibaba Cloud. See
 [Get a kubeconfig for your cluster](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig).
- **With your own cloud CLI**, under your own cloud login. The rest of this section is about this
 way.

The cluster card and `alethia cluster get` (its **Kubeconfig** row) both show the exact command for a cluster, built from
the values the cluster's last successful deploy recorded — see
[Accessing a cluster with kubectl](/reference/cli/clusters#accessing-a-cluster-with-kubectl). The
command per cloud:

 
 
 aws eks update-kubeconfig --name {cluster-name} --region {region}
 
 
 gcloud container clusters get-credentials {cluster-name} --region {region} --project {gcp-project-id}
 
 A zonal cluster gets `--zone {zone}` instead of `--region {region}`.
 
 
 az aks get-credentials --resource-group {resource-group} --name {cluster-name}
 
 
 Alethia does not record the ACK cluster ID yet. Find it in the ACK console, then call
 `DescribeClusterUserKubec

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Pre-Installed Components
records.text:
Every cluster comes with these components installed via ArgoCD (see [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)):

 Component Purpose 
 ----------- --------- 
 **ArgoCD** GitOps continuous delivery 
 **AWS Load Balancer Controller** Ingress via ALB/NLB (AWS) 
 **External DNS** Automatic DNS record sync 
 **External Secrets Operator** Cloud secrets → Kubernetes Secrets 
 **Karpenter** Just-in-time node provisioning (AWS) 
 **Metrics Server** CPU/memory metrics for HPA 
 **Storage Class** GP3 EBS / Persistent Disk / Managed Disk

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Live Updates
records.text: The Clusters page polls every 5 seconds while the tab is focused (TanStack Query pauses the interval in the background) — the interim reconciliation cadence. When a project's default environment reaches `ACTIVE` (deploy completes), the next poll surfaces the new cluster.

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Data Source
records.text: Cluster information comes from the DEPLOY job's `finalizeDeployment()` server action, which extracts OpenTofu outputs (cluster name, endpoint, ARN, ArgoCD URL, database/cache endpoints) and writes them to the project's component tables.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.text: Alibaba Connector. Keyless + account-free access via a RAM OIDC provider and AssumeRoleWithOIDC.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Alibaba Connector
records.text:
Connecting Alibaba registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **keyless and account-free**. Alethia's control plane is its own OIDC issuer;
you register a **RAM OIDC provider** that trusts it and a **RAM role** that trusts that provider. Alethia
assumes the role by presenting a short-lived minted assertion (STS `AssumeRoleWithOIDC`) — Alethia holds
no Alibaba account, generates no AccessKey, and stores nothing but the role ARN. See
[Security Architecture](/concepts/security).

 
**Is this safe?** You create the trust entirely in **your own** Alibaba account — Alethia holds no Alibaba
account and generates no AccessKey. It signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that Alibaba STS verifies
and swaps for a ~1-hour credential. The only thing stored is the **RAM role ARN** (a public identifier).
**Revoke anytime** by deleting the role.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The connect dialog gives you two equivalent options — a one-line `aliyun` command for the
**Alibaba Cloud Shell** (nothing to install), or the **OpenTofu module** for teams that manage
infrastructure as code. Both create everything in **your** Alibaba account:

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Create the RAM OIDC provider
records.text:
A RAM OIDC provider named `alethia` trusting Alethia's issuer (`https://alethialabs.io/api/oidc`), with
client id `sts.aliyuncs.com`. The provider name is fixed — Alethia derives its ARN from your role ARN.
The provider pins the issuer's **CA certificate fingerprints** (the stable intermediate/root, not the
rotating Cloudflare edge leaf); if the issuer's cert chain ever rotates its CA, re-run the setup to refresh
them.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Create the RAM role
records.text:
A role whose trust policy allows `AssumeRoleWithOIDC` from that provider, scoped to Alethia's workload
identity (`oidc:sub = alethia-connector`, `oidc:aud = sts.aliyuncs.com`) — a wrong subject/audience is
rejected.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Attach provisioning permissions
records.text:
The setup attaches **4 enumerated custom RAM policies** — `ComputeCluster` (ACK + its transitive node-pool
ECS + API-server/Service SLB), `Network` (VPC/vSwitch/NAT/SNAT + EIP), `Data` (RDS/KVStore/OSS/Tablestore/
KMS), and `EdgeReg` (Container Registry/AliDNS/MNS) — each listing the **specific
create/read/modify/delete/tag actions** the templates issue, never a `service:*` wildcard or an admin
policy. Service-linked roles ACK/NAT need are covered by a narrow `ram:CreateServiceLinkedRole`-only policy.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Paste the role ARN into Alethia
records.text:
Run `tofu output` and paste `role_arn` — it looks like `acs:ram:: :role/ `. That's the
only value Alethia needs (the OIDC-provider ARN is derived from it).

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console mints an OIDC assertion (audience `sts.aliyuncs.com`) and calls Alibaba STS
 `AssumeRoleWithOIDC` with your role + provider ARNs
2. Alibaba validates the assertion against the RAM OIDC provider and returns temporary credentials
3. A successful assume is the proof of access → `Connected` / `Disconnected`

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- The **RAM role ARN**
- The derived **RAM OIDC provider ARN** (`acs:ram:: :oidc-provider/alethia`)
- The **account id** (parsed from the role ARN)

**No credentials, ever.** Revoke access by deleting the RAM role (or the OIDC provider) in your account.

records.title: AWS Connector
records.text: AWS Connector. Keyless, issuer-direct IAM role — an IAM OIDC provider trusting the Alethia issuer, set up in AWS CloudShell or with OpenTofu.

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: AWS Connector
records.text:
Connecting AWS registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **keyless and issuer-direct**: your account registers an **IAM OIDC provider** that trusts
Alethia's OIDC issuer, plus an IAM role Alethia assumes via **`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`** — no access keys, no
external id, and no trust in an Alethia AWS account. This is the same model GCP, Azure, and Alibaba use. See
[Security Architecture](/concepts/security) for the full model.

 
**Is this safe?** You create the trust entirely in **your own** AWS account — Alethia never sees a key.
It signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that AWS verifies and swaps for a ~1-hour credential. The
only thing Alethia stores is the **role ARN** (a public identifier). **Revoke anytime** by deleting the
IAM role (and its OIDC provider).

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: Setup Methods
records.text:
Two equivalent, keyless paths — the **AWS CloudShell** script (nothing to install) or the **OpenTofu**
module. Both create the same IAM OIDC provider + `AlethiaProvisionerRole` in your account.

 
 
 

 ### Open AWS CloudShell
 Open [AWS CloudShell](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudshell/home) — the `aws` CLI is
 preinstalled and already authenticated. (Or run the script locally with a configured `aws` CLI.)

 ### Run the setup script
 Paste the one-liner from the connect sheet — `curl -sO …/alethia-aws-setup.sh && bash alethia-aws-setup.sh`.
 It creates the **IAM OIDC provider** for the Alethia issuer + `AlethiaProvisionerRole` (whose trust
 allows **only** `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` from that provider, pinned to audience
 `sts.amazonaws.com` and subject `alethia-connector`), attaches the five least-privilege policies, and
 prints `role_arn`. Self-hosters pass their issuer as the first argument.

 ### Copy Role ARN
 Copy the `role_arn` the script prints and paste it into the form, then click "Connect."

 
 
 
 

 ### Apply the OpenTofu module
 Download the module ("Download module" in the connect sheet) and run `tofu apply`. It creates the
 IAM OIDC provider + role that tr

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
After submitting, Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console mints a short-lived assertion and calls `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` on your role
2. Calls `sts:GetCallerIdentity` to confirm the assumed identity (proof of access)
3. Runs a small capability probe (representative reads) → the cloud identity is `Connected`, or `Degraded`
 when provisioning permissions are missing, or `Disconnected` when auth fails

If verification fails, the error message explains what went wrong (e.g., trust policy misconfiguration,
missing permissions). Existing resources (VPCs, subnets, …) are discovered separately by the
server-side [asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory), not during this probe.

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: IAM Role Permissions
records.text:
What the role may *do* is independent of *who may assume it* (the OIDC trust above) — a separate axis.

**Exactly what Alethia provisions in your account** (feature-gated — a given Project uses a subset): EC2/VPC
(subnets, NAT, route tables, security groups, VPC endpoints), EKS (cluster, managed node groups, add-ons, the
IRSA OIDC provider + controller roles), RDS (Aurora), ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey), Route 53, ACM, Secrets
Manager, DynamoDB, SQS/SNS, ECR, S3, KMS envelope keys, CloudWatch Logs + Kinesis Firehose, EventBridge
(Karpenter), Application Auto Scaling, and the in-cluster controller IAM roles (external-dns, AWS Load
Balancer Controller, EBS CSI, Karpenter).

 
**Least-privilege by default — no account admin, fully action-enumerated.** The setup attaches **five scoped
policies** instead of `AdministratorAccess`: `…-ComputeNet`, `…-ComputeScale`, `…-Data`, `…-Edge` — the
data-plane, each listing the **specific `ec2:`/`eks:`/`rds:`/… actions** the templates issue (not
`service:*`; split into net/scale to fit AWS's 6144-char managed-policy limit) — plus an action-enumerated
`…-IAM` policy. The IAM policy lets the templates create the EKS/IRSA roles they need but **explicitly

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
Only the **Role ARN** (`arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AlethiaProvisionerRole`) is stored. No access keys,
secret keys, session tokens, or external id are ever persisted — every credential is a short-lived assertion
minted at call time.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.text: Azure Connector. Keyless Azure access — a managed identity in your own subscription, no client secrets.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Azure Connector
records.text:
Connecting Azure registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **keyless** and
**customer-side**. You create a **user-assigned managed identity** in your own subscription (a plain ARM
resource — no App Registration, no directory-admin rights) with a Federated Identity Credential that
trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer. Both the console (verification) and the runner (provisioning) authenticate
**as that identity** by presenting a short-lived OIDC assertion; Azure validates it and issues an ARM
access token. **You store no client secret**, and there is **no platform Entra app** — parity with the GCP
Workload Identity Federation model. See [Security Architecture](/concepts/security).

 
**Is this safe?** You create the identity in **your own** subscription and grant it a least-privilege role.
Alethia signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that Entra ID verifies and swaps for a ~1-hour
credential. The only things stored are your **tenant, subscription, and managed-identity client id** (all
public). **Revoke anytime** by deleting the managed identity.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The connect dialog gives you a one-line `az` command (or an OpenTofu module). It runs entirely in **your**
subscription:

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Create the managed identity + federated credential
records.text:
`az identity create` provisions a user-assigned managed identity, and
`az identity federated-credential create` adds a credential trusting the Alethia issuer (subject
`alethia-connector`, audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`). No App Registration, no secret.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Assign the least-privilege role
records.text:
The script creates and assigns the **Alethia Provisioner** custom role — scoped to exactly the services
the project templates create, with an ABAC condition that limits role-assignment writes to the single
DNS Zone Contributor role (no path to self-escalation).

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Enter details in Alethia
records.text:
Paste back the three values the script prints:
- **Tenant ID** — your Entra directory ID
- **Client ID** — the managed identity's application id
- **Subscription ID** — the target Azure subscription

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
Same as other providers — Alethia verifies access **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console mints an OIDC assertion for your managed identity and presents it to your tenant
2. Azure validates it against the identity's federated credential and returns an ARM access token
3. A small ARM read confirms provisioning access → `Connected` / `Degraded` / `Disconnected`

Existing VNets, subnets, and DNS zones are discovered separately by the server-side
[asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- **Tenant ID**
- **Client ID** (your managed identity's application id)
- **Subscription ID**

**No client secrets, ever.** Revoke access by deleting the managed identity (or its role assignment)
in your subscription.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.text: Chart Repositories. Connect a private Helm or OCI chart source so Alethia can scan and deploy charts it holds.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Chart Repositories
records.text:
A **chart repository** connector stores the credential Alethia uses to read Helm charts from a private
source — an OCI registry such as GitHub Container Registry, or a classic HTTPS chart repository.

It is the sibling of a [container registry](/guides/design-project/container-registry) connector, and
the difference matters: a container registry credential becomes a Kubernetes `imagePullSecret` so your
*workloads* can pull *images*. A chart repository credential becomes an ArgoCD **repository
credential**, so *Alethia* can read *charts*. Connecting one does not let your pods pull images, and
connecting the other does not let Alethia read a chart.

You only need a chart repository if your charts are private. Public charts work without any connector.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Providers
records.text:
Connect these from **Connectors → Chart repositories**. Every provider authenticates with a username
and a token.

 Provider Registry host Credential 
 ---------- --------------- ------------ 
 **HTTPS Helm Repository** You supply the full repository URL Username · Password / token 
 **GitHub Container Registry** `ghcr.io` Username · Password / token 
 **Docker Hub** `registry-1.docker.io` Username · Access token 
 **GitLab Container Registry** `registry.gitlab.com`, or your own Username · Password / token 
 **Scaleway Container Registry** Your Scaleway host, e.g. `rg.fr-par.scw.cloud` Secret key 
 **Generic OCI Registry** You supply the host — Harbor, JFrog, or any OCI-compliant registry Username · Password / token 

 
**Amazon ECR and ECR Public are not available yet.** ECR authenticates with a token that expires after
twelve hours, so there is no stable password to store. Supporting it needs a credential that refreshes
itself inside the cluster, which is tracked separately. Charts in every other provider above work today.
 

Only the token is secret. The repository URL and registry host are stored as ordinary configuration and
appear in the project's configuration snapshot; the

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Selecting one on a project
records.text:
A connector holds a credential. To use it, add a **chart repository** to the environment on the canvas
and pick the connected provider. Adding it per environment means staging and production can read charts
from different registries.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: How Alethia matches a chart to a credential
records.text:
Alethia does not ask which credential a chart should use. It matches the chart's **host** against the
chart repositories you connected, taking the most specific match:

- An OCI chart matches by URL prefix, so a credential for `oci://ghcr.io` covers
 `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/payments`.
- An HTTPS chart repository matches exactly.

This is the same rule ArgoCD applies, which is what keeps one credential in play from end to end: the
same match authenticates the [safety scan](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts#the-safety-scan)
when you attach a chart and ArgoCD's pull when it deploys. A chart whose host matches nothing you
connected is read anonymously — correct for a public chart, and a clear authentication failure for a
private one.

The credential is delivered to the Runner out of band, when it claims the job. It is never written into
the project's configuration, the job record, or the job logs.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Where the charts are used
records.text:
The same connector serves both kinds of chart:

- [Bring-your-own charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) — your own packaged application.
- Marketplace add-ons, when you point one at a private mirror instead of its public chart.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Registries on a private network
records.text:
By default the Runner refuses to pull a chart from a private or link-local address. The Runner holds
platform credentials, so an operator-supplied chart URL that resolves inside the network — or to the
cloud metadata service — would be a way to reach things it should not.

If your registry genuinely sits on an internal network (a self-hosted Harbor or JFrog on RFC1918
space), set `ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1` on the Runner. See
[Self-hosted runner](/guides/runners/self-operated#environment-variables). Loopback and link-local addresses stay
blocked either way.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Adding a provider
records.text:
The provider set is defined in the connector catalog. To add one, follow the recipe in
[Pluggable connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable#adding-a-new-provider) — a chart repository
provider supplies a repository credential rather than an OpenTofu module, so it needs no module path.

See also: [Bring Your Own Helm Charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) ·
[Pluggable Connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable) ·
[Managing Connections](/guides/connectors/managing-connections)

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.text: Cross-Account Secret Managers. Read secrets from a cloud secret manager in a different account, project, or subscription — keyless.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.text:
A Project's workloads sometimes need secrets that live in a **different** cloud account than the cluster — a central AWS Secrets Manager account, a shared GCP Secret Manager project, an Azure Key Vault in another subscription, or an Alibaba KMS Secrets Manager in another RAM account. The **cross-account secret manager** connectors let the cluster read those secrets **keylessly**: no access key is created, and Alethia never holds admin in the account that owns the secrets.

 Connector Reads from Auth method 
 ----------- ----------- ------------- 
 **AWS Secrets Manager (cross-account)** Secrets Manager in another AWS account `iam_role` 
 **GCP Secret Manager (cross-project)** Secret Manager in another GCP project `service_account` 
 **Azure Key Vault (cross-subscription)** Key Vault in another Azure subscription (same tenant) `service_principal` 
 **Alibaba KMS Secrets Manager (cross-account)** KMS Secrets Manager in another RAM account `ram_role`

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
Each cluster runs the [External Secrets Operator](/guides/design-project/secrets). It already authenticates to the cluster's own cloud with the cluster's workload identity (IRSA on AWS, Workload Identity on GCP, workload identity on Azure, RRSA on Alibaba). A cross-account connector points that same identity at a secret manager in another account through a **trust grant the secret owner creates**:

1. **You bootstrap a least-privilege read grant** in the account that owns the secrets, using a small OpenTofu module Alethia ships. The grant trusts your cluster's identity and allows **read only**.
2. **You paste the grant's references** (a role ARN, a project id, a vault URL) into the connector. No key is stored — only references.
3. **The operator reads across the boundary.** Alethia renders an additional `ClusterSecretStore` that resolves secrets from the other account, alongside the cluster's native store.

This is the same [zero-credential model](/concepts/security) the rest of Alethia uses: the secret owner grants the least privilege, and the control plane only references it.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Set up a cross-account connector
records.text: Each connector needs a one-time bootstrap in the account that **owns the secrets**. The OpenTofu modules live in the Alethia repository under `infra/connector/ /secrets-xacct/`, each with a README.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: AWS Secrets Manager
records.text:
Run `infra/connector/aws/secrets-xacct` in the secrets account. It creates a read-only role that trusts your cluster's external-secrets identity and grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on the secrets you name. Enter the printed **Target Role ARN**, the **target account id**, and the **region** in the connector.

Name the secret ARNs you intend to share. The module has no wildcard fallback, so it refuses to apply rather than granting read on every secret in the account.

You can also set an `external_id` on the module to require an `sts:ExternalId` on the assume. If you do, enter the same value in the connector's **External ID** field: the operator sends it with the assume, and AWS rejects the read when the two disagree. This control is AWS-only — the other three clouds bind the grant to a specific principal instead, so there is nothing equivalent to set.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: GCP Secret Manager
records.text: Run `infra/connector/gcp/secrets-xacct` in the secrets project. It grants your cluster's external-secrets service account `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on each secret you name. Enter the **target project id** in the connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Azure Key Vault
records.text: Run `infra/connector/azure/secrets-xacct` in the subscription that owns the vault. It assigns your cluster's workload identity the **Key Vault Secrets User** role on the target vault. Enter the **target subscription id** and the **vault URL** in the connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Alibaba KMS Secrets Manager
records.text: Run `infra/connector/alibaba/secrets-xacct` in the secrets account. It registers your cluster's OIDC issuer as a RAM OIDC provider and creates a read-only KMS role that trusts your cluster's external-secrets service account. Enter the printed **Target Role ARN** and **Target OIDC Provider ARN** in the connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Keep the grant working when you rebuild a cluster
records.text:
Each grant above names your cluster's external-secrets identity. On AWS that identity has a stable
name, so a rebuild keeps working. On GCP and Azure it does not:

- **GCP** treats a recreated service account as a new identity, even with the same name. The old
 grant is left pointing at the deleted one.
- **Azure** generates a new object id for the managed identity, and the role assignment binds that
 id.

So on those two clouds, destroying and recreating a cluster breaks the cross-account read until you
re-run the bootstrap.

To avoid that, create the identity yourself once and tell the cluster template to use it:

 Cloud Variable 
 --- --- 
 GCP `external_secrets_service_account_email` 
 Azure `external_secrets_identity_name` and `external_secrets_identity_resource_group` 

The template then federates and grants against your identity instead of creating its own, and never
creates, changes or deletes it. Grant that identity access in the secrets account once, and it keeps
working across rebuilds.

Leave the variables unset to keep the default behavior, where the template owns the identity.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: What is not supported
records.text:
Two combinations are out of scope, by cloud-platform limits rather than choice:

- **Hetzner** has no cloud secret manager. Use the [HashiCorp Vault connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) for secrets on Hetzner.
- **Azure cross-tenant** is not available keyless. An Azure managed or workload identity cannot be used across tenants. The Azure connector reads across **subscriptions within one tenant**; a vault in a different tenant needs an app registration and federated credential in that tenant, which is outside this connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Pluggable Connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable) — API-key connectors for DNS, secrets, registry, and observability.
- [Secrets](/guides/design-project/secrets) — choosing a secrets provider per Project.
- [Security model](/concepts/security) — how Alethia keeps the zero-credential guarantee.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.text: GCP Connector. Workload Identity Federation setup with OIDC token exchange.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: GCP Connector
records.text:
Connecting GCP registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that uses **Workload Identity Federation (WIF)** with **direct OIDC** — your project's WIF pool
trusts Alethia's issuer directly (no AWS hop), and Alethia federates in with a short-lived minted JWT. No
service account JSON keys are created or stored. See [Security Architecture](/concepts/security).

 
**Is this safe?** You create the trust entirely in **your own** GCP project — no service account key is
ever generated. Alethia signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that GCP verifies and swaps for a
~1-hour access token. The only thing stored is the **WIF trust configuration** (no secret). **Revoke
anytime** by deleting the pool or unbinding the service account.
 

The connect sheet gives you two one-shot paths that create everything for you. When they finish, you enter
just **two values** — your **Project ID** and **Project Number** — and Alethia assembles the WIF credential
configuration for you (there is no JSON to copy). Both paths pin the same values the console mints: issuer
`https://alethialabs.io/api/oidc`, audience `alethia-gcp-wif`, subject `alethia-connector`, and the fixed
pool `alethia-pool` / provi

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console presents an OIDC token to GCP's Security Token Service (Workload Identity Federation)
2. GCP validates the token against the registered issuer/subject and returns a short-lived access token
3. A small Compute read confirms provisioning access → `Connected` / `Degraded` / `Disconnected`

Existing resources (VPC networks, subnets, DNS zones) are discovered separately by the server-side
[asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Service Account Permissions
records.text:
What the service account may *do* is independent of *who may impersonate it* (the WIF trust above).

**Exactly what Alethia provisions in your project** (feature-gated — a given Project uses a subset):
Compute/VPC (networks, subnets, Cloud Router + NAT, firewall rules, Cloud Armor), GKE (cluster + node
pools), Cloud SQL, Memorystore (Redis), Cloud DNS, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager, Cloud Storage,
Firestore, Pub/Sub, and the workload-identity service accounts + bindings for in-cluster controllers.

 
**Least-privilege by default — no `roles/editor`.** The provisioner service account gets **11 predefined
roles + 6 custom roles**:

- **11 predefined roles** for services whose Google-maintained admin set is already tightly scoped and
 churns with new features (`container.admin`, `compute.networkAdmin`, `compute.securityAdmin`,
 `servicenetworking.networksAdmin`, `cloudsql.admin`, `redis.admin`, `dns.admin`, `artifactregistry.admin`,
 `secretmanager.admin`, `cloudkms.admin`, `iam.serviceAccountUser`) — hand-enumerating those buys nothing.
 `cloudkms.admin` creates the customer-managed key that encrypts Kubernetes Secrets in etcd. It grants no
 permission to *use* the key: `cryptoKe

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Optional APIs you enable yourself
records.text:
Alethia cannot turn APIs on in your project. Enabling one needs
`serviceusage.services.enable`, which would let the provisioner switch on **any** API in your
project, including billable ones you did not ask for. There is no narrower version of that
permission, so Alethia does not hold it. The provisioner can only *read* whether an API is on
(`serviceusage.services.get`), which is what lets a deployment tell you a prerequisite is missing
instead of silently doing nothing.

One feature needs an API you enable once per project:

 Feature API Enable with 
 --- --- --- 
 Container registry → **Vulnerability scanning** `containerscanning.googleapis.com` `gcloud services enable containerscanning.googleapis.com --project ` 

Artifact Registry has no per-repository "on" switch for scanning — a repository can only *follow the
project default* or opt out. So the switch does nothing unless the API is enabled for the project.

If you turn the switch on without it, the deployment **stops before it changes anything** and tells
you which API to enable. Nothing is half-applied, and no repository is created claiming to be
scanned when it is not. Enable the API, then deploy again.

Leaving the switch

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Password-free Cloud SQL
records.text:
Alethia can run your app against Cloud SQL with **no database password**: the pod impersonates a
Google service account through GKE Workload Identity and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy mints a
short-lived IAM token from it.

This is **opt-in on Google Cloud**, and it needs one value from you. After running the setup, take
the `alethia-appdb` account it created and set it in Alethia as:

cloud_sql_app_service_account_email = alethia-appdb@ .iam.gserviceaccount.com

The Terraform module outputs it as `cloud_sql_app_service_account_email`; the shell script prints it
at the end. Leave it unset and your apps keep using password authentication — nothing breaks, and
turning on IAM auth without it simply warns that keyless is not wired.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Why you create this account instead of Alethia
records.text:
`roles/cloudsql.client` and `roles/cloudsql.instanceUser` can only be granted **on the whole
project**. A Cloud SQL instance does not carry its own IAM policy, so there is no way to scope those
roles to a single database instance the way Alethia scopes DNS to one zone and Secret Manager to one
secret.

Granting a project-wide role needs `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` — the permission that
lets a principal grant itself *anything*. Alethia deliberately does not hold it. So this one grant
is made by you, once, at setup, rather than by the provisioner on every deployment.

 
**One database identity per Google Cloud project.** Every Alethia environment in the project shares
the `alethia-appdb` account, so an app in one environment can log in to another environment's Cloud
SQL instance. What it may *do* inside a database is still scoped by the SQL grants Alethia issues
per database. If you need environments isolated at the identity level, run them in **separate Google
Cloud projects**.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: How this differs from AWS and Azure
records.text:
On AWS and Azure the equivalent identity is created per environment during deployment, because both
let the role be scoped to the individual database — AWS through IRSA and RDS IAM auth, Azure through
Entra. Google Cloud's IAM model does not offer that scope for Cloud SQL, so Google Cloud is the one
provider where password-free database auth needs a setup step and shares one identity per project.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- **GCP Project ID** and **Project Number**
- **WIF configuration** — assembled by the console from those two IDs: the pool + provider audience, the
 service account impersonation URL, and the token-file credential source. The provisioner service account
 is referenced by that impersonation URL; there's no separate key field.

No service account JSON keys. Access is revoked by deleting the WIF pool or unbinding the service account.

records.title: Git Providers
records.text: Git Providers. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket OAuth integration with automatic token refresh.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Git Providers
records.text: Git provider connectors give Alethia access to your repositories for GitOps. Three providers are supported, each through OAuth.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Supported Providers
records.text:
Provider Auth Method Token Refresh 
 ---------- ----------- --------------- 
 GitHub OAuth 2.0 Automatic via refresh token 
 GitLab OAuth 2.0 Automatic via refresh token 
 Bitbucket OAuth 2.0 Automatic via refresh token

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Click Connect
records.text: Click "Connect" on the provider card in the Connectors page.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: OAuth Authorization
records.text: You're redirected to the provider's authorization page. Grant the application access to your repositories.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Callback
records.text: The provider redirects back to Alethia with an authorization code. Better Auth exchanges it for access and refresh tokens.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Token Storage
records.text: Better Auth stores the provider tokens in its `account` table — one row per linked account.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Token Refresh
records.text:
Git tokens have limited lifetimes. The `getValidProviderToken()` server action wraps Better Auth's `getAccessToken`, which handles refresh transparently:

1. Better Auth reads the linked account from the `account` table
2. If the access token has expired, it refreshes using the stored refresh token against the provider's token endpoint
3. It returns a valid access token and persists the refreshed one

This happens transparently whenever a Git operation is needed.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: What Tokens Are Used For
records.text:
- **Repository listing** — the Design a Project form shows repos from your connected provider
- **ArgoCD access** — after deploying, ArgoCD uses the token to watch repositories for changes
- **Template cloning** — infrastructure templates can be sourced from your repositories

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Disconnecting
records.text:
Disconnecting a Git provider:

1. Calls `deleteProviderToken()`, which unlinks the account via Better Auth (`unlinkAccount`) — deleting its `account` row
2. Existing ArgoCD installations that use this token will lose repository access

 
Disconnecting a Git provider affects all projects that use repositories from that provider. ArgoCD will show "sync failed" until a new token is provided.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.text: Connection Health & Inventory. How Alethia verifies cloud connections and keeps their asset inventory fresh — server-side, no runner.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Connection Health & Inventory
records.text:
Once a cloud account is connected, Alethia does two things **entirely server-side in the console** — no
[Runner](/concepts/runner) is involved. The runner is provisioning-only; it never tests connections or lists
resources.

 
 Every cloud identity is **platform-managed**: the control plane (the hosted service, or your own console when
 self-hosted) mints the short-lived credentials on demand — it federates off the Alethia OIDC issuer, so it
 holds no standing cloud credential (Alibaba is even account-free). There is no "bring the token to a
 self-hosted runner" path.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Connection health
records.text:
The moment you connect (and continuously afterward), Alethia runs an **instant health probe**:

1. **Auth** — assume the customer role / exchange the federated token / present the API token, using the
 platform credentials. Success proves access.
2. **Provisioning-capability probe** — a small set of representative reads to confirm the cloud identity can
 actually see what Alethia provisions into.

The result is one of three statuses, surfaced on the connector card:

 Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 **Connected** Authenticated and the capability probe passed. Ready to provision. 
 **Degraded** Authenticated, but some provisioning permissions look missing — provisioning may fail until the role/policy is widened. The missing permissions are listed. 
 **Disconnected** Authentication failed (revoked trust, a trust policy that no longer pins the Alethia issuer, expired/invalid token). 

Health is re-checked on a schedule and can be re-run on demand with **Re-verify**. Because it's a direct
API call, it resolves in well under a second — there is no queue and no job to wait on.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Asset inventory
records.text:
Alethia keeps a normalized inventory of the resources you provision alongside (VPCs/networks, subnets,
NICs, Kubernetes clusters, databases, caches, queues, topics, NoSQL tables, container registries,
secrets, storage buckets, DNS zones, and regions). It powers the **"use existing VPC"** picker on the
canvas and gives the verification agent real-world context.

The inventory is maintained server-side:

- **On connect** — a first sync populates the baseline.
- **Reconciliation sweep** — an in-process scheduler (no external cron) re-lists per cloud identity via the
 cloud SDKs on a TTL cadence (health ~10 min, inventory ~1 h), upserts the typed `cloud_*` tables,
 soft-removes anything no longer present, and **backfills** cloud identities that were never synced. This is
 the reliable backstop and is **on by default**.
- **Event-driven updates (opt-in, near-real-time)** — a per-cloud forwarder can stream change events so
 the inventory reflects a new/deleted resource within seconds (**AWS** EventBridge → Lambda; **GCP**
 Cloud Asset Inventory → Pub/Sub → Cloud Function; **Azure** Event Grid → Function App; **Alibaba**
 ActionTrail → EventBridge → Function Compute). Each normalizes
 the

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Data custody — how the inventory is stored
records.text:
The inventory is a **minimized, encrypted, expiring projection** — the cloud stays the source of truth:

- **Minimized** — only the identifiers features need (resource id, name, region, kind + low-sensitivity
 typed fields). We do **not** store resource tags (they routinely carry owner emails / cost centers /
 secrets); only the `Name` tag becomes the row name.
- **Encrypted at rest** — reconnaissance-sensitive attributes (CIDRs, IPs, endpoints, DNS domains) are
 sealed in a single AES-GCM `sensitive` blob per row, decrypted only in-app when a feature needs them.
- **Expiring + purged** — soft-removed rows are garbage-collected after a retention window
 (`ALETHIA_INVENTORY_RETENTION_DAYS`, default 7); **disconnecting a cloud identity purges its inventory
 entirely**.

Storing this metadata doesn't weaken the keyless model — a resource id or CIDR is not a
credential, and a breach grants no cloud access (that still requires the role trust, which Alethia holds
no key for).

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: What the Runner does NOT do
records.text:
For clarity, the [Runner](/concepts/runner) is **provisioning-only**. It does **not**:

- test cloud connections (server-side, above),
- discover or list cloud resources (server-side asset inventory, above),
- cache resource lists.

It claims `PLAN` / `DEPLOY` / `DESTROY` (and the runner-lifecycle + drift) jobs, runs OpenTofu, streams
logs, and runs the [verify gate](/concepts/runner). See [Runner Jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution).

records.title: Hetzner Connector
