records.text: Hetzner Connector. Scoped, project-scoped API token — encrypted at rest, decrypted only on the runner. Provisions a self-managed Talos Linux Kubernetes cluster on cheap Hetzner VMs.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: Hetzner Connector
records.text:
Connecting Hetzner Cloud registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **token-based**. Unlike AWS, GCP, Azure, and Alibaba — which are
**keyless** (Alethia federates into a role you grant via short-lived, minted OIDC assertions) —
Hetzner Cloud offers **no OIDC or workload-identity federation**. Its only auth primitive is a
**project-scoped API token**. So Alethia connects with a token you create, **encrypted at rest
(AES-GCM)** and **decrypted only on the runner** at provision time — never written into a project
snapshot. This is the best-available model for a cloud without federation. See
[Security Architecture](/concepts/security) for the full model.

 
**Is this safe?** The token is stored **encrypted** (AES-256-GCM) and is only ever decrypted on the
runner during a provisioning job — it never appears in a job's config snapshot. A Hetzner token is
scoped to a **single Hetzner project** (the tightest boundary Hetzner offers). **Revoke anytime** by
deleting the token in the Hetzner Cloud Console — that instantly cuts Alethia's access.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: What Hetzner provisions
records.text:
Hetzner Cloud has no managed Kubernetes or managed data services. Instead, Alethia provisions a
**self-managed [Talos Linux](https://www.talos.dev/) Kubernetes cluster** on Hetzner's inexpensive
VMs (ARM `CAX` or x86 `CX`/`CPX`/`CCX`), with Cilium networking and the Hetzner CSI driver for block
storage. Data services (Postgres, cache, queue) that would be managed cloud resources on a
hyperscaler run **in-cluster via Helm** — CloudNativePG (Postgres), Valkey (cache), and RabbitMQ
(queue) — deployed through ArgoCD. See
[Health & Inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory) for how cloud identities are probed.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
### Create a project-scoped API token
 In the [Hetzner Cloud Console](https://console.hetzner.cloud/), open your project, then
 **Security → API Tokens → Generate API token**. Give it **Read & Write** permission —
 provisioning creates servers, networks, and volumes. The token is scoped to just that one
 project.

 ### Paste into Alethia
 Paste the token into the Alethia connect sheet and click **Connect**. Alethia encrypts it at rest
 (AES-GCM) and verifies it immediately against the Hetzner Cloud API.

 
 
 
 

 ### Run a self-hosted runner
 If you operate your own runner, set **`HCLOUD_TOKEN`** in the runner's own environment. Alethia
 then stores **no token at all** — the runner supplies it directly at provision time. This is the
 zero-storage path for federation-less clouds.

 ### Connect
 Mark the cloud identity self-managed; provisioning jobs claimed by your runner use its environment's
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN` and Alethia never persists a credential.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
After you submit, Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner): it decrypts
the stored token and calls a cheap authenticated Hetzner Cloud API endpoint
(`GET https://api.hetzner.cloud/v1/datacenters`).

- `200` → the cloud identity is **Connected**
- `401` / `403` → the token was rejected (bad or revoked) → **Disconnected**

On success, Alethia also syncs the project's **regions** (used for placement) into the asset
[inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory). If verification fails, the error explains what
went wrong.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- **Managed:** only your **encrypted API token** (AES-256-GCM), decrypted solely on the runner at
 provision time — never in a project snapshot.
- **Self-hosted runner:** **nothing** — the runner carries `HCLOUD_TOKEN` in its own environment.

Rotate or revoke the token in the Hetzner Cloud Console at any time to cut access.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.text: Connectors Overview. Connect cloud providers and Git accounts to enable infrastructure provisioning.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Connectors
records.text: The **connector** catalog is the registry of provider *types* you can connect. Each account you actually connect becomes a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) — the credential anchor a project provisions against. The catalog spans the **federated clouds** (AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba) and the **token clouds** (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Civo), plus Git providers (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and **pluggable per-category providers** (DNS, secrets, registry, chart repositories, observability). At least one cloud identity and one Git provider must be connected before provisioning; pluggable providers are optional — they let a project use a tool you already run instead of the cloud-native default.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: How It Works
records.text:
Connectors are displayed as cards organized by category:

 Category Providers Auth 
 ---------- ----------- ------ 
 **Cloud Providers** AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba keyless federation off the Alethia OIDC issuer (no stored keys) 
 **Token Clouds** Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Civo the customer's own API token (encrypted at rest) 
 **Git Providers** GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket OAuth 
 **DNS** Cloudflare API key 
 **Secrets** HashiCorp Vault API key 
 **Registry** Docker Hub API key 
 **Chart repositories** GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, GitLab, Scaleway, generic OCI, HTTPS API key 
 **Observability** Datadog, Grafana Cloud API key 

Each card shows:
- Provider icon and name
- Connection status — a grayscale status badge (dot + label, no color): **Connected**, **Needs Reconnection**, or **Not Connected**
- Connected account identifier (AWS Account ID, GCP Project, GitHub username)
- Action button (Connect / Disconnect / Reconnect)

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Connection Status
records.text:
Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 **Connected** Credentials valid and verified 
 **Needs Reconnection** Git token expired, automatic refresh failed 
 **Not Connected** No credentials on file 
 **Coming Soon** Provider supported but not yet implemented

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Cloud Provider Connections
records.text:
The four **federated clouds** use the platform's [zero-credential model](/concepts/security) — the customer's
role/pool/provider trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer directly, and Alethia federates in with a short-lived minted
assertion. **No static keys are stored.**

 
 Keyless IAM role via an IAM OIDC provider 
 Workload Identity Federation — enter Project ID + Number, config assembled for you 
 Federated credential on your own managed identity — no platform Entra app 
 RAM AssumeRoleWithOIDC (account-free) 
 

The **token clouds** (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Civo) instead use the customer's own API token — there is no
account to federate into. The token is encrypted at rest (`ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`). Only the console holds that key: it
decrypts the token when a runner claims a job and hands it to that runner, so no runner can read a
stored credential.

After connecting, Alethia verifies the credentials **instantly, server-side** (an auth + provisioning-permission probe — no runner, no job) and marks the cloud identity `Connected`, `Degraded`, or `Disconnected`. Existing resources (VPCs, subnets, DNS zones) are discovered + kept fresh by the server-side, event-driven asset inventory

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Git Provider Connections
records.text: Git connections use standard OAuth. See [Git Providers](/guides/connectors/git-providers) for details.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Pluggable Connectors
records.text:
DNS, secrets, registry, chart repository, and observability providers authenticate with an **API key / token**. Secret fields are encrypted at rest (`ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`). The console decrypts them only to hand them to the runner running the job that needs them, and they are never stored in a Project snapshot. After connecting, a verification ping confirms the credential works.

 
 Cloudflare · Vault · Docker Hub · Datadog · Grafana Cloud 
 Private Helm and OCI chart sources

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Disconnecting
records.text:
- **Cloud providers**: Removes the `cloud_identities` record. Existing projects referencing that identity can no longer run jobs.
- **Git providers**: Removes the Better Auth `account` record and revokes the OAuth grant.
- **Pluggable connectors**: Removes the `connector_credentials` record. Projects referencing that provider fall back to failing validation until reconnected.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.text: Managing Connections. Add a second account to a cloud provider, re-verify a connection, rename an account, and disconnect one — all from the connector detail sheet.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Managing Connections
records.text:
Every account you connect becomes a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`). A single provider can hold
**more than one** connected account — each verified account is a distinct identity row. Cloud connections
are **org-scoped**: every member of the org sees them (subject to their role), and mutating a connection
requires the `manage_identities` permission.

This page covers the day-2 actions on the connector detail sheet: adding another account, re-verifying,
renaming, and disconnecting. To connect an account for the first time, see the per-provider guides linked
from [Connectors Overview](/guides/connectors).

 
 These actions are managed **entirely server-side in the console** — no [Runner](/concepts/runner) and no job. A
 re-verify is a direct API call — a live probe against the provider, not a queued job. See
 [Connection Health & Inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Open the connector detail sheet
records.text:
Every action below starts from the same place.

1. Open the **Connectors** page.
2. Select the provider card.

The detail sheet lists each connected account for that provider, with its status and per-account actions.
If you don't have the `manage_identities` permission, the mutating actions are hidden.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Add another account
records.text:
Connect a second account to a provider that already has one — for example a second AWS account or a second
GCP project.

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Select **Add another account**.
3. Complete the provider's connect flow.

Each **Connect** starts a fresh pending identity, so verifying it adds a new account row rather than
replacing the existing one. The provider's own guide describes the credential steps (for example
[AWS](/guides/connectors/aws) or [GCP](/guides/connectors/gcp)).

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Re-verify a connection
records.text:
Re-check an account's health without re-entering its credentials — use this when an account shows
**Limited permissions** or **Verification failed**, for example after you widen a role or policy to
clear a permissions gap. The per-account **Re-verify** action is shown only for those two states.

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Find the account.
3. Select **Re-verify**.

Alethia flips the account to `testing`, re-runs the auth and provisioning-permission probe against the
stored credentials, and updates the status to one of:

 Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 **Connected** Authenticated and the capability probe passed. 
 **Limited permissions** Authenticated, but some provisioning permissions look missing. The missing permissions are listed. 
 **Verification failed** Authentication failed.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Rename an account
records.text:
Give an account a recognizable label instead of its default (for example `AWS Account (123456789012)`).

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Find the account.
3. Select **Rename**.
4. Enter a new name and confirm.

The name is trimmed and stored per account. Renaming does not change the account's credentials or status.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Disconnect an account
records.text:
Remove Alethia's access to a single account.

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Find the account.
3. Select the account's disconnect action.

Disconnecting resets the account to its pending state and:

- **clears all stored credentials** for that identity,
- **unlinks any projects** that referenced it (`projects.cloud_identity_id` is set to `null`), so those
 projects can no longer provision against it,
- **purges the account's asset inventory** — Alethia keeps no projection of a cloud it can no longer
 access.

 
 Disconnect targets a **single account**. Other accounts connected to the same provider are untouched.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Related
records.text:
The connector catalog and how cloud identities are authenticated. 
 How Alethia verifies connections and keeps their asset inventory fresh.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.text: Pluggable Connectors. Bring your own DNS, secrets, registry, chart repository, and observability tools via API-key connectors.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Pluggable Connectors
records.text:
Beyond cloud and Git, Alethia supports **pluggable per-category connectors** that let a Project mix in the tools you already use instead of the cloud-native default — Cloudflare for DNS, HashiCorp Vault for secrets, Docker Hub for a registry, a private Helm or OCI source for charts, and Datadog / Grafana Cloud for observability.

These connectors authenticate with an **API key / token** (`auth_method = api_key`) rather than cloud federation or OAuth.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Categories and providers
records.text:
Category Cloud-native default Pluggable provider Credential fields 
 ---------- ---------------------- -------------------- ------------------- 
 **DNS** Route 53 / Cloud DNS / Azure DNS **Cloudflare** API token 
 **Secrets** Secrets Manager / Secret Manager / Key Vault **HashiCorp Vault** Address, token 
 **Registry** ECR / Artifact Registry / ACR **Docker Hub** Username, access token 
 **Chart repositories** — (public charts need no credential) **[GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, GitLab, Scaleway, generic OCI, HTTPS](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories)** Username, password / token 
 **Observability** — (none) **Datadog** API key, app key 
 **Observability** — **Grafana Cloud** Instance ID, API token 

The catalog is data-driven — each provider is one row in the `connectors` table, seeded from a single manifest (`packages/core/categories/catalog.json`). See [Connectors Architecture](/concepts/connectors) for how this works end to end.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Connecting a provider
records.text:
1. Open **Connectors**, pick the provider card, and choose **Connect**.
2. Fill in the API credential — the form fields are generated from the provider's credential specification.
3. Alethia runs a lightweight **verification ping** against the provider's API (e.g. Cloudflare's token-verify endpoint, Vault's token lookup, Docker Hub login, Datadog's key-validate endpoint). A verified credential turns the card green; an unverified one is still saved so you can retry.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: How credentials are stored
records.text:
Secret fields (tokens, passwords) are **encrypted at rest** with AES-256-GCM before being written to the `connector_credentials` table; non-secret fields (a Vault address, a Docker Hub username) are stored in clear. The encryption key comes from `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (see [Configuration](/guides/self-hosting/configuration)).

 
Secrets are **never** placed in a Project's `config_snapshot`. They are decrypted and attached to a job only at **claim time**, then injected into the runner's OpenTofu variables in memory — preserving the [zero-credential model](/concepts/security).

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Using a connector in a Project
records.text:
Once connected, pick the provider per component in the [Project designer](/guides/design-project):

- [DNS & WAF](/guides/design-project/dns) — choose **Cloudflare** instead of cloud-native DNS.
- [Secrets](/guides/design-project/secrets) — choose **Vault**.
- [Container Registry](/guides/design-project/container-registry) — choose **Docker Hub**.
- [Chart repositories](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories) — add one per environment so Alethia can read your private charts.
- [Observability](/guides/design-project/observability) — choose **Datadog / Grafana Cloud**.

At provision time the runner composes the chosen provider's module into the plan and **skips** the cloud-native resource for that category.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Chart repositories
records.text:
A chart repository works differently from the categories above: it provisions nothing. It tells Alethia which credential to use when ArgoCD pulls a Helm chart from a private repository.

1. Connect the provider under **Chart Repos** on the Connectors page.
2. On the Project canvas, add a **Chart repository** component (**Add → DevOps → Chart repository**) and pick the connected provider. Providers that serve a single fixed host — GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub — need nothing more. For a self-hosted or generic registry, give the bare registry host (`registry.acme.io`, no scheme and no path); for an HTTPS Helm repository, give the full `https://` URL.
3. Deploy. Before it syncs any chart, the runner writes an ArgoCD **repository credential** for that repository. ArgoCD matches a chart to a credential by URL prefix, so the host you enter must match the host your charts are addressed by.

You need one only for a **private** repository. Public charts, including everything in the add-on marketplace, pull without a credential.

To use a private chart, attach it with **Add → Bring your own Helm chart**, choose **OCI registry**, and give the whole reference including the chart name (

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Adding a new provider
records.text:
Pluggable connectors are an open-ended catalog. Adding a sixth provider takes four steps and **no** changes to routes, the runner core, or the form engine:

1. Add a row to `packages/core/categories/catalog.json` (category, slug, auth_method, icon, credential + provider_config fields). Set `icon_url` to a path under `packages/assets/static` — the convention is `/icons/ / -32x32.png` — after committing the file there, or to `null` if no mark ships for the provider. `null` renders a monogram tile and issues no request; a path with no file behind it is rejected in step 4.
2. Add a `CategoryProvider` Go impl under `packages/core/categories/` (its `Tfvars`/`Validate` behavior).
3. Add the OpenTofu module under `infra/templates/categories/ / /`. A chart-repo provider has no module — it implements `RepoCred` instead, and must also get a host rule in `apps/console/lib/connectors/helm-registry-hosts.ts` so the console resolves the same credential URL the Go provider seeds.
4. Run `pnpm -F console gen:connectors` to regenerate the registry + catalog seed. It fails, naming the connector, if any `icon_url` does not resolve to a committed file under `packages/assets/static`.

See [Connectors Ar

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.text: Dashboard Overview. The main dashboard page — stats, cloud identity status, and recent jobs.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Dashboard Overview
records.text: The dashboard is the landing page after login. It provides a quick summary of your infrastructure state.

The dashboard shell wraps all authenticated pages with:

- **Live status** — job and environment status refresh by polling, fast while something is in flight (see [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime))

The overview page shows four stat chips at the top:

Below the stats:

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Connectors Panel
records.text: Shows connected and disconnected [cloud identities](/guides/connectors) as badges. Connected providers show a green indicator and account identifier (AWS Account ID, GCP Project, GitHub username). Disconnected providers link to the connectors page.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Recent Jobs
records.text:
A data table showing the 5 most recent jobs with columns:
- **Type** — job type with icon (PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY, etc.)
- **Status** — color-coded badge (green=SUCCESS, red=FAILED, yellow=PROCESSING, gray=QUEUED)

- **Created** — relative timestamp

Clicking a job row navigates to the [job detail page](/guides/jobs/job-detail).

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Notifications
records.text:
The notifications bell in the header shows a badge with the count of unread job state changes. Clicking it opens a popover with recent notifications. Clicking a notification navigates to the relevant job. "Mark all read" clears the count.

Notifications are driven by the real-time subscription to `jobs` — every status change (QUEUED → PROCESSING → SUCCESS/FAILED) creates a notification.

records.title: Dashboard Overview

**Main Navigation:**

records.title: Project Detail

records.title: Project Detail

The **Duplicate & Edit** action opens the Design a Project form pre-filled with the project's current configuration. If you select a different cloud identity (e.g., switching from AWS to GCP), the configuration is converted automatically. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion) for how this works.

Conversion warnings are displayed in the form if any settings couldn't be mapped directly (e.g., instance types, WAF rules, DNS zones).

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.text: Bring your own Helm charts. Attach your own Helm chart, scan it for safety, and describe the workloads it deploys as first-class canvas nodes you can bind to provisioned infrastructure.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: Bring your own Helm charts
records.text:
Not every workload starts as a Dockerfile in a repo. When you already package an application (or a
third-party one) as a **Helm chart**, you can bring it straight onto the canvas: Alethia deploys the
chart as-is, scans it for safety, and **describes what it actually deploys** so the chart stops being
an opaque box and becomes something you can see, configure, and wire into the rest of your
architecture.

The guiding principle: **Alethia describes and binds your chart — it never rewrites it.** Your chart
stays the single unit that gets deployed (as one hardened ArgoCD Application). Everything below is
about *understanding* and *connecting* that chart, not re-authoring it.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: Attaching a chart
records.text:
Open the canvas command menu (⌘K) and choose **Bring your own Helm chart** from the **Sources**
group. The first step, **Source**, picks where the chart comes from: a Git repository, or an OCI
registry. The remaining steps follow that choice — **Repository → Chart path → Ref → Review** for Git,
**Registry → Version → Review** for OCI. On **Review** you set the target namespace; left blank, it is
`default`.

For what the deployed chart may create, how it syncs, and how to remove it, see
[Bring-your-own charts](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts).

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: From a Git repository
records.text:
Attach the chart from a [connected Git provider](/guides/connectors/git-providers):

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Repository** The Git repo that holds the chart 
 **Chart path** The chart directory within the repo (e.g. `charts/payments`) 
 **Ref** The branch, tag, or commit to deploy 
 **Namespace** The Kubernetes namespace to install into 
 **Values** Your chart values (schema-validated knobs, or raw `values.yaml`)

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: From an OCI registry
records.text:
Attach the chart by its `oci://` reference. There is no chart path — the repository path *is* the
chart:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Chart reference** `oci:// / / ` (e.g. `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/payments`) 
 **Chart version** The chart version to deploy. `*` deploys the latest release 
 **Namespace** The Kubernetes namespace to install into 
 **Values** Your chart values (schema-validated knobs, or raw `values.yaml`) 

To use a **private** registry, connect it as a
[chart repository](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories) on the environment. Alethia matches your
chart's host against the chart repositories you connected and authenticates with that credential —
both when it scans the chart and when ArgoCD pulls it at deploy time. A public chart needs no
connector.

If your registry sits on an internal network rather than the public internet, the Runner needs an
opt-in as well — see
[`ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE`](/guides/runners/self-operated#environment-variables).

At deploy time the Runner renders the chart into a hardened, per-project ArgoCD `AppProject` locked to
your repo and namespace. See [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd) for how the Ap

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: The safety scan
records.text:
Before a chart is trusted to run, Alethia renders it (`helm template`) inside a **sandboxed,
network-isolated** environment and runs the [Elench](/concepts/elench/architecture) verification engine over
the resulting Kubernetes manifests — checking for privileged containers, host access, wildcard RBAC,
missing resource limits, and mutable image tags. The result is attached to the chart as a verify
report you can read on the canvas. The render holds **no secrets and has no network egress** — it only
reads the local chart.

This works the same way for both chart sources. The Runner fetches the chart first — cloning the Git
repo, or pulling it from the OCI registry — and only then renders it in the isolated sandbox. Fetching
happens outside that sandbox, so your registry credential is never exposed to the chart being
rendered.

 
Charts hosted in **Amazon ECR** cannot be scanned yet. ECR issues a short-lived token rather than a
stored password, so it is served by a different mechanism that is still in progress. Charts in every
other supported registry — GitHub Container Registry, GitLab, Docker Hub, Scaleway, and generic OCI
registries — scan normally.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: Described workloads
records.text:
A Helm chart is rarely one thing — it can render several Deployments, a StatefulSet, a CronJob, and
more. From the **same render** the safety scan produces, Alethia **describes each workload the chart
deploys** as its own node:

 What's described From 
 ------------------ ------ 
 **Kind** Deployment · StatefulSet · DaemonSet · CronJob · Job 
 **Image** The workload's primary container image 
 **Ports** The container ports it exposes 
 **Environment** The environment variable **names** it reads (values are never captured) 
 **Resources** The CPU/memory requests and limits it declares 
 **Replicas** The rendered replica count (Deployments and StatefulSets) 

These are **read-mostly descriptions** — they mirror what your chart renders, refreshed every time the
chart is re-scanned. They are deliberately kept separate from Alethia-built services, so a described
workload is never accidentally deployed twice: your chart's ArgoCD Application remains the one and
only thing that deploys it.

 
Environment is captured as variable **names only** — a described workload never stores a rendered
value, so a secret baked into a chart's manifests is never read back into Alethia.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: On the canvas
records.text:
Once a chart is scanned, its workloads appear as **child nodes beneath the chart node** — a line from
the chart to each thing it deploys. A workload node is drawn as a read-mostly card with a dashed, "not
owned by the design" treatment that sets it apart from an Alethia-built service, so you can tell at a
glance which nodes you author and which your chart brings.

Select a workload to open its **inspector**. The top of the panel is the description above —
image, ports, environment variable names, resources, and replicas, all read-only because they mirror
the chart. Below it is the only part you edit: the **overlay** — bindings, a couple of overrides, and
the value-paths those write to.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: Binding a chart to your infrastructure
records.text:
Because each workload is described, you can **bind** it to the databases, caches, queues, and secrets
you provisioned elsewhere on the canvas — the same [bindings](/guides/design-project/databases) model
Alethia-built services use. A binding injects the provisioned connection details into the running
chart by writing into the chart's **values** (for example, pointing the chart at an existing secret):

- **Endpoints and ports** are written as plain values.
- **Credentials** are written as a **reference** to a keyless, cluster-provisioned Kubernetes Secret —
 never as a plaintext value in your chart's values or Git. This keeps the
 [keyless](/concepts/security) guarantee intact end to end.

Binding works by writing into a **declared path** in your chart's values (for example
`postgresql.auth.existingSecret`). Alethia suggests the path from the chart's own conventions, and you
can override it. A chart that exposes no way to accept an existing secret is flagged honestly rather
than having a credential forced into it.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: Overrides: replicas and environment
records.text:
Beyond bindings, a described workload carries a small **editable overlay** you set from the inspector
without touching the chart:

- **Replicas** — override the rendered replica count.
- **Environment** — add or override environment variables (name → value).

Like bindings, these are written into the chart's values at deploy — they never re-author the chart,
and they survive a re-scan. Everything else on the card stays a read-only mirror of what the chart
renders.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: Value-path overrides
records.text:
Every binding and override needs to know **where** in your chart's values to write. Alethia infers
these paths from common chart conventions (`replicaCount`, `image.tag`,
`*.existingSecret` / `auth.existingSecret`) when it scans. When your chart's shape is non-standard, the
inspector's **value-paths** editor lets you correct any knob → dot-path mapping by hand — your override
always wins over the inferred default, and it's preserved across re-scans.

 
Bring-your-own Helm charts are an **opt-in** capability, enabled per deployment and — in the current
trusted-charts phase — scoped to charts you own on your own cluster. Described workloads and binding
roll out behind the same gate. Ask your operator whether it's enabled on your instance.

records.title: Bring your own Helm charts
records.heading: How it fits together
records.text:
1. **Attach** the chart from a connected repo (repo · chart path · ref · values) or an OCI registry
 (chart reference · version · values).
2. **Scan** — the Runner fetches the chart, renders it in the sandbox, and Elench verifies the
 manifests.
3. **Describe** — from that render, each workload the chart deploys becomes a canvas node.
4. **Bind & override** — from a workload's inspector, connect it to your provisioned infrastructure and
 set its replicas/environment overlay; bindings and overrides are written into the chart's values
 (credentials as keyless secret references) at the inferred or overridden value-paths.
5. **Deploy** — your chart, unchanged, syncs as a single ArgoCD Application with the bound values applied.

See also: [The Canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas) · [Repositories](/guides/design-project/repositories) · [Bring-your-own charts](/concepts/bring-your-own-charts) · [Bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.text: Bring your own IaC. Point a project environment at your own OpenTofu root module so Alethia provisions from it instead of the built-in template, behind a static safety scan.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Bring your own IaC
records.text:
Alethia normally provisions an environment from its built-in per-cloud template. **Bring-your-own IaC**
lets you point that environment at a git repo holding your **own OpenTofu root module** — Alethia
plans, scans, and applies *your* module instead. This is a **replace-mode** capability: the module
takes over the environment, and the built-in template no longer applies.

This guide covers writing a minimal module, attaching it, reading its safety scan, and detaching it.
For why the safety gate exists, what it blocks, the variable and cluster-output contracts, and who
may run a module, see [bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

 
Bring-your-own IaC is **opt-in**, enabled per instance with `ALETHIA_BYO_IAC_ENABLED=true`. With the
flag off, attaching, scanning, and provisioning a module all refuse. Ask your operator whether it's
enabled on your instance.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- Link the git provider that hosts your module. The attach dialog reads from your
 [connected git providers](/guides/connectors/git-providers) — if you have none, the repository
 selector offers a connect step.
- Use an environment with **no deployed (or in-flight) template infrastructure**. A replace-mode
 module would orphan existing template state, so attaching is rejected until you destroy that
 environment first.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Write a minimal module
records.text:
The smallest valid module needs no cluster and no cloud. A `random`/`null` module exercises the whole
path (attach → scan → plan → deploy → destroy) at zero spend. Put it in a repo directory, for example
`envs/dev/`:

hcl

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: main.tf — a minimal bring-your-own IaC module

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Platform context from the frozen Alethia contract (declare only what you use).
records.text:
variable "alethia_project" { type = string }
variable "alethia_environment" { type = string }

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Your own variables (any name NOT starting with alethia_).

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Attach a module
records.text:
The attach flow is a four-step dialog: **Repository → Path & ref → Variables → Review**.

1. Open the canvas command menu (⌘K) and choose **Bring your own IaC** from the **Sources** group.
2. **Repository** — select the git repo that holds your module.
3. **Path & ref** — set the **root-module path** (the directory inside the repo that holds the root
 `*.tf`; leave blank for the repo root) and, optionally, the **git ref** (a branch, tag, or commit;
 leave blank for `HEAD`).
4. **Variables** — add any non-secret tfvars the module needs. Each variable is a name, a type, and a
 value.
5. **Review** — confirm the repo, path, ref, and variable count, then select **Attach source**.

Attaching pins a single IaC source on the environment and **queues a safety scan automatically** — you
don't need to trigger the scan yourself.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Variables
records.text:
Variables on the Variables step are **scalar, non-secret tfvars** only:

 Field Rule 
 ------- ------ 
 **Name** Letters, digits, and underscores; must start with a letter or underscore. Names must be unique. 
 **Type** `string`, `number`, or `bool`. 
 **Value** Must parse as the chosen type (`number` must be numeric; `bool` must be `true` or `false`). 

 
Never put secrets here. These values are stored as plain tfvars. Keep credentials in your cloud's
secret store or your module's own data sources.
 

Leave the list empty to run the module with its own defaults.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Read the safety scan
records.text:
Once attached, the module appears on the canvas as an **External IaC** card carrying its provenance —
repo, ref, path, the commit the scan pinned, and a scan-status chip. Select the chip to open the
**IaC safety scan** sheet.

The scan runs the [static safety gate](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac#the-static-safety-gate) and
`tofu validate` against the commit it pinned. The sheet shows:

- A **verdict** — "No blocking issues found", or "Issues found — resolve before deploying".
- A **`tofu validate`** status pill and a count per severity. A finding is `error` (blocks the
 deploy) or `warning` (surfaced, not blocking).
- **Finding cards**, worst-first — each with a rule id, a `file:line` coordinate, and a detail message.
- The **providers** and **modules** the scan discovered.

Re-run the scan any time with **Rescan** in the scan sheet (open it from the node's scan-status chip)
— for example after pushing a fix to the module.

 
Only a clean scan pins the commit a deploy will apply. A **not-ok scan clears the deploy pin**, so
provisioning stays locked until a clean re-scan. This also protects against a swap between scan and
apply: the pinned commit is exactly what runs.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Provision from the module
records.text:
While an enabled source exists, that environment's plan, deploy, and destroy run **your module**
instead of the built-in template. The module's resources appear as their own read-only cards on the
board; the component palette is disabled for a BYO environment, because the module — not the design —
is the source of truth.

The External IaC card tracks live state: it marks the environment **DEPLOYED** or **NOT DEPLOYED** and
shows the commit the last deploy applied alongside the pinned commit.

At plan time, the same verify verdict template provisioning gets (keyless / least-privilege / OIDC-sub)
is attached to each deploy's **Plan** tab.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: Detach a module
records.text:
To return an environment to the built-in template, open the External IaC card and select the detach
(**✕**) control.

 
You can only detach a source that has **never deployed**. Once a deploy has applied the module (or the
environment is in an active or in-flight status), detaching would drop the only handle to that live
infrastructure — destroy the environment first, then detach.

records.title: Bring your own IaC
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Bring-your-own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac) — the safety gate and module contract.
- [Bring your own Helm charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) — attach a single Helm
 chart instead of a whole module.
- [The Canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas) — where sources and their cards live.
- [Git providers](/guides/connectors/git-providers) — connecting the repo host.

records.text: When enabled, the cache replicates data across availability zones for automatic failover. If the primary node fails, a replica in another AZ is promoted automatically. This adds ~50% to the cost (replica nodes).

records.title: Cluster
records.text: Cluster. Kubernetes cluster configuration — version, instance types, node scaling, Karpenter, and cluster admins.

records.title: Cluster

records.text: The cluster section configures the Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes.

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Kubernetes Version** Select Provider-specific versions (e.g., 1.32 for EKS, 1.31 for GKE/AKS). Read-only on Hetzner, which installs one pinned version 
 **Instance Type** Select A single instance/machine type; the option label shows vCPU and memory per node

 **Desired Nodes** Number Target node count (default: 2) 
 **Max Nodes** Number Maximum node count for autoscaling (default: 5) 
 **Capacity** Select AWS only. **On-demand** (the default) or **Spot**. Spot nodes cost less, but AWS can take a node back with two minutes' notice 
 **Autoscaler** Provider default Provider-specific autoscaler (Karpenter on AWS, Autopilot on GKE, Cluster Autoscaler on AKS), enabled at cluster creation 
 **Cluster Admins** Array IAM users/emails with admin access

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Kubernetes Service
records.text:
- **Elastic Kubernetes Service** with managed node groups
 - Versions: 1.29–1.32
 - Autoscaler: **Karpenter** — just-in-time node provisioning based on pod requirements
 - IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) configured automatically
 - OIDC provider created for workload identity
 
 
 - **Google Kubernetes Engine** with node pools
 - Versions: 1.28–1.31
 - Autoscaler: **GKE Autopilot** — fully managed node provisioning
 - Workload Identity enabled by default
 
 
 - **Azure Kubernetes Service** with node pools
 - Versions: 1.28–1.31
 - Autoscaler: **Cluster Autoscaler** — scales node count based on pending pods
 - Azure AD integration for RBAC
 
 
 - Self-managed **Talos Linux** Kubernetes on Hetzner Cloud servers
 - Version: Kubernetes **1.35.6**. The Talos release sets this version, and you cannot choose
 another one.
 - The **Kubernetes Version** field is read-only and shows 1.35.6.
 - If a cluster already has a different version set, for example from the CLI, its next deploy
 fails with an error that names 1.35.6. To fix it, clear the version, or set it to 1.35.

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Instance Types
records.text:
A single instance type is selected from a dropdown, with each option's label showing the node's vCPU and memory. On any cloud you can instead size the node group portably (vCPU and memory per node) and the runner maps that capability to the nearest instance type at provision time.

 Category AWS GCP Azure 
 ---------- ----- ----- ------- 
 General t3.medium, t3.large e2-medium, e2-standard-2 Standard_D2s_v5, Standard_D4s_v5 
 Compute c5.large, c5.xlarge c2-standard-4 Standard_F2s_v2 
 Memory r5.large n2-highmem-2 Standard_E2s_v5 
 GPU g4dn.xlarge a2-highgpu-1g Standard_NC4as_T4_v3 

 
On GCP, `e2-medium` and `n1-standard-1` cannot run the cluster add-ons, and a deploy onto either is
refused before it spends anything.

GKE reserves a flat 1060 millicores on every shared-core E2 machine type, and 6% of a single-core
node. Both shapes therefore leave 940 millicores for your pods — and GKE's own system DaemonSets,
plus the Calico network-policy controller the cluster runs, take almost all of it. A cluster on one
of these shapes comes up looking healthy, then never finishes installing GitOps and never enforces
network policy.

`e2-standard-2` is the smallest GCP shape that works, and it

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Node Scaling
records.text:
Three numbers control the node group size:

- **Min**: Floor for the autoscaler (nodes will never scale below this)
- **Desired**: Initial node count at creation
- **Max**: Ceiling for the autoscaler (nodes will never scale above this)

Each value is bounded individually (1–100); the form does not enforce a min ≤ desired ≤ max ordering.

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Cluster Admins
records.text:
An array of identities with admin access to the cluster:

 
 
 IAM user or role ARNs (or IAM user names), entered as a free-text list. Admins are bound to the cluster-admin `system:masters` group at cluster creation.
 
 
 Google email addresses granted `roles/container.admin`.
 
 
 Azure AD Object IDs granted cluster admin RBAC.

records.title: Container Registry
records.text: Container Registry. ECR, Artifact Registry, and ACR configuration — tag mutability and image scanning.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Container Registry
records.text: The container registry section creates managed Docker image registries for your application containers. Multiple registries can be added per project.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Fields Per Registry
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Repository name (e.g., `api`, `frontend`, `worker`) 
 **Provider** Select Cloud-native registry or a [pluggable connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Tag Mutability** Select `MUTABLE` (tags can be overwritten) or `IMMUTABLE` (once pushed, a tag is permanent) 
 **Scan on Push** Toggle Automatically scan images for vulnerabilities on push

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Registry Provider
records.text:
By default a cloud-native registry (ECR / Artifact Registry / ACR) is created. Select **Docker Hub** to use a Docker Hub repository instead:

- Requires a connected [Docker Hub connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) (username + access token).
- Optional **namespace / organization** (defaults to the username).
- Instead of creating cloud registry repos, the composed module wires a Kubernetes `imagePullSecret` so workloads can pull from Docker Hub; the cloud-native registry is skipped.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Services by Provider
records.text:
**ECR** (Elastic Container Registry)
 - Private repositories with IAM-based access
 - Lifecycle policies (auto-expire old images)
 - Integration with EKS for pull authentication
 
 
 **Artifact Registry**
 - Docker and OCI image support
 - IAM-based access control
 - Vulnerability scanning via Container Analysis
 
 
 **ACR** (Azure Container Registry)
 - SKU tiers: Basic, Standard, Premium
 - Geo-replication (Premium)
 - Integration with AKS for pull authentication

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Tag Mutability
records.text:
Mode Behavior Use Case 
 ------ ---------- ---------- 
 **MUTABLE** Same tag (e.g., `latest`) can be pushed multiple times Development, CI/CD with `latest` tag 
 **IMMUTABLE** Once a tag is pushed, it cannot be overwritten Production (ensures deployed image is never changed) 

 
Immutable tags prevent accidental overwrites in production. A `v1.2.3` tag always points to the same image digest, making rollbacks deterministic.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: After Provisioning
records.text:
The registry card in project detail shows:
- **Repository URL** — full push/pull endpoint (e.g., `123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api`)
- **Status** — ACTIVE or CREATING

records.title: Cost
records.text: Cost. The cost chip — an environment's monthly cost, taken from its last plan's Infracost breakdown.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: Cost
records.text:
The cost chip sits in the top-right of the Architecture canvas. It shows the environment's estimated monthly infrastructure cost, taken from the **last plan** — not a live client-side estimate.

For a deeper technical explanation, see [Cost Estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation).

records.title: Cost
records.heading: Where the number comes from
records.text:
The runner runs [Infracost](/concepts/cost-estimation) on every **PLAN** and posts the cost breakdown back with the job. The chip reads the resulting monthly total (`monthlyCost`) off the environment's status — so the cost is only ever a real figure the platform computed, never a guess made in the browser.

The chip only appears once a project and environment exist (an existing environment on the Architecture route). In the design-only create flow there is nothing planned yet, so there is no chip.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: States
records.text:
The chip is honest about what it knows:

 State When What it shows 
 ------- ------ --------------- 
 **Not priced** The environment has never been planned (`monthlyCost` is null) A dashed chip reading `Not priced`, tooltip "Run a plan to price this environment." 
 **Priced** A plan has run `Monthly $X.XX` (two decimals), tooltip "From the plan on ` `" when the capture time is known 

A never-planned environment shows `Not priced` rather than `$0.00` — a fabricated zero is worse than an admitted unknown, because you would believe it.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: The full breakdown
records.text:
The single headline number is the chip. The **per-resource breakdown** lives in the plan's artifact panel, under the Plan tab. The console parses the Infracost breakdown JSON (`parseCostBreakdown`) into a ranked list of cost-bearing resources:

- Each resource carries its `monthlyCost`, `hourlyCost`, `resourceType`, and any priced sub-resources.
- Free or cost-unknown resources (monthly cost `0` or absent) are skipped — the list only ranks priced ones.
- Resources are sorted by monthly cost, most expensive first.
- The plan also carries `totalMonthlyCost` and `totalHourlyCost`.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: Limitations
records.text:
- The figure is only as fresh as the **last plan** — change the design and the number is stale until you plan again.
- Infracost prices what appears in the OpenTofu plan JSON. Usage-based resources (NoSQL, messaging, object storage) and data-transfer costs are not estimated up front.
- A malformed or partial breakdown degrades to "unknown cost" rather than surfacing a wrong number.

records.title: Databases
records.text: Databases. Managed relational databases — Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure Database with engine selection and capacity.

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Databases
records.text: The databases section configures managed relational database instances. Multiple databases can be added per project, each with its own engine, version, and capacity settings.

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Fields Per Database
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Unique per project, lowercase, used in resource naming 
 **Engine** Select Provider-specific engine (see below) 
 **Engine Version** Auto-set Determined by engine selection 
 **Min Capacity** Number Minimum capacity (ACUs for Aurora, vCPUs for Cloud SQL) 
 **Max Capacity** Number Maximum capacity for auto-scaling 
 **Port** Number Database port (default: 5432 for PostgreSQL, 3306 for MySQL) 
 **IAM Auth** Toggle Authenticate with short-lived cloud IAM tokens instead of a password. PostgreSQL and MySQL, on AWS, GCP and Azure. See [Keyless database auth](/guides/design-project/keyless-database-auth)

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Engines by Provider
records.text:
**Aurora Serverless v2** — auto-scaling managed database

 Engine Version Capacity Unit 
 -------- --------- --------------- 
 Aurora PostgreSQL 16.6 ACUs (0.5–128) 
 Aurora MySQL 8.0 ACUs (0.5–128) 

 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) scale automatically between min and max. Each ACU provides ~2 GiB of memory. At $0.14/ACU-hour, a 0.5–4 ACU database costs approximately $51–$408/month.
 
 
 **Cloud SQL** — managed database instances

 Engine Version Capacity Unit 
 -------- --------- --------------- 
 Cloud SQL PostgreSQL 15 vCPUs (1–96) 
 Cloud SQL MySQL 8.0 vCPUs (1–96) 
 
 
 **Azure Database Flexible Server** — managed database

 Engine Version Capacity Unit 
 -------- --------- --------------- 
 Azure PostgreSQL 16 vCores (1–64) 
 Azure MySQL 8.0 vCores (1–64)

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Adding Multiple Databases
records.text:
Click **"Add Database"** to add another instance. Each database gets its own card in the form. The first database defaults to:
- Name: `primary`
- Engine: Aurora PostgreSQL (or equivalent)
- Capacity: 0.5–4 ACUs

Common patterns:
- **Primary + Read Replica**: One write database + one read-optimized database
- **Multi-service**: Separate databases per microservice (e.g., `users-db`, `orders-db`)

records.title: Databases
records.heading: After Provisioning
records.text:
Once deployed, the database card in the [project detail](/guides/dashboard/project-detail) Services tab shows:
- **Writer endpoint** — primary connection string
- **Reader endpoint** — read replica connection (Aurora only)
- **Master credentials** — stored in Secrets Manager (ARN shown, copy button)
- **Status** — ACTIVE, CREATING, or FAILED

 
**IAM authentication** lets a workload connect using its own cloud identity and a short-lived token
instead of a stored password — nothing to rotate, no secret in the cluster. A service bound to an
IAM-auth database picks this up automatically.

It covers **PostgreSQL and MySQL on AWS, GCP and Azure**. Alibaba Cloud and Hetzner have no
token-based database login, so a database on either stays on the password path even with the toggle
on. See [Keyless database auth](/guides/design-project/keyless-database-auth) for how it works per
cloud and its current rollout status.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.text: DNS & WAF. Domain configuration, managed certificates, and Web Application Firewall options.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: DNS & WAF
records.text: The DNS section is optional (controlled by a master toggle). When enabled, it configures domain management, SSL/TLS certificates, and web application firewall protection.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Enabled** Toggle Master switch for DNS configuration 
 **DNS Provider** Select Cloud-native (Route 53 / Cloud DNS / Azure DNS) or a [pluggable connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Zone ID** Select or text Existing DNS hosted zone 
 **Domain Name** Text input Auto-filled from zone, or manually entered 
 **Managed Certificate** Toggle Auto-provision SSL/TLS certificate (cloud-native only) 
 **WAF Options** Toggles Provider-specific WAF configuration (cloud-native only)

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: DNS Provider
records.text:
The **DNS Provider** selector decouples *what* the Project needs (a managed zone) from *who* provides it:

- **Cloud-native** (default) — uses the cluster cloud's DNS service; the managed-certificate and WAF toggles apply.
- **Cloudflare** — manages records on Cloudflare instead. Requires a connected [Cloudflare connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable); set the **Zone ID** and the **Proxied** option (orange-cloud). The cloud-native DNS/cert resources are skipped at provision time.

When a pluggable provider is selected, its credential is pulled from `connector_credentials` on the runner at provision time — never stored in the Project.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: DNS Zones
records.text:
The zone selector shows existing DNS zones from Alethia's server-side [asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory):

 
 
 **Route 53** hosted zones (public only). Zone ID format: `Z1234567890ABC`.
 
 
 **Cloud DNS** managed zones. Zone name format: `my-zone`.
 
 
 **Azure DNS** zones. Zone name format: `example.com`.
 
 

 
DNS zones are provider-specific. When duplicating a project across providers, the zone ID and domain are cleared and must be re-configured. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: Managed Certificates
records.text:
When enabled, the platform provisions a TLS certificate automatically:

 Provider Issued by Validation 
 ---------- ----------- ------------ 
 AWS ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) DNS validation via Route 53 
 GCP cert-manager, in your cluster ACME DNS01 via Cloud DNS 
 Azure cert-manager, in your cluster ACME DNS01 via Azure DNS 
 Alibaba Not available — bring your own — 
 Hetzner Not available — bring your own — 

Certificates are renewed automatically before expiration.

On **GCP and Azure** the certificate is a free Let's Encrypt one, issued and renewed inside your
cluster by cert-manager and served by the cloud's own ingress — the GKE Ingress reads it from a
Kubernetes Secret, and the Application Gateway has it lifted onto its listener by AGIC. Neither
cloud provisions a cloud-native certificate any more.

On **AWS** the certificate stays in ACM. That is not an oversight: an Application Load Balancer can
only reference a certificate by ARN in ACM or IAM, and ACM will not bind a certificate whose private
key it never held — so a cert-manager certificate cannot terminate an ALB at all. ACM is free and
renews itself, so nothing is lost by it.

On **Alibaba and Hetzner** nothing issu

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: In-cluster certificates
records.text:
On AWS, GCP and Azure the same toggle also installs `cert-manager` in the cluster and creates a
`ClusterIssuer` named `letsencrypt-prod`. Reference it from an Ingress to get a Let's Encrypt
certificate for any hostname in your zone:

metadata:
 annotations:
 cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod

The issuer solves ACME **DNS01** challenges, so it works before you have a public ingress, and it
can issue wildcard certificates. It writes its challenge records with the same cloud identity
`external-dns` uses, so there is no API key to supply.

 
Not available on Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner. `cert-manager` ships no DNS01 solver for either DNS
service, so Alethia creates no issuer rather than one whose challenges never complete. Bring your
own certificate on those clouds. The deploy records the skip and its reason with the environment's
other infrastructure-service decisions.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: Web Application Firewall
records.text:
WAF protects web applications from common attacks (SQL injection, XSS, bot traffic).

Alethia provisions a WAF on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure only. On Alibaba Cloud the switch is disabled and
says why: WAF 3.0 is an account-level purchase there, so a project that owned one would release the whole
account's firewall when it was destroyed. Buy a WAF 3.0 instance in your own account instead and put it in
front of your ingress from the WAF console. Hetzner sells no web application firewall at all.

 
 
 Two WAF options (can enable both):

 Option Protects Cost 
 -------- ---------- ------ 
 **CloudFront WAF** CDN-level protection ~$5/mo base 
 **Application WAF (ALB)** Load balancer level ~$5/mo base 

 AWS WAFv2 with managed rule groups (AWS Managed Rules, Bot Control).
 
 
 **Cloud Armor** — DDoS and application-layer protection at the load balancer.
 
 
 **Azure WAF** — protection via Application Gateway or Front Door.
 
 

WAF costs are reflected in the [cost sidebar](/guides/design-project/cost-sidebar) immediately when toggled.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.text: Design a Project Overview. The infrastructure design canvas — add services as nodes, configure each in its inspector, then Plan and Deploy.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Design a Project
records.text: The design **canvas** is where you define infrastructure. You add services as nodes, configure each one in its inspector, and Plan then Deploy the environment. The canvas is the sole design surface — the legacy multi-section form has been removed.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: The canvas
records.text:
Every project opens on its **Architecture** view. The root **Project node** holds the project's basics — name, environment stage, and cloud region — and pins the stack's core cloud account, which is chosen once when the project is created. Every other service you add is a node wired to the graph.

Under the hood the canvas persists through an abstract Zod schema and a graph ⇄ form round-trip, so a shared `react-hook-form` context still backs a few inspector fields (repository and region pickers). You interact with nodes and inspectors, not a form.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Adding services
records.text:
Add services from the **Add** palette or the `⌘K` command palette. The **Add** palette groups services by domain (Workloads, Data, Storage, Messaging, Security, Networking, Compute, DevOps) and matches on each entry's label and subtitle. The `⌘K` command palette groups services into **Core** and **Periphery** and searches across every provisionable service by name — its per-cloud service names (e.g. `rds`, `postgres`, `redis`, `s3`) and synonyms. Selecting one drops its node on the canvas and opens its inspector; kinds with variants (for example a database engine) ask you to pick the variant first.

The palette is filtered by the project's cloud: a service the target cloud can't provision (Hetzner has no managed pub/sub or NoSQL, for instance) isn't offered, and a singleton already on the canvas is disabled. Services not yet backed by an OpenTofu module show a `Soon` badge.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Configuring a node
records.text:
Each node opens its **inspector** — a set of collapsible config sections. The node's effective provider drives its fields, region choices, and provider-specific advanced knobs. The cloud account is not set per node; it is inherited from the Project root.

Existing resources you can reuse (VPCs, subnets, and the like) come from Alethia's server-side
[asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory), which stays current automatically
(event-driven + a reconciliation sweep). There's no manual refresh.

 
The cloud account is chosen once, at project creation — there is no in-canvas provider switch. When you duplicate a project onto a different cloud, the platform converts the config and surfaces conversion warnings. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Services
records.text:
Name, environment, region 
 VPC/VNet, CIDR, NAT gateway 
 Kubernetes, instance types, node scaling, Karpenter 
 Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure Database 
 Redis, Valkey, Memorystore 
 DynamoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB 
 SQS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus 
 Route53, certificates, WAF 
 Password generation, secret stores 
 ECR, Artifact Registry, ACR 
 Git repos for GitOps 
 Monthly cost from the last plan

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Save, Plan, Deploy
records.text:
Saving a project writes a `projects` row and its **default environment** (a `project_environments` row with status `DRAFT`), then a component row per node in the relevant tables (`project_network`, `project_cluster`, `project_databases`, and so on). The project then appears in the project listing.

From the Architecture view you drive the environment with the **Run** menu and the staged-changes bar:

- **Plan** (`PLAN`) — dry-run the OpenTofu plan and price it with Infracost.
- **Deploy** — apply the staged changes. **Destroy** lives in Project settings.
- **Audit**, **Detect drift**, and **Probe cluster** run their respective jobs against the live environment.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Validation
records.text:
Each service's config is validated by its own Zod schema (`lib/validations/project-form.schema.ts`). For example:

- Project name: free-text display name, max 50 characters; the URL slug is derived via `slugify` (must contain at least one letter or number).
- Bucket names: 3–63 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens; must start and end with a letter or digit.
- Component names (database, cache, queue, topic, table, secret) are required.

A service the target cloud can't provision, or a service binding to a resource that isn't in the environment, is rejected fail-closed at deploy time rather than silently dropped.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.text: Keyless Database Auth. Bind a service to a PostgreSQL or MySQL database that authenticates with short-lived cloud IAM tokens instead of a password — no secret in the cluster, nothing to rotate.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: Keyless Database Auth
records.text:
When you turn on **IAM Auth** on a database, a service bound to it connects using its own **cloud
identity** and a **short-lived token** — not a stored password. No database password sits in the
cluster to leak or rotate. The workload proves who it is to the cloud, and the cloud hands the
database a token that expires in about an hour.

This is the "hold zero keys" principle applied to the last mile — the app→database hop that
previously still needed a password. It works the same way for **PostgreSQL and MySQL**.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: How a binding decides
records.text:
You don't declare "keyless" on the binding. It is **derived** from the database it points at:

- The database's **IAM Auth** toggle is on → the binding's credential facets go keyless.
- The toggle is off → the binding uses the usual provisioned-password path (a Kubernetes Secret
 synced by the External Secrets Operator).

So the database's own configuration is the single source of truth. Flip the toggle and re-deploy;
nothing on the service changes.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: What you bind
records.text:
For a keyless database, wire the binding's facets as usual, but **omit the password**:

- `endpoint` → resolves to `127.0.0.1` (the app talks to a local auth proxy, see below).
- `port` → the engine's port: **5432** for PostgreSQL, **3306** for MySQL.
- `username` → the workload's cloud login identity (filled in for you from the provision).
- `password` → **not needed** and ignored — there is no password.

The port follows the database's engine, not the binding. A MySQL database always gets 3306, on every
cloud, and the proxy in front of it listens on the same port the app is told to dial.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: How it works per cloud
records.text:
All three clouds converge on the same shape: the app connects to a **local proxy sidecar** on
`127.0.0.1`, and the sidecar authenticates upstream with the pod's own identity. Your application
code is unchanged — it connects to localhost with no password and never learns that tokens exist.

There are two mechanisms. GCP has a native auth proxy. AWS and Azure have none, so the pod runs
**`alethia db-authproxy`** — a subcommand of the runner image, already a pinned sidecar.

`db-authproxy` is a handshake and a pipe, not a pooler. For each new upstream connection it gets a
short-lived database token from the pod's Workload Identity. It dials the real database over TLS,
presenting that token as a cleartext password, then byte-splices the two connections. It does no
pooling, no routing and no query parsing.

Two properties follow from minting the token **in-process**:

- **Nothing is ever at rest.** There is no token file, no rotation store and no admin socket. The
 token exists only in the sidecar's memory, and is reused across connections while it stays valid.
- **Rotation stops being a problem.** Both engines authenticate once, at connect time, so an expiring
 token can never invalida

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: The app gets a scoped role, never admin
records.text:
The app's cloud identity logs in, but it maps to a **least-privilege database role**, never a
superuser. A one-shot **bootstrap Job**, which Alethia adds to your GitOps repo, creates that role.
The Job runs as an ArgoCD **PreSync hook**, so it finishes before the app deploys. It connects as the
database administrator, runs the grants, and deletes itself on success.

What the role gets depends on the engine:

- **PostgreSQL** — `CONNECT` on its own database, plus `USAGE` and `CREATE` on the `public` schema.
- **MySQL** — `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, INDEX, REFERENCES`, scoped to the
 app's own database. Never `*.*`, never `GRANT OPTION`, never `SUPER`.

All three clouds get the same privileges for a given engine. They differ only in how the login is
**bound** to the cloud identity:

 Cloud PostgreSQL MySQL 
 --- --- --- 
 **AWS** a role granted the `rds_iam` group, so it authenticates by IAM token a user created `IDENTIFIED WITH AWSAuthenticationPlugin`. No identity id appears in the SQL — the IAM policy's user name is the binding 
 **GCP** OpenTofu already created the IAM service-account user, so the Job only grants the same — grants only, against the trunc

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: Where it doesn't apply
records.text:
On these clouds the canvas shows **IAM authentication** as unavailable and says why, so you cannot
turn it on. If a database carries the setting anyway — imported from another cloud, written by the
CLI, or created before this gate — the deploy **fails** with the same explanation. It does not fall
back to a password: a database you marked as password-free never quietly gets one.

- **Alibaba Cloud (ApsaraDB RDS)** — ApsaraDB has no IAM/RAM token-based database login. RAM controls
 the *management* API, not database logins, so there is no token for a keyless connection to
 authenticate with.
- **Hetzner** — Hetzner databases are in-cluster ArgoCD add-ons, not a managed cloud service with an
 IAM plane, so there is no keyless identity to use.

To use keyless auth on one of these, move the database to AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure. Otherwise
leave IAM authentication off and use the generated-password path, which is fully supported.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: Rollout status
records.text:
Keyless database auth is **behind a feature flag** while it completes real-cloud verification. The
runner enables it with `ALETHIA_KEYLESS_DB_AUTH_ENABLED=true`. With the flag off, an IAM-auth
database binding uses the normal password path unchanged.

Keyless renders schedule the runner image twice: as the `db-authproxy` sidecar, and as the bootstrap
Job. A published runner image carries its own reference, so there is nothing to set. Set
`ALETHIA_RUNNER_IMAGE` only to name a different image than the one running — a private mirror or an
air-gapped registry. A runner built from source has no published reference, so keyless renders fail
closed there; run a published image to exercise this path.

If a keyless binding can't be fully wired at deploy time (a missing identity, for example), it
**fails closed**: the binding is omitted and the reason is surfaced on the deployment's **Deploy** tab
rather than shipping a workload pointed at nothing. The same holds for the bootstrap Job — if its
admin credential can't be resolved, the Job is skipped and reported instead of wedging the sync.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Databases](/guides/design-project/databases) — the IAM Auth toggle.
- [Security Architecture](/concepts/security) — the keyless / hold-zero-keys model.

records.title: Messaging
records.text: Messaging. Queues and topics — SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus configuration.

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Messaging
records.text: The messaging section configures message queues and publish/subscribe topics. Queues and topics are configured independently.

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Queues
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Queue name 
 **Ordered (FIFO) delivery** Toggle Per-key ordering. See [What "ordered" means](#what-ordered-means) 
 **Visibility Timeout** Number 0–43,200 seconds (displayed as human-readable: s/m/h)

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: What ordered means
records.text:
Ordered delivery means one thing on every cloud Alethia supports:

> Messages tagged with the same ordering key are delivered to consumers in the order the service
> received them. Messages with different keys have no relative order and are still processed
> concurrently.

Three consequences apply everywhere. Read them before you turn the toggle on.

**It is per key, never a total order.** No cloud orders a whole queue. AWS orders within a message
group, Azure within a session, and Google Cloud within an ordering key. A queue with no keys is
unordered even with the toggle on.

**It is an application change, not only an infrastructure change.** Your publisher must set a key on
every message. On Azure your consumer must also accept a session instead of receiving plain
messages — once sessions are on, a client that sends or receives regular messages stops working.

**It costs throughput, and on AWS money.** AWS charges more per request for a FIFO queue and caps it
at 300 messages per second, or 3,000 batched. Google Cloud caps each ordering key at 1 MB/s and
raises delivery latency. Azure gives each session to exactly one receiver at a time.

 
Changing this setting on a queue that al

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Topics
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Topic name 
 **Subscriptions** JSONB (backend) Configured per consumer after provisioning 

 
 
 **SNS** (Simple Notification Service) — fan-out messaging. Subscribers can be SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email, or SMS.
 
 
 **Pub/Sub Topics** — message publishing endpoint. Subscribers create pull or push subscriptions.
 
 
 **Service Bus Topics** — publish/subscribe messaging with subscription filters.

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Cost
records.text: Messaging services are usage-based (per message/request), so they show $0 in the cost sidebar. Actual costs depend on message volume and size.

records.title: Network
records.text: Network. VPC/VNet configuration — create new or use existing, CIDR blocks, NAT gateways.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Network
records.text: The network section configures the virtual network that contains all provisioned resources.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Create New vs. Use Existing
records.text: Two modes controlled by a toggle:

records.title: Network
records.heading: Create New Network
records.text:
Provisions a new network from scratch. Fields:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **CIDR Block** IP address range (e.g., `10.0.0.0/16`) 
 **NAT Gateway** Single (cost-optimized) or HA (one per availability zone) 

 
 
 Creates a **VPC** with:
 - Public and private subnets across availability zones
 - Internet Gateway for public subnets
 - NAT Gateway(s) for private subnet internet access
 - Route tables for each subnet type
 - Default security group
 
 
 Creates a **VPC Network** with:
 - Custom-mode subnets in the selected region
 - Cloud NAT with Cloud Router
 - Firewall rules for internal communication
 
 
 Creates a **Virtual Network (VNet)** with:
 - Subnets for cluster nodes and services
 - NAT Gateway for outbound traffic
 - Network Security Groups (NSGs)

records.title: Network
records.heading: Use Existing Network
records.text:
Instead of creating a network, attach the project to one that **already exists** in the account — its id
comes from Alethia's server-side [asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory) (network id,
name, CIDR, region).

**How it works — brownfield attach (AWS · GCP · Azure).** When you pick "existing", Alethia records the
network id and, at deploy time, the [Runner](/concepts/runner) does **not** create a network. Instead the OpenTofu
template *reads* your existing network and wires the cluster into it:

- **AWS** — the runner looks up the VPC's subnets and passes them in (public/private split).
- **GCP** — the template `data`-sources the VPC network and resolves its subnetwork in the project's
 region (including that subnet's pod/service secondary ranges) for GKE.
- **Azure** — the template `data`-sources the VNet and uses one of its subnets for AKS.

 
Existing networks must be in the same region as the project. The list comes from Alethia's server-side
[asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory), which stays fresh automatically (a
reconciliation sweep, plus optional event forwarders) — there's no manual refresh.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Reuse existing resources
records.text:
"Use existing network" is one case of a deliberately **narrow** idea: reuse the **shared substrate you
deploy _into_**, instead of creating a duplicate. The test for whether reuse is a provisioning concern is
simple — **does the rest of the infrastructure graph attach to it?**

- ✅ **Network (VPC/VNet + subnets)** — the cluster and nodes attach into its subnets. Available today on
 AWS, GCP, and Azure (a provision-new vs use-existing toggle; at deploy time the template `data`-sources
 the existing network rather than creating one). The list comes from the server-side
 [asset inventory](/guides/connectors/health-and-inventory).
- 🚧 **Kubernetes cluster** — your workloads deploy _onto_ it (nobody wants a fresh cluster per app). Same
 toggle, on the roadmap.

That's the whole scope. **Databases, caches, queues, storage, etc. are _not_ "reuse" targets** — nothing
downstream attaches to them in the graph. If a database already exists, there's nothing to provision:
the app simply needs its **connection endpoint + secret**, which is a *connection/config* concern (a value
you supply), not a provisioned component. Trying to model that as "provision vs existing" just reintroduces
a credenti

records.title: Network
records.heading: CIDR Block Validation
records.text:
The form validates CIDR notation in real-time and shows a breakdown. For `10.0.0.0/16`:

 Field Value 
 ------- ------- 
 Total addresses 65,536 
 Usable IPs 65,531 
 Range 10.0.0.0 – 10.0.255.255 
 Size Large 

Common ranges:
- `/16` — 65,536 addresses (recommended for production)
- `/20` — 4,096 addresses (suitable for small environments)
- `/24` — 256 addresses (minimal, development only)

records.title: Network
records.heading: NAT Gateway Cost Impact
records.text:
NAT gateways have significant cost implications:

 Mode AWS Cost Description 
 ------ --------- ------------- 
 Single ~$35/mo One NAT in a single AZ (cost-optimized, single point of failure) 
 HA ~$105/mo (3 AZ) One NAT per AZ (high availability, 3x cost) 

The [cost sidebar](/guides/design-project/cost-sidebar) reflects the NAT gateway choice immediately.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Allowed CIDR Blocks
records.text: Optional field for restricting inbound access. Enter CIDR ranges that should be allowed to connect to resources within the network. Default: open to the VPC CIDR only.

records.title: The node inspector
records.text: The node inspector. Open a resource's docked side panel to rename it, read its status, cost and activity, edit its configuration, and remove it — all without leaving the canvas.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: The node inspector
records.text:
The node inspector is the docked side panel that opens beside the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas)
when you select a resource. It replaces the old full-page configuration form: everything you used to
edit in a form, you now edit here, on the same board you designed. The panel is split into
**Overview**, **Cost**, **Activity** and **Settings** tabs (the cluster adds a **Deploy** tab), with an
editable header and a status strip above them.

 
The inspector is the **Architecture view** only. It appears when a node is selected and slides away
when nothing is.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Open the inspector
records.text:
1. Open a project's **Architecture** view.
2. Click a resource card.

The panel docks on the right. Clicking a different card swaps the panel to that resource; clicking an
empty area of the board, or the **✕** in the panel header, closes it.

Some cards open a purpose-built panel instead of the generic inspector:
