- A **Secrets vault** (or any collapsed collection) opens its member list — see [Secrets](/guides/design-project/secrets).
- An **external** card from a bring-your-own IaC module opens a read-only resource list — see
 [Bring your own charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts).
- A described **chart workload** opens its own describe-and-bind panel.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Rename a resource
records.text:
The resource name lives in the panel header, next to the type badge.

1. Click the name field in the header.
2. Type the new name.

Only resources that carry an editable name show an input here — the **project** (its project name) and
the array-style resources you can add many of (databases, caches, secrets, …). For array resources the
name is forced to lowercase as you type, to match cloud naming rules. Resources with no name of their
own show a fixed label instead.

 
The cloud account is **not** set in the inspector. It is chosen once, at project creation, so there is
no per-node cloud selector.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Read the status strip
records.text:
Under the header, a strip shows the resource's **resolved status** — a grayscale dot and a mono label —
followed by the most actionable line for that state (a config issue, a failure message, or a probe
reason). If the real cloud has diverged from what Alethia recorded, a `N drifted` chip rides alongside
the state; hover it to see the OpenTofu addresses that diverged.

Status merges the design's readiness with the environment's server truth, and picks one state to show.
See [The canvas → Status without colour](/guides/design-project/the-canvas) for the full vocabulary and
precedence order.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Check what a resource produced and costs (Overview)
records.text:
The **Overview** tab is a read-only summary of the selected resource:

 Section Shows 
 --- --- 
 **Type / Status** The resource kind and its resolved status label (with the status message, if any) 
 **Environment** For the project only — the real environment's name, stage, and provisioning status 
 **Endpoints** What the deploy produced (for example a database hostname or ArgoCD URL), each with a copy button 
 **Cost** The resource's estimated monthly cost from the last plan 
 **Recent activity** The environment's latest jobs, condensed to the most recent few 
 **Drift** Each drifted OpenTofu address, listed on its own 
 **Configuration** The resource's scalar configuration values 

Sections that have nothing to show are omitted — Endpoints appears only once the resource is deployed,
and Cost appears only once the resource has been priced.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Break down cost by resource (Cost)
records.text:
The **Cost** tab shows the resource's monthly spend, itemised by OpenTofu address.

1. Open the **Cost** tab.
2. Read the **Monthly** rollup at the top.
3. Read the **Breakdown** — one line per OpenTofu address, sorted from most to least expensive.

The rollup and the per-line detail both come from the last plan's Infracost breakdown, and the tab
notes when that plan ran.

 
A resource that has never been priced says **"Not priced yet"** rather than showing `$0` — run a plan
and its estimated monthly cost appears here. See [Cost Sidebar](/guides/design-project/cost-sidebar) for
the pre-plan estimate.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Review recent jobs (Activity)
records.text:
The **Activity** tab lists the environment's recent job history. Activity is scoped to the
**environment**, not the single resource — a deploy provisions the whole board, so a node has no jobs of
its own. Each row shows the job type, its status dot, and how long ago it ran. An environment with no
jobs yet reads **"No activity yet for this environment."**

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Edit configuration (Settings)
records.text:
The **Settings** tab is where you change the resource. Its fields are built from the resource's own
config schema, so each kind shows only the knobs that apply to it.

1. Open the **Settings** tab.
2. Expand a section to reveal its fields.
3. Edit a field — changes apply to the design immediately.

Portable fields sit in the top sections, which open by default. **Advanced**, cloud-specific sections
are collapsed by default and badged with the provider they belong to (for example `AWS only`), so you
open the door to non-portable ground deliberately. A section whose fields don't apply to your project's
cloud is not shown at all.

For the **project** panel on a provisioned environment, Settings also shows the environment's name and
stage read-only — the stage is a fact of the environment you're viewing, not a field you pick on the
board.

 
A **core** resource placed on a different cloud than the project is **gated**: Settings shows a notice
that it can be drawn but the project will not provision until the resource is colocated.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Duplicate or delete a resource
records.text:
Structural actions live in the collapsed **Danger zone** at the bottom of the **Settings** tab.

- **Duplicate resource** — create a copy with the same configuration. Available for the array-style
 resources you can have many of.
- **Delete resource** — remove the resource from the canvas. You can undo this with **⌘Z**.

The Danger zone is hidden for the project root (which can't be deleted) and for out-of-band resources
such as marketplace add-ons and bring-your-own charts, which are managed where they were installed.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Destroy an environment
records.text:
When you inspect the **project** in an editable environment, the Settings tab also carries a separate
**Destroy environment** action.

1. Open the project's **Settings** tab.
2. Click **Destroy**.
3. Confirm in the dialog.

This queues a `DESTROY` job that tears down the environment's provisioned cloud infrastructure. It
cannot be undone.

records.title: NoSQL
records.text: NoSQL. DynamoDB, Firestore, and Cosmos DB table configuration with key schema and billing modes.

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: NoSQL
records.text: The NoSQL section configures managed NoSQL database tables. Multiple tables can be added per project.

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: Fields Per Table
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Table/collection name 
 **Hash Key** Text input Partition key name (default: `id`) 
 **Hash Key Type** Select `S` (String), `N` (Number), `B` (Binary) 
 **Range Key** Text input Optional sort key name 
 **Range Key Type** Select `S`, `N`, or `B` 
 **Billing Mode** Select `PAY_PER_REQUEST` or `PROVISIONED` 
 **Point-in-Time Recovery** Toggle Enable continuous backups 
 **Table Type** Select `standard` or `global` (multi-region replication)

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: Services by Provider
records.text:
**DynamoDB** — fully managed key-value and document database

 - Hash key (partition key) + optional range key (sort key)
 - On-demand or provisioned capacity billing
 - Global tables for multi-region replication
 - KMS encryption at rest
 - Point-in-time recovery (continuous backups up to 35 days)
 
 
 **Firestore** — document-oriented NoSQL database

 - Document-based model (collections → documents → fields)
 - Serverless with automatic scaling
 - Multi-region replication built-in

 
 Firestore uses a document model rather than a key-value model. When converting from DynamoDB, hash/range keys map to document IDs. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).
 
 
 
 **Cosmos DB** — globally distributed multi-model database

 - Partition key (maps to hash key)
 - Multiple APIs: SQL (document), Table (key-value), MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin
 - Multi-region writes for global distribution
 - Serverless or provisioned throughput (RU/s)

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: Billing Modes
records.text:
Mode Description Best For 
 ------ ------------- ---------- 
 **PAY_PER_REQUEST** Pay per read/write operation, no capacity planning Unpredictable workloads, development 
 **PROVISIONED** Reserved read/write capacity units Predictable workloads, cost optimization 

 
NoSQL tables show $0 in the cost sidebar because pricing is usage-based (per operation), not estimable from configuration alone. Actual costs depend on read/write patterns.

records.title: Observability
records.text: Observability. Ship cluster metrics, logs, and traces to Datadog or Grafana Cloud.

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Observability
records.text: The observability section ships cluster metrics, logs, and traces to an external monitoring platform. Unlike DNS or secrets, observability has **no cloud-native default** — it is a connector-only component, so enabling it means choosing a provider and connecting its credential.

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Enabled** Toggle Master switch for observability 
 **Provider** Select Datadog or Grafana Cloud 
 **Provider options** Varies Provider-specific configuration (see below)

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Providers
records.text:
Installs the **Datadog agent** via Helm. Requires a connected [Datadog connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) (API key + application key). Choose the **site** (e.g. `datadoghq.com`, `datadoghq.eu`).
 
 
 Installs the **Grafana Agent** remote-writing metrics to Grafana Cloud. Requires a connected [Grafana Cloud connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) (instance ID + API token) and the **remote-write URL**.
 
 

 
Want a self-hosted metrics stack instead of an external platform? Add the **kube-prometheus-stack** [add-on](/reference/cli/addons) — it installs Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager in-cluster. Prometheus is an add-on (an in-cluster workload), not an observability connector (a credential to an external system).

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Credentials
records.text:
Provider credentials are connected on the [Connectors](/guides/connectors/pluggable) page and encrypted at rest. They are decrypted and injected into the runner's OpenTofu variables at provision time — never stored in the Project snapshot.

 
Observability is a **target-state** component — the connector backends and modules exist; the Project-designer selector is rolling out. Track the [Connectors Architecture](/concepts/connectors) page for the current contract.

records.title: Project Basics
records.text: Project Basics. Project name, environment stage, and the OpenTofu (iac_version) default — the Project node's basics.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Project Basics
records.text: The Project node — the root of the design canvas — establishes the project identity and its default target environment. A project owns **N environments** (`project_environments`); creating a project seeds the default one.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
The Project node's inspector has two sections — **General** (name, environment) and **Placement** (region).

 Field Type Validation Description 
 ------- ------ ----------- ------------- 
 **Project Name** Text input Required, max 50 chars — free-text display name The URL slug is derived from it via `slugify`; also drives resource naming and OpenTofu state paths 
 **Environment** Radio cards Required `development`, `staging`, or `production` — seeds the default environment's `stage` 
 **Region** Region picker Required The cloud region, grouped by geography and keyed to the project's cloud account 

The cloud account is chosen once when the project is created, not per node. OpenTofu itself is pinned to `1.11.4` (the `iac_version` field); the canvas does not expose a version picker.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Project Name
records.text:
The project name is a free-text display name. Alethia derives a URL slug from it (lowercasing and replacing spaces and punctuation with hyphens) via `slugify`. The derived slug is used for:
- Resource naming in OpenTofu (e.g., `{slug}-{env}-eks-cluster`)
- State file path (see [OpenTofu State](/concepts/terraform-state))

The display name appears in the UI (project cards, job listings).

 
You can type any display name — Alethia slugifies it so the identifier is always safe for cloud resource naming constraints across every provider. The name must contain at least one letter or number.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Environment Stage
records.text:
`stage` is a property of the **environment**, not the project. A project can own several environments
(dev / staging / prod), each independently provisionable with its own `stage`. The three options:

 Stage Purpose Naming Convention 
 ------- --------- ------------------ 
 `development` Dev/testing `{project}-dev-*` 
 `staging` Pre-production `{project}-staging-*` 
 `production` Production workloads `{project}-prod-*` 

The environment stage affects OpenTofu state isolation — each stage gets its own state file, even within the same project and region.

records.title: Repositories
records.text: Repositories. The apps repository an environment syncs through ArgoCD — what it must contain, what an overlay path changes, what Alethia commits back into it, and what the ArgoCD project around your manifests permits.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Repositories
records.text:
The repositories section names the Git repository ArgoCD syncs your application manifests from.
It is optional. An environment without one still gets ArgoCD, but ArgoCD manages none of your
applications.

This page is the contract that repository must meet: what it must contain, what changes when you
name an overlay path, what Alethia commits back into it, and what the ArgoCD project around your
manifests permits.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **ArgoCD apps repository** Repository selector The Git repository ArgoCD syncs manifests from 
 **Overlay path** Text A repository-relative subdirectory this environment syncs. Empty means the repository root 

The selector lists repositories from your connected Git provider (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket).
It reads that list through the stored OAuth token — see [Authentication](/concepts/authentication).

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: What the repository must contain
records.text:
**This section describes a dedicated cluster.** The `apps` Application, the `addons` Application
 and the `apps-overlays` ApplicationSet are rendered only for an environment placed on its own
 cluster. A namespace or vcluster placement gets a single Application instead — see
 [What a placed environment gets](#what-a-placed-environment-gets).
 

Naming a repository creates one ArgoCD Application called `apps`. It points at that repository,
tracks `HEAD` — the repository's default branch — and syncs one path. No field changes the tracked
revision.

The synced path is the overlay path, or the repository root when the environment names none. Your
manifests go there. A path with nothing in it produces an Application that manages nothing, which is
the usual reason a deploy succeeds and the cluster stays empty.

Two layout details follow from how the Application is declared:

- **The root Application reads one directory, not a tree.** It does not recurse. A plain directory
 of manifests must keep them in the synced directory itself. A Kustomize or Helm source at that
 path resolves its own subdirectories as normal.
- **`addons/` is a separate Application.** Alethia also creates an `addons

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Overlay discovery
records.text:
An environment that names **no** overlay path also gets an `apps-overlays` ApplicationSet. It scans
the repository root for `overlays/*` directories and creates one Application per directory, named
after it (`overlays/dev` becomes `apps-dev`). A repository with no `overlays/` directory produces
none, which is harmless.

This is the standard Kustomize layout — a `base/` plus one directory per environment under
`overlays/`. Discovery runs **only** while the environment names no overlay path. See
[Naming an overlay path](#naming-an-overlay-path).

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: How the sync behaves
records.text:
The Application syncs automatically, prunes, and self-heals. In practice:

- A commit to the default branch deploys on its own. No Alethia deploy, no approval step.
- Deleting a manifest deletes the resource it created.
- Editing a resource by hand puts it back at the next sync.
- A manifest may name any namespace, but **the namespace has to exist already**. `CreateNamespace`
 creates only the Application's own destination namespace, and this Application declares no
 destination namespace at all — it names a server and nothing else. A manifest pointing at a
 namespace that is not there fails to sync. Create the namespace in the same directory (ArgoCD
 applies a `Namespace` object like any other resource) or out of band.

 
 **Write access to the default branch is deploy access to the environment.** The Application tracks
 `HEAD`, so anyone who can push can change what runs. Restrict the branch if that is not what you
 want.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Naming an overlay path
records.text:
An overlay path makes one environment deliver one subdirectory — `overlays/dev` for a development
environment, `overlays/prod` for production — out of a repository shared by several environments.

 
 **An overlay path turns overlay discovery off.** Naming a path removes the `apps-overlays`
 ApplicationSet for that environment. This is deliberate. The discovery generator is anchored at
 the repository root and matches every `overlays/*` directory, so an environment that also
 discovers adopts the directories other environments are already delivering. Two Applications then
 own the same resources, both self-healing, and ArgoCD reports an ownership conflict. An explicit
 path replaces discovery rather than adding to it.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Path rules
records.text:
The path is user input that lands in an ArgoCD Application, so it is validated when you save it and
again by the runner before it touches the cluster:

 Rule Accepted Refused 
 ------ ---------- --------- 
 Empty or `.` means the repository root an empty value, or `.` — 
 Relative to the repository root `overlays/dev` `/overlays/dev` 
 Already normalized — no traversal, no doubled or trailing separator `overlays/dev` `../shared` · `overlays//dev` · `overlays/dev/` 
 Each segment starts with a letter or digit, then letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-` `env-1.2_a` `overlays/'dev'` · `overlays/$env` 
 At most 512 characters — a longer path 

A path that breaks a rule is refused, never corrected. Rewriting `../../shared` to `shared` would
hand you a different directory from the one you asked for.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: What Alethia commits back into the repository
records.text:
Alethia can push to the repository. Both cases below need a Git token, and both leave your own files
alone. **Both are dedicated-cluster only** — a namespace or vcluster placement never receives a
scaffold or a seeded add-on manifest, for the reason given in
[What a placed environment gets](#what-a-placed-environment-gets).

**Generated service manifests.** If the project has services that render, Alethia scaffolds
manifests for them, commits them, and pushes. It does this **only** when the repository root holds
no `.yaml` or `.yml` file. That test looks at files at the root and does not look inside
directories, so a repository whose manifests all live under `overlays/` or `k8s/` still reads as
empty and gets scaffolded manifests at its root. A single manifest at the root opts the repository
out for good.

 
 **Generated manifests land at the repository root.** An environment with an overlay path syncs a
 subdirectory, so it does not deliver them. Bring your own manifests, or leave the overlay path
 empty, if you want the scaffold to be what runs.
 

**GitOps add-on manifests.** Enabling a marketplace add-on in GitOps mode writes
`addons/ .yaml`, commits it, and pushes. The write i

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: What a placed environment gets
records.text:
A namespace or vcluster placement is wired before the deploy reaches the code that renders the
`apps` and `addons` Applications, the `apps-overlays` ApplicationSet, the generated service
manifests and the seeded add-on files. None of those exists for a placed environment.

What it gets instead is a single Application, `app- - `, under an AppProject named
`tenant- - `. It syncs the same repository at the same `apps_path` — the field
means the same thing on all three placements — and the AppProject bounds it as the table under
[What the apps project permits](#what-the-apps-project-permits) describes.

Two consequences worth stating, because the sections above would otherwise imply the opposite:

- **Overlay discovery does not run.** There is no ApplicationSet, so `overlays/*` directories are
 not turned into Applications. A placed environment syncs exactly one path.
- **Nothing is committed back.** Bring your own manifests; no scaffold arrives.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Access to the repository
records.text:
Each deploy, Alethia connects ArgoCD to the repository:

1. **With a Git token.** The token from your connected Git provider is applied as an ArgoCD
 repository Secret named `repo-apps` in the `argocd` namespace. Every deploy re-applies it.
2. **Without one, if the repository is public.** Alethia probes the repository anonymously over
 HTTPS and, if the probe succeeds, skips the credential. ArgoCD then clones anonymously.
 Only `https://` URLs are probed — an `ssh://` or `git@host:path` repository always needs a token.
3. **Neither.** The deploy fails, and the error says so: connect the Git provider for the job owner,
 or make the repository public. A half-wired cluster that reports success is worse than a failure
 you can act on.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: What the apps project permits
records.text:
Your manifests run under an ArgoCD AppProject, and the project is what bounds them. Which project
depends on how the environment is placed — see
[Fabrics and placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement).

 Dedicated cluster (`apps`) Namespace placement vcluster placement 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Source repositories The one apps repository The one apps repository The one apps repository 
 Destinations Any namespace in the cluster Its own namespace only Any namespace inside its own vcluster 
 Cluster-scoped resources Allowed, any kind None Allowed inside the vcluster 
 Blocked namespaced kinds None `Role`, `RoleBinding`, `NetworkPolicy`, `ResourceQuota`, `LimitRange`, ArgoCD `Application` and `AppProject` None 

Two things are true of every row. The project pins `sourceRepos` to the apps repository you
configured, so an Application under it cannot be re-pointed at a source you did not choose. And a
namespace placement is confined to its own namespace, because the cluster is shared; a dedicated
cluster and a vcluster are not shared, so both are permissive inside their own boundary.

 
 **This is why CRD-bearing infrastructure belongs in the apps repository rather than in a
 bring-your-own c

records.title: Secrets
records.text: Secrets. Managed secrets with auto-generation, presets, and cloud-native secret stores.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Secrets
records.text: The secrets section creates entries in your cloud provider's secret management service. Secrets can be auto-generated with configurable parameters or set to custom values after provisioning.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Fields Per Secret
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Secret name (alphanumeric + hyphens only) 
 **Provider** Select Cloud-native store or a [pluggable connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Generate** Toggle Auto-generate a random value 
 **Length** Number 8–128 characters 
 **Special Characters** Toggle Include `!@#$%^&*()` in generated value

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Secrets Provider
records.text:
By default secrets are created in the cluster cloud's native secret store. Select **HashiCorp Vault** to manage them in a Vault instance instead:

- Requires a connected [Vault connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) (Vault address + token).
- Per-Project knobs: the KV **mount path** and **KV version** (1 or 2).
- The cloud-native secret resources are skipped at provision time; Vault entries are managed by the composed module.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Presets
records.text:
Quick-add buttons create secrets with recommended settings:

 Preset Length Special Chars Use Case 
 -------- -------- -------------- ---------- 
 PostgreSQL Password 32 Yes Database master password 
 API Token 48 No Application API key 
 JWT Secret 64 No Token signing key 
 Redis Password 32 No Cache authentication 
 Custom Secret 32 No User-defined

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Secret Store by Provider
records.text:
**AWS Secrets Manager** — $0.40/secret/month + $0.05 per 10,000 API calls.
 Supports automatic rotation, cross-account access, and integration with RDS for database credential management.
 
 
 **Secret Manager** — $0.06 per 10,000 access operations.
 Supports automatic replication, IAM-based access control, and versioning.
 
 
 **Key Vault** — $0.03 per 10,000 operations.
 Supports secrets, keys, and certificates. Integrates with Azure AD for access control.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Integration with Kubernetes
records.text: After provisioning, secrets are synced to Kubernetes via the **External Secrets Operator** (installed by ArgoCD — see [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)). This creates Kubernetes `Secret` resources from cloud secret store entries, keeping them in sync automatically.

records.title: Services
records.text: Services. A service is a first-class canvas node for your own code — built from a repo or a prebuilt image, run as a Kubernetes workload with validated ports, environment, resources, health, and bindings.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Services
records.text:
A **service** is the customer's own application code on the cluster. Unlike the infrastructure kinds (databases, caches, secrets), a service is built from your source and run as a Kubernetes workload. The runner turns each service into Kubernetes manifests at deploy time.

A service is a first-class node kind on the [canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas): it carries its own validated configuration and it binds to the backing infrastructure it depends on.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Adding a service
records.text: Services lead the Add palette in the **Workloads** group. Selecting **Service** drops a node on the canvas and opens its config sheet.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Identity
records.text:
Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Name** Text Required. Unique per project and environment. 
 **Type** Choice The Kubernetes workload kind. Defaults to **Deployment**. 

The workload type is one of:

 Type Description 
 ------ ------------- 
 **Deployment** Long-running, load-balanced. 
 **Job** Runs once to completion. 
 **CronJob** Runs on a schedule. 
 **StatefulSet** Stable identity and storage.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Source
records.text:
A service's image comes from one of two sources:

 Source Fields 
 -------- -------- 
 **Repository** `Repository URL` (required) and an optional `Path` (subdirectory to build from). Alethia builds and pushes the image. 
 **Prebuilt image** `Image` (required) — a pushed image reference deployed as-is, e.g. `ghcr.io/org/api:1.4.0`.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Build
records.text:
The build fields apply only when the source is a **Repository**. Both are optional:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Dockerfile** Path to the Dockerfile. 
 **Context** Build context directory. 

For a prebuilt image, the Build section does not apply.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Networking
records.text:
Add the container ports the workload exposes. Each port has:

 Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Container port** Number Required. 1–65535. 
 **Protocol** Choice `TCP` or `UDP`. Optional. 
 **Name** Text Optional.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Environment
records.text:
Add plain environment variables as `name` / `value` pairs.

 
Environment variables added here are plain values. To inject a resource's endpoint or credentials,
use a **binding** (below) — Alethia delivers credentials as a Kubernetes `secretKeyRef`, never as a
plain value in the manifest.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Bindings
records.text:
A binding connects the service to a backing resource on the canvas and declares which environment variables that connection injects. Alethia resolves each binding at deploy time — keyless.

A binding targets one resource kind:

 Target kind 
 ------------- 
 Database 
 Cache 
 Queue 
 Secret 

Each binding declares any number of injected variables. Each maps an environment variable name to a **facet** of the connection:

 Facet Delivered as 
 ------- -------------- 
 `endpoint` Templated value in the manifest 
 `port` Templated value in the manifest 
 `username` Kubernetes `secretKeyRef` 
 `password` Kubernetes `secretKeyRef` 
 `connection string` Kubernetes `secretKeyRef` 

The non-secret facets (`endpoint`, `port`) are written into the manifest as templated values; the credential facets (`username`, `password`, `connection string`) are delivered as a `secretKeyRef` and never written into the manifest.

A binding can also target a [bring-your-own IaC](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) resource by its OpenTofu address, in which case the facets resolve against the customer module's declared output names.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Runtime
records.text:
Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Replicas** Number Defaults to `2`. The inspector accepts 1–5. 
 **CPU request** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `100m`. 
 **Memory request** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `128Mi`. 
 **CPU limit** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `500m`. 
 **Memory limit** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `512Mi`. 

Resource requests and limits are optional. When they are left unset, the runner's template defaults apply.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Health
records.text:
A service can gate its rollout on a probe. When the health check is enabled:

 Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Probe type** Choice `HTTP` (check an HTTP endpoint) or `TCP` (open a TCP connection). 
 **Path** Text HTTP probes only, e.g. `/healthz`. 
 **Port** Number 1–65535. 

When the health check is disabled, no probe is configured.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [The canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas) — how nodes and edges model your project.
- [Databases](/guides/design-project/databases) — a common binding target; see also [keyless database auth](/guides/design-project/keyless-database-auth).
- [Secrets](/guides/design-project/secrets) — bind a service to a managed secret.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.text: Starter Templates. Three public template repositories you can copy to start an apps repository, a bring-your-own Helm chart, or a full AI stack — and which of Alethia's two trust levels each one targets.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: Starter Templates
records.text:
Alethia publishes three public template repositories. Each is a working starting point for one
thing you can point an environment at, and each is small on purpose: every path in it is a path the
product actually reads.

They are templates, not forks. Use the **Use this template** button to create your own copy. None
of them reports back to Alethia.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: The three repositories
records.text:
Repository What it is Trust level 
 --- --- --- 
 [alethia-starter-apps](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-apps) An apps repository ArgoCD syncs your manifests from Apps repository 
 [alethia-starter-chart](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-chart) A bring-your-own Helm chart Alethia installs as an add-on Bring-your-own chart 
 [alethia-starter-ai](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-ai) A retrieval-augmented generation stack that spans both Both 

All three are licensed Apache-2.0. Each carries a `TEMPLATE_VERSION` file and a semantic-version
`CHANGELOG.md`. A change to a chart's `values.schema.json` is a major bump, because that file is
the interface your values are written against.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: Pick one when you create a project
records.text:
When you create a project with **Start from a template**, the **Template** section offers three
choices. Each one gives you a starter repository to copy:

 Template Starter repository 
 --- --- 
 Standard alethia-starter-apps 
 AI Workloads alethia-starter-ai 
 Custom None. You attach your own repositories. 

The choice does not change the cluster. All three create the same node pool, with no GPU. Use
**Use this template** to copy the starter, then attach your copy to the environment as this page
describes.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: The two trust levels
records.text:
Your manifests run under one of two ArgoCD projects. They are not the same shape, and which one
applies is decided by how you attach the code — not by what the code does.

 Apps repository Bring-your-own chart 
 --- --- --- 
 Cluster-scoped resources Any kind None 
 `Role`, `RoleBinding`, `ServiceAccount` Allowed Blocked 
 Source repositories Any Only the one you configured 

 
 A chart that installs CustomResourceDefinitions cannot be a bring-your-own chart. A
 CustomResourceDefinition is cluster-scoped, so the project rejects it. This is a limit on what a
 chart **creates**, not on what it is for. Many database charts ship an operator and are blocked
 for that reason alone.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: alethia-starter-apps
records.text:
An apps repository. Point an environment at your copy and three Applications converge: the root,
`apps-dev` and `apps-staging`.

 Path What it is for 
 --- --- 
 `kustomization.yaml` The root manifest. Without one, the root Application manages nothing 
 `namespace.yaml` The namespace the root delivers into 
 `base/` The application, defined once 
 `overlays/dev/`, `overlays/staging/` Discovered automatically; become `apps-dev` and `apps-staging` 
 `addons/` Keeps the `addons` Application out of ComparisonError 

To use it:

 
 Create your own repository from the template. 
 Open the environment, go to **Repositories**, and set **ArgoCD apps repository** to your new
repository. Leave **Overlay path** empty. 
 Deploy. 
 

For what an apps repository must contain, and what Alethia commits back into it, see
[Repositories](/guides/design-project/repositories).

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: alethia-starter-chart
records.text:
A bring-your-own Helm chart. It renders a Deployment, a Service and a ConfigMap. Every one of them
is namespaced and none of them is RBAC, which is the contract a bring-your-own chart must meet.

The repository mechanises that contract in `hack/check-byo-contract.sh`. Run it against your own
chart before you attach it, and the build fails if a change breaks the contract.

 
 Create your own repository from the template. 
 In Alethia, go to **Add-ons → Bring your own chart**. 
 Set **Chart repository** to your repository, **Chart path** to `chart`, and **Ref** to `HEAD`
or a tag. 
 Deploy. Alethia creates the namespace, registers a per-repository credential, and applies the
chart. 
 

For the safety scan and how a chart's workloads appear on the canvas, see
[Bring your own Helm charts](/guides/design-project/bring-your-own-charts).

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: alethia-starter-ai
records.text:
A retrieval-augmented generation stack: a vector database, a CPU embedding server, CPU inference,
model serving and job queueing. It is also the worked example of where the line between the two
trust levels falls.

It splits across both:

 Component Goes in Why 
 --- --- --- 
 KServe, Kueue, the GPU operator `addons/`, the apps repository They install CustomResourceDefinitions, which are cluster-scoped 
 Qdrant, embeddings, inference, the RAG application `chart/`, a bring-your-own chart A Deployment, a Service and a PersistentVolumeClaim are none of the blocked kinds 

Qdrant is the instructive case. It is a database, and it could have gone on either side. What puts
it in the chart is that this particular chart ships no operator.

records.title: Starter Templates
records.heading: KServe needs cert-manager
records.text:
KServe signs its admission webhook with a cert-manager certificate. Without cert-manager, KServe
does not start. Alethia installs cert-manager as part of the platform. The add-on marketplace has
no cert-manager entry, and you must not add one to `addons/`. A second copy fights the platform
copy over the same CustomResourceDefinitions.

How you get cert-manager depends on how you created the project:

 You created the project What to do 
 --- --- 
 From the **AI Workloads** template Nothing. Alethia installs cert-manager for you on every cloud, and you need no domain 
 From another template, or you copied the repository yourself Turn on a managed certificate. On the DNS component, set **Domain name** and turn on **Managed TLS certificate**. This works on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure 

A managed certificate installs cert-manager and also gives it a public issuer for your domain.
KServe does not need that issuer. KServe creates its own self-signed issuer in its own namespace.

 
 **This template provisions no GPU.** It runs CPU-only by default. A GPU node pool is the most
 expensive thing you can provision by accident, so enabling one is a deliberate change you commit
 yourself. See th

records.title: Object Storage
records.text: Object Storage. Object storage buckets are a first-class canvas node with their own fields, S3-safe naming rules, and per-provider backing services.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Object Storage
records.text:
A **bucket** is a first-class node on the [architecture canvas](/guides/design-project/the-canvas) — the same standing as a database, cache, or container registry. Add one from the palette's **Storage** group to provision object storage for files and assets. Multiple buckets can be added per project.

Each bucket is scoped to the project's cloud account and environment. Its name is unique per project, per environment.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Fields Per Bucket
records.text:
Field Type Default Description 
 ------- ------ --------- ------------- 
 **Name** Text input `assets` Bucket name (S3-safe — see [Naming rules](#naming-rules)) 
 **Versioning** Toggle Off Keep every version of an object; restore or roll back at any time (on Azure this applies to the whole project — see [Azure](#azure)) 
 **Encryption at rest** Toggle On Server-side encryption with the cloud's managed keys 
 **Public access** Toggle Off (private) Allow unauthenticated reads (static assets); off keeps the bucket private 
 **CORS origins** Text Empty Comma-separated origins allowed to read from the browser 

The name, versioning, and encryption fields are grouped under **General**; public access and CORS origins are grouped under **Access**.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Naming rules
records.text:
Bucket names use the strictest cloud rules, so one name works on every provider:

- 3–63 characters.
- Lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens only.
- Must start and end with a letter or digit (no leading or trailing hyphen).

The name field lowercases input and strips disallowed characters as you type; the full rule is validated on save.

 
A single S3-safe name is portable across AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud, and Hetzner, so a bucket you design on one provider provisions unchanged on another.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Backing service by provider
records.text:
Buckets are supported on every provider. The name and toggles map to each cloud's object-storage service:

 Provider Service 
 ---------- --------- 
 **AWS** S3 
 **GCP** Cloud Storage 
 **Azure** Blob Storage 
 **Alibaba Cloud** OSS 
 **Hetzner** MinIO (Object Storage)

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Hetzner
records.text:
Compute-only Hetzner projects provision buckets natively via Object Storage (the `aminueza/minio` OpenTofu provider). Two fields differ on Hetzner:

- **Encryption at rest** is not shown — Hetzner Object Storage always encrypts at rest, so there is no per-bucket toggle.
- **CORS origins** is not shown — the provider does not apply CORS to Hetzner's S3 backend.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Azure
records.text:
Two fields behave differently on Azure, because Blob Storage puts the setting on the storage account rather than the container. An Azure project has one storage account, which holds every bucket in the project.

- **Versioning** is an account setting. Turning it on for one bucket versions **every** bucket in that project. Leaving it on for a bucket that no longer needs it costs storage; the alternative — ignoring a bucket that asks for it — loses data on the first overwrite, so Alethia turns versioning on for the account whenever any bucket asks for it.
- **Public access** is applied per bucket, as it is everywhere else. The account permission that allows public containers is opened only when at least one bucket asks for public access, and stays closed otherwise.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Google Cloud
records.text:
**Public access** on Google Cloud does two things: it stops Cloud Storage from refusing public grants on that bucket, and it grants read access to everyone. Uniform bucket-level access stays on for every bucket regardless — it controls per-object ACLs, not public reads, and Cloud Storage will not let it be turned off again once a bucket has had it for 90 days.

 
Many Google Cloud organizations set the `constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` organization policy, which blocks public grants everywhere in the organization. Under that policy a public bucket is refused when the project is deployed, and the deployment says so rather than failing part-way through.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Cloud placement
records.text: A bucket inherits the project's cloud account and region. When left unset, its per-resource cloud identity and region fall back to the project's own — so a bucket lands in the same account and region as the rest of the project unless it is placed on another connected account.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: On the canvas
records.text:
The bucket card summarizes its configuration without opening the inspector:

- **Access** — `public` or `private`.
- **Versioning** — `on` or `off`.
- **CORS** — the number of allowed origins, or `none`.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: After provisioning
records.text: Each bucket carries a lifecycle status — `PENDING`, `CREATING`, `ACTIVE`, `UPDATING`, `FAILED`, `DESTROYING`, or `DESTROYED` — and an estimated monthly cost that rolls up into the [cost sidebar](/guides/design-project/cost-sidebar).

records.title: The canvas
records.text: The canvas. How the architecture canvas is designed — what a card tells you, how status reads without colour, why some resources collapse into one card, and how detail changes with zoom.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The canvas
records.text:
The Architecture view is where a project's infrastructure is designed, deployed, and kept honest.
This page explains how to *read* it — the conventions are deliberate, and once you know them the
board tells you a great deal at a glance.

The canvas is **fully grayscale**. Nothing on it is colour-coded. That is a constraint, not an
oversight: colour is the first thing to fail under a projector, a screenshot, colour-blindness, or a
dark room. So every distinction you can see is carried by **shape, structure, and type** instead —
and the one exception is the cloud provider's own brand mark, which stays in its original colours
because it belongs to someone else.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: What a card tells you
records.text: Every resource is a card, and every card is built from the same four parts.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The glyph and the eyebrow
records.text:
Top-left: the service's icon and its kind, in uppercase mono. This is the fastest read — *what kind
of thing is this*.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The facts
records.text:
The middle of the card is a small grid of the **two or three facts that actually matter for that
service**. This is what makes a database look like a database and not like a DNS zone:

 Resource Reads as 
 --- --- 
 Database `PostgreSQL 16 · 0.5–4 · 7 d` 
 Cache `Valkey · cache.t3.medium · 2 · multi-AZ` 
 Bucket `private · on · 2 origins` 
 Cluster `1.31 · 2–5 · m5a.large` 
 Topic `3 subscriptions · push · pull` 

A fact with no value yet draws a **muted dash**, so an unconfigured resource reads as unconfigured
without having to open it.

The facts are **cloud-honest**. On a compute-only cloud like Hetzner there is no managed database
service, so a database is deployed as a CloudNativePG cluster *inside your Kubernetes cluster* — and
the card says exactly that (`Runs as · CloudNativePG`) rather than implying a managed service that
doesn't exist. The same is true of caches (Valkey) and queues (RabbitMQ).

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The provider chip
records.text:
Which cloud account this resource lands in. A resource with no chip of its own **inherits the
project's** cloud — that's the common case, and the chip says `inherits core`.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The classification rule
records.text:
The thin band across the **top edge** of the card says what kind of citizen the resource is:

 Rule Meaning 
 --- --- 
 Solid, full ink **Root** — the project itself, the anchor everything inherits from 
 Solid, strong **Core** — must sit on the project's cloud (network, cluster, data services) 
 Hairline **Periphery** — may live on a different cloud (DNS, buckets, registry, secrets, GitOps) 
 Dashed **External** — not managed by this design (a bring-your-own Helm chart or IaC module)

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Status without colour
records.text:
Status is shown by a **dot**, read by its fill and shape, with a short mono label beside it. There is
no red and no green anywhere.

 Dot State Means 
 --- --- --- 
 Solid **Live** / **Ready** Nominal. The calm state — it shows only the dot, no label. 
 Hollow ring **Needs setup** / **Not deployed** Designed but incomplete, or never applied. 
 Haloed **Queued** / **Updating** / **Update pending** / **Destroying** Something is pending. 
 Blinking **Applying** A runner is changing this resource right now. 
 Hollow-centre **Failed** / **Unreachable** A real, actionable break. 
 Faint **Gated** / **Destroyed** Inert — it won't provision, or it's gone. 

The canvas stays **calm when everything is fine**: a healthy resource shows a dot and nothing else.
Anything that wants your attention carries a label. If the board is quiet, it's quiet because there
is nothing to say.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: One state, chosen deliberately
records.text:
A resource often has several truths at once — its design is invalid, *and* it's live, *and* it has
drifted. The canvas picks one to show, in a fixed order:

1. **Failed** — a real break outranks everything.
2. **In flight** (queued · applying · updating · destroying) — what's *happening* outranks what's *wrong*.
3. **Needs setup** — the design itself is invalid, so the next deploy will not work. This is shown
 *even for a resource that is currently live*, because the deploy you are about to run is the thing
 that matters.
4. **Gated** — valid, but it won't provision (see below).
5. **Destroyed**, then **Not deployed**.
6. **Unreachable** — it exists, but the cluster's API server didn't answer the last probe.
7. **Update pending** — live, but the design has moved ahead of what's deployed.
8. **Live** / **Ready**.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Drift is an overlay, not a state
records.text:
If the real cloud has diverged from what Alethia recorded, the resource is still **Live** — it just
carries a `2 drifted` chip alongside. Drift never replaces the state, it rides on top of it. The
resource's panel lists exactly which OpenTofu resources diverged.

Drift that can't confidently be traced back to a specific resource is reported **at the environment**
rather than pinned to a card it might not belong to. An honest "2 resources drifted, unattributed" is
better than a wrong badge on your database.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Gated
records.text:
A **core** resource placed on a different cloud than the project is drawn as **gated**. It can be
designed and drawn, but the project will not provision until it's colocated. This mirrors the
provisioner's own rule — the canvas will never let you believe something will deploy when it won't.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Regions — where a resource actually runs
records.text:
The board draws two nested regions, and puts each resource where it really lives:

- The **VPC** — your network. It holds the cluster, and every managed data service.
- The **cluster** — nested inside the VPC. It holds what runs as a workload in Kubernetes.

Everything else — DNS, buckets, the container registry, secrets, the GitOps repository — sits
**outside both**. That isn't an accident of layout: those are exactly the resources that have no VPC,
which is why they're the ones allowed to live on a *different cloud* from the rest of the project.

Drawn flat, a managed database and an in-cluster Grafana look like the same kind of thing. They are
not: the database runs *in* the VPC but *outside* Kubernetes, and Grafana runs *inside* the cluster.
The regions make that difference visible at a glance.

 
On a compute-only cloud like Hetzner there is no managed data plane, so databases, caches and queues
deploy as Helm charts **inside your cluster** — and the board draws them there. The same design lays
out differently on a different cloud, because it genuinely *deploys* differently.
 

Regions are derived from the resources inside them, so dragging a card simply re-shapes the region
a

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Collections — when one card stands for many
records.text:
A real project has thirty or forty secrets. Thirty cards would bury the architecture: the canvas
would stop being a picture of your system and become a wall of near-identical boxes.

So high-cardinality resources **collapse into a single card** — a vault. Secrets work this way today.
The card shows the count, a few names, and **the state of its unhappiest member**: a vault holding one
failed secret can never read *Live*. Collapsing hides the clutter, never the trouble.

Open the vault to get the full list, filter it, add or remove entries, and click through to any single
secret to configure it exactly as you would any other resource. Nothing is taken away — only the
board is kept readable.

 
This is a rendering decision, not a data model. Every secret is still an individual resource with its
own configuration, its own status, and its own line in the deploy diff.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Bring your own IaC — still an architecture
records.text:
An environment can be provisioned from **your own OpenTofu module** instead of the built-in template.
When it is, the module — not the component design — is the source of truth, so you can't add
components to it.

That doesn't make it a black box. Alethia inventories the module's resources and draws them, so a
bring-your-own environment reads as an architecture like any other:

- Resources are grouped into cards **by kind and by OpenTofu module** — the `aws_vpc` and its
 subnets become one **Network** card; the `aws_eks_*` resources a **Cluster** card. A real module is
 fifty to two hundred resources, and drawn one per card they would bury the architecture, so the
 same collapsing rule that governs the Secrets vault applies here.
- The cards sit in the **same VPC and cluster regions** as a template environment, because that is
 genuinely where they run.
- They are drawn **dashed** — external. Alethia plans, prices, drifts and audits these resources; it
 does not own their definition. Changing one means editing your OpenTofu module, so the cards are
 read-only. Open one to see every resource inside it: its address, what the last plan would do to
 it, what it costs, and whether it ha

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Detail follows zoom
records.text:
Cards shed **detail** before they shed **legibility**, so a large architecture stays readable:

 Zoom Shows 
 --- --- 
 Far out The glyph, the name, and a status dot 
 Middle Header, name, and the single most important fact 
 Close in The full card — facts, provider, status, everything 

Zoom out to see the shape of the system; zoom in to work on it.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Reading the board quickly
records.text:
- **Everything quiet, dots only** — the environment is healthy and matches its design.
- **A hollow-centre dot** — something failed or a cluster stopped answering. Start there.
- **A blinking dot** — a deploy is in flight right now.
- **Dashed borders** — resources you brought yourself; Alethia plans and verifies them but does not
 own their definition.
- **Faint dots** — inert. Either gated (won't provision) or already destroyed.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.text: Fleet Pools. Configure a managed warm pool of runners for a cloud so the fleet controller keeps capacity sized to demand.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Fleet Pools
records.text:
A **warm pool** is a declarative target for one cloud's managed runners: a floor of always-ready
runners, a ceiling on spend, and a version to converge to. The **fleet controller** — a 60-second
loop — reads every pool each tick and provisions, drains, or replaces runners to match. Editing a
pool in the console takes effect on the next tick, with no redeploy.

Pools live in the **Pools** panel on the [Runners](/guides/runners) page. For the runner agent
itself, see [Runners](/guides/runners).

 
Warm pools apply to **managed** runners only — the fleet Alethia operates and bills by provisioned
hours. You don't register or deploy them yourself; you configure a pool and the controller keeps it
sized. Self-operated runners are added from **Add Runner** instead.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- **This is a self-managed deployment.** The Pools panel is shown only on self-managed installs,
 where the operator is you. On the hosted SaaS the panel is hidden and the fleet actions refuse.
- **You can manage the fleet.** Creating, editing, pausing, and deleting pools is gated to
 owner/admin. Without that capability the panel is read-only and the **Add pool** button is hidden.
- **A cloud provider is wired for real VMs.** Set `FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud` to provision runners on the
 Hetzner VM fleet. Until then a pool is **advisory** — the controller logs the actions it *would*
 take but creates nothing, and the panel shows a "pools are advisory" notice.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Open the Pools panel
records.text:
1. Go to the [Runners](/guides/runners) page.
2. Find the **Pools** panel in the left column. It lists one card per configured pool, or an empty
 state when none exist.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Add a pool
records.text:
Click **Add pool** to open the wizard. It walks five steps — **Cloud → Placement → Capacity →
Version → Review** — and validates each before you advance.

 
There is **one pool per cloud**. A cloud that already has a pool is disabled in the picker, and a
pool's cloud can't change after creation — edit or delete the existing pool instead.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Choose the cloud
records.text:
Pick the **cloud provider** whose runners this pool manages. Optionally set a **display name** shown
on the pool card; it defaults to the provider name.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Set placement
records.text:
Enter **locations** as comma-separated region codes for that cloud (for example, Hetzner `fsn1,
nbg1`). The controller spreads runners across them, so a degraded region doesn't take the pool down.
At least one location is required.

Set a **minimum per location** to keep that many runners in every listed location. Leave it `0` for
no per-region floor.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Set capacity
records.text:
Field Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Warm minimum** Runners kept booted and ready at all times, even with zero queued jobs. 
 **Maximum** The hard ceiling — the most runners the pool will ever provision, no matter how deep the queue. 
 **Idle buffer** Extra idle runners kept above current demand (N+1 headroom) so a new job rarely waits for a boot. `0` scales exactly to demand. 
 **Slots / runner** How many jobs one runner executes at once. Higher packs more work per VM but shares its CPU and memory. 

A live preview reads the numbers back in plain English. When a runner takes more than one slot, it
also shows the maximum concurrent jobs (maximum × slots per runner).

Two rules are enforced: the maximum must be at least the warm minimum, and the idle buffer can't
exceed the maximum. If the per-location minimum times the number of locations exceeds the maximum,
the wizard warns you to raise the maximum or lower the floor.

Expand **Advanced scaling** for two more knobs:

 Field Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Rollout surge** Extra runners the controller may run above the ceiling during a version rollout, so it replaces old runners without dropping capacity. 
 **Scale-down grace** Consecutive 60-second

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Choose a version source
records.text:
Pick how the pool tracks runner versions:

- **Channel** — track a moving release stream (usually `stable`). The controller resolves the
 channel to the newest release each tick and auto-updates the pool.
- **Pinned** — hold one exact version until you change it.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Review and create
records.text:
Check the summary and click **Create pool**. The controller wakes immediately and begins converging
the pool toward its target.

 

New capacity is always created at the target version. When you change the version, the controller
rolls runners over one step per tick — draining an outdated runner only while it can surge a
replacement first, so online capacity never drops below the warm floor.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Read a pool card
records.text:
Each card derives its numbers from the pool's configured target joined with the runners it observes:

- **Warm capacity** — online runners over the target, drawn as a segmented meter. Filled segments are
 online runners, hatched segments are online-and-busy, dashed segments are the gap to target. A note
 line shows how many are below floor, busy, and draining.
- **Rollout** — the percentage of live runners already on the target version, with the target and a
 progress bar while a rollout is in flight.
- **Versions** and **Locations** — how live runners are distributed; a tally is flagged when it's off
 the target version or a location has an offline runner.
- **Health** — **Healthy**, or **Degraded** when the pool is below its warm floor or any runner is
 offline. A paused pool is dimmed and labelled **Paused**.
- **Economics** (manager-only) — a month-to-date footer with provisioned hours, estimated cost, and
 utilization.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Edit, pause, or delete a pool
records.text:
Open the **⋮** menu on a pool card (visible to managers):

- **Edit** reopens the wizard on that pool. Its cloud is fixed; every other knob is editable, and
 changes converge live on the next tick.
- **Pause** stops the pool. The controller reconciles a paused pool as a teardown target — it drains
 every runner to zero and closes each runner's usage session, so pausing leaves no billable orphans.
 **Resume** rebuilds the warm floor over the next few ticks.
- **Delete** removes the pool. The controller drains and reaps its runners on the next tick before
 the row is removed. This cannot be undone.

 
Pausing and deleting both drain a pool to zero. A busy runner is drained first — it stops claiming
new work and finishes its in-flight job — before it's destroyed, so no running job is dropped.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.text: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster. Use `alethia cluster kubeconfig` to get a short-lived kubeconfig for a cluster without a cloud login of your own. Choose the tier, the lifetime and the shape, reach a private endpoint, revoke access, and fix each refusal.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.text:
`alethia cluster kubeconfig` gets you a short-lived kubeconfig for a cluster that Alethia
provisioned. You do not need a login to the cloud account. A runner in your organization mints the
credential inside the cluster's network and seals it to a one-time key that the CLI makes. Only
the machine that ran the command can open the result.

This page shows you how to get the kubeconfig and how to choose its tier, lifetime and shape. It
also tells you how to reach a private endpoint, how to revoke access, and how to fix each refusal.
For every flag and default, see the
[`alethia cluster kubeconfig` reference](/reference/cli/clusters#alethia-cluster-kubeconfig).

 
 If you already have a login to the cloud account, you can also use your own cloud CLI. The
 **Kubeconfig** row of `alethia cluster get` and the cluster card show that command. See
 [kubeconfig commands](/guides/clusters#kubeconfig-commands).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Before you begin
records.text:
Make sure that:

- The `alethia` CLI is installed and you are signed in. See [Install the CLI](/get-started/install-the-cli).
- The cluster runs on AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner. Other clouds cannot mint a
 kubeconfig through Alethia.
- The environment has at least one successful deploy, and it is not being destroyed.
- The environment has a `dedicated` placement. An environment placed on a shared cluster as a
 `namespace` or `vcluster` cannot get a kubeconfig, because the credential would give access to
 the whole shared cluster. See [Fabrics & Placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement).
- A runner is online for your organization. The mint runs as a job on it. See [Runners](/guides/runners).
- Your role allows the tier you want. See [Choose the access tier](#choose-the-access-tier).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Run the command
records.text:
alethia cluster kubeconfig

The CLI lists your clusters and asks which one you want. To skip the question, name the cluster.
The selector matches a project name, a cluster name or a cluster ID:

alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Wait for the runner
records.text:
The CLI sends the request, and then waits while a runner mints the credential. On an idle runner
this takes a few seconds. A runner that is busy with a deploy can take longer. The CLI waits for up
to 10 minutes.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Use the context
records.text:
The CLI adds the context `alethia- - ` to your kubeconfig and makes it the current
context. It prints the context name and a command to try:

kubectl --context alethia-api-backend-production get namespaces

 
 

By default the CLI merges the context into the first file in `$KUBECONFIG`, or into
`~/.kube/config`. It replaces an older context with the same name, and it does not change your
other contexts. To write a separate file instead, use `--output`:

alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --output api-backend.kubeconfig

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: From the console
records.text:
The console can also download a read-only kubeconfig. Open **Clusters**, find the cluster's card,
and click **Download kubeconfig (1h, read-only)**. The button is the last row of the card's
**Cluster access** block, under the kubeconfig command or the note that replaces it. The block
appears only when the cluster has an API endpoint.

Only people who hold the `cluster:access_readonly` permission see the button: owners, admins and
operators by default. Other people see nothing in its place. The request checks the permission
again.

One click gets you this:

- a **static** kubeconfig, which holds the credential itself and needs only `kubectl`;
- the **read-only** tier, with the access that [What read-only allows](#what-read-only-allows)
 lists;
- a lifetime of **1 hour**;
- a file called `alethia- - .kubeconfig`, which your browser saves. It uses the same
 `alethia- - ` name as the context that the CLI writes.

The console cannot change the tier, the lifetime or the shape. For an admin kubeconfig, another
lifetime or the exec shape, use the CLI.

While the runner mints the credential, the card shows **Minting on the runner…**. When the file is
saved, the card shows its name and when

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Browser support
records.text:
The download needs a browser that can make an X25519 key with WebCrypto: Chrome 133 or later,
Firefox 130 or later, or Safari 17 or later. Other browsers do not get a fallback. The card shows
this message instead:

This browser cannot create the X25519 key the download is sealed to. Use the CLI instead: alethia cluster kubeconfig.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Messages on the card
records.text:
The console and the CLI share the same checks and the same rate limit. So the same causes and
fixes apply as in [Troubleshoot](#troubleshoot), but the card words them differently.

 Message What to do 
 --- --- 
 The billing guard's own sentence, or: Your plan's usage limit is reached, so no new kubeconfig can be minted. The mint uses runner minutes. Check your plan's usage. 
 You need cluster read-only access to download a kubeconfig. Ask an owner or admin for a role that holds `cluster:access_readonly`. 
 This cluster was not found. Reload the page. The cluster may have been removed. 
 This cluster has not finished provisioning, so there is no kubeconfig to mint yet. Deploy the environment, or wait for its deploy to finish. 
 This cluster's cloud cannot mint a kubeconfig through Alethia. Use the cloud's own CLI. 
 Too many kubeconfig requests. Try again in a few minutes. Wait. The limit counts the CLI's requests and the console's together. 
 The kubeconfig could not be requested. Try again. Click the button again. 
 The runner did not finish the kubeconfig in time. Try again. Check that a runner is online for your organization, then try again. 
 The kubeconfig arrived but could n

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Choose the access tier
records.text:
There are two tiers. Read-only is the default. Each tier is a separate permission, and a request
gets exactly the tier it asks for. No cloud changes a read-only request into an admin one.

 Tier Flag Who can get it In-cluster identity 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Read-only none (the default) Owners, admins and operators: the `cluster:access_readonly` permission The `alethia-view` ServiceAccount in the `alethia-system` namespace, bound to the `alethia:view` ClusterRole 
 Admin `--admin` Owners and admins only: the `cluster:access_admin` permission The cloud's own admin credential for the cluster 

A viewer can get neither tier. A custom role can hold either permission. See
[Roles & permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: What read-only allows
records.text:
The `alethia:view` ClusterRole grants only the `get`, `list` and `watch` verbs. It is the built-in
Kubernetes `view` role, written out rule by rule, plus nodes, namespaces and events. It does not
aggregate from `view`, so a custom role that a cluster operator aggregates into `view` cannot widen
it.

 API group Resources 
 --- --- 
 core `pods`, `pods/log`, `pods/status`, `services`, `services/status`, `endpoints`, `configmaps`, `persistentvolumeclaims`, `persistentvolumeclaims/status`, `replicationcontrollers`, `replicationcontrollers/scale`, `replicationcontrollers/status`, `serviceaccounts`, `bindings`, `events`, `limitranges`, `resourcequotas`, `resourcequotas/status`, `namespaces`, `namespaces/status`, `nodes` 
 `apps` `deployments`, `replicasets`, `statefulsets`, `daemonsets`, with their `scale` and `status` subresources, and `controllerrevisions` 
 `batch` `jobs`, `cronjobs`, with their `status` subresources 
 `autoscaling` `horizontalpodautoscalers`, `horizontalpodautoscalers/status` 
 `policy` `poddisruptionbudgets`, `poddisruptionbudgets/status` 
 `networking.k8s.io` `ingresses`, `ingresses/status`, `networkpolicies` 
 `discovery.k8s.io` `endpointslices` 
 `events.k8s.io`

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Get an admin kubeconfig
records.text:
alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --admin

On AWS, GCP and Azure, the admin credential is your organization's cloud identity for the cluster.
On Alibaba Cloud it is a certificate that ACK issues to that identity. On Hetzner it is an admin
certificate from the cluster's Talos API. In each case every user maps to the same identity in
the cluster. The read-only tier also uses one shared ServiceAccount for every user. So the
cluster's own audit log cannot tell your users apart. Alethia's record of each request does. See
[What Alethia records](#what-alethia-records).

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Choose how long the credential lasts
records.text:
`--ttl` sets the credential's lifetime. The default is `1h`. The shortest is `15m` and the
longest is `8h`. The value must be a whole number of seconds, such as `90m` or `2h30m`.

alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --admin --ttl 4h

A read-only credential lasts the TTL on every cloud. The cluster's API server sets the final
expiry, and a cluster that limits token lifetimes can make it shorter.

**For an admin credential, the TTL is a ceiling, not a guarantee.** The admin credential is the
cloud's own, and the cloud sets its lifetime. On AWS, GCP, Azure and Hetzner it lasts at most
about an hour, whatever the TTL. The runner reports the credential's real expiry, never a shorter
one. For a static kubeconfig, the CLI prints that expiry when it writes the file.

{/* Hetzner's row is the managed template's admin_kubeconfig_cert_lifetime, 1h since #5330
 (infra/templates/project/hetzner/variables.tf). The 8h refusal is mintAdminLifetimeCap in
 apps/runner/internal/agent/kubeconfig_mint.go (#5331). */}

 Cloud Read-only Admin 
 --- --- --- 
 AWS The TTL 14 minutes, whatever the TTL. The exec plugin gets a new token when it expires. 
 GCP The TTL The access token's own lifetime, about

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Choose exec or static
records.text:
A kubeconfig gets its credential in one of two shapes.

 Exec (the default on AWS, GCP and Azure) Static (`--static`, and always on Hetzner and Alibaba Cloud) 
 --- --- --- 
 What the file holds No credential. It runs `alethia cluster token` to get one. The credential itself: a bearer token or a client certificate 
 When the credential expires `alethia cluster token` mints a new one, so `kubectl` keeps working The file stops working. Run the command again for a new one. 
 What the machine needs The `alethia` CLI on the `PATH` wherever `kubectl` runs, with a valid session Only `kubectl` 
 If someone copies the file It is useless without a signed-in `alethia` CLI It works for anyone until it expires 

Hetzner and Alibaba Cloud issue certificates, so their kubeconfig is always static. You do not need
to pass `--static` for them: the CLI asks for exec, and if the cloud refuses, it asks again for
static.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: How the exec shape caches the credential
records.text:
`alethia cluster token` keeps each credential in a cache until 60 seconds before it expires. So
only the first `kubectl` call in each credential's lifetime waits for a runner. If several `kubectl`
calls start at the same time, they share one mint. The cache is in the CLI's configuration
directory:

 OS Cache directory 
 --- --- 
 Linux `~/.config/alethia/kubecache` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/alethia/kubecache`) 
 macOS `~/Library/Application Support/alethia/kubecache` 
 Windows `%AppData%\alethia\kubecache` 

The directory has mode `0700` and each file has mode `0600`. The CLI refuses a cache file that
other users can read.

A cached token is valid for at most its TTL: one hour by default, eight hours at most. It stays in
the cache until it expires, or until `alethia logout` deletes the cache. See
[Revoke access](#revoke-access).

Each new token comes from a new mint, with the tier, TTL and organization that you chose when you
ran `alethia cluster kubeconfig`. Each mint checks your permission again. So if someone removes you
from the organization or changes your role, `kubectl` stops working when the current token expires.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Use a kubeconfig on another machine or in CI
records.text:
To print the kubeconfig instead of writing it to a file, use `--output -`. This is the only way
the CLI writes a credential to stdout:

alethia cluster kubeconfig api-backend --static --output - > api-backend.kubeconfig

A static file works on any machine with `kubectl` until it expires. Treat it as a password.

An exec kubeconfig works on another machine only if that machine has the `alethia` CLI and a
session. In CI, use a service token: set `ALETHIA_TOKEN`, or pass `--token`. See
[Running in CI](/reference/cli/authentication#running-in-ci). A machine that did not run
`alethia cluster kubeconfig` has no record of your choices, so it always mints read-only credentials
with a 1-hour TTL, in its active organization.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Reach a cluster with a private endpoint
records.text:
The runner checks whether the cluster's API endpoint is reachable from the internet. If it is
private, the CLI still writes the kubeconfig and prints this note:

Note: this cluster's API endpoint is private. kubectl needs network access to it from this machine (a VPN or a bastion); the credential alone is not enough.

The credential is valid, but `kubectl` must reach the endpoint. Connect to the cluster's network
first, for example through a VPN or a bastion host. Alethia does not proxy traffic to the cluster.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Revoke access
records.text:
A short lifetime is the main control. These are the other controls, and their limits:

- **Remove the person's access.** Remove them from the organization, or change their role so that
 it does not hold the `cluster:access_*` permissions. They cannot get a new credential after that.
 An exec kubeconfig stops working when its current token expires. A static file, or a token
 already in the cache, works until it expires.
- **Revoke every read-only credential for a cluster.** Delete the ServiceAccount. Every token it
 issued stops working at once, for every user. You need admin access to do this:

 kubectl -n alethia-system delete serviceaccount alethia-view
 
 The next read-only request creates the ServiceAccount again. To find every object that the
 read-only tier created, use the label `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=alethia`.
- **Admin credentials cannot be revoked through Alethia.** They end at their real expiry, as shown
 in [the lifetime table](#choose-how-long-the-credential-lasts). On Hetzner the admin
 certificate lasts about an hour, and only a rotation of the cluster's certificate authority ends
 it earlier.
- **End access from a machine.** Run `alethia logout`. It deletes y

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: What Alethia records
records.text:
Alethia writes an audit record **before** it returns a credential. It writes one record when you
request a kubeconfig, and one when the CLI collects it. Each record holds:

- who asked, and from which IP address;
- the cluster, the tier, the shape and the requested TTL;
- the client (the CLI or the console) and whether the call used a session or a service token.

The record never holds the credential. Alethia does not store the credential either: the console
holds only the sealed copy, and it deletes that copy when the CLI or your browser collects it, or
10 minutes after the request.

A refused request appears in [Activity](/guides/access/activity-log) as a denied attempt, like
every other refused action.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Troubleshoot
records.text:
`alethia cluster kubeconfig` prints each error after `Error:`. `alethia cluster token` prints
each error after `alethia cluster token:`, and `kubectl` shows that line.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Refusals from the control plane
records.text:
Status Message What to do 
 --- --- --- 
 401 your session is not valid — run `alethia login`, then try again Run `alethia login`. 
 402 your organization's plan does not allow another kubeconfig right now: … (see `alethia usage`) The mint runs on a runner, so it uses runner minutes. Run `alethia usage` to see the limit you reached. 
 403 your role cannot mint a kubeconfig for this cluster (owners, admins and operators can) Ask an owner or admin for a role that holds `cluster:access_readonly`. 
 403 your role cannot mint an admin kubeconfig for this cluster (owners and admins can); drop --admin for read-only access Run the command again without `--admin`, or ask for a role that holds `cluster:access_admin`. 
 404 the cluster was not found in the active organization (`alethia org switch`, or pass --org) Switch to the cluster's organization with `alethia org switch`, or pass `--org`. 
 409 The cluster has not been provisioned, so there is nothing to mint a kubeconfig for — deploy the environment first (`alethia project apply`) Deploy the environment. A draft environment, one being destroyed, and one with no successful deploy cannot get a kubeconfig. 
 422 This cluster's cloud cannot

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Messages while the CLI waits
records.text:
Message What to do 
 --- ---
