 the kubeconfig request expired before a runner completed it — check that a runner is online for this organization (`alethia runner list`), then try again No runner collected the job within 10 minutes. Check that a runner is online with `alethia runner list`. 
 timed out waiting for a runner to mint the kubeconfig — check that a runner is online … The same as above, measured on your machine's clock. 
 the kubeconfig request is gone (already collected, or expired and swept) — run the command again Run the command again. A credential can be collected only once. 
 your role no longer allows collecting this kubeconfig (it changed after the request) Your role changed while the mint ran. Ask for the permission again. 
 the minted credential had already expired when it arrived; check this machine's clock, then try again Set your machine's clock correctly.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Reasons a runner gives
records.text:
When a mint fails, the CLI prints `the runner could not mint the kubeconfig:` and one of these
reasons. The runner sends only these fixed sentences, never the cloud's own error text.

 Reason What to do 
 --- --- 
 The runner could not mint the credential. A cause with no specific sentence. Read the mint job's log with `alethia jobs logs --latest --type MINT_KUBECONFIG`. 
 The cluster was not found in the cloud account. The cluster no longer exists, or it was renamed outside Alethia. Check it in the cloud console. 
 The runner could not reach the cluster's API endpoint. Check that the runner's network can reach the cluster's API endpoint. 
 The runner could not assume the cluster's cloud identity. Check the cloud identity in [Connectors](/guides/connectors). 
 The cloud refused to issue a credential for this cluster. The cloud identity cannot get cluster credentials. Check its permissions in the cloud. 
 The read-only identity could not be prepared in the cluster. The runner could not create or check the `alethia-view` ServiceAccount or the `alethia:view` ClusterRole. Check whether someone changed them. 
 This cloud cannot issue the requested kubeconfig shape. Run the command again

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Other errors
records.text:
Message What to do 
 --- --- 
 --ttl must be whole seconds from 15m to 8h Pass a TTL from `15m` to `8h`. 
 --output takes a file path here (or - for stdout), not a format In this command `--output` takes a file name. To write a file called `json`, pass `./json`. 
 if any flags in the group [merge output] are set none of the others can be Pass `--merge` or `--output`, not both. 
 … is locked by another writer (kubectl?) Another program is writing your kubeconfig. If nothing is running, delete the `.lock` file that the message names. 
 kubecache: insecure cache file A cache file can be read by other users. Delete the file that the message names, then run the command again. 
 a cluster id is required `alethia cluster token` needs a cluster ID when it does not run at a terminal. Get a new kubeconfig with `alethia cluster kubeconfig`.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: kubectl says "You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)"
records.text:
The credential expired, or someone revoked it. With a static kubeconfig, run
`alethia cluster kubeconfig` again.

With an exec kubeconfig, the cache can still hold a token that was revoked, for example after
someone deleted the read-only ServiceAccount. The cache serves that token until 60 seconds before
it expires. Delete the cache directory from
[the table above](#how-the-exec-shape-caches-the-credential), then run `kubectl` again. The next
mint creates the ServiceAccount again.

records.title: Get a kubeconfig for your cluster
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Cluster commands](/reference/cli/clusters) — every flag of `alethia cluster kubeconfig` and `alethia cluster token`.
- [Clusters](/guides/clusters) — the cluster card, and the commands that use your own cloud CLI.
- [Fabrics & Placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement) — which environments have their own cluster.
- [Roles & permissions](/concepts/access-control/roles-and-permissions) — the built-in roles and custom roles.

records.title: How-to guides

Alethia, start with [Get started](/get-started) or a [tutorial](/tutorials).

Connect AWS, GCP, Azure, Hetzner, Alibaba Cloud, Git providers, and chart repositories.

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.text: Jobs Overview. Job list page with status and type filtering, search, and real-time updates.

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Jobs
records.text: Every infrastructure operation is modeled as a **job**. The Jobs page shows all jobs with filtering, search, and real-time status updates. For the technical deep dive on how jobs are queued and claimed, see [Job queue](/concepts/job-queue).

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Job List Page
records.text: Located at `/{org}/~/jobs`, the page shows:

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Filters
records.text:
The page follows the console filter standard — one filter bar backed by server-side filtering and facet counts. Each control is a multi-select popover, the counts come from the unfiltered facet universe, and every selection syncs to the URL:

- **Search** — free-text match over project name and slug, environment name, Runner name, and the error message.
- **Date range** — a quick-range preset picker (default: last 12 months) plus a custom range.
- **Authors** — the org member who initiated each job.
- **Environments** — the job's target environment.
- **Projects** — the target project (hidden when the list is scoped to a single project).
- **Statuses** — QUEUED, CLAIMED, PROCESSING, SUCCESS, FAILED, CANCELLED.
- **Types** — PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY plus the Runner-lifecycle and scan/utility job types; each option shows its live count.

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Data Table
records.text:
Column Description 
 -------- ------------- 
 Type Job type with icon and description 
 Status Grayscale status badge with inline run duration 
 Project Target project name with its cloud provider icon (hidden in a project-scoped view) 
 Runner Name (or short ID) of the runner that claimed the job 
 Environment Target environment name and stage 
 Initiated Relative time plus the initiating member's avatar 

Click any row to navigate to the [job detail page](/guides/jobs/job-detail).

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Live Updates
records.text: The list stays current through TanStack Query polling: it refetches every 5 seconds while any visible job is in-flight (QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING) and every 30 seconds otherwise, so new rows and status changes appear without a page refresh. (Per-job log streaming on the detail page uses a Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE subscription — see [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime).)

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Runner Select Popover
records.text:
When triggering Plan, Apply, or Destroy from a project, the **Runner Select Popover** appears:

- Lists all registered Runners with a grayscale status dot (state is shown by the dot, never color)
- "Any available" option for automatic assignment
- Only ONLINE Runners can be selected; DRAINING and OFFLINE Runners are disabled

The selected Runner's ID is stored as `assigned_runner_id` on the job.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.text: Job Detail & Logs. Real-time log streaming, status polling, and job actions.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Job Detail & Logs
records.text: The job detail page (`/{org}/~/jobs/{id}`) shows the full execution state of a job with real-time log streaming. For the underlying streaming architecture, see [Real-time updates](/concepts/realtime).

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Header
records.text:
- Job type icon and label
- Status badge
- Duration (elapsed or final run time)
- Job ID (first 8 chars)
- Runner ID (first 8 chars) — the runner that claimed the job (shown once a runner has claimed it)
- Created time (relative)
- Action buttons

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Log Viewer
records.text:
A full-height, monospace, auto-scrolling log area showing the runner's `tofu` (OpenTofu) output in real-time. Each log row carries a `stream_type` of `STDOUT`, `STDERR`, or `SYSTEM`:

- **STDERR** — rendered in the destructive (error) style
- **STDOUT** and **SYSTEM** — rendered in the normal foreground style

Logs are streamed via a Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE subscription (`/api/stream/jobs/{id}`) over the `job_logs` table, filtered by `job_id`. The server sends the backlog on connect, then pushes new rows in near-real-time as the Runner writes them.

Auto-scroll pins to the bottom as new logs arrive.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Collapsible Details
records.text:
Three expandable sections below the logs:

- **Job Details** — full metadata (ID, type, runner, project, and the created/started/completed timestamps)
- **Config Snapshot** — the project configuration at time of job creation (JSON)
- **Execution Metadata** — OpenTofu outputs, cost data, cluster info, and the **`verify_result`** report (JSON)

For PLAN and DEPLOY jobs, `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` carries the [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) report — the fail-closed policy evaluation over the plan JSON. The Console renders it as the **Verify Report** in the project's Plan tab; see [engine internals](/concepts/elench/engine-internals).

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Actions
records.text:
Button When Visible Effect 
 -------- ------------- -------- 
 **Cancel** QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING Sets status to CANCELLED, Runner terminates gracefully 
 **Apply** PLAN job with SUCCESS status Opens Runner Select Popover → creates DEPLOY job 
 **Re-run** Any terminal status (SUCCESS, FAILED, CANCELLED) Creates a new job with the same configuration

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Status Polling
records.text: The page polls `getJob(jobId)` every 3 seconds while the job is in-flight (QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING), then idles once it reaches a terminal state. This query drives the header status and any error message — the full log streaming happens via the Realtime subscription.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Status Banner
records.text:
When the job reaches a terminal state, a banner appears:

- **SUCCESS** — neutral banner with a checkmark ("Job completed successfully.")
- **FAILED** — destructive banner with the error message ("Job failed")
- **CANCELLED** — muted banner ("Job cancelled")

records.title: Job types
records.text: Job types. Reference for every provisioning job type Alethia runs, with its Console label and what it does.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Job types
records.text:
Every infrastructure operation is modeled as a [job](/guides/jobs). Each job has a **type** drawn from the `provision_job_type` enum. The Console renders each type with a label, an icon, and a short description from a single catalog (`lib/jobs/format.ts`), shared by the jobs data table and the overview's recent-jobs card.

The table below lists every job type. It is the one catalog in these docs: other pages link here
rather than repeat it. For which runner handler executes each type, see
[Job execution](/concepts/runner/job-execution).

 Type Label Description 
 ------ ------- ------------- 
 `PLAN` Plan Dry-run infrastructure plan 
 `DEPLOY` Deploy Provision infrastructure from config 
 `DESTROY` Destroy Tear down infrastructure 
 `DEPLOY_RUNNER` Deploy Runner Provision a runner into your cloud account 
 `UPDATE_RUNNER` Update Runner Update a runner to a newer version 
 `DESTROY_RUNNER` Destroy Runner Tear down a provisioned runner 
 `ANALYZE_REPO` Analyze Repo Scan a repository for infrastructure config 
 `DETECT_DRIFT` Detect Drift Refresh-only check for drift between state and live cloud 
 `AUDIT` Audit Audit bring-your-own IaC (an OpenTofu/Terraform plan or Kubernetes manifes

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Infrastructure jobs
records.text:
`PLAN`, `DEPLOY`, and `DESTROY` run OpenTofu against a project's configuration.

- `PLAN` is a dry run. It produces a plan and the fail-closed [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) report, which the runner forwards on `execution_metadata["verify_result"]`.
- `DEPLOY` provisions the infrastructure. An **Apply** action on a successful `PLAN` job creates a `DEPLOY` job; see [Job Detail & Logs](/guides/jobs/job-detail#actions).
- `DESTROY` tears the infrastructure down.

An environment promotion does not add a new type — it reuses `PLAN`, then `DEPLOY`.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Runner jobs
records.text: `DEPLOY_RUNNER`, `UPDATE_RUNNER`, and `DESTROY_RUNNER` manage the lifecycle of a runner provisioned into your cloud account.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Scan jobs
records.text:
These jobs inspect code or configuration and provision nothing.

- `ANALYZE_REPO` clones the repository and scans it statically into a `RepoDigest`, which drives
 repo-first onboarding.
- `CHART_SCAN` clones (or pulls) the chart, runs `helm template` in the sandbox with no secrets and no
 egress, and evaluates the rendered manifests with Elench verify.
- `IAC_SCAN` clones the module, pins the commit, inventories providers and modules, and runs
 `tofu validate` plus the static safety gate. Its result gates the environment's `PLAN` and `DEPLOY`
 jobs (both require a fresh scan that pinned the commit to apply). `DESTROY` is not gated on the
 scan — it runs the commit that created the deployed state, so a failed re-scan never traps live
 infrastructure.
- `AUDIT` evaluates input carried on the job — an existing `show -json` plan or a set of Kubernetes
 manifests — and posts the Elench verify report to `execution_metadata.verify_result`, exactly like a
 `PLAN` job's gate.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Reconciliation jobs
records.text:
- `DETECT_DRIFT` runs `tofu plan -refresh-only` and records a per-environment drift posture — see
 [Drift detection](/concepts/drift).
- `PROBE_CLUSTER` dials the cluster's Kubernetes API server and records reachability in
 `environment_probes`. An unreachable cluster is a **successful** probe with `reachable=false`; the
 job only fails when the probe itself could not run.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Build jobs
records.text: `BUILD` builds and pushes service images in-cluster. For each service whose source is a repository, it schedules an in-cluster kaniko Job that builds from the git context and Dockerfile and pushes to the provisioned registry, then reports a per-service image digest map in `execution_metadata.build_result`.

records.title: Job types
records.heading: Break-glass jobs
records.text: `STATE_SURGERY` is an operator-initiated, two-person-approved, fully-audited repair of a corrupt or stranded OpenTofu state. It is queued as a normal job so it flows through the same claim and state-lock path as any other job. The runner-side executor ships **inert** and fail-closed: it refuses to run unless the runner explicitly opts in via `ALETHIA_BREAKGLASS_STATE_SURGERY_ENABLED`.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.text: Plan and apply in the console. Plan an environment, review the plan and its verify report, apply that exact plan, or destroy the environment — from the console.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Plan and apply in the console
records.text:
Infrastructure provisioning follows a strict **Plan-Review-Apply** workflow. Nothing is provisioned without explicit user confirmation.

This guide covers the console. To run the same workflow from a terminal, see the CLI reference
[Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply). For what the runner does inside each job, see
[Plan jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/plan-jobs) and [Deploy jobs](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs).

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Generate Plan
records.text:
From the [project detail page](/guides/dashboard/project-detail), click **Plan**. Select a Runner to execute. A `PLAN` job is queued.

The runner plans the environment against its config snapshot, evaluates the
[verify gate](#verify-gate) over the plan JSON, optionally prices it with Infracost
([cost estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation)), and uploads the plan artifact.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Review Plan
records.text:
The Plan tab in project detail shows:

**Plan Summary Bar:**
- Resources to **create** (green count)
- Resources to **update** (yellow count)
- Resources to **destroy** (red count)
- Estimated monthly cost

**Resource Groups:**
Collapsible sections grouped by resource type (e.g., "AWS EKS", "AWS VPC", "AWS RDS"). Each resource shows:
- Resource address (e.g., `module.eks.aws_eks_cluster.main`)
- Action: create / update / delete
- Per-resource monthly cost (from Infracost)

**Verify Report:**
The Plan tab renders the [verify gate](#verify-gate) result (`execution_metadata["verify_result"]`) — per-control pass / fail / `not_evaluable` outcomes over the plan JSON. See [engine internals](/concepts/elench/engine-internals).

**Cost Breakdown:**
Total estimated monthly cost with per-resource itemization.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Apply
records.text:
Click **Apply** to provision. Select a Runner. A `DEPLOY` job is queued, bound to the plan you
reviewed: the runner applies that plan's saved artifact (see [Applying the reviewed plan](#config-hash-validation)).
The verify gate runs again before `tofu apply` and is **fail-closed**. After the apply, the runner
installs ArgoCD ([GitOps](/concepts/gitops-argocd)) and reports cluster metadata back to the Console.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Finalization
records.text:
When the `DEPLOY` job succeeds, the Console records the cluster, database and cache endpoints on the
environment and sets its status to `ACTIVE`. See
[Deploy jobs → Finalization](/concepts/runner/job-execution/deploy-jobs#finalization).

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Verify gate
records.text:
Between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`, the runner runs the [Elench](/concepts/elench) verification gate
over the OpenTofu **plan JSON**: per-control `pass`, `fail`, or an honest `not_evaluable` for anything
the plan cannot prove. A hard control failure **blocks before `tofu apply`** unless an authorized
override waives it — see [Verify override](/guides/jobs/verify-override). `PLAN` jobs attach the
report too, so you see the outcome in the **Plan** tab before you apply. For the control catalog and
the signed evidence receipt, see [Engine internals](/concepts/elench/engine-internals).

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Config hash validation
records.text:
An apply bound to a plan applies **that plan**, not a fresh one:

- The `PLAN` job must have finished with `SUCCESS`, or the `DEPLOY` job fails.
- The runner downloads the plan's saved artifact and applies it. If the artifact cannot be fetched,
 the runner logs a warning and plans again from the `DEPLOY` job's own snapshot.
- When both jobs carry a configuration hash, the runner compares them and fails on a mismatch with
 `configuration changed since plan was generated`. Jobs queued through the jobs API — which the CLI
 uses — carry that hash; jobs queued from the console do not, so the saved artifact is what binds a
 console apply to its plan.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Destroy Workflow
records.text:
Destroy follows a simpler flow — no plan step required:

1. Click **Destroy** from project detail
2. Select a Runner
3. A `DESTROY` job is queued
4. The Runner runs `tofu destroy -auto-approve`
5. Environment status → DESTROYING → DESTROYED

 
Destroy permanently removes all cloud resources (VPC, cluster, databases, etc.). OpenTofu state is preserved so accidental destroys can be recovered by re-applying, but data in databases will be lost.

records.title: Plan and apply in the console
records.heading: Free plan limits
records.text:
Community (free) organizations have two limits on provisioning jobs:

- **Concurrency** — at most **2 jobs** run at once (enforced when a runner claims a job). Extra jobs wait in the queue rather than being rejected. Team raises this to 8; Enterprise has no concurrency cap.
- **Daily volume** — at most **25 provisioning jobs you start** in any rolling 24-hour window (an operator can change the number with `ALETHIA_FREE_DAILY_JOB_QUOTA`). Reaching it blocks the next plan/apply/destroy/scan with an upgrade prompt; the limit clears as older jobs age out of the window. Paid plans have no daily cap.

Only jobs **you** start count toward the daily limit. Background jobs the platform runs on your behalf — drift detection, cluster probes, reconciliation, and ephemeral-environment cleanup — are never counted and never blocked, so day-2 automation keeps running regardless of the cap.

Requests for a short-lived cluster kubeconfig are not counted toward the daily limit and are not blocked by it, so you can always reach a cluster you have deployed. They have their own rate limit of 20 requests in 10 minutes for each person, and their runner time counts toward your included provisioning minutes

records.title: Verify Override
records.text: Verify Override. Waive specific failing verify controls on a queued DEPLOY job so a fail-closed apply can proceed deliberately.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Verify Override
records.text:
The [verify gate](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) is **fail-closed**: a hard control
failure blocks before `tofu apply`. A verify override is the deliberate, accountable exception —
it waives **specific** failing control IDs on one DEPLOY job so the apply can proceed, without ever
disabling the gate wholesale.

An override is time-boxed and stamped with the actor who authorized it, so the waiver stays auditable
and the runner seals it into the apply's evidence receipt as a recorded exception.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- The failing controls must come from the [verify report](/guides/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate).
 Read `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` on the PLAN job (the **Verify Report** in the Plan tab,
 or **Execution Metadata** on the [job detail page](/guides/jobs/job-detail)) to get the exact
 control IDs that failed — for example `LEASTPRIV-001` or `AZURE-FED-001`. See the
 [control catalog](/reference/control-catalog) for what each ID checks.
- You need **edit** authority on the job.
- The DEPLOY job must be **QUEUED** — set the override after clicking **Apply** but before a runner
 claims and processes the job. An override cannot be set once the job leaves the QUEUED state.

 
An override waives a security control on a single apply. Only the control IDs you list are waived;
every other control still evaluates fail-closed.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Record the override
records.text:
The override is recorded by the `recordVerifyOverride` server action:

recordVerifyOverride(jobId, controls, reason, ttlHours);

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Collect the failing control IDs
records.text: List the exact IDs from the verify report as `controls`. The array must contain at least one ID.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Write a reason
records.text: Provide a non-empty `reason` explaining why the waiver is justified. It is stored with the override.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Set an expiry (optional)
records.text:
Pass `ttlHours` to bound how long the waiver is valid. It defaults to **24** hours. The action
computes `expiry` as the current time plus `ttlHours`, stored as an RFC3339 timestamp.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Submit
records.text:
The action verifies your edit authority, confirms the job is QUEUED, and writes the waiver to
`jobs.verify_override`.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: What gets stored
records.text:
The action writes a JSONB `verify_override` value on the job:

 Field Source 
 ------- -------- 
 `controls` The control IDs you passed 
 `reason` Your reason (trimmed) 
 `by` Stamped server-side to the authorizing actor — you cannot set it 
 `expiry` Now + `ttlHours` (default 24), as an RFC3339 timestamp

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: What the runner does
records.text:
When a runner claims the DEPLOY job, it reads `jobs.verify_override` and passes it to the fail-closed
gate. The gate applies the waiver only to the listed controls, lets the apply proceed, and records the
waiver as an exception in the signed [evidence receipt](/concepts/elench/engine-internals) for the apply.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Errors
records.text:
The action rejects an override that cannot be honored:

- **No control IDs** — the `controls` array is empty.
- **No reason** — `reason` is blank.
- **Job not found** — no job matches the ID in your scope.
- **Job is not QUEUED** — the job has already been claimed or has reached a terminal state.

records.title: Runners
records.text: Runners. Registering, monitoring, and managing Runner execution agents.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Runners
records.text: Runners are the execution agents that run OpenTofu (the `tofu` binary) on behalf of users. The Runners page manages their lifecycle. Every runner sits on a two-axis taxonomy — **operator** (`managed` `self`) × **provisioning** (`deployed` `registered`, for `self` only). For how Runners work internally, see the [Runner Agent](/concepts/runner) documentation.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Runners Page
records.text: A two-column layout: the left column stacks the warm **Pools** (managed-fleet, self-managed operators only) and the **Versions** changelog; the right column is a filterable, paginated grid of runner cards.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Filter Bar
records.text:
Follows the console filter standard: a name search plus chip and facet filters.

- **Search** — filter by Runner name
- **Cloud** — supported providers (or "Any")
- **Status** chips — Online, Offline, Draining
- **Operator** chips — Managed, Self · Deployed, Self · Registered
- **Region** and **Version** facet popovers

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Runner Cards
records.text:
Each runner renders as a card (grayscale — status reads through a badge dot + mono label, never colour):

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 Name Runner name, with a star if it's the default runner 
 Status Badge: ONLINE, OFFLINE, DRAINING — plus in-flight lifecycle states PROVISIONING, UPDATING, DESTROYING while a job acts on the runner 
 Operator Badge: `Managed`, `Self · Deployed`, or `Self · Registered` 
 Cloud Supported provider icons (or "Any") 
 Region Deployment location — shown for **managed** runners 
 Version Runner release version (click to view release notes; an "update available" badge appears when outdated) 
 Provisioned / Last seen Managed runners show provisioned hours; self runners show time since last heartbeat 
 Active job The in-flight job (if any), linking to the job detail — QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING 
 Actions Default-runner star toggle; **Destroy** (self · deployed with cloud resources) or **Remove** (registered runners)

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Versions Panel & Updates
records.text: The **Versions** panel (left column) shows the latest release, a changelog of recent releases, and — when runners are behind the latest version — an **"Update all"** button that queues `UPDATE_RUNNER` jobs for the runners it can roll in place (deployed runners with a stored token). Runners it can't roll are flagged as needing a re-deploy.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Adding a Runner
records.text:
Click **Add runner** to open a sheet that chooses between two paths — **Deploy to a cloud** or **Register your own**:

 
 
 Provisions a Runner into your **AWS** account automatically (an existing runner runs OpenTofu to stand it up — ECS Fargate via `infra/templates/runner/aws`). This is a `self`-operated, `deployed` runner:

 1. Select an AWS cloud identity and region
 2. Click Deploy → queues a `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job
 3. The job provisions: ECS task definition, IAM roles, CloudWatch log group, security groups
 4. After ~2 minutes, the Runner appears as ONLINE

 **This path is AWS only.** The account picker lists verified AWS identities alone, because `infra/templates/runner/` holds one template. A deploy into GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner is refused when you queue it — in this form and in `alethia runner deploy`. Use **Register your own** for those clouds; a registered Runner provisions every cloud Alethia supports, wherever it runs.

 A deployed Runner is one always-on ECS Fargate task (`desired_count = 1` in `infra/templates/runner/aws/main.tf`); it does not scale with the queue. Only the managed fleet scales — see [Warm-pool scaling](/concepts/runner/scaling).
 
 
 For br

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Status Indicators
records.text:
Status is determined by heartbeat recency:

 Status Meaning Heartbeat 
 -------- --------- ----------- 
 **ONLINE** Ready to accept jobs Seen within the last 45 seconds (runners heartbeat ~every 10s) 
 **DRAINING** Finishing current job, not accepting new ones Sent with DRAINING flag 
 **OFFLINE** Missed heartbeat, jobs will be requeued No heartbeat for > 45 seconds (the sweep flips stale ONLINE or DRAINING runners to OFFLINE)

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Live Updates
records.text: The Runners page polls every 10 seconds while the tab is focused (TanStack Query pauses the interval in the background), so heartbeat-driven ONLINE/OFFLINE changes, new registrations, and job assignments surface on the next poll.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Version Tracking
records.text:
Each Runner reports its version on heartbeat. The page shows:
- Current version per Runner
- Latest available version (from the `runner_releases` table)
- A **Release Notes** popover showing the changelog for each version

When a new Runner release is published via the CI pipeline, existing runners are rolled onto the new image via `UPDATE_RUNNER` jobs — ECS force-new-deployment for self·deployed AWS runners; VM replacement for the managed Hetzner fleet.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.text: Self-operated runners. Running a runner you operate yourself — registered or deployed — for on-premises or air-gapped environments.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Self-operated runners
records.text:
A runner is described by two axes: **operator** and **provisioning**. Self-operation is the
**operator = `self`** case — you run the runner rather than letting Alethia operate it in the
managed fleet. Within `self`, the **provisioning** axis says who placed it:

- **`deployed`** — provisioned into your cloud by an existing runner running `tofu` (Console
 "Deploy" tab / `alethia runner deploy`). **AWS only** — it lands on ECS Fargate from
 [`infra/templates/runner/aws/`](/concepts/runner/infrastructure-templates/aws).
- **`registered`** — you bring your own runner (your own IaC, or just `alethia runner start`) and
 register it for a token. Any cloud, plus on-premises, air-gapped, or development hosts.

 
 **Deployed runners are available on AWS only.** `infra/templates/runner/` holds one template,
 `aws`, so there is no runner template for GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner. The Console form
 offers AWS accounts alone, and both the Console and `alethia runner deploy` refuse a deploy for
 the other clouds at the moment you queue it.

 This limits **where the runner itself runs**, not what it provisions: one registered runner —
 the page you are reading — provisions every cloud Alet

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
The runner is a single Go binary and is **CLI-free** — it does **not** need `aws`, `gcloud`, or
`azure-cli`. Cloud auth is minted in-process (keyless OIDC), and cluster tokens come from
`runner kube-token`, so the only host tools it shells out to are:

 Tool Purpose Minimum version 
 ------ --------- ----------------- 
 OpenTofu (`tofu`) Infrastructure provisioning 1.9+ 
 kubectl Kubernetes cluster access — (unpinned; matched to the target cluster) 
 Helm Chart installation (ArgoCD, components) — (unpinned) 

The official runner image bundles all three (plus the `tofu` provider cache). When running the
binary directly you install them yourself; the container path needs nothing extra.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Registration
records.text:
Before running, the runner must be registered with Alethia:

1. Register the runner via the Console or API (or, in the managed fleet, self-register with a
 bootstrap token).
2. Receive a `runner_id` and `runner_token` (shown once).
3. Pass these as environment variables.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Running
records.text:
Set the required environment variables and start the binary. Note there are **no S3 credentials** —
tofu state flows through the Console state proxy, authenticated by a per-job token the runner
fetches itself:

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Optional
records.text:
./runner

The runner will:
1. Register / confirm with the Console.
2. Start the heartbeat goroutine (30s).
3. React to push wakes (sub-second pickup) with a 30s safety poll as a fallback, and execute claimed jobs keylessly.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Environment variables
records.text:
Variable Required Description 
 ---------- ---------- ------------- 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` Yes Alethia control-plane base URL 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_ID` Yes Assigned runner ID 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_TOKEN` Yes Authentication token 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_OPERATOR` No Defaults to `self` when unset; set it explicitly to `self` for clarity (legacy `ALETHIA_RUNNER_MODE=self-hosted` still works) 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_PROVIDERS` No Comma-separated clouds this runner serves (e.g. `aws`); unset = any 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_SLOTS` No Concurrent jobs per runner (default `1`). Above `1`, the runner supervises N isolated worker subprocesses — run the container with an init (`docker --init` / compose `init: true`) so orphaned tools are reaped 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_INSTANCE_ID` No Distinct self-registration id when several runners share a host 
 `ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE` No Set to `1` to let Helm chart pulls reach a registry on a private network — a self-hosted Harbor or JFrog on RFC1918 space. Off by default, so a chart URL cannot be used to reach inside your network. Loopback and link-local (cloud metadata) addresses stay blocked either way. See [Chart repositories](/guides/connectors/chart-repositories) 
 `IN

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: On-premises infrastructure
records.text:
For organizations that need infrastructure provisioned from within their network (private cloud,
bare metal):
- Run the runner on a bastion host or CI/CD runner.
- It polls Alethia over HTTPS (outbound only — no inbound ports required).
- `tofu` provisions resources reachable from the internal network.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Self-managed token clouds (DigitalOcean / Hetzner / Civo)
records.text:
These clouds have no role federation — they authenticate with a single API token. For true
zero-trust, keep that token in your own runner instead of storing it in Alethia:

- In the connect sheet, pick **"Self-hosted runner — token stays in your infra"** (the cloud
 identity is recorded with no token).
- Set the matching env var on this runner — `HCLOUD_TOKEN`, `CIVO_TOKEN`, or
 `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN`.
- Those jobs are flagged `requires_self_runner`, so `claim_next_job` excludes managed runners from
 them — only this runner, which holds the token, runs them. Alethia stores nothing.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Air-gapped environments
records.text:
For high-security environments without internet access:
- Pre-download OpenTofu providers and modules.
- Configure a local provider mirror.
- The runner communicates with Alethia over an approved network path.

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Development and testing
records.text:
For local development:
- Run the runner alongside the Alethia dev console.
- Point `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` at `http://localhost:3000`.
- Exercise job execution without any cloud deploy. (`pnpm dev:runner` stands one up natively.)

records.title: Self-operated runners
records.heading: Differences from managed / deployed
records.text:
Aspect Managed (Hetzner fleet) Self · Deployed (AWS ECS) Self · Registered (this page) 
 -------- ------------------------- --------------------------- ------------------------------- 
 Substrate Hetzner VM warm pool ECS Fargate Any host you manage 
 Deployment In-app scaler, automatic `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job (`tofu`) Manual 
 Scaling 60s warm-pool loop, by queue depth ECS `desired_count` (you) You start/stop it 
 Tool management Baked into the GHCR image Baked into the GHCR image You install `tofu`/kubectl/Helm 
 Updates New image + drain-replace `UPDATE_RUNNER` (force-redeploy) Manual binary update 
 Monitoring Console fleet cockpit + logs CloudWatch + Console Local stdout/stderr + Console 
 Network Platform account Customer VPC Your network 
 Billing Provisioned hours (`runner_usage_sessions`) Your AWS bill Not billed by Alethia

records.title: Configuration
records.text: Configuration. The .env keys that configure a self-hosted Alethia bundle.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Configuration
records.text:
All configuration is environment variables in `.env` (copy from `.env.example`).
The installer generates the secret values; the rest you set. Internal service
URLs (Postgres, SeaweedFS) are wired by compose — you don't set those.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Ingress
records.text:
Key Notes 
 --- --- 
 `ALETHIA_DOMAIN` Your domain; Caddy gets TLS for it. Empty → plain HTTP on `:80`. 
 `ALETHIA_ACME_EMAIL` Let's Encrypt contact email. 
 `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` Public origin, e.g. `https://alethia.example.com`. 
 `ALETHIA_TRUSTED_IP_HEADER` Single-value client-IP header that your ingress overwrites. Defaults to `cf-connecting-ip`. 

The bundled Caddy configuration overwrites `cf-connecting-ip` before it forwards a request.
If you use another ingress, set `ALETHIA_TRUSTED_IP_HEADER` to a header that ingress controls.
Strip any value supplied by the client, set the real client address, and keep the app container
unreachable from the public network. Production authentication returns `503` when the header is
missing or is not one valid IPv4 or IPv6 address. This refusal prevents all users from sharing one
rate-limit bucket.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Secrets (generated by the installer)
records.text:
Key Generate with 
 --- --- 
 `CLI_JWT_SECRET` `openssl rand -hex 32` — signs CLI/runner tokens (shared with the runner). 
 `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` `openssl rand -hex 32` — signs sessions/cookies. 
 `ALETHIA_DB_PASSWORD` / `ALETHIA_APP_DB_PASSWORD` strong random — bundled Postgres roles. 
 `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY` `openssl rand -base64 32` — AES-256-GCM key encrypting api-key [connector](/guides/connectors/pluggable) secrets (Cloudflare/Vault/Docker Hub/…). Required to connect pluggable connectors. The installer does not generate this one — set it yourself.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Database & storage
records.text:
Defaults target the bundled `postgres` + `seaweedfs`. To use a managed Postgres or
S3/R2 instead, point `ALETHIA_DATABASE_URL` / `ALETHIA_STORAGE_*` at them and set
`ALETHIA_STORAGE_AUTO_CREATE_BUCKETS=false`.

 Key Notes 
 --- --- 
 `ALETHIA_DB_USER` / `ALETHIA_DB_NAME` bundled Postgres user/db 
 `ALETHIA_STORAGE_ENDPOINT` S3 endpoint (bundled SeaweedFS by default) 
 `ALETHIA_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` must match `deploy/seaweedfs/s3.json` for the bundle

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Email (Resend / SMTP / SES)
records.text:
Transactional email is pluggable. The transport is chosen by `EMAIL_PROVIDER` when
set (`resend` `smtp` `ses`), else auto-detected from whichever provider's
credentials are present, in precedence order **Resend → SMTP → SES**. With none
configured, sign-in/account emails are logged to the console instead of sent (a
fresh install works with zero email setup). From-addresses must be verified sending
identities/domains for the chosen provider.

**Resend (recommended)** — react-email templates render natively, HTTP API (no SMTP
ports to open), and domain verification is self-serve. Get an API key at resend.com,
verify your sending domain, then:

 Key Notes 
 --- --- 
 `RESEND_API_KEY` Resend API key. Selects Resend (unless `EMAIL_PROVIDER` overrides). 

**Generic SMTP** — bring any provider (Postmark, Mailgun, SES-SMTP, a local Mailpit):

 Key Notes 
 --- --- 
 `SMTP_HOST` SMTP server host. Selects SMTP. 
 `SMTP_PORT` Default `587`. 
 `SMTP_USER` / `SMTP_PASS` Optional auth credentials. 
 `SMTP_SECURE` Implicit TLS on connect. Defaults to `true` on port 465, else `false`. 

**AWS SES** — set `ALETHIA_SES_REGION` to select it (requires SES production access
to mail arbitrary recipients)

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: OAuth providers (optional)
records.text:
Only the providers you configure appear on the sign-in screen.

 Key 
 --- 
 `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` / `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` 
 `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` / `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` 
 `GITLAB_APPLICATION_ID` / `GITLAB_SECRET` 
 `BITBUCKET_KEY` / `BITBUCKET_SECRET` 

Set each provider's callback URL. GitHub and Google are native social providers and use
`https:// /api/auth/callback/ `. GitLab and Bitbucket are registered
through the generic OAuth plugin and use `https:// /api/auth/oauth2/callback/ `.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Cloud connectors (optional)
records.text:
Key Default Notes 
 --- --- --- 
 `NEXT_PUBLIC_CONNECTOR_ASSETS_ORIGIN` hosted bucket Origin serving the connector setup artifacts the AWS/GCP/Azure connect flows hand out (`alethia-bootstrap.yaml`, `alethia-{gcp,azure}-setup.sh`). Point it at your own console origin — the files ship in `apps/console/public/`, e.g. `https://alethia.example.com`. The AWS CloudFormation quick-create flow needs an S3-hosted template, so AWS uses the bucket default or the OpenTofu method.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Managed runner fleet (optional)
records.text:
By default, runners are static — you register them yourself (see [Runners](/guides/runners)).
Set `FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud` to let the in-app scaler provision warm runner VMs on Hetzner Cloud and
scale them by queue depth. Unset / `manual` → no managed fleet (the scaler is a no-op).

 Key Default Notes 
 --- --- --- 
 `FLEET_PROVIDER` `manual` `hcloud` provisions real Hetzner VMs; `manual` = no-op. 
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN` — Hetzner Cloud API token. Required when `FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud`. 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` — Low-privilege shared token fleet VMs present to self-register. 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` — Console URL the VMs call back to (must be reachable from them). 
 `HCLOUD_SERVER_TYPE` `cax21` Hetzner server type (ARM CAX recommended for runner workloads). 
 `HCLOUD_IMAGE` `ubuntu-24.04` Base OS image for fleet VMs. 
 `HCLOUD_SSH_KEYS` — Comma-separated Hetzner SSH key IDs. 
 `FLEET_RUNNER_IMAGE_TAG` `latest` Runner image tag pulled from GHCR. 
 `FLEET_RUNNER_SLOTS` `1` Concurrent job slots per fleet runner. 
 `FLEET_BOOT_GRACE_SECONDS` `180` Seconds a freshly-booted VM is exempt from scale-down (cloud-init grace). 

Warm pools are managed in the console **Fleet** page (DB-backed).

records.title: Email
records.text: Email. Set up transactional email via Resend, generic SMTP, or AWS SES, with reputation-isolated sending subdomains (auth, product, marketing).

records.title: Email
records.heading: Email (Resend / SMTP / SES)
records.text:
Alethia sends transactional email through a **pluggable transport** — pick
**Resend**, a **generic SMTP** server, or **AWS SES**. Until you configure one,
sign-in codes and other emails are **logged to the server console** (run
`docker compose logs app`), so a fresh self-host works with zero email setup.
This page is what you do to send real email.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Choosing a provider
records.text:
The transport is chosen by `EMAIL_PROVIDER` (`resend` `smtp` `ses`) when set,
else auto-detected from whichever provider's credentials are present, in
precedence order **Resend → SMTP → SES**.

- **Resend (recommended).** react-email templates render natively, it's an HTTP API
 (no SMTP ports to open — friendly to containers/serverless), and domain
 verification is self-serve. Sign up at [resend.com](https://resend.com), add your
 domain, verify the DKIM + MAIL FROM DNS records it shows you (the same
 reputation-isolated subdomains below apply), create an API key, and set
 `RESEND_API_KEY`. That's the whole setup.
- **Generic SMTP.** Bring any provider — Postmark, Mailgun, SES-SMTP, or a local
 [Mailpit](https://github.com/axllent/mailpit) for testing. Set `SMTP_HOST`
 (+ `SMTP_PORT`/`SMTP_USER`/`SMTP_PASS`/`SMTP_SECURE` as needed).
- **AWS SES.** Powerful but its sandbox→production review frequently **denies
 legitimate new senders** (young account / fresh domain / OTP-heavy use case), and
 in the sandbox you can only mail *verified* addresses. If you already have SES
 production access it works great — the full runbook is below. Otherwise prefer
 Resend or SMTP.

> The hosted ale

records.title: Email
records.heading: Why subdomains
records.text:
Mail is split across **dedicated sending subdomains**, one per *stream*, so a
reputation hit on one stream can never poison another — which matters most for
auth mail (a sign-in code in spam = a locked-out user). The root domain is
reserved for your human/corporate mail and never sends app email.

 Stream Subdomain From-address (env) Used for 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Auth / security `auth.alethialabs.io` `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM` sign-in codes, email verification, password reset 
 Product / general `mail.alethialabs.io` `EMAIL_FROM` welcome, org invites, job notifications 
 Marketing *(future)* `marketing.alethialabs.io` — bulk/marketing — give it its **own** SES identity and ideally a separate IP pool / configuration set, so a campaign flagged as spam never touches auth or product deliverability 
 Human / corporate `alethialabs.io` (root) — your mailboxes only; locked down with DMARC, the app never sends from it 

Swap `alethialabs.io` for your own domain throughout.

records.title: Email
records.heading: SES setup steps (one-time)
records.text:
_For Resend or SMTP, follow that provider's domain-verification flow instead — the
subdomain design above still applies. The steps below are the AWS SES path._

records.title: Email
records.heading: 1. Verify the sending domains in SES
records.text:
In the SES console (in your chosen AWS region), create a **domain identity** for
each sending subdomain you'll use now — `auth.alethialabs.io` and
`mail.alethialabs.io`. (Add `marketing.alethialabs.io` later when you need it.)

records.title: Email
records.heading: 2. Enable DKIM
records.text:
For each identity, turn on **Easy DKIM**. SES gives you **3 CNAME records** per
domain — add them to your DNS. DKIM-signs every message and is required for DMARC
alignment.

records.title: Email
records.heading: 3. Set a custom MAIL FROM
records.text:
For each identity, set a **custom MAIL FROM** subdomain (e.g.
`bounce.auth.alethialabs.io`, `bounce.mail.alethialabs.io`) and add the records
SES shows:

- an **MX** record pointing at the SES regional mail endpoint, and
- an **SPF** `TXT` record: `"v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all"`.

This aligns SPF (and bounces) with your domain so DMARC passes.

records.title: Email
records.heading: 4. Add a DMARC policy
records.text:
Add a `TXT` record at `_dmarc.alethialabs.io`. Start in monitor mode and tighten
once reports look clean:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@alethialabs.io

Progression: `p=none` → `p=quarantine` → `p=reject`.

records.title: Email
records.heading: 5. Leave the SES sandbox
records.text:
New SES accounts are **sandboxed** — they can only mail verified addresses.
Request **production access** in the SES console to send to anyone.

records.title: Email
records.heading: 6. Grant send permission
records.text:
SES authenticates with AWS credentials. Either:

- attach an **IAM role** with `ses:SendEmail` / `ses:SendRawEmail` to the host
 running the console (cleanest — no secrets in env), **or**
- create an **IAM user** with that permission and set `ALETHIA_SES_ACCESS_KEY_ID`
 / `ALETHIA_SES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`.

records.title: Email
records.heading: 7. Configure the console
records.text:
Set these in `.env` (then `docker compose up -d app`):

ALETHIA_SES_REGION=eu-west-1 # the region you verified the domains in

records.title: Email
records.heading: Only if NOT using an IAM role:
records.text:
ALETHIA_SES_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
ALETHIA_SES_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...

AUTH_EMAIL_FROM="Alethia "
EMAIL_FROM="Alethia "

records.title: Email
records.heading: Optional — per-stream configuration sets (see "Bounce & complaint handling").
records.text:
ALETHIA_SES_AUTH_CONFIG_SET=alethia-auth
ALETHIA_SES_GENERAL_CONFIG_SET=alethia-general

`ALETHIA_SES_REGION` is the switch — set it and SES is used; leave it empty and
emails are logged. `EMAIL_FROM` falls back to `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM` if unset.

records.title: Email
records.heading: DNS records, at a glance
records.text:
Per sending subdomain (`auth.`, `mail.`, …):

 Record Host Type Value 
 --- --- --- --- 
 DKIM ×3 ` ._domainkey. ` CNAME ` .dkim.amazonses.com` (from SES) 
 MAIL FROM MX `bounce. ` MX `feedback-smtp. .amazonses.com` (priority 10) 
 MAIL FROM SPF `bounce. ` TXT `v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all` 

Once per root domain:

 Record Host Type Value 
 --- --- --- --- 
 DMARC `_dmarc.alethialabs.io` TXT `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@alethialabs.io`

records.title: Email
records.heading: Bounce & complaint handling (production)
records.text:
Optional, but recommended for a hosted deployment: track bounces and complaints
so the app stops mailing dead or complaining addresses (which protects your
sending reputation).

How it fits together:

- Each stream sends through an SES **configuration set**
 (`ALETHIA_SES_AUTH_CONFIG_SET` / `ALETHIA_SES_GENERAL_CONFIG_SET`).
- The configuration set publishes `Bounce` / `Complaint` events to an **SNS
 topic**, which posts them to the console at **`/api/webhooks/ses`**.
- That handler verifies the SNS signature and, on a **permanent** bounce or a
 **complaint**, adds the recipient to the **suppression list**. Every send then
 skips suppressed addresses.

For the hosted platform this whole stack — identities, DKIM, MAIL FROM, the
configuration sets, the SNS topic + subscription, account VDM, and reputation
alarms — is codified in OpenTofu at **`infra/email-ses/`** (see its `README.md`).
Self-hosters can either run that stack against their own domain or wire the same
pieces by hand; leaving the config-set vars unset keeps the simpler send-only
behavior.

records.title: Email
records.heading: Verify
records.text:
1. Open the console and request an email sign-in code.
2. It should arrive from `no-reply@auth.alethialabs.io` (check spam on the first
 send). If nothing arrives, `docker compose logs app` shows either the SES
 send error or — if SES isn't configured — the code itself.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.text: Enterprise setup. The end-to-end runbook for turning on the licensed Enterprise edition — packages, migrations, OpenFGA, and the license.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Enterprise setup
records.text:
The ordered checklist to take a deployment from Community to
 Enterprise . None of this is needed for the open-source edition — see
[Licensing](/editions/licensing) for the mechanism this turns on.

 
 Everything below is **additive and reversible.** If the license is removed, the deployment degrades back to
 Community behavior without data loss.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A commercial **license key** for Alethia Enterprise.
- The Enterprise package `@alethia/ee` (ships with the Enterprise distribution; absent from the open-source build).

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Install the Enterprise dependencies
records.text:
`@alethia/ee` and its peers add the organization/SSO/OpenFGA machinery:

pnpm install

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: brings in @alethia/ee, @openfga/sdk, @better-auth/sso (+ samlify, jose)
records.text: The core never imports these — they're loaded only through the `lib/enterprise.ts` seam at runtime.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Run the database migrations
records.text:
The org/team/SSO/authz tables ship as ordinary migrations (inert in Community — never written without the
plugins). Apply them:

pnpm -F console db:migrate # applies all pending migrations + programmables (RLS, triggers)

Then reconcile the Better Auth org/team/SSO tables against the plugin's expected shape:

npx @better-auth/cli generate

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: (Optional) Bring up OpenFGA
records.text:
Enterprise runs fine on the Postgres engine. To use the [OpenFGA fine-grained engine](/concepts/access-control/openfga),
start the `enterprise` compose profile (OpenFGA + its own datastore):

docker compose --profile enterprise up -d openfga

Create a store, then point the app at it:

OPENFGA_API_URL=http://openfga:8080
OPENFGA_STORE_ID= 

On boot the app writes the authorization model (generated from the registry) and backfills tuples from your
existing grants and hierarchy. Leaving `OPENFGA_*` unset keeps `PostgresRbacPDP` as the engine.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Activate the license
records.text:
Install the signed license so the Enterprise entitlements resolve to `true`. The license is a compact
EdDSA (ed25519) JWT that Alethia Labs mints offline; the console verifies it **offline** against the
issuer public key you bake in — no phone-home:

ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY= 
ALETHIA_LICENSE_PUBLIC_KEY= 

Restart the console. The org switcher, Members, Teams, Roles (custom), Access, SSO, and activity export now light
up.

 
 `ALETHIA_LICENSE_ACTIVE=true` is a **non-production dev bypass only** — it is ignored in production,
 where a signed `ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY` is required. Verification is fail-closed: a missing, expired, or
 forged license leaves the instance unlicensed and degrades to per-org billing (Community), never a boot
 crash.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: (Optional) Register an SSO provider
records.text:
In **Settings → Single Sign-On**, register your IdP over [OIDC or SAML](/guides/access/sso). Members signing
in with a matching email domain are routed to it and provisioned into the org.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Verify
records.text:
- Create an organization, invite a second member, and confirm the [invite lifecycle](/guides/access/members-and-invitations).
- In **Settings → Access**, grant a role to a member or team, then add a **deny** exception
 ([grants & scopes](/guides/access/grants-and-scopes)) and confirm it takes effect.
- If OpenFGA is on, run the parity check — the two engines must agree across roles, scopes, and actions.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: What you get
records.text:
Once the license is active, the full Enterprise surface is available — see the
[feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix) and the [Access Control](/concepts/access-control) reference.

records.title: Helm chart
records.text: Helm chart. Run the Alethia bundle on any managed Kubernetes cluster with the Helm chart.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Helm chart (deploy/helm/alethia)
records.text:
For teams already on Kubernetes, the chart deploys the same bundle as the
[compose stack](/guides/self-hosting) — console, docs, runner, and (optionally) bundled Postgres + object
store — wired behind a single Ingress (console at `/`, docs at `/docs`).

> **x86 only.** The published app-bundle images are built `linux/amd64`, so every pod carries a
> `nodeSelector` of `kubernetes.io/arch=amd64`. Use an x86 node pool, or clear it with
> `--set nodeSelector=null` once you publish multi-arch images.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: What it deploys
records.text:
- **console** Deployment + Service. Two init containers run first: `wait-for-postgres`, then
 `migrate` (idempotent — applies schema/programmables and sets the app-role password).
- **docs** Deployment + Service.
- **runner** Deployment (self-registers with the console over the in-cluster Service URL).
- **postgres** StatefulSet + headless Service + PVC — *optional* (`postgres.enabled`).
- **seaweedfs** StatefulSet + headless Service + PVC + ConfigMap (S3 identity) — *optional*
 (`objectStore.enabled`).
- **Ingress** (`/docs*` → docs, `/` → console) with optional cert-manager TLS.
- **Secret** holding the connection strings + app secrets (or bring your own via
 `secrets.existingSecret`).

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A Kubernetes cluster with an **x86 node pool**, an **Ingress controller** (e.g. ingress-nginx),
 and a **default StorageClass** (for the bundled Postgres/object-store PVCs).
- **cert-manager** with a `ClusterIssuer` if you want automatic TLS.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Install
records.text:
helm install alethia deploy/helm/alethia \
 --namespace alethia --create-namespace \
 --set domain=alethialabs.io \
 --set secrets.cliJwtSecret="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
 --set secrets.betterAuthSecret="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
 --set postgres.password="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
 --set postgres.appPassword="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
 --set objectStore.secretKey="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
 --set ingress.tls.clusterIssuer=letsencrypt-prod

Then point DNS for your domain at the ingress controller's external IP.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Bring your own Postgres / object store
records.text:
Disable the bundled ones and point at managed services:
helm install alethia deploy/helm/alethia \
 --set postgres.enabled=false \
 --set postgres.host=db.internal --set postgres.port=5432 \
 --set postgres.user=alethia --set postgres.password=... \
 --set postgres.database=alethia --set postgres.appPassword=... \
 --set objectStore.enabled=false \
 --set objectStore.endpoint=https://s3.amazonaws.com \
 ...

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: App secrets (OAuth, email, …)
records.text:
Provider client IDs/secrets, `ALETHIA_SES_*` (email), and other app env go under `secrets.extraEnv` as a
map — they're merged into the chart-managed Secret and exposed to the console/runner via `envFrom`:
secrets:
 extraEnv:
 ALETHIA_SES_REGION: eu-central-1
 AUTH_EMAIL_FROM: Alethia 
 GITHUB_CLIENT_ID: ...
 GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET: ...
Or manage everything yourself in one Secret and set `secrets.existingSecret=my-secret` (it must hold
`ALETHIA_DATABASE_URL`, `ALETHIA_APP_DATABASE_URL`, `ALETHIA_APP_DB_PASSWORD`,
`ALETHIA_STORAGE_ENDPOINT`, `CLI_JWT_SECRET`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`).

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Upgrade
records.text:
helm upgrade alethia deploy/helm/alethia --reuse-values --set image.tag=v1.2.3
The migrate init container re-runs on each rollout, so schema changes apply automatically.

records.title: Helm chart
records.heading: Key values
records.text:
Value Default Notes 
 --- --- --- 
 `image.registry` / `image.tag` `ghcr.io/alethialabs-io` / `latest` Pinned across components 
 `nodeSelector` `kubernetes.io/arch=amd64` `null` to disable 
 `domain` `alethialabs.io` Ingress host 
 `postgres.enabled` `true` `false` → set `postgres.host` 
 `objectStore.enabled` `true` `false` → set `objectStore.endpoint` 
 `ingress.className` `nginx` Ingress controller class 
 `ingress.trustedIpHeader` `x-real-ip` Header the ingress overwrites with the client IP for authentication throttling 
 `ingress.tls.clusterIssuer` `letsencrypt-prod` cert-manager issuer 

The default matches ingress-nginx, which overwrites `X-Real-IP` before forwarding a request. If you
use another ingress controller, set `ingress.trustedIpHeader` to a single-value client IP header
that controller overwrites. Authentication returns HTTP 503 in production when that contract is
missing or malformed, instead of placing every client in one shared rate-limit bucket.

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.text: Self-Hosting. Run the whole Alethia platform on your own infrastructure with one docker-compose bundle.

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.heading: Self-Hosting Alethia
records.text:
Alethia ships as a single **docker-compose bundle** — the control plane (console),
docs, Postgres, S3-compatible object storage (SeaweedFS), and a runner — behind a
Caddy reverse proxy with automatic HTTPS. It runs on **any cloud's VM** (AWS, GCP,
Azure, Alibaba, Hetzner) or your own hardware. No managed database or object store
required; nothing is welded to a single SaaS.

The whole stack is permissively licensed (Better Auth · Drizzle · SeaweedFS ·
Postgres · Caddy) — only Alethia's own code is AGPL.

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.heading: Quickstart (one command)
records.text:
On a fresh Linux VM with a domain pointed at it:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/main/deploy/install.sh \
 DOMAIN=alethia.example.com ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com sh

The installer ensures Docker, fetches the repo to `/opt/alethia`, generates secrets
into `.env`, and starts the bundle from prebuilt public images. Caddy obtains TLS
for your domain automatically. Omit `DOMAIN` to serve plain HTTP on `:80` for a
quick IP-only test.

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.heading: Quickstart (manual)
records.text:
git clone https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs.git && cd alethialabs
cp .env.example .env # then edit: secrets, OAuth, email (RESEND_API_KEY / SMTP_* / ALETHIA_SES_*)
docker compose up -d # builds locally; or use the prod overlay (below) for prebuilt images

Production (prebuilt images + TLS), after setting `ALETHIA_DOMAIN`/`ALETHIA_ACME_EMAIL` in `.env`:

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/prod/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.heading: Requirements
records.text:
- A Linux VM: **2+ vCPU / 4–8 GB RAM** (8 GB comfortable), ~25 GB disk.
- **Docker** + the Compose v2 plugin (the installer adds them).
- A **domain** (for automatic HTTPS). DNS `A`/`AAAA` → the VM's IP.
- Outbound network for image pulls and to reach the clouds you provision into.

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.heading: What's in the bundle
records.text:
Service Role 
 --- --- 
 `app` Console (Next.js control plane) 
 `docs` This documentation, served at `/docs` 
 `blog` Blog (Next.js), served at `/blog` 
 `postgres` Application database (Drizzle) 
 `seaweedfs` S3-compatible object storage (OpenTofu state + plan artifacts) 
 `runner` Executes provisioning jobs (OpenTofu) — runs as a self-operated runner 
 `caddy` Single ingress, automatic TLS 
 `pgweb` Optional DB browser (`--profile tools` → `:8081`)

records.title: Self-Hosting
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- **[Configuration](/guides/self-hosting/configuration)** — every `.env` key (DB, storage, auth, OAuth, email).
- **[Terraform](/guides/self-hosting/terraform)** — provision a hardened control-plane VM on a specific cloud (Hetzner, AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba), closed-origin behind a Cloudflare Tunnel (no open web ports).
- **[Helm chart](/guides/self-hosting/helm)** — run the same bundle on a Kubernetes cluster instead of a single VM.
- **[One-click deploy](/guides/self-hosting/one-click)** — Launch Stack (AWS) / Deploy to Azure buttons, no tooling.
- **[Upgrading & backups](/guides/self-hosting/upgrading)** — updates, Postgres dumps, volume snapshots.

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.text: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup). Provision the platform cloud identity so your instance can verify and provision into customer AWS/GCP/Azure accounts. Every cloud federates keylessly off Alethia's own OIDC issuer.

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: Managed cloud connectors — operator setup
records.text:
Your customers connect their cloud accounts from **Connectors** in the console. For that to work, your
instance is its **own OIDC issuer** that customers' clouds trust directly. This page is the operator side;
the per-cloud *customer* flows live under [Connectors](/guides/connectors).

There is almost nothing to stand up: the issuer's signing key is auto-generated, so **AWS, GCP, Azure, and
Alibaba all work out of the box** — no platform cloud account, no platform Entra app, no per-cloud operator
step. Token clouds (Hetzner / DigitalOcean / Civo) use the customer's own API token and need nothing here.

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: The model: every cloud federates off Alethia's OIDC issuer
records.text:
There is a single root of trust — **Alethia's own OIDC issuer** (`/api/oidc`, signing key
`ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`, auto-generated by `bootstrap-secrets.sh`). Every managed cloud trusts that
issuer directly and exchanges a short-lived, audience-scoped assertion for cloud credentials — **no platform
cloud account, no static key anywhere:**

How each cloud federates against the issuer — the customer-side trust, the audience, and what the role
may do — is explained once, in [Security architecture](/concepts/security#the-alethia-oidc-issuer-workload-identity);
the runner side is in [Cloud credentials](/concepts/runner/cloud-credentials).

The only load-bearing operator secret is the issuer's signing key (`ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`, set by
default). AWS, GCP, Azure, and Alibaba need nothing else.

For the underlying protocols — the [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) issuer, the per-cloud
[workload-identity federation](/reference/standards/workload-identity) exchange, and the
[JOSE](/reference/standards/jose) assertion signing — see the standards reference.

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: AWS / GCP / Alibaba — nothing to configure
records.text:
These three are keyless **and** account-free on the operator side: the customer's IAM role (AWS) / WIF pool
(GCP) / RAM OIDC provider (Alibaba) trusts your issuer directly, and the console mints an assertion per call.
As long as `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` is set (it is, by default), their **Connectors** tiles show **Connect**
immediately. Verify by connecting a test account (customer side: [AWS](/guides/connectors/aws) ·
[GCP](/guides/connectors/gcp) · [Alibaba](/guides/connectors/alibaba)) — each verifies to **Connected** via
a server-side probe (no runner).

If a tile is unexpectedly greyed out, confirm the issuer's JWKS is reachable (the customer cloud validates
assertions against it):

curl -fsS https://alethialabs.io/api/oidc/jwks >/dev/null && echo OK

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: Azure — keyless via the Alethia OIDC issuer
records.text:
Azure is fully **keyless** — **no client secret** anywhere, and **no platform Entra app**. Alethia's
control plane is its own workload-identity OIDC issuer (`/api/oidc`, key `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`,
auto-generated by `bootstrap-secrets.sh`). **There is no one-time operator step for Azure** — like
AWS/GCP/Alibaba, availability tracks the issuer key alone.

The customer runs the connect script (`infra/connector/azure`) in their own subscription — see
[Connectors → Azure](/guides/connectors/azure) and
[Security architecture → Azure](/concepts/security#azure-federated-identity). It must trust the issuer
your instance actually serves: issuer `${APP_URL}/api/oidc`, subject `alethia-connector`, audience
`api://AzureADTokenExchange`.

The issuer must be **publicly reachable** — Azure fetches `${APP_URL}/api/oidc/jwks` to validate the
assertion, and that route 404s until `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` exists (auto-generated by
`bootstrap-secrets.sh`, so run that before you expect Azure to verify).

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: Alibaba — keyless + account-free
records.text:
Alibaba is **keyless and account-free**: the console assumes the customer RAM role via STS
`AssumeRoleWithOIDC` with an assertion minted by the **same OIDC issuer** as Azure — Alethia holds **no
Alibaba account** and no AccessKey. There is **nothing to set here** (no `ALETHIA_ALIBABA_*`); availability
tracks the OIDC issuer key alone (`ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`, auto-generated).

The customer side is in [Connectors → Alibaba](/guides/connectors/alibaba). No operator action is
needed beyond having the issuer key.

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: Rotating the issuer signing key
records.text:
The issuer's signing key (`ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`) is the trust root for **all four** managed clouds, so
treat it like a CA key. It rotates with **zero downtime** via a two-key overlap — the JWKS publishes the old
and new key at once, and each assertion's `kid` header selects the right one, so in-flight assertions keep
verifying while new ones are signed by the new key. `scripts/rotate-oidc-key.sh` drives it against the vault:

bash

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: 1. Mint a new primary; park the outgoing key in ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS (published, not signing).
records.text:
./scripts/rotate-oidc-key.sh
gh workflow run deploy-console.yml # publish both keys; start signing with the new one

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: 3. Retire the old key.
records.text:
./scripts/rotate-oidc-key.sh --finalize
gh workflow run deploy-console.yml # redeploy without the previous key

`./scripts/rotate-oidc-key.sh --status` shows what's currently in the vault (key fingerprints, never private
material). The script refuses to start a second rotation while one is unfinalized. No cloud-side change is
needed — Azure/Alibaba/AWS/GCP all re-fetch the JWKS and validate against whichever key signed the assertion.

records.title: Managed cloud connectors (operator setup)
records.heading: Reference
records.text:
- Vault key catalog: `deploy/prod/.env.production.example`; operator inputs:
 `deploy/prod/secrets.local.env.example`.
- The emit list in `.github/workflows/deploy-console.yml` is the gate — a key only reaches the app if
 it's emitted there.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.text: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook). Turn on the managed fleet so your instance provisions Kubernetes into customer AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, and Hetzner accounts — connectors, runner images, fleet pools, per-cloud verification, and the optional untrusted-BYO container sandbox.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Managed provisioning — operator runbook
records.text:
With the **managed** operator, your instance runs the provisioning runners itself: a cheap Hetzner VM fleet claims each
customer's plan/deploy job, assumes into the customer's cloud (keyless OIDC, or a token for Hetzner), runs
OpenTofu against Alethia's own project templates, and streams state + logs back through the console. The
customer never runs a runner.

All five clouds — **AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, Hetzner** — provision end-to-end. This page is the operator
checklist to enable it and verify each cloud. The per-cloud *customer* connect flow and the OIDC-issuer
platform setup live in [Managed cloud connectors](/guides/self-hosting/managed-cloud-connectors); this page assumes
you've done that and covers the **fleet** side.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Architecture (what happens on a deploy)
records.text:
1. A customer connects a cloud (keyless OIDC for AWS/GCP/Azure/Alibaba; an API token for Hetzner) and
 creates a project, then queues a **plan** or **deploy**.
2. The in-app **scaler** (`lib/fleet`, 60s tick) sizes a per-provider warm pool and creates a Hetzner VM.
 Its cloud-init runs the per-cloud runner image `ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner- ` and the VM
 **self-registers** with a per-VM, short-TTL, instance-bound bootstrap token.
3. The runner claims the job, mints a **per-job cloud token** (OIDC) and a **per-job tofu-state token**, and
 runs `tofu init/plan/apply` against the baked project template. Tofu **state** goes to the console HTTP
 state proxy (`/api/jobs/[id]/state`) — no storage credential ever touches the runner.
4. The kubeconfig comes from the cloud (EKS/GKE/AKS API) or a tofu output (ACK/Talos), post-apply Helm/ArgoCD
 runs, and the job completes. The VM is disposable (SLOTS=1).

The fleet holds **no** storage master key and **no** shared bootstrap token — both were drained from the
cloud-init (E0 2b/0b). Untrusted **BYO** execution additionally requires the container sandbox — see
[Untrusted BYO](#untrusted-byo-container-sandbox-3b) at the end.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A working self-hosted deploy (console + migrate + storage reachable). See [Configuration](/guides/self-hosting/configuration).
- The **OIDC issuer** signing key `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` — auto-generated by `scripts/bootstrap-secrets.sh`.
 Its discovery + JWKS routes (`/api/oidc/...`) must be **publicly reachable** (Azure/Alibaba validate the
 assertion). This is set up in [Managed cloud connectors](/guides/self-hosting/managed-cloud-connectors).
- Object storage configured (`ALETHIA_STORAGE_*` on the **console** — NOT the fleet).

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: 1. Per-cloud connector setup (one-time)
records.text:
Do this once per cloud you want to offer. Full detail in
[Managed cloud connectors](/guides/self-hosting/managed-cloud-connectors); summary:

 Cloud Platform operator step Customer step 
 --- --- --- 
 **AWS** none (issuer key only) `tofu apply infra/connector/aws` → paste **role ARN** 
 **GCP** none (issuer key only) `tofu apply infra/connector/gcp` → paste **credential config** 
 **Alibaba** none (issuer key only) `tofu apply infra/connector/alibaba` → paste **role ARN** 
 **Azure** none (issuer key only) `tofu apply infra/connector/azure` → paste **tenant + client + subscription ids** 
 **Hetzner** none paste a Hetzner **API token** (token auth — no OIDC) 

The connect UI for each provider only lights up once its platform prerequisite is satisfied
(`computePlatformConfigured`): AWS/GCP/Azure/Alibaba all track the issuer signing key alone, Hetzner is
always available.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: 2. Runner images
records.text:
Managed provisioning of a cloud requires its **per-cloud runner image** to be published to GHCR. The deploy
pipeline (`deploy-console.yml`) builds and pushes all five on a push to `main`:

ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner-aws runner-gcp runner-azure
ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner-alibaba runner-hetzner

`runner-alibaba` and `runner-hetzner` carry no cloud CLI (Alibaba is keyless OIDC with a static kubeconfig
from the ACK output; Hetzner is Talos with a static kubeconfig from the talos output). Confirm the tags exist
for the tag your fleet pins (`FLEET_RUNNER_IMAGE_TAG`, default `latest`):

for c in aws gcp azure alibaba hetzner; do
 docker manifest inspect ghcr.io/alethialabs-io/runner-$c:latest >/dev/null && echo "runner-$c OK"
done

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: 3. Fleet enablement
records.text:
The fleet is off until you select the Hetzner provider and give it a token. Set on the **console** env:

 Var Required Notes 
 --- --- --- 
 `FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud` yes selects the Hetzner backend (default `manual` = no-op) 
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN` yes Hetzner API token for the **fleet** project (distinct from a customer connector token) 
 `HCLOUD_SSH_KEYS` recommended comma-separated Hetzner SSH key IDs (break-glass access) 
 `ALETHIA_RUNNER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` auto seeded by the runner script on first run; the scaler mints per-VM tokens from it 
 `HCLOUD_SERVER_TYPE` no default `cax21` (arm64) 
 `FLEET_RUNNER_IMAGE_TAG` no default `latest` 
 `FLEET_RUNNER_SLOTS` no default `1` (one job per VM) 

Then create **one fleet pool per cloud** you want to provision. Pools are DB rows (`fleet_pools`), created
from the console fleet UI (self-managed deployments) — the `createFleetPool` action, gated on the `fleet`
resource. Each pool sets `provider`, `warm_min`, `max`, `locations`, etc.; the scaler re-reads enabled pools
every tick (no restart). A paused (`enabled=false`) pool is skipped.

> The fleet UI + pool reads/writes are only available on a **self-managed** deployment
> (`isFleetOperatorDeploy

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: 4. Per-cloud verification
records.text:
For each cloud, end to end:

1. **Connect** the cloud in the console (paste the role ARN / credential config / token). The cloud identity
 verifies server-side (no runner needed).
2. **Create a project** targeting that cloud and a small cluster.
3. **Plan** — a VM spins up in that cloud's pool, claims the job, and returns a plan + a `verify.Report`
 (Elench) in the console Plan tab. Confirm:
 - a `fleet- -…` server appears in Hetzner and self-registers as a runner,
 - the plan streams logs and completes,
 - no `ALETHIA_STORAGE_*` / bootstrap secret is in the job env (they're not injected).
4. **Deploy** — apply provisions the cluster; the kubeconfig is captured (EKS/GKE/AKS API call, or the
 ACK/Talos tofu output) and post-apply Helm/ArgoCD runs.
5. **Destroy** — tears the cluster down and purges the tofu state (`DELETE …/state`).

Repeat for AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, Hetzner. Alibaba provisions a real managed **ACK** cluster; Hetzner
provisions a self-managed **Talos** cluster.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Troubleshooting
records.text:
- **VM boots but never registers** — check the per-VM bootstrap token TTL (`FLEET_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS`,
 default 3600) vs. a slow multi-GB image pull, and the boot grace (`FLEET_BOOT_GRACE_SECONDS`).
- **`runner- ` image pull fails** — the tag isn't published for that cloud; re-check step 2.
- **Cloud auth fails on plan** — the customer's connector `tofu apply` is missing (no managed identity /
 role), or the issuer isn't publicly reachable (`${APP_URL}/api/oidc/jwks` must resolve).

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Untrusted BYO (container sandbox, 3b)
records.text:
Everything above provisions Alethia's **own** (trusted) templates — safe to run in-process (Passthrough).
Running **untrusted** customer code (BYO Helm/IaC) on the managed fleet additionally requires the per-job
**container sandbox**: a nested rootless-podman container per job with an allowlisted env, its own PID
namespace, and a default-deny domain-allowlist egress net (so it cannot reach the `169.254.169.254` metadata
service, which serves the VM's cloud-init).

The Go backend and the fleet plumbing ship **inert**. Turn-on is **config-only** on the fleet — but the
