isolation must be **proven on a real VM first**, because nested podman + `/dev/fuse` + IMDS egress cannot be
tested in CI.

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Turn-on sequence
records.text:
1. **Enable the sandbox on a canary pool** — set on the fleet cloud-init env (`renderCloudInit`, gated by
 `FLEET_SANDBOX_CONTAINER=1`). This renders the default-deny egress net + squid forward proxy and starts
 the runner with the container backend + proxy env. **Do NOT set `FLEET_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` yet** — with
 it unset the container backend **fail-closes on managed** (jobs refuse), which proves the runtime works
 before you trust egress.

 FLEET_SANDBOX_CONTAINER=1
 FLEET_EGRESS_EXTRA_DOMAINS= # optional
 FLEET_EGRESS_PROXY_IMAGE=ubuntu/squid@sha256: # pin a digest in prod
 
2. **Run the real-VM canary** on a live Hetzner VM. All must pass:
 - `podman run --rm true` (as `runner`) succeeds — proves subuid/subgid + fuse-overlayfs +
 crun + the `--device /dev/fuse` + seccomp/apparmor/systempaths relaxations.
 - From inside the nested child: it **cannot** read `/proc/1/environ`, `$ALETHIA_RUNNER_TOKEN`, or the
 storage/bootstrap secrets, and sees only its own PID tree.
 - `curl --max-time 3 http://169.254.169.254/...` from the child **times out** — with the proxy env set
 AND unset (the `--internal` net + iptables belt + non-allowlisted domain all deny it).
 - Through the pro

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: Fleet env — 3b knobs
records.text:
Var Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `FLEET_SANDBOX_CONTAINER` render the egress net + proxy + container-backend runner (master switch) 
 `FLEET_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` set `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED=1` — **only after** the canary passes 
 `FLEET_SANDBOX_ENFORCE_MANAGED` fleet-wide kill-switch: a managed pool lacking the container backend refuses 
 `FLEET_EGRESS_EXTRA_DOMAINS` extra allowlist domains (comma-separated) 
 `FLEET_EGRESS_PROXY_IMAGE` the forward-proxy image (pin a digest)

records.title: Managed Provisioning (5-cloud runbook)
records.heading: If nested podman is fragile
records.text:
Nested rootless podman + fuse-overlayfs on the arm64 Hetzner kernel is the fragile layer. Fallbacks, in order:
switch the containers `storage.conf` driver to `vfs` (slower but robust) → add `--cap-add SETUID --cap-add
SETGID` to the outer run for `newuidmap` → escalate to a microVM SKU (sysbox/Kata) — a larger fleet change.

Until the canary passes, managed **untrusted** BYO stays flag-gated trusted-only; the trusted 5-cloud
provisioning above is unaffected.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.text: One-click deploy. Launch the Alethia bundle on AWS or Azure with a single button — no OpenTofu, no shell.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: One-click deploy
records.text:
The fastest way to stand up a control plane on a public cloud: a button that opens the cloud's own
console with a prefilled template. Each template provisions **one x86 VM**, opens 22/80/443, and runs
the [installer](/guides/self-hosting) via cloud-init — the same bundle as everywhere else.

> **x86 only.** The published app-bundle images are `linux/amd64`, so both templates default to x86
> instances (AWS `t3`, Azure `Dsv5`).

> **Domain afterwards.** Leave the domain blank to come up on HTTP at the public IP first, then point
> DNS at it and redeploy with the domain set for automatic HTTPS. Or pre-create the DNS record so the
> first boot can obtain TLS.

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: AWS — Launch Stack (CloudFormation)
records.text:
Template: [`deploy/oneclick/aws-cloudformation.yaml`](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/main/deploy/oneclick/aws-cloudformation.yaml)

Creates an EC2 `t3.medium` (Ubuntu 24.04 amd64, gp3 root), a security group (22/80/443), and an
Elastic IP. Parameters: `Domain`, `AcmeEmail`, `InstanceType`, `KeyName` (an existing key pair),
`AllowedSshCidr`, `VolumeSize`. The AMI resolves from Canonical's public SSM parameter, so it's
current in every region. Read `PublicIp` from the stack **Outputs**.

You can also launch it from the CLI:
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name alethia \
 --template-file deploy/oneclick/aws-cloudformation.yaml \
 --parameter-overrides Domain=alethia.example.com AcmeEmail=you@example.com KeyName=my-key \
 --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: Azure — Deploy to Azure (ARM template)
records.text:
Template: [`deploy/oneclick/azure-arm.json`](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/main/deploy/oneclick/azure-arm.json)

Creates a `Standard_D2s_v5` (x86, Ubuntu 24.04 amd64) VM with a static public IP, VNet,
and an NSG (22/80/443). Parameters: `domain`, `acmeEmail`, `adminUsername`, `sshPublicKey`,
`vmSize`, `location`. Read `publicIp` from the deployment **Outputs**.

From the CLI:
az deployment group create --resource-group alethia-cp \
 --template-file deploy/oneclick/azure-arm.json \
 --parameters domain=alethia.example.com acmeEmail=you@example.com \
 sshPublicKey="$(cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub)"

records.title: One-click deploy
records.heading: When to use what
records.text:
One-click [Terraform](/guides/self-hosting/terraform) [Helm](/guides/self-hosting/helm) 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Best for a quick managed VM, no tooling repeatable IaC + CI (plan/apply) existing Kubernetes 
 State the cloud's stack/deployment your S3 state bucket the cluster 
 DNS manual / pre-created Cloudflare, automated your ingress + DNS 

All three land on the same bundle — switch later without reinstalling.

records.title: Scaling out
records.text: Scaling out. Run the console across multiple replicas — realtime SSE fan-out already works without a shared broker, and an optional Redis service backs the enterprise fan-out.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Scaling out
records.text:
One console container handles most self-host workloads. When you need more
throughput or redundancy, run several console replicas behind the ingress. This
page shows how, and explains what does and doesn't need a shared service.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Why replicas work without a shared broker
records.text:
The console streams realtime updates to the browser over Server-Sent Events (SSE)
— job logs, support messages, and runner wake/cancel. In the open-source build,
that fan-out rides on **Postgres `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`**, not a message broker.

A Postgres trigger runs `pg_notify(' ', json)` on insert; each console
instance holds one dedicated `LISTEN` connection per channel and dispatches to its
own SSE subscribers. Because every replica listens independently, **the fan-out
scales to multiple instances with no Redis** — a `NOTIFY` from any writer reaches
the subscribers on every replica.

The channels wired today are `job_logs`, `support_messages`, `runner_wake`, and
`runner_cancel`.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Run more than one replica
records.text:
The `app` service binds no host port of its own — Caddy fronts it at `app:3000`
— and sets no fixed container name, so Compose can run several copies. Scale it up:

docker compose up -d --scale app=3

Each replica connects to the same bundled Postgres and object storage, so the
replicas are interchangeable for stored state.

> **Rate limiting is per-instance.** The console's built-in sliding-window rate
> limiter keeps its counters in memory on each instance, with no cross-replica
> coordination. It still blunts accidental double-submits per replica, but a limit
> is not shared across the fleet.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: The optional Redis service
records.text:
The Compose stack ships a Redis service dedicated to scale-out SSE fan-out:

yaml

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: docker-compose.yml
records.text:
redis:
 image: redis:7-alpine
 profiles: ["scale-out"]
 volumes:
 - redis-data:/data
 restart: unless-stopped

It sits behind the `scale-out` [Compose profile](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/profiles/),
so it **never starts in the default bring-up**. The enterprise tier swaps a
Redis-backed fan-out implementation in behind the same realtime interfaces; the
open-source `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` transport above needs no Redis.

To start the profiled service:

docker compose --profile scale-out up -d redis

> The open-source build does not require Redis to run multiple replicas. Enable the
> `scale-out` profile only for the enterprise Redis-backed fan-out.

records.title: Scaling out
records.heading: Next
records.text:

- **[Helm chart](/guides/self-hosting/helm)** — run the same bundle on Kubernetes instead of a single VM.
- **[Upgrading & backups](/guides/self-hosting/upgrading)** — updates, Postgres dumps, volume snapshots.

records.heading: What it creates

 system disk
- `alicloud_vpc` + `alicloud_vswitch` (AZ auto-picked to one that has the x86 type)

- **Automation:** `aliyun ecs RunCommand`.

records.heading: Access — SSM Session Manager
records.text:
No SSH port is open. The SSM agent (preinstalled on the AMI) dials out; connect with:

- A Cloudflare **API token** with **DNS edit + Zero Trust (Tunnel)** perms, the **zone id**, and the

records.heading: Apply

account's default VPC with an auto-assigned public IP (egress only).

A single x86 Gen2 **`Standard_D2s_v5`** (2 vCPU / 8 GB) Linux VM fronted by a Cloudflare Tunnel.

records.heading: What it creates

- `azurerm_linux_virtual_machine` (`Standard_D2s_v5`, Ubuntu 24.04 amd64) with a 30 GB StandardSSD OS
 disk; **Trusted Launch** (secure boot + vTPM); a system-assigned **managed identity**; boot

No Bastion, no open SSH. Automation via **`az vm run-command`** (control-plane, no port); interactive
break-glass via the **Serial Console**:
az vm run-command invoke -g -n alethia-cp --command-id RunShellScript --scripts '…'
az serial-console connect -g -n alethia-cp

records.heading: Apply

records.text: GCP. Provision the Alethia control plane on an x86 Compute Engine VM, closed-origin behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, SSH via IAP.

records.title: GCP
records.heading: GCP (infra/cp-gcp)
records.text:
A single x86 **`e2-standard-2`** (2 vCPU / 8 GB) Compute Engine VM fronted by a Cloudflare Tunnel.
**≈ $57/mo** (e2-standard-2 + 30 GB pd-balanced; Infracost, on-demand, `europe-west4`).

records.heading: What it creates
records.text:
- `google_compute_instance` (`e2-standard-2`, Ubuntu 24.04 amd64) with a 30 GB `pd-balanced` boot
 disk; **Shielded VM** (secure boot + vTPM); a dedicated least-priv service account
- `google_compute_firewall` — **SSH (`22`) from the IAP range `35.235.240.0/20` only**; no 80/443

records.title: GCP
records.heading: Access — IAP (no public SSH)
records.text: gcloud compute ssh alethia-cp --zone --tunnel-through-iap

records.title: GCP
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A GCP **project** with the Compute Engine + IAP APIs enabled.
- A **service-account JSON key** (provider auth → `GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS`).

records.heading: Apply
records.text:
cd infra/cp-gcp

records.title: Hetzner
records.text: Hetzner. Provision the Alethia control plane on a Hetzner Cloud x86 VM, closed-origin behind a Cloudflare Tunnel.

records.title: Hetzner
records.heading: Hetzner (infra/cp-hetzner)
records.text:
The cheapest target, and the one the hosted alethialabs.io runs on: a Hetzner Cloud **CX33** (Intel
x86, 4 vCPU / 8 GB) with an attached data volume, fronted by a Cloudflare Tunnel. **≈ €14/mo**
(Hetzner list price: `cx33` €13.10 + 25 GB volume €1.19; not priced by Infracost).

records.title: Hetzner
records.heading: What it creates
records.text:
- `hcloud_server` (`cx33`) + `hcloud_volume` (25 GB, holds Postgres + object storage) + attachment
- `hcloud_firewall` — **SSH only** (`22`); no 80/443 (ingress is the tunnel)
- `cloudflare_zero_trust_tunnel_cloudflared` (+ config) and **proxied** `cloudflare_record` CNAMEs
 (apex + `www`) onto ` .cfargotunnel.com`
- cloud-init: installs Docker, moves Docker's data-root onto the volume, clones the repo

records.title: Hetzner
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A Hetzner Cloud **project + API token** (`HCLOUD_TOKEN`).
- A Cloudflare **API token** with **DNS edit + Zero Trust (Tunnel)** perms, the **zone id**, and the
 **account id**.
- An SSH **public key** (SSH is the admin channel on Hetzner).

records.title: Hetzner
records.heading: Apply
records.text:
cd infra/cp-hetzner
cp backend.hcl.example backend.hcl # fill S3 endpoint + creds
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # hcloud_token, cloudflare_* (token/zone/account), ssh_public_key, domain

tofu plan && tofu apply

records.heading: Tuning
records.text:
`server_type` (`cx33` default; `cx43` if busy), `data_volume_size`, `location` (any EU region),
`ssh_allowed_cidrs` (SSH source restriction).

records.title: Hetzner
records.heading: Also here — inbound email
records.text:
Hetzner owns the zone-global Cloudflare **Email Routing** for the apex addresses (support@, sales@,
…) — see [Email](/guides/self-hosting/email). It's gated off until you import the existing routing.

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.text: Terraform (per-cloud). Provision a hardened control-plane VM on any of five clouds — closed-origin behind a Cloudflare Tunnel — with OpenTofu.

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.heading: Terraform modules
records.text:
The repeatable IaC path. Each cloud has a self-contained OpenTofu stack under `infra/cp- /`
that provisions **one** control-plane VM and fronts it with a **Cloudflare Tunnel**, so the box has
**no public web ports**. It lands on the same [bundle](/guides/self-hosting) as the [one-click](/guides/self-hosting/one-click) VM
and the [Helm](/guides/self-hosting/helm) chart — pick this when you want version-controlled infrastructure with a
plan/apply CI loop.

> **Pick one.** The stacks all serve the **same domain/zone**, so they are alternatives — apply
> **one instead of another**, never two at once (two would fight over the apex DNS + tunnel). The
> hosted alethialabs.io runs on Hetzner.

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.heading: Status
records.text:
Cloud Module Box (x86) Cost/mo Admin access (no open web port) Page 
 --- --- --- --- --- --- 
 Hetzner `infra/cp-hetzner` `cx33` ≈ €14 SSH, key-only (firewall SSH-only) [Hetzner](/guides/self-hosting/terraform/hetzner) 
 AWS `infra/cp-aws` `t3.large` ≈ $72 SSM Session Manager [AWS](/guides/self-hosting/terraform/aws) 
 GCP `infra/cp-gcp` `e2-standard-2` ≈ $57 IAP tunnel [GCP](/guides/self-hosting/terraform/gcp) 
 Azure `infra/cp-azure` `Standard_D2s_v5` ≈ $90 `az vm run-command` + Serial Console [Azure](/guides/self-hosting/terraform/azure) 
 Alibaba `infra/cp-alibaba` `ecs.g7.large` ≈ $75–95 ECS Session Manager [Alibaba](/guides/self-hosting/terraform/alibaba) 

> **x86 boxes.** The published app-bundle images are `linux/amd64`, so every module provisions an x86
> host (the per-cloud *runner* images are arm64, but they run on the managed fleet, not this box).

> **Costs** are on-demand estimates at each module's default region. AWS/GCP/Azure are from
> **Infracost**; Hetzner and Alibaba (which Infracost doesn't price) are **list prices**. See each
> cloud's page for the breakdown; a monthly/subscription commitment is cheaper on most clouds.

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.heading: The model — closed origin, zero standing inbound
records.text:
Every stack follows the same shape:

- **Ingress is a Cloudflare Tunnel.** `cloudflared` (a service in the bundle) dials **out**; nothing
 dials in. The firewall / security group exposes **no 80/443**. Apex and `www` are **proxied**
 `CNAME`s onto ` .cfargotunnel.com`, and TLS terminates at Cloudflare's edge.
- **The connector token is an output.** The stack exports `tunnel_token` (sensitive); set it as
 `TUNNEL_TOKEN` in the box's `.env` and the compose `cloudflared` connects with nothing else
 (`config_src = "cloudflare"`, remotely-managed).
- **The public IP is egress-only** (image pulls, `git`, dialing the tunnel out); inbound is closed.
- **Hardened + asserted.** Each stack ships a `checks.tf` that fails the plan if the posture regresses
 (no web ingress, disk encryption / verified boot, tunnel remotely-managed).

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.heading: Shared workflow
records.text:
Every module is the same three steps:

cd infra/cp- 
cp backend.hcl.example backend.hcl # S3-compatible state backend (endpoint + creds)
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # cloud creds, domain, cloudflare_* ids
tofu init -backend-config=backend.hcl
tofu plan && tofu apply

Then wire the tunnel token into the bundle `.env`:


State lives in an S3-compatible bucket (`TF_STATE_S3_*`), one key per stack
(` -cp/terraform.tfstate`). DNS records are **proxied** CNAMEs onto the tunnel — there is no
open origin. See each cloud's page for the exact GitHub secrets.

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A **Cloudflare account + zone** and an API token with **DNS edit** and **Zero Trust (Cloudflare
 Tunnel)** permissions — you pass `cloudflare_account_id` and `cloudflare_zone_id`.
- An **S3-compatible state backend** (`backend.hcl`).
- The chosen cloud's own credentials.

records.title: Terraform (per-cloud)
records.heading: Not managed here
records.text:
Cloudflare **Email Routing** is zone-global and lives only in `cp-hetzner` (see [Email](/guides/self-hosting/email)),
so the stacks don't collide on the shared zone.

records.title: Upgrading & Backups
records.text: Upgrading & Backups. Update a self-hosted Alethia bundle and back up its data.

records.title: Upgrading & Backups
records.heading: Upgrading
records.text:
Re-run the installer (it's idempotent — it pulls the latest images and restarts):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/main/deploy/install.sh sh

Or manually from `/opt/alethia`:

git pull
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/prod/docker-compose.prod.yml pull
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/prod/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d --remove-orphans

Database migrations run automatically on boot (the one-shot `migrate` service runs
before `app` starts). Your `.env` is never overwritten.

records.title: Upgrading & Backups
records.heading: Backups
records.text:
Two things hold state: **Postgres** and the **object store** (OpenTofu state +
plan artifacts). OpenTofu state is the only un-regenerable data — back it up.

**Postgres** (schedule via cron):

docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U alethia alethia gzip > backup-$(date +%F).sql.gz

**Object storage** — snapshot the `seaweedfs-data` volume, or `aws s3 sync` it to
an off-box bucket. If you point `ALETHIA_STORAGE_*` at managed S3/R2, use that
provider's backups instead.

On managed hosts, also enable the provider's **volume/server snapshots** for an
off-box copy (e.g. Hetzner backups, EBS snapshots).

records.title: Upgrading & Backups
records.heading: Inspecting the database
records.text: docker compose --profile tools up -d pgweb # → http://localhost:8081

records.title: Introduction
records.text: Introduction. Comprehensive documentation for the Alethia Console web platform, alethia CLI, and Runner execution agents.

records.title: Introduction
records.heading: Introduction
records.text:
Documentation for **Alethia** — the multi-cloud Kubernetes control plane by Alethia Labs. Configure
infrastructure visually in the Console, deploy from the terminal with the `alethia` CLI, and let Runners
execute OpenTofu and reconcile GitOps. New to Alethia? Start with [Get started](/get-started).

 
 **Two editions, one codebase.** Alethia is open-core: a free, open-source Community 
 edition (the complete single-tenant product) and a licensed Enterprise edition
 (multi-member organizations, teams, SSO, custom roles, and the fine-grained access portal). See
 [**Editions**](/editions) for the full comparison.
 

 
 
 Sign up, connect a cloud, design a project, and deploy it. Install the `alethia` CLI.
 
 
 Learn by building something real, start to finish, on a cloud you own.
 
 
 Do one task: connect an account, design a project, run jobs, manage access, or self-host.
 
 
 Every CLI command and flag, the API, configuration variables, controls, and the glossary.
 
 
 How Alethia works: the domain model, provisioning, runners, isolated execution, security, and Elench.
 
 
 Community vs Enterprise: the feature matrix, licensing, and how Alethia compares.

records.title: Auth APIs
records.text: Auth APIs. Device code flow endpoints for CLI authentication — generate, exchange, refresh.

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: Auth APIs
records.text: These endpoints implement the **Device Authorization Grant** (RFC 8628) for CLI authentication. See [Authentication Flows](/concepts/authentication) for the complete flow.

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: POST /api/auth/cli/generate
records.text:
Called by the **browser** (authenticated user) to approve a CLI login attempt.

**Requires:** Active browser session (Better Auth session cookie).

**Body:**
{
 "device_code": "uuid-from-cli"
}

**Effect:**
- Upserts a `cli_logins` record keyed by the device code, storing the user's profile ID (which signifies approval) and the user's first linked git provider access token (held in the `verification_code` column for the CLI to pick up on exchange)
- Returns `{ "success": true }`

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: POST /api/auth/cli/exchange
records.text:
Called by the **CLI** to exchange the approved device code for tokens.

**No authentication required** — the browser must have already approved the device code (its `cli_logins` record must have a `profile_id` set).

**Body:**
{
 "device_code": "uuid-from-cli"
}

**Validation:**
- Looks up the `cli_logins` record by device code
- Verifies that `profile_id` is set (meaning the browser approved the login)

**Response:**
{
 "access_token": "jwt...",
 "refresh_token": "jwt...",
 "provider_token": "git-oauth-token",
 "user_email": "user@example.com"
}

**Token Details:**
- **Access token**: 1-hour TTL, HS256 signed with `CLI_JWT_SECRET`
- **Refresh token**: 90-day TTL, same signing

JWT payload:
{
 "sub": "user-uuid",
 "email": "user@example.com",
 "type": "access",
 "iss": "urn:example:issuer",
 "aud": "urn:example:audience"
}

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: POST /api/auth/cli/refresh

records.title: Auth APIs
records.heading: GET /api/auth/[...all]
records.text:
Better Auth's catch-all handler owns the OAuth callback at `/api/auth/[...all]` after provider authentication, along with email-OTP verify, session, account linking, and sign-out.

Better Auth persists the provider's access token to the `account` table. The CLI `generate` endpoint later reads it from there (via `auth.api.getAccessToken`) to hand the git provider token to the CLI.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.text: CLI APIs. API endpoints used by the alethia CLI for project, job, and runner management.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: CLI APIs
records.text: These endpoints are called by the alethia CLI. Authentication is via `Authorization: Bearer {jwt}` header with a CLI-issued JWT. See [Authentication Flows](/concepts/authentication).

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/configurations
records.text: List all project configurations for the authenticated user.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/configurations/{name}
records.text: Get a configuration by name.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/configurations/by-project-name/{project_name}
records.text: Look up a project by name.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: POST /api/jobs
records.text:
Create a new job. Accepts:

{
 "job_type": "PLAN",
 "configuration_id": "project-uuid",
 "assigned_runner_id": "runner-uuid",
 "plan_job_id": "plan-job-uuid"
}

Valid job types: PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY, DESTROY_RUNNER.

If `configuration_id` is provided, the server auto-resolves `cloud_identity_id`, computes config hash, and creates a config snapshot.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/jobs
records.text: List all jobs for the authenticated user. Supports a `?status={status}` filter.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/jobs/{id}
records.text: Get job status and metadata.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/jobs/{id}/logs
records.text: Get job logs (same format as the Runner API).

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: POST /api/cli/jobs/{id}/cancel
records.text: Cancel a QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING job.

records.title: CLI APIs
records.heading: GET /api/cli/runners
records.text: List all registered Runners.

records.title: API Overview
records.text: API Overview. Alethia API endpoints — authentication methods, base URLs, and route categories.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: API Reference
records.text: Alethia exposes three categories of API routes, each with its own authentication mechanism.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: Authentication Methods
records.text:
Category Auth Header Token Type Used By 
 ---------- ----------- ------------ --------- 
 **Runner APIs** `X-Runner-ID` + `X-Runner-Token` SHA-256 hashed token Runner agents 
 **CLI APIs** `Authorization: Bearer {jwt}` HS256 JWT (1h access, 90d refresh) alethia CLI 
 **Release APIs** `Authorization: Bearer {secret}` Static secret (`RELEASE_API_SECRET`) CI/CD pipeline 

See [Authentication Flows](/concepts/authentication) for details on each mechanism.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: API Categories
records.text:
Job claiming, heartbeat, status updates, log streaming, plan artifacts.
 
 
 Configurations, jobs, runners, repositories.
 
 
 Device code flow: generate, exchange, refresh.

records.title: API Overview
records.heading: Request Format
records.text:
All APIs accept and return JSON. Errors return a consistent format:

{
 "error": "Human-readable error message"
}

HTTP status codes:
- `200` — success
- `201` — created
- `400` — validation error
- `401` — authentication failure
- `404` — not found
- `409` — conflict (e.g., duplicate release version)
- `500` — internal error

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.text: OIDC APIs. The public, unauthenticated discovery and JWKS endpoints of the Alethia workload-identity OIDC issuer.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: OIDC APIs
records.text:
Alethia is its own OpenID Connect identity provider for cloud workload-identity federation. It mints a short-lived, signed JWT so managed cloud connectors can federate **keylessly** — the private signing key never leaves the vault, and a customer's cloud verifies the token against Alethia's published public keys.

This surface is deliberately minimal. It has no interactive or user-facing endpoints — it is not a general OAuth server. Only two routes are public: the discovery document and the JWKS. Both serve static signed material.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Base URL
records.text:
The issuer is served under `/api/oidc` on the app origin. The full issuer URL is:

${APP_URL}/api/oidc

This value is the token `iss` claim and the URL a customer's cloud is configured to trust.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Authentication
records.text:
Both endpoints are **public, unauthenticated, and `GET`-only**. Anyone can fetch them. Only public key material is served — no private key fields are ever exposed.

Responses are cacheable:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=300

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Availability

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: GET /api/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration
records.text:
Returns the OIDC discovery document. A customer's cloud fetches this to locate the JWKS before verifying a minted token.

**Response:**

{
 "issuer": "https://app.example.com/api/oidc",
 "jwks_uri": "https://app.example.com/api/oidc/jwks",
 "response_types_supported": ["id_token"],
 "subject_types_supported": ["public"],
 "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": ["RS256"],
 "scopes_supported": ["openid"],
 "claims_supported": ["iss", "sub", "aud", "iat", "exp"]
}

Only `issuer` and `jwks_uri` are load-bearing for federation. The remaining fields satisfy the validators that fetch discovery.

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: GET /api/oidc/jwks

records.title: OIDC APIs
records.heading: Minted Token
records.text:
The issuer mints tokens server-side for a cloud's token exchange; there is no public token endpoint. The token is an RS256-signed JWT with these characteristics:

 Field Value 
 ------- ------- 
 `alg` (header) `RS256` 
 `kid` (header) Thumbprint of the signing key 
 `typ` (header) `JWT` 
 `iss` The issuer URL (`${APP_URL}/api/oidc`) 
 `sub` `alethia-connector` — a single stable, non-secret workload subject, never per-customer 
 `aud` The cloud's expected audience (for example `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, or the Alibaba OIDC client id) 
 `iat` Issued-at timestamp 
 `exp` Expiry — a maximum lifetime of 600 seconds 

The `sub` claim must match the Azure federated-credential subject and the Alibaba RAM-role OIDC condition. The `aud` claim scopes the token to one cloud so it cannot be replayed at a different cloud.

records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Auth APIs](/reference/api/auth-apis) — device code flow for CLI authentication.
- [Runner APIs](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethialabs/blob/dev/docs/contributing/runner-apis.md) — endpoints used by Runner agents.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.text: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO). Manage RBAC roles and access grants, and inspect SSO providers, from the alethia CLI.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: Access Control
records.text:
Alethia's authorization model has three CLI-manageable parts:

- **Roles** are permission bundles. Four **built-in** templates ship with every org
 (`owner`, `admin`, `operator`, `viewer`) and are read-only; **custom** roles are org-scoped
 and editable.
- **Grants** bind a **principal** (a user or a team) to a role **or** a single permission, at a
 resource scope, as an **allow** or an explicit **deny** (deny wins).
- **SSO providers** are the configured OIDC/SAML identity providers (read-only from the CLI).

All commands operate on the **active organization**, set with
[`alethia org switch`](/reference/cli/organizations), or on the organization named by the global
`--org ` for a single invocation. `--org` selects a scope rather than granting one: naming an
organization you are not a member of is refused with `403`. Every command accepts it, along with the
global [`-o, --output `](/reference/cli/identity#output-formats) and `--no-input` flags.

 
Authoring **custom roles** and **access grants** requires an **Enterprise** license. Listing roles
(the built-in templates) and reading SSO providers work on any plan. SSO provider secrets and
config JSON are never returned by the API.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia roles list
records.text:
Lists the active organization's roles — the four built-in templates (flagged) followed by any
custom roles, with a permission count.

alethia roles list
alethia roles list -o json

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia roles create
records.text:
Creates a custom role. Repeat `--permission` for each `resource:action` key the role should carry;
with no `--permission` on a terminal, the keys are offered as a checklist read from the control
plane's own catalog, so a permission added to the product appears here without a CLI release.

alethia roles create deployers --permission project:plan --permission project:deploy
alethia roles create

{/* fieldspec: alethia roles create */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Name What the custom role is called `[name]` — 
 Permissions The resource:action keys the role carries, offered from the server's own catalog `--permission` — 

A role with no permissions is accepted, so `--no-input` without `--permission` is not an error — it
creates a role that grants nothing yet.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia roles delete
records.text:
Deletes a custom role. Name it with `--name`, or pick from the org's custom roles; grants
referencing the role are removed with it.

alethia roles delete --name deployers --yes
alethia roles delete

{/* fieldspec: alethia roles delete */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Role Which custom role to delete; built-in templates cannot be deleted `[role_id]` `--name` 

The four built-in templates cannot be deleted. They are not offered in the picker and naming one
with `--name` is refused, because the control plane's delete filters them out and still answers
`ok` — so asking for one used to print `Role deleted` having changed nothing.

Destructive, so it confirms; `--yes` skips the prompt and is required with `--no-input`.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia grants list
records.text:
Lists the active organization's access grants.

alethia grants list
alethia grants list -o json

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia grants add
records.text:
Assigns a grant. A grant binds a principal to **exactly one** of a role (`--role`) or a single
permission (`--permission`), at a resource scope. Omit `--resource` for an **org-wide** grant.

`--principal` takes an **email** (or a team name) as readily as an id, and `--role` takes a **role
name**; anything that is not already a uuid is looked up against the active org. With no
`--principal` on a terminal, the whole grant is asked for, one question at a time.

alethia grants add --principal ada@example.com --role deployers
alethia grants add --principal platform --principal-type team --permission project:deploy --resource-type project
alethia grants add

With no `--principal` on a terminal you are asked for all seven, in order, and every one of them
that has a list behind it is a **picker over live values** — the members and teams of the org, its
roles or the server's permission catalog, and the projects, runners or cloud accounts of the kind
you scope to.

{/* fieldspec: alethia grants add */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Principal kind Whether the grant binds a user or a team `--principal-type` — 
 Principal Who the

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: The resource is picked, not typed
records.text:
Once you have chosen a **kind**, the form lists that kind's live resources and you choose one:
projects from `alethia project list`, runners from `alethia runner list`, cloud accounts from
`alethia connector list`. Nothing has to be copied out of another command's output.

Every one of those lists opens with **Every _kind_ in this organization** — the id-less scope, which
is what `--resource-type project` with no `--resource` has always meant and what `grants list`
renders as a bare `project`. Choosing it is how you grant over a whole kind.

The `org` kind asks nothing at all. `org` *is* org-wide: the control plane treats a grant as
org-wide when the kind is `org` **or** the id is absent, so an id given alongside `--resource-type
org` would be stored on the grant and then ignored by everything that reads it. `--resource` with
the `org` kind is therefore **refused** rather than sent — and since `org` is the default kind, that
refusal is what you get from `--resource ` with no `--resource-type`, which would otherwise have
granted over the whole organization while the command line read as one project.

A kind this CLI has no list for is still askable — you are asked for the id, and th

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia grants remove
records.text:
Revokes a grant. A grant has no name — it *is* the binding — so pass the id you have, or pick one
from the org's grants.

alethia grants remove --yes
alethia grants remove

{/* fieldspec: alethia grants remove */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Grant Which grant to revoke; pick it from the org's grants rather than copying an id `[grant_id]` — 

Destructive, so it confirms; `--yes` skips the prompt and is required with `--no-input`. When the
CLI picks the grant for you, it prints which one on stderr before it asks.

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia sso list
records.text:
Lists the active organization's configured SSO identity providers (OIDC and SAML). Read-only —
registering a provider is done in the console. Secrets and config JSON are never shown; `Enabled`
reflects whether the provider's domain is verified.

alethia sso list
alethia sso list -o json

records.title: Access (Roles, Grants & SSO)
records.heading: alethia sso get
records.text:
Shows a single provider as a detail card. Name it by the email domain it serves, or pick from the
org's providers.

alethia sso get --domain example.com
alethia sso get

{/* fieldspec: alethia sso get */}

 Field What it is Flag or argument Name it by 
 ----- ---------- ---------------- ---------- 
 Provider Which configured provider to show; name it by its email domain `[id]` `--domain`

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.text: Add-on Commands. Enable, reconfigure, disable and inspect the marketplace add-ons in a project environment.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Add-on Commands
records.text:
The `addon` group (alias `addons`) manages the **marketplace add-ons** (observability, databases,
caches, … — OSS Helm charts deployed via ArgoCD) in an environment: enable one, reconfigure it,
disable it, or list what is installed.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call `/cli/projects/ /addons`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**
(`alethia org switch`). Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different organization —
it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: No id is copied between commands
records.text:
`enable` and `disable` take the add-on id as an **optional** first argument. Omit it on a terminal
and the add-ons installed in the environment are offered to choose from, so nothing has to be read
out of one command's output and pasted into the next. The add-on the CLI resolved is printed on
**stderr**, so `-o json` still emits a document that parses.

Pass `--project` and the id is the only thing missing; omit `--project` too and you are asked for
that as well. With `--no-input` (or a non-terminal stdin/stdout) nothing is asked: the command
fails naming the argument to pass, so a script never blocks on a prompt it cannot answer.

 
One handoff remains, and it is the CLI's only one here: installing an add-on that is **not yet
enabled** needs its catalog id, and the CLI has no endpoint that enumerates the marketplace
catalog — browse it in the console. The picker offers what is installed, which covers every
reconfigure and every disable.

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon list
records.text:
List the add-ons installed in a project environment.

alethia addon list --project my-project
alethia addon list -p my-project -e staging
alethia addon list -p my-project -o json

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment name, stage, or id. Omit to use the project's default environment. 

Columns: **Add-on** (the catalog id), **Enabled** (✓ / —), **Mode** (`managed` `gitops`),
**Version**, **Status**, **Sync**, **Health**, **Last synced**.

**Sync, not Health, is the column to read first.** Health is the workload's own report — a chart
with no readiness probe reports `Healthy` the moment its pods schedule. Sync is whether ArgoCD has
applied the manifest the control plane asked for at all, so an add-on stuck `OutOfSync` is the
failure that otherwise looks like a working install. `Last synced` reads `never` for an add-on
whose Application has not synced once, which is a different statement from a sync whose timestamp
we could not read.

Add `-o json` for the full view, which also carries each add-on's `namespace`; `-o csv` for the
rows. Backing call:

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon enable
records.text:
Enable an add-on in an environment, or reconfigure one already enabled.

bash

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Reconfigure: pick from what is installed
records.text: alethia addon enable -p my-project

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Enable with the catalog defaults
records.text: alethia addon enable kube-prometheus-stack -p my-project

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: With settings, in one environment
records.text: alethia addon enable loki -p my-project -e staging --set retention_days=7

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: GitOps delivery: the manifest is written to your apps repo, and you own it
records.text: alethia addon enable falco -p my-project --mode gitops

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: Advanced: a raw Helm values override
records.text:
alethia addon enable loki -p my-project --values-file ./loki-values.yaml

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[addon-id]` No Catalog id (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from the installed add-ons. 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment name, stage, or id. Omit for the project's default. 
 `--mode` No Delivery mode: `managed` (Alethia applies it) or `gitops` (written to your apps repo). 
 `--set` `key=value` No An add-on setting. Repeatable; values are JSON-typed when they parse. 
 `--values-file` No Path to a raw Helm values YAML override (Advanced). 

`--mode` is checked against the `addon_mode` database enum before anything is sent, so a typo is
refused by name instead of costing a round trip; the two spellings are matched case-insensitively.

Re-running `enable` on an installed add-on **updates** it. Settings are merged over what is stored,
so you can change one value without restating the rest — and a secret you do not resend is
preserved rather than blanked.

Each add-on's settings are validated against **that add-on's own schema**, server-side, so an
u

records.title: Add-on Commands
records.heading: alethia addon disable
records.text:
Disable an add-on in an environment.

alethia addon disable falco -p my-project -e staging
alethia addon disable falco -p my-project --yes
alethia addon disable -p my-project

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[addon-id]` No Catalog id (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from the installed add-ons. 
 `--project`, `-p` No Project name or id. Omit it on a terminal and you are asked. 
 `--env`, `-e` No Environment name, stage, or id. 
 `--yes`, `-y` No Skip the confirmation prompt. Required with `--no-input`. 

 
 Disabling removes the add-on's workloads from the cluster on the next sync. Data held in its
 volumes may not survive — take a backup first if it matters. The add-on the CLI resolved is
 named on stderr **before** the confirmation, so what you are confirming is always something you
 can read. The command requires `--yes` when it cannot prompt, and fails rather than exiting 0
 having done nothing.

- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.text: Agent Commands. Inspect agent identities — machine/agent personas scoped to your account or organization.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: Agent Commands
records.text:
The `agent` group (alias `agents`) reads **agent identities** — machine/agent personas, each with a
persona, a mission, an allowed tool scope, and a memory namespace, scoped to your account or org.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call `/cli/agents[/…]` with your
[CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and resolve within your tenancy — an agent id from another org
returns not-found, never its persona/mission.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: No id is copied between commands
records.text:
`get` takes the agent id as an **optional** first argument. Omit it on a terminal and the
identities you can see are offered to choose from, so the id never has to be read out of
`agent list` and pasted back in. The identity the CLI resolved is printed on **stderr**, so
`-o json` still emits a document that parses.

Only an **id** is accepted as the argument, and it is passed through byte for byte. A persona is
not resolved to an id on purpose: personas are not unique, so "the one whose persona matches"
would silently read a different identity the day a second agent takes the same persona. With
`--no-input` (or a non-terminal stdin/stdout) nothing is asked and the command fails naming the
argument to pass.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: alethia agent list
records.text:
List the agent identities you can see.

alethia agent list
alethia agent list -o json

Columns: **ID**, **Persona**, **Tools** (count of allowed tools), **Namespace** (memory
namespace), **Version**. Add `-o json` for the raw objects. Backing call: `GET /cli/agents`.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: alethia agent get
records.text:
Show one agent identity's persona, mission, and tool scope.

alethia agent get
alethia agent get ag_01J8Z9QK3F
alethia agent get ag_01J8Z9QK3F -o json

 Argument Required Description 
 ---------- ---------- ------------- 
 `[agent-id]` No The agent identity's id. Omit it on a terminal to pick from a list. 

Renders a field/value card: **id**, **persona**, **mission**, **tool scope** (the allowed tools),
**namespace**, **project** (the project it is scoped to, or `—` for an org-wide identity),
**created**, **version**. Add `-o json` for the full object. Backing call:
`GET /cli/agents/ `.

records.title: Agent Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text: - [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Authentication
records.text: Authentication. Device Authorization Grant flow for people, service-account tokens for pipelines, token storage, and automatic refresh.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Authentication
records.text:
alethia authenticates two ways, for two different callers:

- **You, at a terminal** — the **Device Authorization Grant** (RFC 8628). You never type a password.
- **A pipeline** — a **service-account token**, supplied through `$ALETHIA_TOKEN`. No browser, no prompt.

For why the CLI authenticates this way, see [Authentication flows](/concepts/authentication); for
the protocol, its endpoints and its deviations from RFC 8628, see
[Device Authorization Grant](/reference/standards/device-code).

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Login
records.text:
alethia login

1. The CLI prints a short `user_code` and opens your browser at the Console's `/cli/login` page.
2. Sign in there with any OAuth provider (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Google) or email OTP, if you are
 not already. The page names the account that is about to be bound, what approval hands over, who
 is asking and how long is left.
3. Check that the code on screen is the one your terminal printed, then approve. Nothing is typed
 back into the terminal.
4. The CLI, which has been waiting with a spinner, receives an access and refresh token pair and
 saves it to `~/.config/alethia/credentials.json`.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Refusing a login you did not start
records.text:
If the code on screen is not the one your terminal printed, or you did not run `alethia login` at all,
press **This isn't me**.

That records the refusal in Console rather than only in the browser. Three things follow:

- The device that is polling is told at once, with the standard `access_denied` error, instead of waiting
 out its own timeout.
- Nothing is handed over — no access token, no refresh token, and none of your linked git provider's
 OAuth token.
- The refusal is final for that link. Opening it again cannot approve it; a genuine sign-in needs a fresh
 `alethia login`.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Force Re-authentication
records.text:
alethia login --force

Re-authenticates even if a valid token already exists. Useful when switching accounts.

On a terminal you do not need the flag. If you are already signed in, `alethia login` names the account
and asks whether to keep that session or sign in again. **Keep this session** is the first option, so
pressing Enter changes nothing. With `--no-input`, or with no terminal, the command asks nothing: it
prints the account, keeps the session and exits 0. Pass `--force` to sign in again from a script.

A first sign-in asks no question. The control-plane URL is not asked for here: pass `--web-origin`, or
use `alethia init` for the guided first-run setup.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Logout
records.text:
alethia logout

Removes `~/.config/alethia/credentials.json` and the kubeconfig credential cache, for every
organization. After that, an exec kubeconfig from `alethia cluster kubeconfig` fails until you run
`alethia login` again. If the CLI cannot delete the cache, `alethia logout` prints the reason and
exits with a non-zero status. See
[Revoke access](/guides/get-a-kubeconfig#revoke-access).

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Token Lifecycle
records.text:
Token TTL Purpose 
 ------- ----- --------- 
 Access token 1 hour `Authorization: Bearer` header on API calls 
 Refresh token 90 days Obtain new access tokens transparently 

Before each API call, alethia checks the access token's expiry and refreshes it automatically when it
is within a minute of expiring — see [Refresh](/reference/standards/device-code#refresh). You never
notice it.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Identity & Active Org
records.text:
After logging in, confirm who you are signed in as and which organization the CLI is scoped to:

alethia whoami # user, active org, role, plan, default runner
alethia config # control-plane URL, active org, on-disk file paths

The active organization is sent as the `X-Alethia-Org` header on every request. Set or change it
with `alethia org switch`. See [Identity & Global Options](/reference/cli/identity) and
[Organizations, Members & Teams](/reference/cli/organizations).

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Running in CI
records.text:
The device flow needs a browser and a person, so a pipeline cannot use it. Mint a **service-account
token** instead:

alethia token create --name "github-actions"

The token is printed **once**, on stdout, with everything else on stderr — so you can pipe it
straight into a secret store without selecting it by eye:

alethia token create --name "github-actions" gh secret set ALETHIA_TOKEN

Then set `ALETHIA_TOKEN` in your job and use the CLI normally. Nothing is written to disk, and no
`alethia login` is needed:

- name: Deploy staging
 env:
 ALETHIA_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ALETHIA_TOKEN }}
 run: 
 alethia project apply --env staging --wait --no-input

Pair it with `--no-input`, which makes the CLI fail rather than prompt — together they mean a job
never hangs waiting for an answer nobody is there to give.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: What a service token can do
records.text:
A token **acts as the person who created it**, inside the **one organization** it was minted for.
That org is fixed when the token is created: an `X-Alethia-Org` header that disagrees with it is
refused, not ignored, so a token issued for one organization can never act on another.

It also stops working the moment its creator leaves that organization — membership is re-checked on
every request, not trusted from when the token was minted.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Minting a token
records.text:
Run `alethia token create` on a terminal with no flags and it asks for the two things it needs:

{/* fieldspec: alethia token create */}

 Field What it is Set without the form 
 --- --- --- 
 Name What this token is for, so a list of tokens is a list of purposes `--name` 
 Expires A token that never expires is a credential nobody remembers to rotate `--expires-in-days` 

The flags are the complete contract: anything the form can ask, a flag can set, so
`--no-input` never needs a prompt.

alethia token create # asks for the name and the lifetime
alethia token create --name ci --expires-in-days 90 # the same, unattended

`--expires-in-days 0` — the default — never expires. That is a deliberate choice rather than an
oversight, and it is why the form asks: a credential with no end date is one nobody remembers to
rotate.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Managing tokens
records.text:
alethia token list # id, name, prefix, created, expires, last used, status
alethia token revoke # pick from the live tokens, or pass an id

`alethia token list` shows `last used: never` for a token nothing has ever presented. That is usually
the most interesting row on the list — a credential that was minted, put somewhere, and forgotten.

`alethia token revoke` with no argument shows the tokens that are still live and revokes the one you
pick, so you never have to copy an opaque id out of `token list` by eye. Already-revoked tokens are
left out of the picker; revoking one again does nothing.

{/* fieldspec: alethia token revoke */}

 Field What it is Set without the form 
 --- --- --- 
 Token The token to revoke; it stops working on its very next request `[id]` 

alethia token revoke # pick from a list
alethia token revoke 3f2b9c14-7a1e-4d68-9c05-2b8e6a1d40f7 # revoke a known id, no prompt

 
Revoke carries **no `--yes`**, unlike every other destructive command. Its asymmetry runs the other
way: revoking a token you did not mean to costs one `alethia token create`, while failing to revoke a
leaked one costs the organization. A confirmation here would fail an incident-response pipe

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Environment Variables
records.text:
Variable Default Purpose 
 ---------- --------- --------- 
 `ALETHIA_WEB_ORIGIN` Production URL (baked at build) Override the Alethia API URL 
 `ALETHIA_TOKEN` unset A service-account token for non-interactive use. When set, the CLI uses it and never reads or writes the credentials file. 

alethia login # authenticates against local dev server

The `--token` flag does the same thing as `$ALETHIA_TOKEN` and takes precedence over it. Prefer the
environment variable in CI: a flag value lands in the process table and in shell history, where an
environment variable does not.

records.title: Authentication
records.heading: Token Storage
records.text:
~/.config/alethia/credentials.json

{
 "access_token": "eyJ...",
 "refresh_token": "eyJ...",
 "user_email": "you@example.com"
}

The access-token expiry is read from the JWT itself (the `exp` claim), so no separate timestamp is
stored. The active-org context is kept separately in `~/.config/alethia/config.json` (see
[Configuration](/reference/cli/configuration)).

 
This file contains authentication tokens. It is not encrypted — protect it with filesystem permissions.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.text: Billing, Usage & Fleet. Inspect the active organization's billing and usage, and configure managed-fleet warm pools, from the alethia CLI.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.text:
Three related views into an organization's plan and the platform's provisioning capacity:

- **`billing`** — the active organization's plan, subscription status, seats, and period boundaries.
- **`usage`** — current consumption: seats, runner-minutes, projects, and AI credits.
- **`fleet`** — the managed pool of warm provisioning runners (platform-operator config).

`billing` and `usage` operate on the **active organization** (set via `alethia org switch`), or on
the organization named by the global `--org ` for a single invocation — which is refused with
`403` if you are not a member of it. Every command accepts the global
[`-o, --output `](/reference/cli/identity#output-formats) flag.

 
`billing` and `usage` are **read-only** — manage the subscription, cards, and invoices in the
console. No Stripe customer ids or charge amounts are ever returned by the CLI.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia billing
records.text:
Shows the active organization's billing state as a detail card: its plan, subscription status, the
purchased seat count, the Stripe subscription id, and the trial / current-period boundaries. An
organization with no subscription reads as the free `community` plan.

alethia billing
alethia billing -o json

 Field Meaning 
 -------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------- 
 `Plan` `community`, `team`, or `enterprise` 
 `Status` Subscription status (`active`, `trialing`, `none`, …) 
 `Seats` Purchased seats (per-seat plans); a dash on flat/no subscription 
 `Subscription` Stripe subscription id, if any 
 `Trial ends` When a `trialing` subscription's trial ends 
 `Period ends` End of the current paid period

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia usage
records.text:
Shows the active organization's current usage as a detail card: billable seats used vs the purchased
cap, managed-runner minutes consumed this period, the project count, and AI credits used in the
trailing week vs the plan's weekly grant.

alethia usage
alethia usage -o json

 Field Meaning 
 ---------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 
 `Seats` Billable seats used **/** purchased cap 
 `Runner minutes` Managed-runner minutes consumed this billing period, written for a person: `0 min`, `47 min`, `2h 15m` 
 `Projects` Projects in the organization 
 `AI credits` Included AI credits used this week **/** the weekly grant 

 
`Runner minutes` has no **/ cap** beside it, unlike `Seats` and `AI credits`. The usage API returns
a consumed figure and no runner-minute allowance, so the CLI shows what you have used and does not
state an allowance nobody sent. The console's usage page reads the allowance from the plan
catalogue; see **Settings → Usage** there for minutes used against minutes included.
 

Use `-o json` or `-o csv` when a script needs the raw counters. Only the card is written for a
person: `runner_minutes` is a plain integer of

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia fleet
records.text:
The **managed fleet** is the platform's pool of warm provisioning runners — one pool per cloud — that
the Fleet Controller reconciles toward a declarative target (warm floor, ceiling, locations, version).

 
Fleet configuration is **platform-operator infrastructure** (the pools are global, not per-org). It
is only available on **self-managed deployments**, to organization **owners/admins**. On the hosted
service `fleet list` returns an empty list, and `fleet set` is refused.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia fleet list
records.text:
Lists the configured warm pools. On a TTY this opens the interactive table; with `--output json csv`
(or `--no-input`) it prints a static table.

alethia fleet list
alethia fleet list -o json

Columns: `Provider`, `Enabled`, `Warm` (floor), `Max` (ceiling), `Slots` (concurrent jobs per
runner), `Locations`, and `Version` (a pinned version, or the tracked channel). The command takes
no input of its own.

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: alethia fleet set
records.text:
Updates the warm pool for one cloud. Only the flags you pass are changed; the rest keep their
stored value. A pinned `--version` and a release `--channel` are **mutually exclusive** — a version
pin clears the channel.

The provider is optional at a terminal: omit it and you choose from the clouds Alethia knows —
`aws`, `azure`, `gcp`, `alibaba`, `digitalocean`, `hetzner`, `civo`. That list is the product's own
`cloud_provider` set rather than a list typed into this page, and **nothing is refused on it**:
which of those clouds a given deployment's fleet controller actually serves is the server's answer,
not the CLI's.

bash

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Choose the cloud at a terminal
records.text: alethia fleet set --warm-min 2

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Raise the AWS pool's warm floor and ceiling
records.text: alethia fleet set aws --warm-min 2 --max 20

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Pin a runner version (clears any tracked channel)
records.text: alethia fleet set gcp --version v1.4.0

records.title: Billing, Usage & Fleet
records.heading: Pause a pool (drains its runners — prompts for confirmation)
records.text:
alethia fleet set azure --enabled=false

{/* fieldspec: alethia fleet set */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Provider Which cloud's warm pool to configure; omit it to choose from the clouds Alethia supports `[provider]` 
 Warm floor How many runners stay provisioned with no work to do `--warm-min` 
 Ceiling The most instances the controller may ever run for this cloud `--max` 
 Slots per runner How many provisioning jobs one runner takes at once `--slots` 
 Enabled Whether the controller provisions for this cloud at all; disabling drains it `--enabled` 
 Release channel A runner channel to track, e.g. stable; mutually exclusive with a pinned version `--channel` 
 Pinned version An exact runner version to hold this pool at; setting it clears the channel `--version` 

 
Disabling a pool drains its runners (a capacity reduction), so `fleet set --enabled=false` prompts
for confirmation on a TTY — and the prompt names the cloud, because with the picker the CLI may
have chosen it. Scripted, pass `--yes`; `--no-input` alone now **fails** rather than exiting 0
having done nothing.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.text: Chart Commands. Attach, scan, list and detach the BYO Helm charts on a project environment.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: Chart Commands
records.text:
The `chart` group (alias `charts`) manages your **BYO Helm charts** — your own charts, pulled from a
connected git repo or an OCI registry and deployed into an environment through ArgoCD alongside the
marketplace add-ons.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These commands call `/cli/projects/PROJECT/byo-charts`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: Common flags
records.text:
Every command in the group takes the same two selectors. They are registered on the group, so they
work in any position.

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Project The project, by name or id; omit it on a terminal and you are asked `--project` 
 Environment The environment, by name, stage or id; empty means the project's default `--env` 

`--project` has the short form `-p` and `--env` has `-e`. On a terminal, omitting `--project` opens
the project picker; with `--no-input`, with `-o json`, or with the output redirected to a file, it
is required — a form drawn into a redirected stream would corrupt the document you are piping.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart list
records.text:
List the BYO Helm charts attached to a project environment.

alethia chart list --project my-project
alethia chart list -p my-project -e staging
alethia chart list -p my-project -o json

Columns: **Chart** (its per-env id and release name), **Repo** (the git or OCI URL), **Path** (the
chart directory, a dash for an OCI chart), **Ref** (the git ref, a dash when it tracks the default
branch), **Status**, **Scan** (chart-safety scan lifecycle: `unscanned`, `scanning`, `done`,
`failed`). Add `-o json` for the full view — the Elench scan report itself is console-only — or
`-o csv` for the rows. The dashes in **Path** and **Ref** are for a person reading a column; under
`-o csv` a chart that has neither gets an empty cell, the same split `alethia config get` makes.
Backing call: `GET /cli/projects/PROJECT/byo-charts`.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart attach
records.text:
Attach a chart from your own repository — git or OCI — to one environment.

alethia chart attach api -p shop -e dev --repo https://github.com/acme/charts --chart-path charts/api --ref v1.2.3
alethia chart attach api -p shop --repo oci://registry.example.com/acme/api
alethia chart attach api -p shop --repo https://github.com/acme/charts --chart-path charts/api --set replicas=2 --values-file ./api-values.yaml

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart attach */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Chart id Your name for this chart; the server slugifies it and the result is the id every later command uses `[id]` 
 Repository Where the chart lives — a git URL, or an oci:// reference to a chart registry `--repo` 
 Chart path Where the chart sits inside a git repository; an OCI chart is named by its URL and needs none `--chart-path` 
 Git ref The branch, tag or commit to deploy; empty tracks the repository's default branch `--ref` 
 Namespace The destination namespace; empty lets the environment place it `--namespace` 
 Values file A path on this machine to a raw Helm values YAML override, sent as the file's content `--values-file` 
 Chart value One key=value chart value, repeatable, JSO

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: The interactive path
records.text:
Run `alethia chart attach` on a terminal with nothing else and it asks for each field it was not
given. A flag you did pass is never questioned again, so a half-written command finishes itself.

The **repository is chosen, not typed**: the form asks which connected provider to look in, then
offers the repositories Alethia can already see, with `Type a URL instead…` at the bottom of the
list for anything else. That is the whole reason this form exists — the URL used to be something you
read off `alethia repo list` and typed back in. If no provider is connected, or the listing fails,
the question falls back to a plain typed line rather than refusing the attach.

`--chart-path` is asked for git repositories only: an OCI chart is named by its URL's last segment.

The run finishes by printing the flags that would have produced the same result, so the command you
answered once is the command you can commit to a repository.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: With --no-input
records.text:
Nothing is asked, and the chart id and `--repo` are required. Leaving one out fails and names it.
Every field above has a flag, so any attach the form can perform, a script can perform.

 
 **A private repository needs no credential flag.** The runner fetches a short-lived token at job
 time from your linked GitHub or GitLab account, scoped to the repositories this project declares,
 and refreshed per job — so nothing is stored against the chart. Link that account once in the
 console and private repositories work.
 

Re-attaching the same id **updates** it, so this is also how you move a chart to a new ref. The
success line echoes the id the server stored, because it slugifies what you send.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart scan
records.text:
alethia chart scan api -p shop -e dev
alethia chart scan -p shop -e dev

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart scan */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Chart Which attached chart to scan; an unscanned chart is refused at deploy `[id]` 

An attached chart is **not deployable until it has been scanned**: the scan renders it and records
the verdict the plan-time gate reads. Re-scan whenever the chart's repository moves.

The id is optional. Omit it on a terminal and the environment's attached charts are offered, so
nothing is copied out of `alethia chart list`. The scan is asynchronous: the queued job id is
printed, and `alethia jobs logs --latest --follow` tails it without repeating that id back.

records.title: Chart Commands
records.heading: alethia chart detach
records.text:
alethia chart detach api -p shop -e dev
alethia chart detach api -p shop --yes

{/* fieldspec: alethia chart detach */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Chart Which attached chart to detach; its workloads leave the cluster on the next sync `[id]` 

Like `chart scan`, the id is optional on a terminal and the attached charts are offered instead.

 
 Detaching removes the chart's workloads from the cluster on the next sync. The command confirms
 first, and the confirmation **names the chart it resolved to** — including the one you picked from
 the list. With `--no-input`, or when stdin is not a terminal, `--yes` is required and the command
 fails without it rather than cancelling quietly.
 

 
 These commands need `ALETHIA_BYO_HELM_ENABLED=true` on the instance. Without it they return **501**
 with the variable named, rather than a permissions error you would go looking for in vain.

records.heading: See also
records.text:

- [IaC Commands](/reference/cli/iac) — your BYO Terraform/OpenTofu source.
- [Repository Commands](/reference/cli/repositories) — the repositories the pickers offer.
