records.title: Probe Commands
records.text: Probe Commands. Inspect a project's cluster-alive probes — the "is it still up?" day-2 signal per environment.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.heading: Probe Commands
records.text:
The `probes` group (alias `probe`) lists the latest **cluster-alive probe** per environment — the
"is it still up?" half of day-2, alongside [drift](/reference/cli/drift)'s "has it diverged?". A
`PROBE_CLUSTER` job dials each environment's cluster API server; this shows the most recent result.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. `probes list` calls `/cli/projects/ /probes`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on the **active organization**, which you
change with `alethia org switch`. Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different
organization — it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.heading: alethia probes list
records.text:
List a project's latest per-environment cluster probes.

alethia probes list
alethia probes list --project my-project
alethia probes list -p my-project -o json

Name the project with `--project`; omit it at a terminal and you are asked which project to read,
from the ones you have.

{/* fieldspec: alethia probes list */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Whose environments to report the latest cluster probe for `--project` 

Columns: **Environment**, **Reachable** (`● up`, `○ down`, or `— never probed`), **Message** (why
unreachable, when down), **Probed** (when the last probe ran, to the minute in UTC). Every
environment is listed; one that has never been probed shows `never probed` rather than being
hidden.

Environment Reachable Message Probed
production ● up — 2026-01-01 00:00
staging ○ down dial tcp: timeout 2026-01-01 00:00
dev — never probed — —

Add `-o json` for the raw probe objects — the `probed_at` there is the wire's unrounded RFC 3339
timestamp, not the table's rendering; `-o csv` for the rows. Backing call:
`GET /cli/projects/ /probes`.

records.title: Probe Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Drift Commands](/reference/cli/drift) — the divergence half of day-2.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Project Commands
records.text: Project Commands. Create, inspect, author and provision projects from the CLI.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Project Commands
records.text:
Projects are infrastructure configurations (an *app* that owns one or more environments). The CLI
can both **read** projects (`list`, `get`) and **author** them — create a project, manage its
environments, and CRUD its component resources — so the whole project lifecycle is scriptable.

All authoring commands operate on the **active organization** (set via `alethia org switch`), or on
the organization named by the global `--org ` for a single invocation — which is refused with
`403` if you are not a member of it. Every command accepts the global
`-o, --output ` flag.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Two rules that hold for every command on this page
records.text:
**Nothing has to be copied out of another command's output.** Every reference takes the name you
already know: `--project` takes a project's name *or* its id, `--cloud-account` takes a cloud
account's label *or* its id, and `--env` takes an environment's name, stage or id. Omit one on a
terminal and you are asked, from a picker of what actually exists.

**Every question has a flag.** The interactive paths below exist so you do not have to assemble
anything by hand — they never let you say something a flag cannot. After a run that asked you
questions, the CLI prints the exact command that reproduces it, so what you answered once can be
committed to a repository:

Same result, without the questions:
 alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account

The one thing a flag cannot say is a list of environments, so a run that declared an environment
matrix through the form prints back the `alethia.yaml` its answers add up to — the file
[`alethia apply`](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply) reads. So `--no-input` always works, and so does a
pipe.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project list
records.text:
List all projects in the active organization.

alethia project list
alethia project list --output json

On a terminal this is the shared navigable table (sort, filter, quit); piped or with
`--output json csv` it is a plain projection.

 Column Description 
 ------ ---------- 
 Project Project name 
 Env The default environment's stage 
 Status Provisioning status 
 Provider Cloud provider 
 Region Cloud region 
 Cost Estimated monthly cost 
 Updated Last change 

**Status**, **Provider**, **Region** and **Cost** are rendered for a person: the status carries a
glyph and is folded to lower case, the provider is upper-cased, an unset provider or region is `—`,
and a project the wire sent no status for reads as `draft` — an inference that tells a reader the
project has not been applied yet, rather than leaving a blank that looks like a broken table.

Under `-o csv` a script gets the values instead: each is the wire value, and each is an **empty
cell when the wire sent nothing** — including the status, because handing a script a status the
server never sent is the one thing a machine format must not do. **Cost** is a bare number and
**Updated** an RFC3339 stamp.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project get
records.text:
Print a project's full configuration.

alethia project get boutique
alethia project get boutique --open
alethia project get # asks which project

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[project_name]` No Project name (positional). Omit it on a terminal to pick from a list. 
 `--open` No Open the project in the web console. (Long-only — `-o` is the global `--output` flag.) 

 
 `get` looks a project up by **name**, so the picker returns a name and refuses one that two
 projects share — that lookup answers a duplicate with whichever project is older, and quietly
 printing another project's region, cluster endpoint and apps repo is worse than an error. Every
 other command takes `--project`, which resolves a name **or** an id.
 

Shows the full project configuration including:
- Project name, provider, region, environment
- Status and estimated monthly cost
- Component summary (network, cluster, databases, caches, etc.)
- Cloud identity reference

When run interactively without `--open`, the CLI offers to open the project in the browser after
printing it.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project create
records.text:
Create a new project in the active organization.

alethia project create # asks for everything, prints the file back

or say it all at once:

alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account

or from the manifest in the current directory, which also declares the environment matrix:

alethia project create --file alethia.yaml

The file in the current directory is read even when `--file` is not passed, and the command prints
the line naming it. A script that must not be steered by whatever `alethia.yaml` happens to be in
the tree passes `--no-manifest`.

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[name]` Yes* Project name (positional). *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--region` Yes* Cloud region to provision into. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--cloud-account` No Cloud account to link, by its **label** or its id. Asked for on a terminal when omitted; a project may be created with none. 
 `--stage` No Initial environment stage: `development` (default), `staging`, `production` 
 `--iac-version` No OpenTofu version to pin (defaults server-side) 
 `--placement-mode` No Placement of the default environment

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Node shape
records.text:
Without `--instance-type` or `--node-size`, the project's cluster gets the catalog's default machine
type for its cloud: `t3.large` on AWS, `e2-standard-2` on Google Cloud, `Standard_D2s_v5` on Azure,
`cpx22` on Hetzner and `ecs.g6.large` on Alibaba Cloud. Pass one of the two flags to choose the node
yourself:

alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account --instance-type t3.xlarge
alethia project create boutique --region eu-west-1 --cloud-account prod-account --node-size 4x16

The shape applies to every `dedicated` environment, because only a dedicated environment provisions
a cluster. A `namespace` or `vcluster` environment runs on the cluster of the environment it is
placed on. The two flags are mutually exclusive, and a create where no environment is `dedicated`
refuses them. To change the shape later, set the cluster's `instance_types` with
`alethia project component add --kind cluster`, which updates the existing cluster.

The created project prints as a card (or the typed object with `--output json`), followed —
when anything was asked for — by the `alethia project create` line that would produce the same
project without the questions. That

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The environment matrix
records.text:
Every environment and **how each is placed onto a Fabric** is declared in `alethia.yaml`, under
`environments:`. The first entry is the default environment and owns the Fabric it provisions, so
it defaults to `dedicated`; later entries default to `namespace` and share that Fabric.

project: shop
cloud:
 account: prod-account
 region: eu-west-1
environments:
 - name: prod
 stage: production
 - name: dev
 stage: development
 namespace: boutique-dev
 - name: staging
 stage: staging
 placement: vcluster

That is **one** cluster hosting three environments. With no manifest and no terminal you get the
default Production + Preview pair instead; on a terminal you are asked for each environment in
turn — name, stage, placement, namespace — and then shown the file your answers add up to, to
save as `alethia.yaml`.

A stage or a placement outside the allowed set is refused locally, naming the whole set, rather
than coming back as a `400`. The file's full reference, components included, is on
[Plan & Apply](/reference/cli/plan-and-apply#alethiayaml).

 
 Placement is the flag with a bill attached. Each `dedicated` environment is a separate cluster with
 its own OpenTofu state; `namespace` and

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project plan · apply · destroy
records.text:
Queue a `PLAN`, `DEPLOY` or `DESTROY` job for one environment of a project.

alethia project plan --project boutique --env dev-1 --runner eu-box --wait
alethia project apply --project boutique --env dev-1 --latest-plan --wait
alethia project destroy --project boutique --yes

Omit `--project` on a terminal and you are asked which project; omit the runner and you are
asked which one (or "Any available"). `destroy` takes the runner by id only, for now.

 Flag plan apply destroy Description 
 ------ ------ ------- --------- ------------- 
 `--project` ✓ ✓ ✓ Project by **name** or id. Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--project-id` ✓ ✓ ✓ Project id. Prefer `--project`, which also takes the name. 
 `--env` ✓ ✓ ✓ Target environment name (default: the project's default environment) 
 `--runner` ✓ ✓ Runner by **name** or id. Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--runner-id` ✓ ✓ ✓ Runner id. Prefer `--runner`, which also takes the name. 
 `--plan-job-id` ✓ Apply a specific `PLAN` job, by id 
 `--latest-plan` ✓ Apply the project's most recent `PLAN` job 
 `-w`, `--wait` ✓ ✓ ✓ Wait for job completion 
 `-y`, `--yes` ✓ Skip the confirmation prompt (required with `--no-input`) 
 `--ca

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Applying the plan you just reviewed
records.text:
`--latest-plan` resolves the project's own most recent `PLAN` job, so a review-then-apply pass
never moves a uuid between two commands:

alethia project plan --project boutique --env prod --wait
alethia project apply --project boutique --env prod --latest-plan --wait

It prints which job it chose before it queues anything. Three things it deliberately does **not**
do:

- It is **opt-in**. Without it (or `--plan-job-id`) the deploy runs its own plan, which is the
 ordinary path — a plan reference is a mode, not a hint: the Runner refuses a deploy whose plan
 did not succeed, or whose configuration moved since the plan was taken.
- It resolves `PLAN` jobs **only**. The project's most recent job is as likely to be the `DEPLOY`
 that followed the plan.
- It takes the most recent `PLAN` **whatever its status**, and refuses when that is not `SUCCESS`,
 naming the job and its status. Skipping past a plan that is still running would apply an older
 one you never asked for.

`--plan-job-id` is still there for a plan you already hold the id of.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project design apply
records.text:
The declarative counterpart to `project component add`. The imperative commands are what you narrate
one step at a time; a design document is what a repository commits and CI replays. Both write the same
tables.

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The document, as it is now
records.text: alethia config export -p shop --out shop.json

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: See what would change — writes NOTHING
records.text: alethia project design apply -p shop -e dev -f shop.json --dry-run

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Apply it
records.text: alethia project design apply -p shop -e dev -f shop.json

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Or send it to the staged-changes tray for review instead
records.text: alethia project design apply -p shop -e dev -f shop.json --stage

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: From a pipe
records.text:
cat shop.json alethia project design apply -p shop -f -

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `-f`, `--file` Yes* Design document path, or `-` for stdin. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `-p`, `--project` Yes* Project name or id. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `-e`, `--env` No Environment name, stage, or id. Omit for the project's default. 
 `--dry-run` No Print the changes that would be made and write nothing. 
 `--stage` No Stage the change for review instead of applying it. 
 `-y`, `--yes` No Confirm an apply whose plan **removes** a component. Required with `--no-input` only in that case. 

Both `--dry-run` and a real apply print one row per component with the action taken:

3 change(s) would be made in dev:
 UPDATE databases orders
 CREATE caches sessions
 DELETE storage_buckets receipts

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The gate is on the plan, not on the command
records.text:
An apply can **delete**: a kind the document omits is a kind the environment loses. So the
confirmation appears exactly where that happens, and nowhere else.

- A plan that only **adds or updates** applies unprompted, including under `--no-input`. A design
 document is what a repository commits and CI replays, and a pipeline that adds a cache does not
 need a human in it.
- A plan that **removes** a component prints what would go, then confirms. Under `--no-input` it
 requires `-y`, `--yes`.

To decide which it is, a real apply asks the server for its own `--dry-run` first, so the prompt
names the components rather than asking in the abstract:

This apply would DELETE 1 component(s) in dev:
 DELETE storage_buckets receipts

If that check cannot be read at all, the apply is **refused** rather than run blind — `--yes`
applies without it.

 
 `--yes` on a `design apply` is not a blanket "this command is destructive" switch. It opts *that
 invocation* into removing components. Leaving it on a pipeline permanently means every later
 replay may remove components too; if a replay is suddenly asking for it, the usual cause is a
 document that stopped declaring something you meant to keep.

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project env
records.text:
A project owns N independently-provisionable environments. The project is named with `--project`
(its name **or** id); omit it on a terminal and you are asked.

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: List a project's environments
records.text: alethia project env list --project boutique

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Add one, answering the same four questions the --env tuple asks
records.text: alethia project env add --project boutique

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Or say it outright
records.text: alethia project env add staging --project boutique --stage staging

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: As a vcluster on a named Fabric, with its own destination namespace
records.text:
alethia project env add staging --project shop --stage staging \
 --placement-mode vcluster --fabric shared --namespace boutique-staging

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: One that provisions its OWN cluster
records.text:
alethia project env add prod --project shop --stage production --placement-mode dedicated

 Command Flags Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `env list` `--project` List the project's environments (default first) 
 `env add [name]` `--project` `--stage` `--region` `--placement-mode` `--fabric` `--namespace` `--lifecycle` Add an environment (name is slugified; region inherits the project's when omitted) 

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--project` Yes* Project name or id. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--stage` No `development` (default), `staging`, `production` 
 `--placement-mode` No `namespace` (default), `vcluster`, `dedicated` 
 `--namespace` No ArgoCD destination namespace for a shared placement (default: derived from the name) 
 `--fabric` No Fabric to place onto, by name (default: the one the project's default environment is on) 
 `--region` No Region (inherits the project's when omitted) 
 `--lifecycle` No `persistent` (default) or `ephemeral` 

An **added** environment defaults to `namespace` placement on the Fabric the project's default
environment already uses — the cheap rung, and the one that makes a second tier fr

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: alethia project component
records.text:
One uniform group authors **all** of a project's component resources. The project is named with
`--project`, and the environment with `--env`.

**Which kinds exist is published by the server, and `component kinds` is how you read it.** This
page used to list them, and that list drifted: it named thirteen while the server accepted fourteen.
A kind has one of two cardinalities — **singleton** (one per project *per environment*, name-less) or
**multi** (named, many per environment) — and `kinds` prints each with its own, so the answer to
"does this one need a `--name`" comes from the same place as the list itself.

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: List the supported kinds
records.text: alethia project component kinds

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: List a project's components (optionally filter by --kind and/or --env)
records.text: alethia project component list --project boutique --kind databases

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Add one by answering questions — kind, name, environment, then field by field
records.text: alethia project component add --project boutique

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Or say it outright. Multi kind → --name required
records.text:
alethia project component add --project boutique --kind databases --name main \
 --set engine=postgres --set port=5432 --set iam_auth=true

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Configure the cluster singleton (--name ignored; upserts)
records.text:
alethia project component add --project boutique --kind cluster \
 --set 'cluster_version="1.35"' --set node_min_size=2 --set 'instance_types=["t3.medium"]'

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Remove components (destructive → confirms)
records.text:
alethia project component remove --project boutique --kind databases --name main
alethia project component remove --project boutique --kind network

 Command Flags Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `component kinds` — List the component kinds the server publishes, with each one's cardinality. Needs a session — the answer is the server's, not a built-in list 
 `component list` `--project` `--kind` `--env` List components (all kinds, or one) 
 `component add` `--project` `--kind` `--name` `--env` `--set` Create a component 
 `component remove` `--project` `--kind` `--name` `--env` `-y`, `--yes` Delete a component (confirms) 

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--project` Yes* Project name or id. *Asked for on a terminal when omitted. 
 `--kind` Yes* Component kind. Optional on `list`, where it filters. *Asked for on a terminal for `add` and `remove`. A kind this CLI's cached list does not hold is still authorable — the picker offers it verbatim and the server decides. 
 `--name` Yes for multi kinds Component name. Ignored by singleton kinds, which upsert. *Asked for on a terminal by `add` and `remove`, as a picker over the components that ex

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Components belong to an environment
records.text:
A component is scoped to one **environment**, not to the project as a whole — so two environments
can hold the same kind with different configuration. `--env` takes an environment id, name or stage:

bash

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: dev and staging deploy DIFFERENT overlays of the same repo
records.text:
alethia project component add --project shop --env dev --kind repositories \
 --set apps_destination_repo=https://github.com/acme/shop --set apps_path=overlays/dev

alethia project component add --project shop --env staging --kind repositories \
 --set apps_destination_repo=https://github.com/acme/shop --set apps_path=overlays/staging

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: Inspect one tier at a time
records.text:
alethia project component list --project shop --env staging

What `--env` defaults to differs by verb, deliberately:

- **`add` and `remove`** default to the project's **default environment**, so a single-environment
 script needs no `--env` at all.
- **`list`** defaults to **every** environment. Narrowing a read silently would hide rows you did
 not ask to hide.

 
 `remove` deletes from **one** environment — the one you named, or the default. It never touches a
 sibling environment's copy. The confirmation names both the component and the tier
 (`Deletes the databases main configuration in staging`), and so does the success line
 (`Component removed in staging`).

records.title: Project Commands
records.heading: The --set field setter
records.text:
`--set key=value` is repeatable and generic. Each value is parsed as JSON when it can be, else taken
literally — so numbers, booleans, and arrays are typed correctly:

--set port=5432 # number
--set iam_auth=true # boolean
--set instance_types='["t3.medium"]' # array
--set 'node_size={"vcpu":4,"memory_gb":16}' # object
--set engine=postgres # string
--set 'cluster_version="1.31"' # string that would otherwise parse as a number

Quote a value that looks like a number but is a string field — `cluster_version=1.31` coerces to the
number `1.31`, which the server refuses.

A cluster is sized one of two ways. `node_size` is a size that works on any cloud: the deploy picks
the closest machine type in the catalog for the cluster's cloud. `instance_types` pins a machine type.
Setting one clears the other in the same write, and a single `add` that sets both fails.

`capacity_type` chooses how the nodes are bought: `on_demand` (the default) or `spot`. Spot nodes cost
less, but the cloud can take a node back at short notice. Only AWS accepts `spot` through this field;
on other clouds a deploy refuses it.

alethia project component add --project boutique --kind cluster --set capacity_type=spot

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.text: Promotion Commands. Inspect environment promotions — status, approval tally, and approval slots.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: Promotion Commands
records.text:
The `promotion` group (aliases `promotions`, `promo`) reads a project's **environment promotions** —
moving a source environment's proven design into a target environment, gated by that environment's
[protection rules](/reference/cli/protection).

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call
`/cli/projects/ /promotions[/…]` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on
the **active organization**, which you change with `alethia org switch`. Approving, rejecting, or
cancelling a promotion stays in the console.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: alethia promotion list
records.text:
List a project's promotions, newest first.

alethia promotion list
alethia promotion list --project my-project
alethia promotion list -p my-project -e production
alethia promotion list -p my-project -o json

{/* fieldspec: alethia promotion list */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Whose promotions to list `--project` 
 Target environment Show only promotions INTO this environment, by name, stage, or id `--env` 

Columns: **ID**, **Source**, **Target**, **Status**, **Created**. Backing call:
`GET /cli/projects/ /promotions`.

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: alethia promotion get
records.text:
Show one promotion's status, approval tally, and approval slots.

alethia promotion get
alethia promotion get --project my-project
alethia promotion get 8f3c1a2b -p my-project

A promotion has no name, so there is nothing to type but its id — which is why **you do not have
to**. Run `promotion get` with no argument at a terminal and you are shown the project's
promotions and pick one; `--env` narrows that list exactly as it narrows `promotion list`. Given an
argument, an unambiguous **id prefix** is enough: `8f3c1a2b` resolves as readily as the full UUID.

{/* fieldspec: alethia promotion get */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Which project the promotion belongs to `--project` 
 Promotion The promotion to open, by id or id prefix; omit it to choose from the list `[promotion]` 

Renders a summary card (source → target, status, **approvals** `N/M`, initiator, created, any
error) followed by the approval slots (status, approver, required role, decided-at). The per-gate
evaluation detail and full config diff stay in the console. Add `-o json` for the full object.

The card is written for a person, and `-o csv` gives a script the values: the stat

records.title: Promotion Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:

- [Staged Commands](/reference/cli/staged) — an environment's pending canvas changes.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Protection Commands
records.text: Protection Commands. Inspect a project's promotion protection rules — the gates that guard deploys into each environment.

records.title: Protection Commands
records.heading: Protection Commands
records.text:
The `protection` group (alias `protect`) lists the **promotion protection rules** configured per
environment: the gates that must pass before a promotion deploys into that environment.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. `protection list` calls
`/cli/projects/ /protection` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on the
**active organization**, which you change with `alethia org switch`. Pass `--org ` to scope a single invocation to a different
organization — it is refused with `403` if you are not a member of it.

records.title: Protection Commands
records.heading: alethia protection list
records.text:
List a project's per-environment protection rules.

alethia protection list
alethia protection list --project my-project
alethia protection list -p my-project -o json

Name the project with `--project`; omit it at a terminal and you are asked which project to read,
from the ones you have.

{/* fieldspec: alethia protection list */}

 Field What it is Set with 
 ------- ------------ ---------- 
 Project Whose environments' promotion gates to read `--project` 

Columns: **Environment**, **Predecessor** (predecessor stage must be deployed + in-sync),
**Verify** (Elench verify must pass), **Approval** (a human must approve), **Approvers** (minimum
approver count), **Soak (min)** (minutes since the predecessor deploy), **Cost Δ** (a plan cost
delta above this USD/mo flips the promotion to pending-approval). A configured gate renders as a
check; an unset gate or limit renders as `—`. Only environments with rules configured appear.

Environment Predecessor Verify Approval Approvers Soak (min) Cost Δ
production ✓ ✓ ✓ 2 30 $100.00
staging — ✓ — — — —

Every one of those renderings is for a person reading a column. Under `-o csv` a script gets the
values instead: a gate is `true` or `false`

records.title: Protection Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Drift Commands](/reference/cli/drift) · [Cost Commands](/reference/cli/cost) — the posture the
 verify/cost gates act on.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Provider Commands
records.text: Provider Commands. Inspect and re-verify connected cloud provider identities from the terminal.

records.title: Provider Commands
records.heading: Provider Commands
records.text:
The `provider` group (alias `providers`) reads and re-verifies an existing **cloud provider
connection**. Use [`alethia connector`](/reference/cli/connector) to create or change a connection;
these commands only inspect and re-probe one.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. These subcommands call `/cli/providers/ /*`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**
(`alethia org switch`), or on the organization named by the global `--org ` flag.
You must be a member of the organization you name; if you are not, the request is refused
with `403`. A service token is pinned to the organization it was minted for, and a request
carrying a different one is refused with `403` rather than quietly rescoped.

records.title: Provider Commands
records.heading: alethia provider status
records.text:
Show the connection status of a cloud provider identity.

alethia provider status aws
alethia provider status gcp -o json

records.title: Provider Commands
records.heading: Or omit the provider for a picker over your connections
records.text:
alethia provider status

 Argument Required Description 
 ---------- ---------- ------------- 
 `[provider]` No `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, `alibaba`, or `hetzner`. Omit for a picker over the accounts you have connected. 

Renders a field/value card: **status** (`connected` `disconnected`), the **identity** id, and the
provider-specific identity fields that are set (AWS account id / role arn, GCP project id / service
account, Azure tenant / client / subscription). Add `-o json` for the raw `ProviderStatus`.

Backing call: `GET /cli/providers/ /status`.

records.title: Provider Commands
records.heading: alethia provider verify
records.text:
Re-run the server-side health probe (auth + provisioning-capability check) against the connected
identity for a provider. The server verifies **inline** — there is no job to poll.

alethia provider verify aws

records.title: Provider Commands
records.heading: Or omit the provider for a picker over your connections
records.text:
alethia provider verify

 Argument Required Description 
 ---------- ---------- ------------- 
 `[provider]` No `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, `alibaba`, or `hetzner`. Omit for a picker over the accounts you have connected. 

The picker lists the accounts you have actually connected, not every provider Alethia
supports: these commands read and re-probe an existing connection, so offering one with no
identity behind it can only produce "no connected identity". Under `--no-input` there is no
picker, so the argument is required and the refusal names the valid providers.

The command resolves the connected identity via `status`, then re-verifies it and renders the
verdict: **identity**, **status**, **verified**, and — when degraded — the **missing permissions**.
It exits non-zero when there is no connected identity to verify or the probe reports the identity is
not connected, so it is safe to use in a script or CI gate.

Field Value
identity id-1
status connected
verified true

Backing call: `POST /cli/providers/ /verify` with `{ identity_id }`.

records.title: Provider Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Connector Commands](/reference/cli/connector) — connect or change a cloud provider account.
- [Identity](/reference/cli/identity) — how connections and keyless credentials work.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Repository Commands
records.text: Repository Commands. Browse the git repositories Alethia can see through a connected git provider.

records.title: Repository Commands
records.heading: Repository Commands
records.text:
The `repo` group (aliases `repos`, `repositories`) lists the repositories reachable through a
connected **git provider** — GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. These are the repositories you can point
a project at when authoring its infrastructure.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API — it authors nothing locally. `repo list` calls
`/cli/repositories/PROVIDER` with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and the git token captured
when you logged in. It is the one listing in the CLI that is NOT org-scoped: the repositories you
can see are the ones your git account can see, so the global `--org ` changes nothing about the
result here.

It is still *checked*, though, and under a [service token](/reference/cli/authentication) it must name the
token's own organization — naming a different one is refused with `403` before this route runs at
all. A scripted `repo list --org ` therefore fails rather than returning the same list.

records.title: Repository Commands
records.heading: alethia repo list
records.text:
List repositories for a connected git provider.

alethia repo list # defaults to --provider github
alethia repo list --provider gitlab
alethia repo list --provider bitbucket -o json

{/* fieldspec: alethia repo list */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Provider Which connected git provider to browse `--provider` 

The provider defaults to `github`; the other accepted values are `gitlab` and `bitbucket`. Omit
`--provider` on a terminal and you are asked which one, with the cursor already on the default — so
Enter is exactly the list `repo list` printed before. Because the value has a default, nothing is
ever refused for omitting it: `repo list --no-input`, and anything running where a prompt cannot be
shown, reads `github` without a question. `--provider` answers it outright either way.

The same provider list backs the repository picker in
[`chart attach` and `iac attach`](/reference/cli/charts), which is what stops a URL printed here from
having to be typed into the next command.

Columns: **Name** (the repo's full `owner/name`, falling back to its short name), **Visibility**
(`public` `private`), **Default branch**, **URL**. In an interactive TTY this renders as a

records.title: Repository Commands
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Connector Commands](/reference/cli/connector) — connect a cloud provider account.
- [Authentication](/reference/cli/authentication) — how the CLI obtains the token these commands use.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Runner Commands
records.text: Runner Commands. Deploy, register, list, and tear down runner agents from the CLI.

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Runner Commands
records.text:
Runners execute infrastructure jobs. Manage them with `alethia runner`.

Every runner is named by its **name** — the one `alethia runner list` shows. No command in this
group needs an id copied out of another command's output. The `--runner-id`,
`--assigned-runner-id` and `--cloud-identity-id` forms still take a raw id for scripts that
already pass one; passing a name form and an id form for the same field together is refused
rather than silently resolved by precedence.

Every field below is a flag, so every command in this group runs under `--no-input`.

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: alethia runner deploy
records.text:
Deploy a new runner into an AWS account. Creates a runner record and queues a `DEPLOY_RUNNER`
job using the latest stable release.

bash

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Interactive: picks the cloud account, then asks for the name and region
records.text: alethia runner deploy

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Unattended: every field named, nothing asked
records.text:
alethia runner deploy --cloud-account prod-account --name eu-runner --region eu-west-1 --no-input

 Flag Description 
 ------ ------------- 
 `--cloud-account` Cloud account to deploy into, by **label** or id (AWS only; asked for on a terminal when omitted) 
 `--cloud-identity-id` Cloud identity id to deploy into — prefer `--cloud-account`, which also takes the label 
 `--name` Runner name (default: `runner- `) 
 `--region` Cloud region (default: `eu-west-1`) 
 `--assigned-runner` Runner that executes the deployment, by **name** or id (any available when omitted) 
 `--assigned-runner-id` Runner id that executes the deployment — prefer `--assigned-runner` 
 `--wait`, `-w` Wait for job completion 

With `--no-input`, `--name` and `--region` take the defaults above and the value used is printed,
and an omitted `--assigned-runner` leaves the job for any available runner. Only the cloud account
has no default: pass `--cloud-account` or `--cloud-identity-id`.

 
 **Deployed runners are available on AWS only.** `infra/templates/runner/` holds one template,
 `aws`, so there is no runner template for GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner. Omit
 `--cloud-account` and the picker lists your ver

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: alethia runner register
records.text:
Register a runner you operate yourself. Nothing is provisioned — this is the command for every cloud
`runner deploy` cannot reach.

alethia runner register my-hetzner-box

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Bound to a cloud account by its label, and unattended for a provisioning script
records.text:
alethia runner register gcp-box-1 --cloud-account prod-account --no-input

 Argument / Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `[name]` Yes* Runner name (positional, or `--name`; asked for on a terminal) 
 `--name` Yes* Runner name, when not passed as the argument 
 `--cloud-account` No Bind the runner to a cloud account, by **label** or id 
 `--cloud-identity-id` No Cloud identity id to bind to — prefer `--cloud-account` 

\* One of the two. On a terminal the name is asked for when omitted, and an optional cloud account
is offered; with `--no-input` a missing name is an error naming the flag.

It prints the two values the runner process needs, as assignments you can paste straight into an env
file or a systemd unit:

✓ Registered runner my-hetzner-box (7f3c…)

ALETHIA_RUNNER_ID=7f3c…
ALETHIA_RUNNER_TOKEN=9a1b…

 
 **The token is shown once.** Only its SHA-256 is stored, so it cannot be re-read or recovered — a
 leak of the runners table yields nothing usable, and a token you lose is a runner you re-register.
 Copy it before the terminal scrolls.
 

Then start the runner with those two variables set and confirm it appears in
`alethia runner list` with a recent

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: alethia runner list
records.text:
List all runners (status, operator, version, last heartbeat). The **Operator** column shows `managed` or, for self runners, `self · deployed` / `self · registered`. This is where the runner names the other commands take come from.

Those cells are for a person reading a column, and `-o csv` gives a script the values instead:
**Operator** is the bare `managed` / `self` (the provisioning half is its own field under
`-o json`), **Status** is the wire status without its glyph, **Default** is `true` / `false` rather
than `◆` on one row and blank on the others, **Version** is an empty cell when unset, and **Last
Heartbeat** is the RFC3339 stamp.

alethia runner list

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: alethia runner destroy
records.text:
Tear down a runner's cloud infrastructure. Queues a `DESTROY_RUNNER` job; another
runner executes the teardown.

bash

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Interactive: picks the runner, then the executor, then confirms
records.text: alethia runner destroy

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Unattended, by name
records.text:
alethia runner destroy --runner eu-runner --no-input --yes

 Flag Description 
 ------ ------------- 
 `--runner` Runner to destroy, by **name** or id (asked for on a terminal when omitted) 
 `--runner-id` Runner id to destroy — prefer `--runner`, which also takes the name 
 `--assigned-runner` Runner that executes the teardown, by **name** or id (any available when omitted) 
 `--assigned-runner-id` Runner id that executes the teardown — prefer `--assigned-runner` 
 `--wait`, `-w` Wait for job completion 
 `--yes`, `-y` Skip the confirmation prompt (**required** with `--no-input`) 

A runner cannot execute its own teardown. Naming the same runner for both the executor and
the target is refused before the job is queued — the interactive picker leaves it out of the
list for the same reason. Omit the executor flags to let the control plane choose.

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: alethia runner remove
records.text:
Remove a runner's database record only (no cloud teardown). Run
`alethia runner destroy` first to tear down cloud resources.

bash

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Interactive: picks the runner, then confirms
records.text: alethia runner remove

records.title: Runner Commands
records.heading: Unattended, by name
records.text:
alethia runner remove --runner eu-runner --no-input --yes

 Argument / Flag Description 
 ------ ------------- 
 `[runner-id]` Runner id to remove (positional) — prefer `--runner`, which also takes the name 
 `--runner` Runner to remove, by **name** or id (asked for on a terminal when omitted) 
 `--yes`, `-y` Skip the confirmation prompt (**required** with `--no-input`) 

 
 `destroy` and `remove` are destructive, so with `--no-input` they refuse unless `--yes` is
 passed. They do not silently do nothing: a scripted teardown that cannot confirm exits non-zero.

records.title: Staged Change Commands
records.text: Staged Change Commands. Inspect an environment's staged (pending) canvas changes — the diff an apply would push.

records.title: Staged Change Commands
records.heading: Staged Change Commands
records.text:
The `staged` group reads an environment's **staged (pending) canvas changes** — the durable diff
between the edited canvas and the environment's live config, i.e. the Pending Changes an apply would
push.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. `staged list` calls `/cli/projects/PROJECT/staged`
with your [CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operates on the **active organization**. Staging,
discarding, or applying changes stays in the console/canvas.

records.title: Staged Change Commands
records.heading: alethia staged list
records.text:
List an environment's staged changes.

alethia staged list --project my-project
alethia staged list -p my-project -e staging
alethia staged list -p my-project -o json

{/* fieldspec: alethia staged */}

 Field What it is How to set it 
 --- --- --- 
 Project The project, by name or id; omit it on a terminal and you are asked `--project` 
 Environment The environment, by name, stage or id; empty means the project's default `--env` 

`--project` has the short form `-p` and `--env` has `-e`. On a terminal, omitting `--project` opens
the project picker; with `--no-input`, with `-o json`, or with the output redirected to a file, it
is required — a form drawn into a redirected stream would corrupt the document you are piping.

Columns: **Op** (`create` `update` `delete`), **Component** (the canvas node kind), **Component
ID** (the target row for update/delete; `—` for create), **Created** (rendered the way the console
writes a date, `9 Mar 2026, 15:04` in UTC, rather than the raw wire timestamp). The per-change payload delta
stays console-only. Prints `No staged changes.` when the environment is in sync. Backing call:
`GET /cli/projects/PROJECT/staged`.

Both of those renderings are for

records.text:
- [Promotion Commands](/reference/cli/promotions) — moving a proven design between environments.
- [Command Reference](/reference/cli) — the full command tree and global flags.

records.title: Verify Commands
records.text: Verify Commands. Pull a job's signed evidence receipt, check its ed25519 signature against a key your control plane vouches for, and read the per-control report.

records.title: Verify Commands
records.heading: Verify Commands
records.text:
Every `PLAN` and `DEPLOY` job carries an **Elench evidence receipt**: the per-control verification
report, sealed to the hash of the exact OpenTofu plan that was applied, and signed with ed25519.
The `verify` group reads that receipt from the terminal.

`alethia verify receipt` checks the signature and **exits non-zero when it cannot**, so you can gate
a deployment pipeline on it. `alethia verify show` prints the report behind the verdict.

 
The CLI is a client of the same Console API. Both commands call `/cli/jobs/ ` with your
[CLI token](/reference/cli/authentication) and operate on the **active organization**
(`alethia org switch`).

records.title: Verify Commands
records.heading: Choosing the job
records.text:
Both commands act on one job. The id is optional, and there are three ways to say which job you
mean:

alethia verify receipt 8f3c2a1e-4b7d-4c2a-9f1e-2d3c4b5a6978 # an id you already have
alethia verify receipt --latest # the most recent PLAN or DEPLOY — no id needed
alethia verify receipt # a picker, on a terminal

`--latest` is the one to use in a script: it needs no terminal, so it works under `--no-input`.
Narrow it until it names one job.

 Flag Description 
 ------ ------------- 
 `--latest` Act on the most recent matching job instead of naming one. Works with `--no-input`. 
 `--type` Narrow to a job type — see [Jobs Commands](/reference/cli/jobs) for the full set. 
 `--status` Narrow to a job status. 
 `--project` Narrow to a project, by name or by an id prefix. 
 `--job`, `-j` The job id, as a flag. The same thing as passing it as an argument. 

Only `PLAN` and `DEPLOY` jobs carry a receipt, so `--latest` and the picker consider **only those
two types** — otherwise the newest job in a busy org is usually a scheduled `DETECT_DRIFT` that
`verify` can do nothing with. Naming a `--type` yourself overrides that, and an id on the command
line is always taken as given.

The receip

records.title: Verify Commands
records.heading: alethia verify receipt
records.text:
Fetch a job's receipt and verify it.

alethia verify receipt --latest
alethia verify receipt 4f3c2b1a-9d6e-4a3b-8c17-5e2f1a9b7c04 -o json
alethia verify receipt --latest --key-file alethia-receipts.pub

 Flag Required Description 
 ------ ---------- ------------- 
 `--key` No Verify against this base64 ed25519 public key instead of the trusted set. 
 `--key-file` No Same, read from a file. 
 `--allow-unsigned` No Exit zero when the receipt carries no signature. 
 `--allow-untrusted` No Exit zero when the signature is self-consistent but its key is not vouched for. 

Plus the selector flags from [Choosing the job](#choosing-the-job).

alethia · verify receipt
 Signature ✓ signature verified against your organization's own recorded key
 Trust org
 Algorithm ed25519
 Key ID 9f2c4a1b7e5d3068
 Verdict pass
 Sealed to plan 3b1f...c204
 Control catalog elench-controls-0.5.2
 Evaluated 9 Mar 2026, 15:04
 Controls 14 pass, 0 fail, 0 warn, 0 n/a

The glyph on the `Signature` row has **three** states, not two:

 Glyph Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `✓` verified against a key that is vouched for, or the one you pinned 
 `◐` the signature is self-consistent, but who signed it is **unestablished** 
 `✗` th

records.title: Verify Commands
records.heading: What a green check means
records.text:
The signature is verified against a key **the control plane vouches for** — your organization's own
recorded signing key, or the Alethia platform key — fetched from `GET /cli/signing-keys`.

This matters more than it looks. A receipt carries the public key it was signed with, so it will
always verify against *itself*, whoever produced it. Checking only that proves the document was not
altered in transit; it does not prove Alethia signed it. Binding the receipt's `key_id` to a
separately-served trusted key is what makes the difference, and a receipt signed by a key outside
that set fails — which is exactly what a forged receipt looks like.

The `Trust` field names the answer:

 Trust Meaning 
 --- --- 
 `pinned` verified against the key you supplied with `--key`/`--key-file` 
 `org` verified against your organization's own recorded signing key 
 `platform` verified against the Alethia platform key — attests "Alethia asserted this" 
 `self` only the receipt's own embedded key verified; who signed it is unestablished 

For verification that depends on nothing the control plane says about itself — the posture an
auditor or a security reviewer will want — pass the public key out of band

records.title: Verify Commands
records.heading: Exit status
records.text:
Exit status is part of the contract, so this can gate a pipeline:

 Situation Exit 
 --- --- 
 Signature verified against a vouched-for or pinned key `0` 
 The job carries no receipt non-zero 
 The receipt is unsigned (`algorithm: "none"`) non-zero, or `0` with `--allow-unsigned` 
 The signature does not match the receipt non-zero — **always**, no flag forgives it 
 The signature is valid but its key is not vouched for non-zero, or `0` with `--allow-untrusted` 

A receipt that fails its own signature check has been altered since it was signed. No flag
downgrades that.

Receipts are unsigned when the runner had no `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` configured. That is a
legitimate state and the receipt still renders — but it is not evidence, so it fails by default.

records.title: Verify Commands
records.heading: alethia verify show
records.text:
Print the per-control report the receipt seals.

alethia verify show --latest
alethia verify show 4f3c2b1a-9d6e-4a3b-8c17-5e2f1a9b7c04 -o json

The selector flags from [Choosing the job](#choosing-the-job) are the only ones this command takes.

Verify: pass (aws, catalog elench-controls-0.5.2) — 14 pass, 0 fail, 0 warn, 1 not evaluable

Control Status Severity Title
KEYLESS-001 pass high No static cloud credentials
LEASTPRIV-001 pass high No wildcard admin policy
OIDC-001 not_evaluable medium OIDC trust is scoped

▸ OIDC-001 — OIDC trust is scoped
 coverage: no OIDC provider in the plan

Controls reporting `not_evaluable` are shown, never hidden. A control the engine could not inspect
is not a control that passed, and a report that quietly dropped them would overstate what was
checked. Any recorded waiver prints with who granted it, why, and when it expires.

`verify show` exits non-zero on a blocking verdict, matching `elench-verify`.

Add `-o json` for the full report object; `-o csv` emits the control rows.

records.title: Control catalog
records.text: Control catalog. The authored controls per cloud, what each detects, the engine's blind spots, framework mapping, and catalog versioning.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Control catalog
records.text:
The current catalog is **`elench-controls-0.5.2`**. `Evaluate` detects the plan's cloud and runs that
provider's control set (a mixed or unknown plan runs all of them, so nothing is silently skipped). Every
control records its `provider`, so a uniform posture UI can never imply coverage a control does not have.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: AWS
records.text:
ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `KEYLESS-001` No static IAM access keys creating an `aws_iam_access_key` (use OIDC federation instead) 
 `OIDC-001` Federated trust bound to a specific subject a federated role — trust `Action` covering `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, literally or via a wildcard grant (`sts:*`, `*`) — whose trust **lacks a `:sub` condition**, or binds `sub` only with a **`StringLike` wildcard** (the "any repo can assume" footgun) 
 `LEASTPRIV-001` No over-broad IAM grants (named patterns) `Action:"*"` + `Resource:"*"`; `Allow` + `NotAction`; attaching `AdministratorAccess` / `PowerUserAccess` / `IAMFullAccess`. **Warns** on sensitive service wildcards (`iam:*`, `kms:*`, …) with `Resource:"*"`. **Not-evaluable** when the policy body is computed or referenced only by ARN. 
 `ACCESS-ANALYZER-001` No sensitive actions grantable (opt-in) a policy AWS IAM Access Analyzer proves *could* grant any action in a sensitive denylist.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: GCP
records.text:
ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `GCP-KEYLESS-001` No static service-account keys creating a `google_service_account_key` (use Workload Identity) 
 `GCP-WIF-001` WIF providers are attribute-conditioned a `google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider` with an empty `attribute_condition` 
 `GCP-LEASTPRIV-001` No project-wide primitive roles binding `roles/owner` (fail) — **warns** on `roles/editor` — via `google_project_iam_member`/`_binding`

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Azure
records.text:
ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `AZURE-KEYLESS-001` No static app/SP secrets creating an `azuread_application_password` / `azuread_service_principal_password` (use a federated identity credential) 
 `AZURE-FED-001` Federated credentials bind a subject an `azuread_application_federated_identity_credential` with an empty or wildcard `subject` 
 `AZURE-LEASTPRIV-001` No Owner/Contributor assignments an `azurerm_role_assignment` of `Owner` (fail) — **warns** on `Contributor` — scope annotated

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Alibaba Cloud
records.text:
Alibaba has a real RAM/OIDC authority surface — **RRSA** (RAM Roles for Service Accounts) is its
workload-identity mechanism, the analogue of AWS IRSA / GCP WIF — so its control set mirrors the AWS
one. RAM trust and policy documents share AWS IAM's statement shape; the one Alibaba-specific
difference is the trust action (`sts:AssumeRole`, not `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`). On both
clouds a wildcard action grant (`sts:*`, `*`) covers the assume call and keeps the role in scope.

 ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `ALI-KEYLESS-001` No static RAM access keys creating an `alicloud_ram_access_key` (use RRSA / AssumeRoleWithOIDC instead) 
 `ALI-OIDC-001` RRSA trust bound to a specific subject an `alicloud_ram_role` whose Federated (RRSA) trust **lacks an `oidc:sub` condition**, or binds it only with a **`StringLike` wildcard** (any pod from the issuer can assume). Service-principal roles are out of scope; a computed trust doc → **not_evaluable**. 
 `ALI-LEASTPRIV-001` No over-broad RAM grants (named patterns) an `alicloud_ram_policy` granting `Action:"*"` on `Resource:"*"` or using `Allow` + `NotAction`; or a **role/user/group** policy attachment of an admin-famil

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Hetzner
records.text:
Hetzner is **token-auth** — the API token is the ceiling, with no OIDC/federation/IAM surface to bind —
so its controls assert **network/firewall posture**, the attack surface a Hetzner plan can actually
misconfigure. They are tuned so the shipped Talos template evaluates to **warns only** (never a
hard block of the nightly apply).

 ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `HCLOUD-FW-001` Every server is behind a firewall an `hcloud_server` with **no firewall anywhere** — no known `firewall_ids`, no configuration reference to an `hcloud_firewall`, and no `hcloud_firewall_attachment` covering it (a bare public node). **Not-evaluable** (never a false brick) for unresolvable expressions, `label_selectors` / `apply_to` selection, or a plan without a configuration section. 
 `HCLOUD-NET-001` No world-open SSH; management ports flagged a firewall rule opening **tcp/22** to the whole internet — including split-CIDR spellings that union to full coverage (Talos runs no SSH daemon; world-open 22 is always wrong). **Warns** on world-open Kubernetes API `6443` / Talos apid `50000`/`50001` (open by design today), any other world-open inbound rule, and very broad partial sources on

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Kubernetes
records.text:
A separate input path — `EvaluateManifests(yaml)` — decodes (multi-doc) manifests and runs the Kubernetes set
(`provider` = `k8s`). It backs the [bring-your-own audit](/concepts/elench/engine-internals) and grades the
manifests Alethia *generates* (which pass by construction).

 ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `CONTAINERSECURITY-001` Containers run non-root, unprivileged, on pinned images a `privileged` container, `runAsUser: 0`, or a mutable `:latest` / untagged image. **Warns** when `runAsNonRoot` is unset (may run as root). 
 `RBAC-001` No wildcard RBAC or anonymous bindings a `ClusterRole`/`Role` rule granting `"*"` verbs on `"*"` resources in `"*"` apiGroups; a binding to `system:anonymous` / `system:unauthenticated` 
 `HOSTACCESS-001` Pods don't reach the host namespace or filesystem `hostNetwork` / `hostPID` / `hostIPC: true`, or a `hostPath` volume 
 `RESOURCES-001` Containers declare CPU + memory limits a container missing CPU and/or memory `limits` (**warn** — reliability, not a breach) 

Coverage is honest the same way the cloud controls are: a control with no in-scope resources is a vacuous
pass, and workload kinds without a decodable pod spec are

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Blind spots
records.text:
The gate inspects what the plan JSON can actually show. It is honest about the rest rather than
 guessing:

 - **Computed bodies** (`after_unknown`) — interpolated IAM/trust/bucket policies → `not_evaluable`.
 - **Managed-policy bodies** — AWS-managed (non-admin) policies attached by ARN, and Alibaba's
 non-admin System policies, have no body in the plan → coverage gap, not a pass.
 - **Cross-state / cross-module** — resources created in another state or module, permission
 boundaries, and SCPs are out of view.
 - **AWS is deepest; Alibaba mirrors it.** GCP/Azure cover the static-credential, federation-binding,
 and primitive-role cases; Hetzner is network **posture** (token-auth has no authority surface to
 audit); the per-cloud `provider` on each control + the report makes coverage explicit.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Framework mapping
records.text:
Each control carries a small, conservative set of framework references (CIS / SOC 2 criteria), surfaced
in the posture and the receipt. These map to controls, not certification — see
[security & compliance readiness](/reference/standards/security-and-compliance) for how the evidence supports an
audit rather than replacing one.

 
 A wrong control-to-framework mapping (e.g. claiming a control satisfies "SOC 2 CC6.1" when it does
 not) is **worse than no mapping** — it manufactures false assurance. Mappings are kept deliberately
 small, owned, and reviewed, never auto-generated.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Catalog versioning
records.text:
`CatalogVersion` is part of the evidence. **Bump it whenever a control's logic changes in a way that
could alter a verdict** — an old receipt is only meaningful against the catalog (and provider schema)
that produced it. The version is recorded on every report and sealed into the receipt.

records.text: Glossary & Naming. The canonical name for every core concept — one term per thing, and the words we deliberately avoid.

records.title: Glossary & Naming
records.heading: Glossary & Naming
records.text:
Alethia uses **one name per concept**. This page is the source of truth: every other page in these
docs defers to the terms below. If you find a doc using a rejected term, it's a bug — the canonical
column is what the product, the schema, and the CLI actually call it.

 
 A quick disambiguation up front: **Alethia** is the whole platform, **Console** is the web app you
 sign into, and **`alethia`** (lowercase) is the CLI binary. **Alethia Labs** is the company.

records.title: Glossary & Naming

records.text:
Concept Canonical term Definition Avoid 
 --- --- --- --- 
 Tenancy boundary **organization** ("org") The top-level owner of every resource. In Community a personal org is created per user; the Enterprise edition turns orgs into shared, multi-member tenants. Enforced by coarse Postgres RLS keyed on `org_id`. ~~workspace~~ 
 Infrastructure app record **project** A declarative infrastructure configuration under an org. A project is an *app* that **owns N environments**. Links to exactly one [cloud identity](#connectivity). — 
 Deployment target **environment** An independently-provisionable target inside a project (`project_environments`). A project owns **N**; each has a `stage` (development / staging / production) and a `lifecycle` (`persistent` or `ephemeral`). The per-environment provisioning **status** lives here. 1:1 phrasing; treating a project as having a single environment 
 Configured resource **component** A cloud resource a project's environment declares — network, cluster, DNS, database, cache, queue, registry, secret, etc. Every component belongs to a `(project, environment)` pair. — 

 
 **A project owns N environments — not one.** A common stale assumption is Project↔

records.title: Configuration
records.text: Configuration. The ALETHIA_SANDBOX_* runner environment variables that select the isolation backend and set its runtime, image, network, egress, memory, and cancellation grace.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Configuration
records.text:
The per-job container sandbox is configured entirely through `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_*` environment
variables read by the **runner**. This page is the reference for those variables — what each one
selects, its default, and the accepted values.

 
 These variables are read on the runner, and the container backend applies only to **untrusted
 bring-your-own** work on the managed fleet. The default backend (`Passthrough`) ignores most of
 them. For the enabling sequence on the fleet, see the
 [managed provisioning runbook](/guides/self-hosting/managed-provisioning).

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Backend selection
records.text:
`ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND` picks the isolation backend:

- `container` selects the per-job `Container` backend.
- Any other value (including unset) selects the in-process `Passthrough` backend — no isolation.

When `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container` is set but the container backend fails to initialize on a
runner whose operator is not `self`, selection is **fail-closed**: the runner falls back to a
`Passthrough` that refuses every job rather than silently running untrusted work unsandboxed.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: The container variables
records.text:
These variables configure the `Container` backend. They are parsed by `NewContainerFromEnv`.

 Variable Default Meaning 
 --- --- --- 
 `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_RUNTIME` `docker` The container CLI to invoke (`docker` for local dev, `podman` for the fleet). The value must resolve on `PATH`, or the backend fails to initialize. 
 `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_IMAGE` the runner's own image ref (`ALETHIA_RUNNER_IMAGE`) The image the per-job container runs. If both this and `ALETHIA_RUNNER_IMAGE` are empty, the backend returns an error — an image is required. 
 `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_NETWORK` runtime default The container `--network` value. Empty uses the runtime's default network. 
 `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` unset (false) Confirms that the runtime constrains egress. The managed fail-closed gate requires it (see below). 
 `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_MEMORY` `2g` The container `--memory` limit. 

 
 The per-job container pid limit is fixed at 512 and is not configurable through an environment
 variable.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Cancellation grace
records.text:
`ALETHIA_CANCEL_GRACE_SECONDS` sets the `SIGINT`→`SIGKILL` grace window applied when a running job
is cancelled mid-flight. The value is an integer number of seconds:

- Unset defaults to 120 seconds.
- A value of `0` sends `SIGKILL` immediately after `SIGINT`.

The grace window lets a foreground container runtime forward the interrupt to OpenTofu, so the
in-flight resource finishes, state is written, and the state lock is released before the process
exits.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Enforcing isolation on the default backend
records.text:
`ALETHIA_SANDBOX_ENFORCE_MANAGED` is the kill-switch for the default (`Passthrough`) path. When it
is set, a `Passthrough` backend **refuses** to run on any runner whose operator is not `self`,
instead of silently running unsandboxed. It never refuses a `self` operator, and when it is unset
(the default) the `Passthrough` backend never refuses at all.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Truthy values
records.text:
`ALETHIA_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` and `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_ENFORCE_MANAGED` are boolean flags. They are
read as true for any of these values (case-insensitive):

1
true
yes
on

Any other value — including unset — is read as false.

records.title: Configuration
records.heading: Fail-closed behavior
records.text:
Two gates depend on the variables above:

- **Managed egress gate.** On an `operator=managed` runner, the container backend refuses to run an
 egress-permitted stage unless `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_EGRESS_ENFORCED` is true. A no-egress stage (such
 as `chart_scan`, which runs with `--network none`) is exempt.
- **Backend fallback.** Requesting `ALETHIA_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container` on a non-`self` runner where
 the backend cannot initialize yields a refusing `Passthrough`, never an unsandboxed run.

records.heading: Where to go next
records.text:

 proxy fit together.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.text: Device Authorization Grant. How `alethia login` / `alethia init` authenticate the CLI over a browser-approval flow modeled on OAuth 2.0's Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) — device code, exchange, CLI JWT, and refresh.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
The **OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant** ([RFC 8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628))
authenticates a client that cannot easily host a browser or receive a redirect — a CLI, a TV, an IoT
device. The device asks the authorization server for a **device code** plus a human-readable
**user code**, tells the user to open a **verification URI** and enter the code, then **polls** a
token endpoint until the user approves (`authorization_pending` / `slow_down`) or the code expires.
The user authenticates in a full browser on another device; the CLI never handles their password.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
`alethia login` (and the guided `alethia init`) run a browser-approval flow in this spirit, with a
couple of deliberate deviations from the literal RFC — documented below so the behaviour is
auditable. The CLI code lives in `apps/cli/cmd/login.go`; the control-plane routes are under
`apps/console/app/api/auth/cli/`.

 >CLI: device_code = new UUID, user_code = 8 chars
 CLI->>ST: register {device_code, user_code, client, version}
 ST->>DB: insert pending row (+ requester IP, user agent, deadline)
 CLI->>BR: open /cli/login?device_code=UUID&user_code=CODE
 CLI->>EX: poll {device_code} every 2s
 BR->>RQ: read the request (requires session)
 RQ-->>BR: account, requester, scopes, deadline
 alt user approves
 BR->>GEN: approve (requires session)
 GEN->>DB: bind device_code -> profile_id (+ git token)
 EX->>DB: claim approved row -> delete (one-time)
 EX-->>CLI: 200 { access_token, refresh_token }
 CLI->>CLI: write ~/.config/alethia/credentials.json
 else user refuses
 BR->>DN: deny (requires session)
 DN->>DB: set denied_at, clear profile_id + stashed token
 EX-->>CLI: 403 { error: access_denied }
 else still deciding
 EX-->>CLI: 404 while pending
 end
`} />

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Start
records.text:
`alethia login` generates a `device_code` (a client-side **UUID**, `uuid.New()`) and a `user_code`
(eight characters from an unambiguous consonant alphabet, printed to the terminal).

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Register the request
records.text:
The CLI `POST`s both codes, its own name and version to `/api/auth/cli/start`. The route records a
pending `cli_logins` row carrying the `user_code`, the requesting IP, the `user-agent`, and a
deadline for the **decision** window. The insert never overwrites an existing row, because the route
is unauthenticated by necessity — the terminal has no session yet.

Registration is best-effort on the client: against a control plane that predates the route the CLI
prints a warning and continues, and the browser then shows less about the request.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Read the request in the browser
records.text:
The CLI opens `${web-origin}/cli/login?device_code= &user_code= `. The page
(`apps/console/app/(private)/cli/login/page.tsx`) requires an authenticated Better Auth session and
shows the `user_code` from the link.

`GET /api/auth/cli/request` answers with the account that approval would bind, what approval hands
over, who is asking, and how long is left — every field from the registration rather than from the
link, so nothing it returns is under the sender's control except the codes, which must match what
was registered.

The page's consent screen (`cli-request.tsx`) reads this route to show those fields.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Approve in the browser
records.text:
The page `POST`s to `/api/auth/cli/generate`. That route binds the `device_code` to
`session.user.id`, and best-effort stashes the user's first linked git provider token (held
transiently in `verification_code`). It refuses a `device_code` that belongs to another account, one
that was already refused, and a `user_code` that disagrees with the registered one.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Or refuse it
records.text:
"This isn't me" `POST`s to `/api/auth/cli/deny`, which is session-gated and rate-limited exactly like
`generate` — an unauthenticated version would let anyone terminate someone else's in-flight login.
The route writes a `denied_at` marker, clears the bound account and anything stashed for it, and the
refusal is terminal: the same link cannot be approved afterwards.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Poll to exchange
records.text:
The CLI polls `POST /api/auth/cli/exchange` with `{ device_code }` every 2 seconds. A **404** means
"pending" (`pollForToken` keeps waiting), a **403** carrying `access_denied` means the user refused
and the poll stops, a **429** means back off and keep waiting, and any other non-2xx is fatal. The
claiming delete is narrowed to approved, unrefused rows, so polling neither consumes the pending row
the browser is reading from nor erases a refusal.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Mint and store
records.text:
Once the row shows a `profile_id`, `exchange` **deletes the record** (single use) and mints two JWTs
with the `jose` library, signed HS256 with `CLI_JWT_SECRET`:

- `access_token` — `type: "access"`, **1 hour** TTL.
- `refresh_token` — `type: "refresh"`, **90 day** TTL.

Both are written to `~/.config/alethia/credentials.json` (`os.UserConfigDir()/alethia/credentials.json`,
mode `0755` dir). The git provider token rides back as `provider_token`.

records.title: Device Authorization Grant
records.heading: Refresh
records.text:
Before each authed call, `getAuthTokenInternal` (`apps/cli/cmd/auth_utils.go`) parses the access
token's `exp`; if it is within 1 minute of expiry it calls `POST /api/auth/cli/refresh` with the
refresh token, which verifies `type === "refresh"` and issues a fresh 1-hour access token. When the
refresh token is gone or invalid, the CLI re-runs the browser flow.

 

 
 **Deviations from RFC 8628 (be precise).** Alethia's flow is *modeled on* the device grant but is
 not a literal implementation:
 • The `user_code` is **compared, not typed**. The CLI mints it, registers it, and prints it;
 the browser URL carries both codes and approval is a click. The user's job is to check that the code
 on screen is the one their terminal printed — the server refuses any other.
 • Both codes are **minted by the client**, not issued by the authorization server. The server
 binds the pair at registration and refuses a mismatch from then on.
 • Pending status is signalled with **HTTP 404**, not the RFC's `authorization_pending` /
 `slow_down` token-endpoint errors; the poll interval is a fixed 2s. A refusal does use the RFC's
 `access_denied`, over HTTP 403.
 • The CLI tokens are **HS256 JWTs** with pl

records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text: - [RFC 8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628) — OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant.

records.title: Standards & Protocols
records.text: Standards & Protocols. The open standards Alethia builds on — OAuth 2.0, OIDC, the Device Authorization Grant, cloud workload identity, JOSE, SAML/SCIM — with the exact code that implements each.

records.title: Standards & Protocols
records.heading: Standards & Protocols
records.text:
Alethia authenticates people, machines, and cloud accounts entirely on published standards — no
bespoke crypto, no proprietary handshake. Every credential is short-lived, scoped, and verifiable
against a spec you can read. This section names each standard, shows the exact file/route/function
that implements it, and links the authoritative spec so you can audit the claim yourself.

Two design rules run through everything here:

- **No long-lived secrets cross a trust boundary.** Console sessions, CLI tokens, and cloud
 federation are all time-boxed. The only durable private keys (`ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY`,
 `CLI_JWT_SECRET`, `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY`) never leave the control plane.
- **Claims are verifiable.** Cloud assertions verify against a published JWKS; verify-gate evidence
 is ed25519-signed; the standards below define the wire format so a third party can check them.

records.heading: Standards matrix
records.text:

 --- --- --- --- 
 [OAuth 2.0](/reference/standards/oauth2) [RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) Console social sign-in (GitHub/Google native, GitLab/Bitbucket generic) via Better Auth Live 
 [OAuth 2.0 PKCE](/reference/standards/oauth2) [RFC 7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636) Better Auth authorization-code exchange for social sign-in Live
