records.title: Standards & Protocols
records.heading: How to read these pages
records.text:
Each page has the same three parts:

1. **What the standard is** — one or two paragraphs, no marketing.
2. **How Alethia implements it** — the real files, routes, functions, env vars, and tables.
3. **The authoritative spec** — the IETF RFC, OASIS document, or `openid.net` reference.

For the security model in prose, see [concepts/security](/concepts/security); for the authorization
layer (roles, grants, the PDP), see [access control](/concepts/access-control).

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.text: JWT, JWS & JOSE. Where Alethia uses JSON Web Tokens and signatures — Better Auth sessions, HS256 CLI tokens, RS256 workload assertions, and the ed25519-signed Elench verify evidence receipts.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**JOSE** (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) is the family of IETF standards for representing keys,
signatures, and encryption over JSON. The two that matter here:

- **JWS** ([RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515)) — a JSON Web Signature: a payload plus
 a detached or compact signature, with a header naming the algorithm (`HS256`, `RS256`, `EdDSA`, …).
- **JWT** ([RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519)) — a JSON Web Token: a set of claims
 (`sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, …) carried as a JWS. A signed JWT is verifiable and tamper-evident:
 anyone with the key (symmetric) or public key (asymmetric) can confirm the claims were not altered.

Alethia uses signed tokens in several distinct places, each with the algorithm that fits its trust
boundary. It never encrypts tokens (no JWE) — every token here is *signed*, not secret-bearing.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
Surface Format Alg Key Lifetime Code 
 --- --- --- --- --- --- 
 Console web session Better Auth session cookie (HTTP-only), backed by the `session` table — signed with `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` rolling `lib/auth/index.ts` 
 CLI access token JWT `HS256` `CLI_JWT_SECRET` 1 hour `api/auth/cli/exchange` 
 CLI refresh token JWT `HS256` `CLI_JWT_SECRET` 90 days `api/auth/cli/exchange` 
 Cloud workload assertion JWT `RS256` `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` ≤ 600s `lib/oidc/issuer.ts` 
 MCP access token OAuth 2.1 token (OIDC provider) — Better Auth `mcp()` plugin short `lib/auth/index.ts` 
 Verify evidence receipt detached ed25519 signature over canonical JSON `EdDSA` / ed25519 `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` per-apply `packages/core/verify` 

 
 The **web session is not a JWT** in this build — there is no `jwt()` plugin. It is a Better Auth
 signed, HTTP-only session cookie referencing a `session` row (validated by Next.js middleware). The
 genuine JWT/JWS surfaces are the CLI tokens, the workload assertions, and the MCP tokens. The verify
 receipt is a JOSE-adjacent EdDSA signature, described below.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: CLI tokens (HS256)
records.text:
`apps/console/app/api/auth/cli/exchange/route.ts` mints access/refresh JWTs with the `jose` library
(`new jose.SignJWT(...).setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256" })`). Claims: `sub` = profile id, `email`,
`type` ∈ {`access`, `refresh`}, `iss`/`aud` set to placeholder `urn:example:*` values, and `exp` of
1h / 90d respectively. `/api/auth/cli/refresh` verifies the refresh token
(`jose.jwtVerify`, matching `iss`/`aud`), rejects any token whose `type !== "refresh"`, and issues a
new 1-hour access token. See [device code](/reference/standards/device-code) for the full flow.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: Workload assertions (RS256)
records.text:
The [workload-identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity) issuer signs its federation assertions RS256 —
the widest-compatible alg for AWS/GCP/Azure token exchange — and publishes the public key at
`/api/oidc/jwks` so clouds verify independently. Key rotation is supported by publishing a second
(previous) key while the primary rolls over.

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: Elench verify receipts (ed25519)
records.text:
The [Elench](/concepts/elench) verify gate emits a per-apply **evidence receipt** — a precise, honest record of
what was checked, against which plan, under which control set (`packages/core/verify/receipt.go`). The
receipt binds to the exact plan via `plan_sha256` and pins `tofu_version` / `provider_versions` /
`catalog_version`. When `ALETHIA_RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` is set (a base64 64-byte ed25519 private key,
`packages/core/verify/signing.go`), `Sign()` produces a `SignedReceipt`: a detached **ed25519**
([RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032)) signature over the receipt's canonical JSON bytes,
plus `algorithm: "ed25519"` and a short `key_id` (`KeyID` = first 8 bytes of SHA-256 of the public
key). `Verify()` recomputes the canonical bytes and checks the signature — any tampering fails.

 
 **Root-of-trust honesty (from the code's own comments).** Signing is *additive evidence*, not a
 precondition — an unset key attaches an **unsigned** receipt rather than blocking the apply. And a
 signature from Alethia's runner only proves "Alethia asserted this". For a receipt to mean something
 to a customer's auditor, sign with a customer-controlled key and/or anchor the signature

records.title: JWT, JWS & JOSE
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519) — JSON Web Token (JWT).
- [RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515) — JSON Web Signature (JWS).
- [RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032) — EdDSA (Ed25519).

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.text: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE. Console social sign-in over OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) with PKCE (RFC 7636), implemented by Better Auth — GitHub/Google natively, GitLab/Bitbucket via the generic OAuth plugin.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**OAuth 2.0** ([RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749)) is the authorization framework
that lets a user grant an application access to a resource without sharing a password. The web flow
Alethia uses is the **authorization-code grant**: the app redirects the user to the provider's
authorization endpoint, the provider redirects back with a short-lived `code`, and the app exchanges
that code at the token endpoint for an access token.

**PKCE** ([RFC 7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636), "Proof Key for Code Exchange") hardens
that exchange against code-interception. The client generates a random `code_verifier`, sends its
SHA-256 hash (`code_challenge`) on the authorization request, and presents the raw verifier at token
exchange — so a stolen `code` is useless without the verifier.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
The [Console](/reference/glossary) delegates web sign-in to **Better Auth** (in-process, Drizzle
adapter). The auth instance is built in `apps/console/lib/auth/index.ts`; the single catch-all route
`apps/console/app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts` serves every Better Auth endpoint (authorization start,
callback, token exchange). Better Auth drives the authorization-code + PKCE handshake — the console
never hand-rolls the flow.

Four social providers are registered, in two ways:

 Provider Registration Scopes requested 
 --- --- --- 
 GitHub native `socialProviders.github` `repo` (+ Better Auth's `read:user`/`user:email` defaults) 
 Google native `socialProviders.google` provider defaults 
 GitLab `genericOAuth` plugin (self-hosted base URL) `read_api read_user read_repository read_registry openid profile email` 
 Bitbucket `genericOAuth` plugin `account repository` 

Native GitHub/Google use Better Auth's built-in provider configs. GitLab and Bitbucket go through the
`genericOAuth` plugin (`import { genericOAuth } from "better-auth/plugins"`), configured with explicit
`authorizationUrl` / `tokenUrl` / `userInfoUrl` in `genericOAuthConfigs`. Each provider is registered
**only when its c

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: Where the token lands
records.text:
On callback, Better Auth exchanges the code (with PKCE) and creates a session — an HTTP-only cookie
backed by the `session` table. Next.js middleware validates it on every request; the
[PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) then resolves the active org and sets `app.current_org` for the
coarse Postgres [RLS](/concepts/security) tenant guard. See
[JWT / JWS](/reference/standards/jose) for the token formats and [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) for enterprise SSO.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: The MCP authorization server
records.text:
Alethia also *acts as* an OAuth 2.1 authorization server for its Model Context Protocol endpoint. The
`mcp()` plugin (also in `lib/auth/index.ts`) lets remote MCP clients register dynamically and obtain
an access token that `/api/mcp` resolves into a PDP-scoped actor — no new authority beyond the token
owner's normal scope.

records.title: OAuth 2.0 & PKCE
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [oauth.net/2](https://oauth.net/2/) — the OAuth 2.0 landing page and flow overview.
- [RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework.
- [RFC 7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636) — Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.text: OpenID Connect. Enterprise SSO with Alethia as the OIDC Service Provider — Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, AWS IAM Identity Center and any OIDC IdP, via @better-auth/sso.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** is a thin identity layer on top of [OAuth 2.0](/reference/standards/oauth2). Where
OAuth 2.0 answers *"is this app allowed to act?"*, OIDC answers *"who is this user?"* — the IdP
returns a signed **ID token** (a JWT) with verified identity claims (`sub`, `email`, group/role
claims), and the Relying Party verifies it against the IdP's published JWKS. It is the protocol behind
"sign in with your company account".

Alethia plays two OIDC roles, kept strictly separate:

- **Relying Party / Service Provider** for enterprise SSO — it *consumes* a customer's IdP so members
 sign in with their corporate identity (this page).
- **Identity Provider** for keyless cloud federation — it *is* an OIDC issuer that clouds trust. That
 is a different subsystem; see [workload identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity).

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
Enterprise SSO is an [Enterprise](/editions)-gated capability contributed by the `@alethia/ee` module
(`ee/src/index.ts`) through the `getAuthPlugins()` seam in `apps/console/lib/auth/plugins.ts`. It wraps
the **`@better-auth/sso`** plugin. Alethia is always the **Service Provider** — it never runs an IdP
of its own for user login (no Hydra, no Alethia-as-IdP).

Each [organization](/reference/glossary) registers its own provider (rows in the `ssoProvider` table,
scoped by `organizationId`), so different orgs can federate different directories. Supported IdPs
include Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, AWS IAM Identity Center, OneLogin, and Ping — any
standards-compliant OIDC provider. The server actions in `apps/console/app/server/actions/sso.ts`
manage provider CRUD and report each row's protocol (`oidc` `saml` `unknown`) from which config
block is present.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Domain verification and JIT provisioning
records.text: Two safeguards gate first sign-in:

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Domain proof
records.text:
Registration is bound to domain ownership. `@better-auth/sso` is configured with
`domainVerification: { enabled: true, tokenPrefix: "alethia-sso" }` — the customer publishes a DNS
`TXT` record at `_alethia-sso- `. Until the domain is verified, sign-in through that
provider is rejected and no email-domain account-linking is trusted.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Entitlement gate
records.text:
A custom `alethia-sso-entitlement-guard` middleware blocks `POST /sso/register` unless the target org
holds the `sso` entitlement — so a non-Enterprise admin cannot register a provider by calling the API
directly. The UI shows the upsell instead.

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Just-in-time member provisioning
records.text:
On first successful SSO sign-in, the user is provisioned into their org with
`organizationProvisioning.defaultRole: "member"` (least-privileged). The
[PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) then authorizes them exactly like any other
[member](/guides/access/members-and-invitations) — mapping better-auth's `member` to Alethia's
viewer-scoped access.

 

 
 **Honest current state.** SSO users are always provisioned as least-privileged members — automatic
 **IdP group-claim → Alethia role** mapping (owner/admin/operator/viewer) is a documented follow-up,
 not yet wired. Directory-driven provisioning/deprovisioning (SCIM) is **not implemented**; see
 [SAML & SCIM](/reference/standards/scim-saml).
 

For the operator-facing setup (fields per protocol, the register flow), see
[access control → SSO](/guides/access/sso).

records.title: OpenID Connect
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [openid.net — How OpenID Connect works](https://openid.net/developers/how-connect-works/).
- [OpenID Connect Core 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) — the specification.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.text: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0. Enterprise directory federation — SAML 2.0 SSO is implemented (Enterprise, Service Provider) with documented hardening follow-ups; SCIM 2.0 provisioning is NOT implemented (just-in-time provisioning only).

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.text:
Two enterprise directory standards, at two different maturities. Read the status on each honestly —
one is live, one is roadmap.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**SAML 2.0** (Security Assertion Markup Language, OASIS) is the long-standing XML protocol for
enterprise SSO. The Identity Provider (IdP) issues a digitally-signed XML **assertion** about the
user; the Service Provider (SP) validates the signature against the IdP's X.509 certificate and logs
the user in. It predates OIDC and is still the default in many enterprise directories.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
Alethia is the **Service Provider** — same posture as [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc). SAML providers are
registered per [organization](/reference/glossary) via the `@better-auth/sso` plugin (`ee/src/index.ts`,
[Enterprise](/editions)-gated). SAML config is stored in the `ssoProvider.samlConfig` column; the
server actions in `apps/console/app/server/actions/sso.ts` parse it to surface the IdP entry point and
a **SHA-256 fingerprint of the signing certificate**, and classify each row's protocol as
`oidc` `saml` `unknown` (a row with neither config is reported `unknown` rather than mislabelled).
Registration collects the IdP entity ID, SSO entry-point URL, and X.509 signing certificate (see
[access control → SSO](/guides/access/sso)).

Domain verification (DNS `TXT` at `_alethia-sso- `) and the same
`alethia-sso-entitlement-guard` gate apply to SAML exactly as to OIDC, and users are provisioned
just-in-time as least-privileged members.

 
 **Documented hardening follow-ups (from `ee/src/index.ts`).** The SAML integration ships with two
 standup items still open: enabling `algorithms.onDeprecated: "reject"` (reject deprecated signature
 algorithms) and turning on `InResponseTo` vali

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**SCIM 2.0** (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, [RFC 7644](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644)
protocol + [RFC 7643](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643) schema) is the REST standard for
**automatic** user/group provisioning and *de*-provisioning. A directory (Okta, Entra) pushes
create/update/delete against the SP's `/scim/v2/Users` and `/scim/v2/Groups` endpoints, so access is
granted and — critically — **revoked** the moment HR changes the directory, with no sign-in required.

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: Reality in Alethia
records.text:
SCIM is **not built**. There is no `/scim/v2` endpoint. Membership is populated only by **just-in-time
provisioning** — a user becomes a member the first time they successfully sign in through SSO, and is
never automatically deprovisioned by the directory.

This is stated honestly in the product itself: the console SSO settings
(`apps/console/components/settings/sso/sso-manager.tsx`) render a plain note that *"automatic user
provisioning/deprovisioning from your IdP isn't available yet — SSO users are provisioned
just-in-time on first sign-in"*, with a "talk to us" link. The code comments record that an earlier
UI advertised a `/scim/v2/ ` URL that never existed; that fake card was removed. The plan
catalog lists SCIM as *"coming soon"*.

 
 Do not represent SCIM as available. If a deployment's compliance posture depends on **automatic
 deprovisioning** (offboarding removing access without an admin action), that requirement is **not
 met today** — plan around JIT provisioning and manual member removal
 ([members & invitations](/guides/access/members-and-invitations)).

records.title: SAML 2.0 & SCIM 2.0
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [OASIS — SAML 2.0 Core](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/v2.0/saml-core-2.0-os.pdf).
- [RFC 7644](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644) — SCIM 2.0 Protocol · [RFC 7643](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643) — SCIM 2.0 Core Schema.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.text: Security & Compliance. The real security controls behind Alethia — tenant isolation via Postgres RLS, keyless cloud credentials, the fail-closed verify gate, least-privilege connector roles, audit logging, and the state proxy — mapped to the standards, with an honest SOC 2 posture.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Security & Compliance
records.text:
This page maps Alethia's **real, shipped** controls to the standards in this section. Every control
below has code evidence. The compliance framing is deliberately conservative — see the SOC 2 note at
the end.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Tenant isolation — coarse Postgres RLS
records.text:
Every tenant-owned table is scoped by `org_id`, and Postgres **Row-Level Security** enforces the
boundary at the database. After authentication, the [PDP](/concepts/access-control/architecture) resolves the
active [organization](/reference/glossary) and sets `app.current_org` via `set_config`; RLS policies
key on that setting, so a query can only ever see its own org's rows even if application code forgets a
`WHERE`. This is *coarse* isolation (org-level), complemented by the fine-grained PDP for
role/resource authorization. See [concepts/security](/concepts/security) and
[access control](/concepts/access-control).

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Keyless cloud credentials — zero stored secrets
records.text:
Alethia stores **no** static cloud credentials. All four managed clouds federate keylessly through the
Alethia OIDC issuer ([workload identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity)); the only durable private key
is the issuer's own signing key, held on the control plane and never shared. Revocation is the
customer deleting the trust in their own account — there is nothing to leak from Alethia's side.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Fail-closed verify gate — Elench
records.text:
On a real apply the [runner](/concepts/runner) runs the [Elench](/concepts/elench) `verify` gate between `tofu plan` and
`tofu apply` (`provisioner.RunDeployV2` over `packages/core/verify`). It is **fail-closed**: a hard
control failure (keyless / least-privilege / OIDC-subject checks) blocks the apply unless an
authorized, time-boxed `verify.Override` waives it — and the waiver is recorded in the evidence
receipt. The report is forwarded on `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` and rendered in the Console
Plan tab. Evidence receipts are ed25519-signable ([JOSE](/reference/standards/jose)).

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Least-privilege connector roles
records.text:
The cloud roles Alethia assumes are scoped down from cloud-admin to the minimum needed to provision
and inspect — not blanket administrative access — narrowing blast radius even within a federated
session.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Runner holds no storage credentials — the state proxy
records.text:
The runner never receives object-storage keys. `tofu` state is read and written through the Console
**state proxy** (`backend "http"` → `/api/jobs/{id}/state`, authenticated by a per-job token in
`TF_HTTP_PASSWORD`). A compromised runner cannot reach the state bucket directly. The runner images
also ship **CLI-free** (no bundled `aws`/`gcloud`/`az`); cluster tokens are minted in-process.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Audit / activity log
records.text:
Membership and authorization-relevant actions (invites, removals, role changes, policy decisions) are
written to the org **activity log** (`recordActivity` / `enforceDecision`, surfaced at
[access control → activity log](/guides/access/activity-log)). It gives a per-org trail of who did
what.

 
 **Known honest limitation.** The activity/audit log today has no dedicated RLS policy or
 write-once (WORM) retention guarantee — it is an application-level trail, not yet a tamper-evident
 store. Note this when scoping evidence requirements; it is a tracked hardening item, not a shipped
 guarantee.

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Control-to-standard map
records.text:
Control Backing standard Evidence 
 --- --- --- 
 Web sign-in [OAuth 2.0 + PKCE](/reference/standards/oauth2) `lib/auth/index.ts`, Better Auth 
 Enterprise SSO [OIDC](/reference/standards/oidc) · [SAML 2.0](/reference/standards/scim-saml) `ee/src/index.ts`, `@better-auth/sso` 
 CLI auth [Device grant](/reference/standards/device-code) · [JWT](/reference/standards/jose) `api/auth/cli/*` 
 Keyless cloud access [Workload identity](/reference/standards/workload-identity) `lib/oidc/issuer.ts`, `lib/cloud-providers/session/*`

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: SOC 2 posture — read this carefully
records.text:
Alethia is **built to support SOC 2** — the controls above map to the Security and Confidentiality
Trust Services Criteria (least-privilege access, no stored credentials, tenant isolation, change
verification, audit trail). This is **SOC 2 readiness / control mapping**, and nothing more.

 
 Alethia is **not SOC 2 certified**, **not SOC 2 compliant**, and no SOC 2 report has been issued.
 SOC 2 is an attestation performed by an independent auditor over an observation period; **no such
 formal audit has been performed and no report exists yet.** Anyone stating otherwise is wrong. The
 accurate phrasing is "designed for SOC 2 readiness" / "controls mapped to SOC 2 criteria".
 

For the security model in prose, see [concepts/security](/concepts/security).

records.title: Security & Compliance
records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text: - [AICPA — SOC 2](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2) — what a SOC 2 report is (and requires).

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.text: Cloud Workload Identity. Keyless cloud connectors — one Alethia OIDC issuer federates into AWS (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity), GCP (Workload Identity Federation), and Azure (federated identity). No static cloud secrets are ever stored.

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: What the standard is
records.text:
**Workload identity federation** lets a workload prove *what it is* to a cloud without holding a
long-lived cloud key. The workload obtains a short-lived, signed **OIDC token** from an issuer the
cloud trusts, presents it to the cloud's token exchange, and receives temporary cloud credentials in
return. Trust is established once (the cloud is configured to trust the issuer's URL, its published
JWKS, and a specific `sub`/`aud`); after that every access is a fresh, expiring assertion. The static
attack surface — access keys, service-account JSON, client secrets — disappears.

Each major cloud has its own exchange built on the same OIDC primitive:

- **AWS** — STS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` against an IAM OIDC identity provider.
- **GCP** — Workload Identity Federation (STS token exchange into a workload identity pool).
- **Azure** — a federated identity credential on an Entra ID app (client-assertion grant).

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: How Alethia implements it
records.text:
The control plane **is its own OIDC issuer**, purpose-built for machine federation and nothing else
(`apps/console/lib/oidc/issuer.ts`). It mints short-lived **RS256** JWTs and publishes the matching
public material so any cloud can verify them:

 Property Value 
 --- --- 
 Issuer `${APP_URL}/api/oidc` 
 Discovery `/api/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration` 
 JWKS `/api/oidc/jwks` 
 Signing alg `RS256` (widest cloud-federation compatibility) 
 Subject (`sub`) `alethia-connector` (single, stable, non-secret) 
 Max token TTL 600 seconds 
 Signing key `ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY` (PKCS8, vault-held) `+ ALETHIA_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS` for zero-downtime rotation 

`mintWorkloadToken()` produces a per-cloud-scoped assertion (audience set per provider); the same
issuer serves both the [Console](/reference/glossary) (server-side inventory/health) and the
[runner](/concepts/runner) (provisioning). **No platform cloud account and no stored customer secret exists
anywhere on the Alethia side** — revocation is the customer deleting the trust in their own cloud.

 api/oidc RS256] --> mint sub=alethia-connector TOK[Short-lived JWT]
 TOK --> AWS[AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity]
 TOK --> GCP[G

records.title: Cloud Workload Identity
records.heading: Per-cloud exchange
records.text:
`apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/session/aws.ts`. The customer's IAM role trusts the Alethia issuer
**directly** as an IAM OIDC provider, so the console/runner federate straight in via
`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityCommand` (`@aws-sdk/client-sts`) presenting a freshly minted assertion.
`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` is an unauthenticated STS action — **no platform AWS account, no
`ExternalId`, no stored key**. Session ≈ 1 hour (`DurationSeconds: 3600`); each caller re-assumes the
role (mints a fresh assertion) when it needs credentials — the session itself is not refreshed in place.

 
 

`apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/session/gcp.ts` + `apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/gcp-wif.ts`. A direct-OIDC Workload Identity
Federation config exchanges the Alethia-minted JWT for a GCP access token. The audience encodes the
pool/provider:
`//iam.googleapis.com/projects/ /locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/ /providers/ `.
Connection validation asserts the audience contains `workloadIdentityPools` (`connections.ts`).

 
 

`apps/console/lib/cloud-providers/session/azure.ts`. Each customer creates a **User-Assigned Managed
Identity** in their **own** subscription with a **federated-identity cred

records.heading: Authoritative reference
records.text:
- [OpenID Connect Core 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) — the token format clouds verify.
- [AWS — `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.html) and [creating an IAM OIDC provider](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_create_oidc.html).
- [GCP — Workload Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation).
- [Azure — Workload identity federation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/workload-id/workload-identity-federation).

records.title: Tutorials
records.text: Tutorials. Learn Alethia by building something real, start to finish, on a cloud you own.

records.title: Tutorials
records.heading: Tutorials
records.text:
A tutorial is a lesson. It has one path, tells you exactly what to type, and ends with something
running that you can look at. Use a tutorial the first time you use Alethia. To do a specific task,
use the [how-to guides](/guides). To understand why the product works the way it does, read the
[concepts](/concepts).

Follow each step exactly. If a step does not give the result the page says it gives, the page has a
bug. Please report it.

records.title: Tutorials
records.heading: Available tutorials
records.text:
**[Deploy Online Boutique to three environments](/tutorials/online-boutique)**: build one cluster
that hosts three environments at three isolation levels, and deliver a twelve-service shop into two
of them. About 40 minutes, most of it waiting for the cluster. Tested on Hetzner Cloud, AWS, and
Google Cloud.

**[Start from a template](/tutorials/start-from-a-template)**: copy two of the public starter
templates. Connect one as a cluster's ArgoCD apps repository and the other as a bring-your-own Helm
chart, and watch both sync. About 30 minutes, most of it waiting for the cluster. Tested on Hetzner
Cloud.

records.title: Tutorials
records.heading: Before you start any of them
records.text:
- [Install the CLI](/get-started/install-the-cli) and run `alethia login`.
- Have an account on a supported cloud, with permission to create clusters and networks.

 
 Tutorials **create real infrastructure that costs money.** Each one ends with a teardown step, and
 you are not finished until you run it.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.text: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments. Build one Kubernetes cluster with three environments at three isolation levels, and deliver a twelve-service shop into two of them — all from the terminal.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.text:
In this tutorial you build **one Kubernetes cluster** that hosts **three environments**. Two of them
run their own copy of Online Boutique, a twelve-service shop, delivered by ArgoCD. You do it all
from the terminal, with one file and one command.

Watch for the second and third environments. They cost no new cluster and no new network. They are
placed onto the cluster that the first environment owns.

It takes about 40 minutes. Most of that is waiting for the cluster.

 
 This tutorial creates **real infrastructure that costs money** while it runs. The last step tears
 it down. You are not finished until you run it.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: What you will build
records.text:
P["prod · dedicated owns the Fabric"]
 F --> D["dev-1 · namespace namespace boutique-dev-1"]
 F --> S["staging · vcluster its own Kubernetes API server"]
 D --> DA["overlays/dev-1 12 services"]
 S --> SA["overlays/staging 12 services, 2 frontends"]
`} />

A **Fabric** is the infrastructure: the cluster, its network, and its DNS. An **environment** is
placed onto a Fabric, and its **placement** sets how isolated it is:

 Placement What the environment gets 
 --- --- 
 `dedicated` Its own Fabric. This is the placement that creates a cluster. 
 `namespace` A namespace on a cluster that already exists. 
 `vcluster` Its own Kubernetes API server, running inside a cluster that already exists. 

In this tutorial, `prod` owns the Fabric and runs no application. `dev-1` and `staging` are placed
onto it, and each one deploys an overlay of the shop from the public
[alethia-examples](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-examples) repository. For the model
behind this, see [Fabrics and placement](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement).

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
You need:

- The `alethia` CLI, [installed](/get-started/install-the-cli) and signed in with `alethia login`.
- An account on Hetzner Cloud, AWS, or Google Cloud, with permission to create a cluster and a
 network.
- A runner to execute the jobs. Check with:

 alethia runner list
 
 If no runner is online, [register one you run yourself](/guides/runners/self-operated).

This tutorial is tested on Hetzner Cloud, AWS, and Google Cloud. If you only want to learn the
product, use **Hetzner**. It is the cheapest, and you connect it with one token.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 1 — Connect your cloud account
records.text:
In the Hetzner Cloud Console, create a **new project** for this tutorial. In that project, go to
 **Security → API tokens** and generate a token with **Read & Write** access.

 Then connect it. The command asks for the token and hides what you type:

 alethia connector hetzner
 
 A Hetzner token can do anything inside its project, so the project is the only boundary you get.
 That is why you use a new, empty one. Hetzner has no keyless option, because it has no OIDC
 provider. See [Connect Hetzner](/guides/connectors/hetzner).
 
 
 With the `aws` CLI signed in to the account you want to use, run:

 alethia connector aws
 
 This deploys a CloudFormation stack. The stack creates an IAM OIDC provider that trusts Alethia,
 and a role that Alethia assumes. No access keys are created. See [Connect AWS](/guides/connectors/aws).
 
 
 Alethia cannot turn on Google Cloud APIs for you. Turn on the two that this tutorial needs. Use
 your own project ID in place of `my-gcp-project`:

 gcloud services enable container.googleapis.com cloudkms.googleapis.com --project my-gcp-project
 
 Then connect the project:

 alethia connector gcp --project my-gcp-project
 
 This creates a service account and

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 2 — Describe the project in one file
records.text:
Create a file named `alethia.yaml`. It declares the project, its three environments, the size of the
cluster, and which overlay each environment deploys. Replace `my-account` with the value from the
**Account** column.

 
 
 yaml title="alethia.yaml"
 project: boutique
 cloud:
 account: my-account
 region: nbg1
 environments:
 - name: prod
 stage: production
 placement: dedicated
 components:
 cluster:
 instance_types: [cpx32]
 node_min_size: 3
 node_desired_size: 3
 node_max_size: 3
 - name: dev-1
 stage: development
 placement: namespace
 namespace: boutique-dev-1
 components:
 repositories:
 apps_destination_repo: https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-examples
 apps_path: examples/online-boutique/overlays/dev-1
 - name: staging
 stage: staging
 placement: vcluster
 namespace: boutique-staging
 components:
 repositories:
 apps_destination_repo: https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-examples
 apps_path: examples/online-boutique/overlays/staging
 
 Three `cpx32` nodes have 4 vCPU and 8 GB each, at about €35 a month per node. You can also use
 the region `fsn1` or `hel1`.
 
 
 yaml title="alethia.yaml"
 project: boutique
 cloud:
 account: my-account
 region: us-east-1
 envir

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 3 — Preview what will be created
records.text:
alethia plan

This compares the file with what already exists in your organization. It lists the project, the
three environments, and their components. It changes nothing and starts no job.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 4 — Apply it
records.text:
alethia apply

The CLI shows the same plan and asks you to confirm. Then it deploys each environment in the order
the file lists them, and waits for each one:

1. `prod` creates the network and the cluster, then installs ArgoCD and the platform add-ons.
2. `dev-1` creates its namespace on that cluster and deploys its overlay.
3. `staging` creates its vcluster on that cluster and deploys its overlay.

The `prod` deploy runs an OpenTofu plan and then a **verify gate** before it builds anything. The
gate refuses the deploy if the plan breaks a control, for example a database open to the internet.
Its verdict is a signed receipt. See [the verification gate](/concepts/elench).

To watch the current job from a second terminal:

alethia jobs logs --latest --follow

When every environment is deployed, the CLI prints `boutique is up.`

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 5 — Check the result
records.text:
List the environments:

alethia project env list --project boutique

You see three environments in one project.

Look at the cluster:

alethia cluster get boutique

The **GitOps** row counts the ArgoCD Applications on the cluster, and how many are synced and
healthy. If a deploy failed, the row names the step that failed instead.

Check the signed receipt from the deploy that built the cluster:

alethia verify receipt --project boutique

A list of jobs opens. Select the `prod` deploy. The command checks the receipt's signature against a
key the control plane trusts, and exits with a non-zero status if the check fails. You can use the
same command to gate a CI pipeline. See [`alethia verify`](/reference/cli/verify).

 
 To use `kubectl`, you need a kubeconfig for the cluster. On AWS and Google Cloud, get one with your
 cloud's CLI, as [Clusters](/guides/clusters) shows. Alethia cannot give you a kubeconfig for a
 Hetzner cluster yet.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 6 — Add a fourth environment
records.text:
Run this:

alethia cluster list

There is **one** cluster. Three environments run on it. Each has its own application and its own
namespace, and `staging` also has its own Kubernetes API server.

To add another environment, add another entry to `alethia.yaml`. The repository has a `dev-2`
overlay that uses the namespace `boutique-dev-2`:

 - name: dev-2
 stage: development
 placement: namespace
 namespace: boutique-dev-2
 components:
 repositories:
 apps_destination_repo: https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-examples
 apps_path: examples/online-boutique/overlays/dev-2

Then deploy only that environment:

alethia apply --env dev-2

No new cluster is created. The node sizes in Step 2 are tested with three copies of the shop
running, so `dev-2` fits. To add more environments than that, first raise `node_desired_size` and
`node_max_size` on `prod`.

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: Step 7 — Tear it down
records.text:
Destroy the environments that are placed on the cluster **first**, and the environment that owns
the cluster **last**. If you add `dev-2`, destroy it first too.

alethia project destroy --project boutique --env dev-1 --yes --wait
alethia project destroy --project boutique --env staging --yes --wait
alethia project destroy --project boutique --env prod --yes --wait

 
 Do not destroy `prod` first. Destroying `prod` removes the cluster, and Alethia does not stop
 you while other environments are still placed on it. After that, the other environments can no
 longer be torn down cleanly, and the cloud identities created for their namespaces can be left
 behind.
 

Then make sure nothing is left. Your cloud provider's console has the final answer. Load balancers,
volumes, and NAT gateways are the resources that most often survive a failed teardown, and they bill
by the hour.

 
 
 hcloud server list
 hcloud load-balancer list
 hcloud volume list
 hcloud network list
 
 
 Every resource Alethia creates on AWS carries the tag `Application=alethia`:

 aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=Application,Values=alethia --region us-east-1
 aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --

records.title: Deploy Online Boutique to three environments
records.heading: What you did
records.text:
You:

- Built one Fabric that carries environments at three isolation levels.
- Delivered a different version of the same application to two environments, through GitOps.
- Had the deploy that built the cluster checked by a signed verify receipt, which you checked
 yourself.
- Did all of it from a terminal, so you can also do it from CI.

This tutorial did not cover scale, failure behavior, or day-2 operations. Next, read about
[promoting changes between environments](/concepts/promotions) and
[drift detection](/concepts/drift).

records.title: Start from a template
records.text: Start from a template. Copy two of Alethia's public starter templates, deploy one as the ArgoCD apps repository of a Hetzner cluster and the other as a bring-your-own Helm chart, and watch both sync.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Start from a template
records.text:
In this tutorial you copy two of Alethia's public starter templates and put both on **one Kubernetes
cluster** on Hetzner Cloud:

- [alethia-starter-apps](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-apps) becomes the
 cluster's **ArgoCD apps repository**. ArgoCD syncs a small application from it into three
 namespaces.
- [alethia-starter-chart](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-chart) becomes a
 **bring-your-own Helm chart**. Alethia installs it as an add-on, in a namespace of its own.

The result is the setup that the starter templates' deploy test proved on Hetzner, with both
Applications synced at the template's own commit. You build it from the terminal, with one file and
a few commands.

Plan for about 30 minutes. Most of that is waiting for the cluster.

 
 This tutorial creates **real infrastructure that costs money** while it runs. The last step tears
 it down. You are not finished until you run it.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: What you will build
records.text:
1 control plane + 2 cpx32 workers"]
 C --> A["ArgoCD apps repository your copy of alethia-starter-apps"]
 C --> B["Bring-your-own chart your copy of alethia-starter-chart"]
 A --> A1["apps · namespace starter"]
 A --> A2["apps-dev · namespace starter-dev"]
 A --> A3["apps-staging · namespace starter-staging"]
 A --> A4["addons · nothing yet"]
 B --> B1["addon-starter-chart · namespace starter-chart"]
`} />

The two templates run under two different trust levels. The apps repository can create any kind of
resource on its cluster. A bring-your-own chart can create only namespaced resources in its own
namespace, and no RBAC. For the full comparison, see [Starter Templates](/guides/design-project/starter-templates).

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
You need:

- The `alethia` CLI, [installed](/get-started/install-the-cli) and signed in with `alethia login`.
- A Hetzner Cloud account.
- A GitHub account, to hold your copies of the two templates.
- A runner to execute the jobs. Check with:

 alethia runner list
 
 If no runner is online, [register one you run yourself](/guides/runners/self-operated).

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 1 — Copy the two templates
records.text:
A template is a starting point, not a dependency. You make your own copy, and Alethia deploys your
copy. Nothing in either template reports back to Alethia.

1. Open [alethia-starter-apps](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-apps) on GitHub.
2. Select **Use this template**, then **Create a new repository**.
3. Name it `my-starter-apps`, and set it to **Public**.
4. Do the same for [alethia-starter-chart](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-chart),
 and name the copy `my-starter-chart`.

Use **public** copies for this tutorial. ArgoCD clones a public repository anonymously, so you do not
have to connect GitHub to Alethia first. That is also how the tested run cloned them. To use a
private copy, first connect GitHub as a [Git provider](/guides/connectors/git-providers).

In the rest of this tutorial, replace `my-github-account` with your GitHub user or organization name.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 2 — Connect Hetzner
records.text:
In the Hetzner Cloud Console, create a **new project** for this tutorial. In that project, go to
**Security → API tokens** and generate a token with **Read & Write** access.

Then connect it. The command asks for the token and hides what you type:

alethia connector hetzner

A Hetzner token can do anything inside its project, so the project is the only boundary you get.
That is why you use a new, empty one. See [Connect Hetzner](/guides/connectors/hetzner).

Now find the name of the account you connected:

alethia connector list

Note the value in the **Account** column. You use it in the next step.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 3 — Describe the project in one file
records.text:
Create a file named `alethia.yaml`. Replace `my-account` with the value from the **Account** column,
and `my-github-account` with your GitHub name.

yaml title="alethia.yaml"
project: starter
cloud:
 account: my-account
 region: nbg1
environments:
 - name: dev
 stage: development
 placement: dedicated
 components:
 cluster:
 instance_types: [cpx32]
 node_min_size: 2
 node_desired_size: 2
 node_max_size: 2
 repositories:
 apps_destination_repo: https://github.com/my-github-account/my-starter-apps

Three things in this file matter:

- **`placement: dedicated` gives the environment its own cluster.** The overlay discovery in
 Step 5 runs only on a dedicated cluster. The template also creates its own `Namespace` objects,
 which a namespace placement refuses.
- **`apps_destination_repo` is your copy of alethia-starter-apps.** It is the repository ArgoCD syncs.
- **There is no `apps_path`.** With no overlay path, ArgoCD syncs the repository root, and it also
 turns each directory under `overlays/` into an Application of its own. If you set a path, that
 discovery stops. See [Repositories](/guides/design-project/repositories).

The cluster is the size the templates are tested on: one cont

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 4 — Preview and deploy
records.text:
Preview what the file creates:

alethia plan

This lists the project, its environment and its components. It changes nothing and starts no job.

Now deploy:

alethia apply

The CLI shows the same plan and asks you to confirm. Then it creates the network and the cluster,
installs ArgoCD and the platform add-ons, and connects ArgoCD to your apps repository. To watch the
job from a second terminal:

alethia jobs logs --latest --follow

When the deploy is done, the CLI prints `starter is up.`

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 5 — Check that the apps repository synced
records.text:
alethia cluster get starter

The **GitOps** row counts the ArgoCD Applications on the cluster, and how many are synced and
healthy. Every Application should be both.

Four of those Applications come from your copy of alethia-starter-apps:

 Application Synced from Namespace What it runs 
 --- --- --- --- 
 `apps` the repository root `starter` one `hello` Deployment and its Service 
 `apps-dev` `overlays/dev` `starter-dev` the same, with 1 replica 
 `apps-staging` `overlays/staging` `starter-staging` the same, with 2 replicas 
 `addons` `addons/` none nothing yet. It is still Synced and Healthy 

You did not declare `apps-dev` or `apps-staging` anywhere. ArgoCD found the two directories under
`overlays/` and made one Application for each. To get a third, add `overlays/prod` to your copy and
push it. No Alethia deploy is needed.

 
 Every Application from the apps repository syncs automatically, prunes, and self-heals. A commit
 to the default branch of your copy deploys on its own, so **write access to that branch is deploy
 access to the cluster.**

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 6 — Attach the chart template
records.text:
Attach your copy of alethia-starter-chart to the `dev` environment as a bring-your-own chart:

alethia chart attach starter-chart --project starter --env dev --repo https://github.com/my-github-account/my-starter-chart --chart-path chart --ref HEAD --namespace starter-chart

Each flag maps to one field of the chart:

 Flag Value Why 
 --- --- --- 
 `starter-chart` the chart's ID Its ArgoCD Application is named `addon-starter-chart` 
 `--chart-path` `chart` The directory in the repository that holds `Chart.yaml` 
 `--ref` `HEAD` The default branch. Use a tag if you want each release to be explicit 
 `--namespace` `starter-chart` Alethia creates this namespace, and the chart may create resources only in it 

Attaching a chart also queues a **safety scan**. The runner renders the chart in an isolated sandbox
and checks what it would create. Follow the scan with:

alethia jobs logs --latest --follow

 
 Bring-your-own charts are an opt-in feature of each Alethia instance. If `alethia chart attach`
 says they are not enabled, ask the operator of your instance.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 7 — Deploy again
records.text:
The chart is attached, but nothing has installed it yet. Run the same command as before:

alethia apply

The file has not changed, so the plan shows no new resources. The deploy still runs, and this time
it renders the chart's ArgoCD Application. It reuses the cluster from Step 4 and creates no new
server.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 8 — Check that the chart synced
records.text:
List the charts attached to the environment:

alethia chart list --project starter --env dev

The **Scan** column shows the result of the safety scan. Then look at the cluster again:

alethia cluster get starter

The **GitOps** row now counts one more Application, `addon-starter-chart`, and it is synced and
healthy. It manages three resources in the `starter-chart` namespace: a Deployment, a Service and a
ConfigMap. None of them is cluster-scoped and none of them is RBAC, which is the contract every
bring-your-own chart must meet.

A bring-your-own chart syncs differently from the apps repository:

- **Prune is off.** A resource you delete from the chart keeps running until you delete it yourself.
- **Self-heal is off.** A change made by hand stays, and the Application reports `OutOfSync`. That
 is information, not an error.

Before you change your chart, run the template's own contract check against it. Run it from a
clone of your copy, with `helm` installed:

hack/check-byo-contract.sh chart

It fails if the chart renders a kind that a bring-your-own chart cannot create.

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: Step 9 — Tear it down
records.text:
alethia project destroy --project starter --env dev --yes --wait

This removes the cluster, its network and everything ArgoCD installed on it. Your two GitHub
repositories stay. They are yours.

Then make sure nothing is left. The Hetzner Cloud Console has the final answer. Servers, load
balancers and volumes bill by the hour, and they are the resources that most often survive a failed
teardown.

hcloud server list
hcloud load-balancer list
hcloud volume list
hcloud network list

records.title: Start from a template
records.heading: What you did
records.text:
You:

- Copied two templates, and deployed your copies rather than the originals.
- Connected one as the ArgoCD apps repository of a dedicated cluster, and saw overlay discovery
 turn two directories into two Applications.
- Attached the other as a bring-your-own chart, which runs in its own namespace under a
 default-deny project.
- Did it all from a terminal, so you can also do it from CI.

The third template, [alethia-starter-ai](https://github.com/alethialabs-io/alethia-starter-ai), uses
both trust levels at once. Read [Starter Templates](/guides/design-project/starter-templates) to see
where it puts each component and why. For the model behind the apps repository, read
[GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd).
